## Vinaya Piṭaka
## Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Prologue (Ganthārambhakathā)

I pay homage with my head to that Buddha, who, through pure wisdom and compassion, liberated all beings worthy of guidance from the suffering of the round of rebirth; who has reached the end of the world and has become the eye of the world; and I pay homage to the Dhamma of that Buddha.

I also pay homage to the Saṅgha, endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla). Taking the essence of all words, according to my own desire for brevity, being urged by monks, and seeing the benefit for the monks,

I shall write, in a concise manner, the explanation of the obscure words (līnapada) in the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā, which was composed by the great teacher Ācariya Buddhaghosa.

One who wishes to expound any treatise should first state these five things: the name, the reason, the author, the extent, and the purpose.

According to that statement: "Samantapāsādikā" is the name of the treatise. "The inability to benefit the monks on other islands" is the reason for composing the treatise. "The one named Buddhaghosa, given by the teachers" is the author. "The number of units (gantha) being more than twenty-seven thousand" is the extent of the treatise. "The long-lasting stability and propagation of the Dispensation (Sāsana)" is the purpose of the treatise.
2:
In that treatise, the objector asks: "In the statement that the author who wishes to speak the five aforementioned points should speak, what kind of qualities does the teacher who speaks possess?" I shall state the answer: Only the expounder (desaka) who is accustomed to knowing the varieties of text and meaning, who is unshakeable by others, who has a pure heart, who is free from envy, who is accustomed to knowing decisions suitable for the disciples, and who strives for the welfare of the assembly of disciples, is called a teacher. (Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā, Ganthārambhakathā).

In that context, it is called 'text' (pāṭha) because it is recited. That text has many varieties, such as text conforming to the meaning and text not conforming to the meaning. How? There are: intentional discourse (sandhāyabhāsita), literal discourse (vyañjanabhāsita), text with a remainder (sāvasesapāṭha), text without a remainder (niravasesapāṭha), text of explicit meaning (nītapāṭha), and text of implicit meaning (neyyapāṭha).

Among those, 'intentional discourse' (sandhāyabhāsita), so called because it expresses various meanings, refers to such passages as "Having killed mother and father..." etc. (Dhammapada 294). (In this context, 'mother' refers to craving and 'father' to conceit.) 'Literal discourse' (vyañjanabhāsita), so called because it expresses only a single meaning, refers to such passages as "Mind is the forerunner of all states..." etc. (Dhammapada 1, 2). 'Text with a remainder' (sāvasesapāṭha) refers to such passages as "Monks, all is burning..." etc. 'Text without a remainder' (niravasesapāṭha), which is the opposite of the former, refers to such passages as "All things in every way come into the range of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha..." etc. 'Text of explicit meaning' (nītapāṭha), which is to be understood exactly as spoken, refers to such passages as "Impermanence, suffering, non-self" etc. 'Text of implicit meaning' (neyyapāṭha), which is to be understood through proper reasoning, refers to such passages as "Monks, there is one person..." etc.

Meaning (attha) also has many varieties: the meaning of the text (pāṭhattha), the natural meaning (sabhāvattha), the meaning to be known (ñeyyattha), meaning conforming to the text (pāṭhānurūpa), meaning not conforming to the text (pāṭhānanurūpa), meaning with a remainder (sāvasesattha), meaning without a remainder (niravasesattha), explicit meaning (nītattha), implicit meaning (neyyattha), and so on.

Among those, the meaning of the text recited to make a particular point known is called 'pāṭhattha', as in "with meaning and with phrasing" etc. The intrinsic nature such as characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and function (rasa) of material and immaterial states is called 'sabhāvattha', as in "one develops right view" etc. The meaning which, when known, leads to welfare and happiness, and is worthy of being known, is called 'ñeyyattha', as in "speaker of the goal, speaker of the Dhamma" etc. The meaning expounded in accordance with the text is called 'pāṭhānurūpa', such as the meaning understood as "the eye is also kamma" because the Blessed One said, "Monks, the eye is old kamma." The meaning expounded by obscuring the sense through the shadow of the phrasing is called 'pāṭhānanurūpa'. The meaning expounded with a remainder, without abandoning some part that should be excluded, is: "Dependent on the eye and forms..."
3:
The word "Uppajjati" (arises) occurs in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Nidānavagga, etc., and in verses such as "All tremble at the rod, all fear death" (Dhammapada). The meaning that is fully drawn out (nītattha) is like the statement: "I and you have run and wandered [in Saṃsāra]." Regarding that wandering: "O bhikkhus, who is the knower, who is the believer... except those who have seen the Dhamma?" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.66). The meaning to be taken directly by the power of the words (nītattha) is like: "Pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches..." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.151). The meaning to be understood by way of conventional designation (neyyattha) is like: "O bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons comparable to clouds" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.101).

Therefore, it is said:
"The meaning known directly from the words is known by the wise as Nītattha. The meaning to be understood by the combination of meanings is called Neyyattha."

One who knows the meaning of the text in such various ways is called a Pāṭhatthavidū. One who cannot be destroyed or shaken by the words of others, even after living long in the views of other sects, is called Asaṃhīra. One who is capable of preaching because of being endowed with development (bhāvanā), tradition (āgama), and realization (adhigama) is called a Vattā; this means one capable of making others understand through brief and detailed methods, reasons, and examples. One who purifies oneself and others is called Suci; this means one free from the stains of immorality and wrong view. Indeed, an immoral person destroys themselves and speaks unacceptably, like a sick doctor lacking food and proper conduct. A person with wrong view destroys others and cannot be a refuge, like a lotus pond infested with snakes and scorpions. One who fails in both is unworthy of association in every way, like a dung-smeared firebrand from a funeral pyre or a dung-smeared cobra. However, one endowed with both is pure and should be associated with and served by the wise in every way, like a treasure mine free of danger. One who is not stingy is called Amacchara; this means one who does not have the "teacher's fist." It means one who does not abandon the fourfold set consisting of Sutta, Suttānuloma, Ācariyavāda, and Attanomati, and who explains only that meaning. Or, it means one who does not abandon the four means of knowledge: Paccakkha (perception), Anumāna (inference), Sadda (testimony), and Atthāpatti (implication).

"One type of statement is Ekāṃsavacana (categorical), another is Vibhajjavacana (analytical). The third should be answered by counter-questioning (Paṭipucchā), and the fourth should be set aside (Ṭhapanīya)."
4:
One who does not abandon these four ways of answering, or one who is devoted to the welfare of listeners, means one who makes an effort for the benefit of the listeners and desires their understanding. Such a teacher is: Piyo (dear) due to pure mind; Garu (venerable) for not abandoning the four ways of answering; Bhāvanīya (inspiring) for being unshakeable; Vattā (speaker) for being a preacher; Vacanakkhama (patient in speech) for being devoted to welfare; Gambhīrakathaṃ kattā (speaker of deep discourse) for being a knower of text and meaning; and does not urge toward the unsuitable because of being Amacchara (unselfish).

"Dear, venerable, inspiring, a speaker, patient in speech, a speaker of deep discourse, and not urging toward the unsuitable" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.37, Nettippakaraṇa 113)—thus is the teacher described.

Now the listener is described: One who respects the Dhamma teacher, is adorned with qualities such as faith and wisdom, is free from deceit and hypocrisy, is wise, and is facing the Deathless (Nibbāna) is a listener. Therein, because of respecting the Dhamma, one does not disparage the discourse. Because of respecting the teacher, one does not disparage the speaker. Because of being adorned with qualities such as faith and wisdom, one does not disparage oneself. Because of the absence of deceit and hypocrisy and because of facing the Deathless, one has an undistracted mind. Because of being wise, one reflects wisely (yoniso manasikāra). For it has been said:

"Bhikkhus, a listener endowed with five qualities is capable of entering the right path (sammattaniyāma) in wholesome states. What are the five? One does not disparage the discourse, does not disparage the speaker, does not disparage oneself, listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted and one-pointed mind, and reflects wisely." (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.151).

Because of being endowed with those characteristics, such a person is a listener for whom the act of hearing becomes a development (bhāvanā).

## Description of the Introduction to the Book

Now begins the work: Therein, the word "Yo" (whoever) is an indefinite designation (aniyamaniddesa). By that word, showing that pure birth, family, lineage, etc., are not the causes for the purification of the stains of defilements or for being worthy of worship, it indicates that anyone, regarding the cause of being the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) as described in the opening verse of this Samantapāsādikā, through the aforementioned root cause...
5:
(Regarding the cause of that state of being a refuge [nāthatta]), making it extremely firm and unshakable, fulfilling it continuously throughout the aforementioned causal period, and finally achieving the result of the aforementioned cause (nāthatta), he accomplishes the benefit of the aforementioned cause and result. It is determined that only such a Noble One (who is the refuge of the three worlds) is worthy of the highest worship.

By this sequence of words:
"This salutation is not a salutation born of fear, delusion, or wrong view. This salutation is shown to be a salutation preceded by wisdom in every aspect."

The "cause" (of that nāthatta) refers to the wholesome deeds known as the thirty perfections (pāramīs), which are extremely difficult to perform. Because they are performed with great hardship, and with great effort of a power that cannot be fully described in words, they are called "atidukkara" (extremely difficult to perform). Precisely because they are so difficult to perform, they produce the result known as nāthatta (the state of being a refuge), which is extremely rare in the world and not shared with others. That result is here called "hetu-phala" (the fruit of the cause). "Hetu-mūla" (the root of the cause) is the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) capable of bringing the aforementioned cause (the perfections) to completion. That Great Compassion, starting from the initial aspiration (paṇidhāna) with the thought, "Having been liberated, I shall liberate [others]," continues uninterrupted until the benefit of the fruit of the cause (hetu-phalappayojana). Regarding that Great Compassion, it is said:

"When the world ends, this great earth, along with its forests, its great mountains like Sineru, and its oceans, has many times gone to destruction due to water, fire, and wind. But how could the Great Compassion, which is the great heat (tapa) of the Bodhisatta, ever go to destruction?"

Because he is endowed with that Great Compassion, it is said: "I pay homage to Him, the Great Compassionate One." "Hetu-kāla" (the causal period) refers to the time divided into four, eight, or sixteen incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and so on. Referring to that time, it is said: "For a time immeasurable even by billions of aeons (kappakoṭi)." In that word (kālaṃ), it should be understood that the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga), as in "māsaṃ adhīte" (studies for a month) or "divasaṃ carati" (travels for a day).

In truth, although that time can be known and measured by way of incalculables (asaṅkheyya), it is said "for a time immeasurable even by billions of aeons" referring to the fact that it cannot be known by way of billions of aeons (kappakoṭi). In that word, it is called "kāla" because it "causes to happen" or "destroys" (kālayati). It means it casts down or destroys the lives of beings. The root "kala" is used in the sense of casting down (vikkhepa). In the word "kappa" (aeon), it is so called because it can only be conceived or compared by metaphors such as a mountain of mustard seeds, and cannot be counted by human days, months, or years. It is called "koṭi" (billion/ten million) because it is the end (koṭi) of the counting sequence such as one, ten, etc. Billions of aeons...
6:
...even by many billions of aeons, it cannot be measured, thus it is immeasurable; for that immeasurable time. While 'performing' (karonto)—since roots have various meanings—it means giving gifts (dāna), guarding virtue (sīla), renouncing the mass of greed/sensual pleasures (nekkhamma), discerning various dhammas such as one's own benefit and the benefit of others (paññā), striving and exerting with various efforts (viriya), enduring the faults of various beings (khanti), making true the promises, conventional truths, and ultimate truths (sacca), determining the welfare of various beings (adhiṭṭhāna), radiating loving-kindness to the entire world (mettā), and abandoning bias such as towards friends or enemies to maintain equanimity towards various beings (upekkhā).

'Reaching weariness' (khedaṃ gato) means reaching it in the sense of experiencing the great suffering of saṃsāra, which has infinite varieties. Saṃsāra's suffering is called 'kheda' (weariness/exhaustion) because it destroys or brings down physical and mental happiness. The phrase 'for the benefit of the world' (lokahitāya) is an indication of the cause, fruit, and purpose mentioned above. Some teachers say it is 'an indication of the reason for experiencing the suffering of saṃsāra.'

It is said: "Even though he was capable of going to the cessation of the suffering of birth and saṃsāra (Nibbāna), out of compassion alone, he remained for a long time in saṃsāra, weary and exhausted."

That interpretation is not appropriate. For the Blessed One does not experience the suffering of saṃsāra for the benefit of the world. Indeed, the experience of suffering by anyone does not bring any benefit to the world. Rather, it is shown this way: it shows the cause (hetu) consisting of the thirty perfections and the fruit (phala) known as the state of being a refuge (nāthatta), which is the result of the perfections. As he said: "Ananda, it is by relying on me as a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta) that beings subject to birth are freed from birth," and so forth. 

In that process, the Blessed One, through the aforementioned causes, sowed the seeds of wisdom that produce the state of being tamable in beings. By the fruit of the cause—the state of having mature faculties—he tamed those beings who had reached the state of being tamable and liberated them from the suffering of saṃsāra. In this way, he did not perform any benefit for the world simply by experiencing the suffering of saṃsāra; therefore, the connection (sambandha) should be made as: "performing extremely difficult deeds for the benefit of the world." According to this construction (yojanā), the attainment of the fruit of the perfections, known as the state of being a refuge (nāthatta), should be understood as starting from the time the very first Bodhisatta appeared. The connection intended is "the Lord who is the refuge (nātha)."

For this meaning, the following statement is evidence:
"Whatever first thought arose for your enlightenment, may that very thought be the worshipped refuge for this world."

The nature of the first thought as a perfection (pāramī) should be established by the simile of a tree starting from its sprout. Here, the phrase 'reaching weariness' (khedaṃ gato)...
7:
If it is asked, "Is the statement 'he reached exhaustion' useless because, according to the aforementioned method, it is impossible to accomplish the attributes?" No, it is not; because it is intended to show the state of non-regression during the intermediate period (before becoming a Buddha). While performing difficult tasks, he indeed reached exhaustion, but it shows that he did not regress by being unable to endure that exhaustion in the intermediate period. Alternatively, it shows the Blessed One's own ability to endure suffering, as he desired to remove the suffering of the world.

"To whomever I may be a giver of noble boons,
I am awake (with compassion) at all times,
Focusing on the mass of suffering of all beings,
Just as a multitude of lotuses bloom."

This means that because the Blessed One, who has such an intention, has the ability to endure suffering himself, it shows the excellence of the meaning that "suffering occurs only in the body." Alternatively, "reached exhaustion" (khedaṃ gato) also appropriately means that he reached the state of increasing his exertion and practice. For in the world, when people see a man exerting himself in work and so on, they are accustomed to saying, "This man is exhausted in his work, this man is exhausted for the sake of beings," and so forth. In this connection, it should be understood that by the word "Nātha" (Protector), the time when he reached and stood in the state of being a Protector, which is the pinnacle accomplished by the attainment of Buddhahood, is shown. Some teachers write that by saying "Mahākāruṇika" (The Great Compassionate One), it refers to one who has already become a Buddha; that writing does not seem good, because that term is also evident during the time of being a Bodhisatta. Therefore, it means that the Bodhisatta, having performed difficult tasks for such a long time and having fulfilled the perfections that are difficult to complete at the end, reached the state of being a Protector, which is the fruit of those perfections, and reached the state of exertion for the benefit of the world. Even if it is said, "He reached Enlightenment (Bodhi)," it clearly shows the cause and its effect. Because of the presence of the specific attribute, it amounts to paying homage only to the Protector who has already attained Buddhahood, not to the Bodhisatta.

Even so, the domain of Vinaya is intended here. And that domain of Vinaya exists from the time of ordination until the time of death. If a person with a sense of shame (lajjī) fulfills even the very easily practiced virtue (sīla) for the sake of his own individual benefit, with the desire to remove only his own suffering during that very short period, who would not reach the happiness that transcends this world and the world beyond? As for the Blessed One, with the desire to remove the suffering of the entire world, he performed (difficult tasks) for an immeasurable time through billions of eons and reached the very difficult and joyless exhaustion; does the commentator not praise his attributes by way of referring to another?

In the word "lokahitāya," it is called "loka" (world) because suffering resides in this (being); or it is called "loka" because it is destroyed by the sufferings of birth, aging, and death. By this word "loka," the world of beings (satta-loka) and the world of birth (jāti-loka) are included. Therefore, for the benefit of that world of beings in this world and the world beyond, or for those who have transcended the world beyond and have cut off the origin of the world...
8:
In the term "loka-hita," the etymological definition is: it is called "loka" because the mass of suffering resides in this world of beings, or because it is oppressed and destroyed by the sufferings of birth, aging, and death. By this word "loka," both the world of beings (satta-loka) and the world of space (okāsa-loka) should be taken. The commentator stated "loka-hita" by combining the benefit of that world in this life and the next life, and the benefit known as living happily in the present moment (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra) in the world of birth and the world of space.

"Nātha" means one who requests (nāthate) in the sense of entreating, "Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma... listen to that," in accordance with the differences in inclinations (āsaya), underlying tendencies (anusaya), temperaments (carita), and dispositions (adhimutti) of all beings. He is "Nātha" because he approaches and torments (tapati) the defilements with compassion that brings about benefit in the present and the future by prescribing training rules (sikkhāpada) according to the transgressions of the monks; or, by way of the Suttanta, he approaches and torments the defilements lying latent in the continuity of those beings with compassion and wisdom; or, by way of the Abhidhamma, he contemplates those various formations (saṅkhāra) by way of characteristics such as impermanence, and having approached with wisdom, he cuts off and torments his own defilements—thus he is "Nātha" also in the sense of tormenting (tapana). He is "Nātha" also in the sense of lordship (issariya) because he is a peerless person in the world with its devas, because he has the teaching of Dhamma that is unhindered by anyone, and because of the exercise of supreme mastery over the mind. He is to be known as "Nātha," the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), in the sense of wishing (āsīsa) known as gladdening, according to the words, "He instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a Dhamma talk"; or in the sense of wishing (āsīsa) by way of the method beginning with "How may I, being liberated, liberate others?" since the time of his initial aspiration. Although all Buddha-qualities such as the Fourfold Intrepidity (vesārajja) and the Fourfold Analytical Knowledge (paṭisambhidā) can be connected with these four factors of a Protector (nāthaṅga), they are not connected here for fear of excessive length.

"Namo" (Homage) refers to the inclination of the mind (citta-nati) which is heavy with great respect for the Buddha-qualities in the ultimate sense, and the inclination of body and speech (vacī-kāya-nati) arising from that mental inclination. It should be connected with the remaining words as "May my homage be." In the word "Mahākāruṇika," the compassion is "Great Compassion" (Mahākaruṇā) because its object is all beings and because it arises from great effort. The Blessed One is "Mahākāruṇika" because he is constantly endowed with that compassion from the time of his initial aspiration until his entry into the city of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). And here, by the word "Mahākāruṇika," he shows the fundamental cause of being a Protector as mentioned before. For a person without compassion, being indifferent to the suffering of others, would consider even the mere aspiration for Buddhahood to be an excessive burden; how then could he fulfill the immeasurably long and extremely difficult causal factors and perform the benefit for the world, which is the purpose and result of the cause known as being a Protector? Therefore, desiring to praise only the attribute of Great Compassion, which is the root of all attributes, he said, "Namo Mahākāruṇika" (Homage to the Great Compassionate One). By this much, it amounts to showing the effect corresponding to the cause, the cause corresponding to the effect, and the fundamental root and the special benefit corresponding to those two.

Thus, the Blessed One, who is such a wonderful and supreme man and who stands in the attribute of a Protector (Nātha), is worthy of receiving the homage of the multitude of humans, devas, brahmas, and disciples who are not protectors (who are without refuge). In this verse beginning with "kappakōṭīhipi," there may be such an objection from a challenger.
9:
The cause corresponding to the effect, the root corresponding to both, and the purpose corresponding to all three—this is the meaning shown.

Thus, the Blessed One, who is a wonderful and supreme man, established in the qualities of a protector (nātha), is worthy of receiving the fulfillment of the veneration of the assembly of unprotected humans, devas, Brahmās, and Arahant disciples.

In this context, an objection (codanā) might arise: "While there are many virtues of the Blessed One, why is only the single virtue of 'Great Compassion' (Mahākāruṇika) mentioned?" To answer this question—

In a faultless treatise, no objection exists,
A faulty treatise is not even called a treatise,
Therefore, your objection does not apply.

I do not make a criticism; rather, I only make an inquiry. Furthermore—

"Just as fruit does not fall from a tree, even if it exists, without shaking it,
So too, let there be objections in treatises; inquiry brings the fruit of meaning through great effort.
If one does not strive well and does not endeavor to take the pot,
Making an objection is a hindrance to the desired wisdom.
Just as a lotus grove blooms with fragrance because of the moon,
So this treatise, free from flawed meaning, is well-adorned with the ointment of meaning."

And also—
Even if it is a good objection, contentious disciples may hurt the teacher;
Therefore, guard against excessive speech.
A disciple who causes distress to the teacher with words like arrows brings defeat upon himself;
Just as a charioteer conquers a horse, the teacher conquers both himself and the disciple.

It is said here—
Even if one had a thousand mouths, and in each mouth a hundred tongues,
One would not be able to utter the names indicating the virtues of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)
Even for an entire aeon.
10:
For example—
"Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire aeon, without speaking of anything else, the aeon would come to an end within that long duration, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."

Because the virtues of the Blessed Ones are infinite, it is impossible to speak of them all without remainder.

To say it another way—
"O Blessed One, endowed with the Ten Powers, just as You are supreme among beings, so too is the pair of Wisdom and Compassion most excellent. Your Wisdom and Compassion are the foundation of all collections of virtues."

The commentator mentions only the virtue of Great Compassion because it is the most excellent of all virtues and the root of Buddhahood. Alternatively, it is said: "Since it is one of the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), by taking Great Compassion, the remaining knowledges are also included by way of association (sahacaraṇa-lakkhaṇa)." Specifically here, because the Abhidhamma is purely the domain of wisdom, the Teacher (commentator) praised the virtue of Wisdom at the beginning of the Abhidhamma Commentary, saying: "As he has compassion for beings, so this Great Seer (Mahesi) has wisdom." This is because His wisdom, which discerns according to the various inclinations (āsaya), latent tendencies (anusaya), temperaments (carita), and dispositions (adhimutti) of various beings, and His Great Compassion for beings, are the governing factors. At the beginning of the Suttanta Commentary, both the virtues of Wisdom and Compassion of the Blessed One are praised: "He whose heart is cooled by compassion, and whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom."

In this Vinaya, however, without regarding inclinations and so forth, out of pure compassion, even though He was a supreme being, He listened to words not fit to be heard, asked about matters not fit to be asked, and spoke words not fit to be spoken to prescribe the training rules (sikkhāpada). Thus, it should be understood that only the virtue of compassion is praised.

Wisdom and compassion are the causes for one's own benefit and the benefit of others,
All the virtues of the Conqueror (Jina) follow these two, wisdom and compassion,
Therefore, the noble teacher has mentioned both these virtues of the Blessed One, who is an ocean of virtues, in this [Vinaya Commentary].

With this much, the verses at the beginning of the commentary are beautified by the meanings of the words spoken in brief.
Saying that this too is a detailed method, I shall summarize those detailed methods from here on.
11:
In the second verse, "asambudhaṃ" means not knowing the true nature of phenomena (dhammas). "Buddhanisevitaṃ" means the Dhamma that is appropriately resorted to by the Buddha, the Follower-Buddhas (anubuddhas) who understand after the Buddha, and the Paccekabuddhas, through the practice of resort (gocarasevanā) and the practice of development (bhāvanāsevanā). "Bhavābhavaṃ" means reaching or going from the present existence to another existence.

Alternatively, "bhava" is eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi), and its opposite "abhava" is annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi). Or "bhava" is prosperity and "abhava" is decline. Or "bhava" is a miserable destination (duggati) and "abhava" is a happy destination (sugati). This is because the letter "a" has the meaning of prosperity (or fullness), as in "appamāṇā dhammā" (immeasurable dhammas) or "asekkhā dhammā" (dhammas of the adept). It is called "bhava" (birth/jāti) because it causes development (bhāvayati). Or it is called "bhava" because it happens (bhavati). This illustrates the arising of various aggregates (khandhas) along with their transformations. "Abhava" means destruction, meaning one reaches the state of birth and the state of death. Here, the death of Arahants should also be taken by way of momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa). Non-existence in various lives is "bhavābhava"; it means reaching that bhavābhava (the designation of non-existence in lives).

"Jīvaloka" refers to the world of beings (sattaloka). Since the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) and the world of space (okāsaloka) cannot go from one existence to another, the world of beings is specifically distinguished by the term "jīvaloka." In the term "avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsī" (destroyer of the net of defilements like ignorance), the nine supramundane states (lokuttara dhammas) are also included. This is because the four Path-dhammas (magga-dhamma) go about destroying defilements, thus they destroy the net of defilements such as ignorance by way of limitation. That destruction exists in the Path-dhamma. Since Nibbāna is the object of those Paths and arises together with them, Nibbāna also has the name "destroyer of the net of defilements like ignorance." As stated in the Sutta: "Friends, the destruction of lust... this is called Nibbāna." Likewise, because there are words describing the destruction of lust etc., this name also applies to the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), and by way of the nature of the Fruit, to the three lower Fruits. Therefore, all nine types of supramundane states are called "avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsī."

Alternatively, it is because of the cause marked by the methods of association (sahacaraṇa) and indication (upalakkhaṇa), or because of taking Nibbāna, which is the opposite of defilements, as the object. Although the word "Dhamma" in that verse does not directly state the "Fruit" (phala), it should be understood as stated; thus, by taking the Path (magga) which is the cause and Nibbāna which is the object, the four Fruits are also included. It is called "Dhamma" because it holds one from falling into hell etc., and establishes one in happy destinations (sugati). Furthermore, it is called "Dhamma" because it prevents unwholesome states that cause one not to fall from happy destinations, and it nurtures, maintains, and increases [wholesome states]. That Dhamma is threefold by way of the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere. Because it brings absolute happiness, and because it is more noble than the dhammas in those three spheres, it is called "dhamma-vara" (the Excellent Dhamma).

Here, an objector might say: "Monks, because of not understanding and not penetrating the four Noble Truths, you and I have for such a long time run and wandered [in saṃsāra]." According to these words, it is established that the world of beings, not knowing the Dhamma of the four Truths, goes from existence to existence. Therefore, because one goes due to not knowing those four Noble Truths, and because those four Noble Truths are specified and determined by the word "tassa" (of that) at the end using the pronoun "ta" (that), the Dhamma of the four Truths also...
12:
...it also arrives at the meaning: 'the Excellent Dhamma that destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance.' Otherwise, making the word 'tassa' (indicated by 'ta') have the same case ending as 'the Excellent Dhamma that destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance' (namo avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsino dhammavarassa tassa) would be improper due to the rule preventing over-extension. The phrase 'of the Excellent Dhamma that destroys ignorance etc.' is a qualitative description (visesana). Therefore, if one says there is no reason for the Truths of Suffering and Origin to become that (Excellent Dhamma)? No, because in the position of having the same case ending as the word 'tassa' (indicated by 'ta'), it is not specifically distinguished. Furthermore, since Fruitions (phala) are not included within the Truth of the Path and the Truth of Cessation, it would contradict the statement that the nine supramundane states are included. If Fruitions are not included, it would contradict the explanation in the Veranjaka section: 'Not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) along with the Noble Fruitions (ariya-phala) [are included].' And it would also contradict the words: 'Lust-free, desire-free, sorrow-free... resort to this Dhamma as a refuge.' Thus, is this verse not contradictory in its preceding and following parts, and contrary to the Dispensation?

It is said in reply: All this [objection] is improper, because of not knowing the meaning of the stated verse. For here, the Teacher has shown the classification of the process (pavatti), the cause of the process (pavatti-hetu), and the object (visaya). How? In that verse, 'asambudhaṃ' means non-realization, which in essence is ignorance (avijjā); and by that, craving (taṇhā) and clinging (upādāna) are also taken. All these three states are the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). In the term 'bhavābhavaṃ', the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) is meant. Existence (bhava), with its divisions of happy and woeful states, is in essence the five aggregates of clinging. According to the statement, 'Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering,' the arising of suffering is called 'pavatti', and the cause of the arising of suffering (samudaya) is called 'pavatti-hetu'. The two truths of Cessation and the Path are the objects (visaya) of the non-knowing of the cause of the process known as ignorance. For is it not stated: 'Therein, what is ignorance? It is non-knowledge regarding suffering... non-knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering'?

And here, the Truth of Cessation was resorted to by the Buddha through the practice of resort (gocara-sevanā), and the Truth of the Path through the practice of development (bhāvanā-sevanā). To this extent, 'asambudhaṃ buddhanisevitaṃ yaṃ' refers to Cessation and the Path, which are the objects functioning as the grammatical object. The meaning of this verse is: 'Homage to the Excellent Dhamma which destroys the threefold net of defilements such as ignorance as mentioned.' The scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) can also be called 'the destroyer of the net of defilements such as ignorance' because it is a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the destruction of defilements according to the Sutta method, and because it has the nature of destroying defilements. In this way, the meaning of the verse 'rāga-virāgā' etc., and the Sutta meaning 'He teaches the Dhamma... proclaims the holy life,' are included without exception.
13:
Alternatively, by this verse, only the Pariyatti Dhamma (the Dhamma of learning) should be taken. With reference to that Pariyatti Dhamma, it was said: "The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning... he proclaims the holy life." That Pariyatti Dhamma also cannot be fully realized by others; it is frequented only by the Buddhas through their own range of experience, and not by others. As it is said: "Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take refuge in the Blessed One... having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it."

In the third verse, although qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so on may be mundane or supramundane as the case may be, because of the phrase "Ariya Saṅgha" at the end, the four aggregates of Dhamma—virtue and so on—are only supramundane. Here also, where it should have been said "by virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge of liberation, etc.," it is expressed as "by the knowledge of liberation, etc.," by using the grammatical method of sarūpekasesa (retaining one of the same form).

In this term "vimuttiñāṇappabhuti," although vimutti (liberation) refers only to the states of fruition (phala) in the Suttas, it should be understood that the knowledge which reviews the Path and so on is called "knowledge of liberation" (vimutti-ñāṇa), because it is said: "Emerging from the Path, he reviews the Path. He reviews the defilements that have been abandoned. He reviews the Fruition. He reviews Nibbāna." The three terms vimutti (liberation), vimokkha (release), and khaya (destruction) are identical in meaning. In the phrase "knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇaṃ), knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇaṃ)," "destruction" refers to the Path (magga), while "destruction of lust" and "destruction of hatred" are synonyms for Fruition and Nibbāna, as found in the Suttas. The destruction of defilements for those who have abandoned them is indeed a natural destruction. By the word pabhuti (and so on), qualities such as the three true knowledges (vijjā), the six supernormal powers (abhiññā), and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) are included. The word yutta (endowed) means being possessed of these qualities or not being deficient in them.

Regarding the phrase "the field for those desiring wholesome merit": according to the Sutta, "the incomparable field of merit for the world," the Saṅgha is the field for wholesome merit because it is the place where wholesome states grow, and because it acts as a strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) according to the Suttanta method. It is certainly the field of wholesome merit, but not the field of the people who desire wholesome merit. Therefore, if it is argued that the phrase "the field of those desiring wholesome merit" is inappropriate—it is not inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. Why? Because the Sutta meaning is possible. In the Sutta, it is said: "the incomparable field of merit for the world." For which world? The Saṅgha is the field for the world that desires merit. Because it is the support (upanissaya) for merit, the Saṅgha is the "field of merit" (puṇṇakkhetta), and it is also called "the field of those desiring wholesome merit." In common usage, just as one says "Devadatta's field" or "Yaññadatta's field," it is also called a "rice field" (sāli-khetta) or a "barley field" (yava-khetta) because it is the support for rice or barley.

"Ariya Saṅgha" means "noble" (ariya) or pure because defilements have been removed. Alternatively, it is called "Saṅgha" because it is a community of those who have reached the state of a Noble One, being united by commonality of virtue and view. Some teachers write that "by the word ariya, the conventional Saṅgha (sammuti-saṅgha) is excluded." That writing is not suitable, because the Saṅgha is already distinguished by the inclusion of the quality of "knowledge of liberation."
14:
By the word 'sirasā' (with the head), although it actually demonstrates the act of physical bowing, the author says 'I pay homage with my head' because he wishes to point out the head, which is the most excellent limb, out of respect for the virtues of the noble Saṅgha. The excellence of the head is due to its being the support for the noble eye-faculty and ear-faculty. The excellence of these faculties should be understood as being the cause for the supreme seeing (dassanānuttariya) and the supreme hearing (savanānuttariya).

In this regard, a questioner (codaka) who is skilled in the sequence of connections asks:
'The opening of a treatise has six divisions: (1) prologue (upogghāta), (2) word (pada), (3) meaning of the word (padattha), (4) word-analysis (padaviggaha), (5) objection (codanā), and (6) explanation (parihāra). Why, instead of stating these, did you first mention the homage to the Triple Gem?'

The answer is: Because it is the custom of the virtuous (satācāra). Indeed, it is the custom of the virtuous to perform the act of honoring the Triple Gem at the beginning of a commentary. Therefore, it is done with the thought, 'May we not be those who fail in the custom of the virtuous.' Even for a teacher endowed with the power of wisdom, who wishes to comment on the Vinaya Piṭaka which is endowed with the fourfold depth, a great fear (awe) arises, like one entering the great ocean. This act of homage and worship, born from the recollection of the virtues of the Triple Gem, is capable of exhausting all fears. As it was taught: 'Thus, for those who recollect the Buddha...' and so forth.

Furthermore, by performing the act of worship to the Teacher (the Buddha), the teacher (the author) instills the correct recognition of the Teacher in the Truly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) for the people of the world who mistakenly regard those who are not teachers as the Teacher. He causes them to abandon the false recognition of non-teachers as the Teacher. He also avoids the fault stated as 'treating the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata as if it were his own.' Because the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santāna) is full of dangers, and fearing that his life, appearance, happiness, and strength might be exhausted before the unfinished task of commenting on the Vinaya is complete, he aspires to the benefits taught as 'For one who is in the habit of paying homage... life, beauty, happiness, and strength increase,' until the conclusion of the commentary.

Moreover, in this homage, the act of worshiping the Blessed Buddha inspires those who are practicing the Buddha-vehicle (Buddha-yāna) to attain the state of a Sammāsambuddha. The act of worshiping the True Dhamma, which is divided into mundane and supramundane (or is purely supramundane), inspires those who are practicing the Paccekabuddha-vehicle to attain the state of a Paccekabuddha. For they desire only the penetration of the True Dhamma. The act of worshiping the Saṅgha of the ultimate sense (paramattha-saṅgha) inspires those who are practicing the Disciple-vehicle (Sāvaka-yāna) to attain the state of the ultimate Saṅgha. Alternatively, for the sake of satisfying the minds of those who hold the view that auspicious acts (mangala) such as paying homage are beneficial, free from danger, long-lasting, and highly esteemed, he performs the auspicious act praised by the Blessed One: 'Worshiping those worthy of worship is an auspicious blessing.'

And the teachers say:
'The Blessed Buddha is an auspicious blessing; the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also auspicious blessings. Auspicious acts and the like, which are beneficial, are accomplished quickly in every way. Knowing that one can obtain many such virtues as mentioned above through the act of worshiping the Teacher, one should be devoted to the worship of the Teacher.'

In this context, because the Teacher is primary, the act of worshiping the Dhamma and the Saṅgha should be understood as the act of worshiping the Teacher, both according to the Dispensation (Sāsana) and the world. Therefore, the teachers said this word: 'The Buddha is the Dhamma...'
15:
'The Blessed Buddha is an auspicious blessing; the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also auspicious blessings. Auspicious acts and the like are accomplished quickly in every way.

Knowing that one can obtain many such virtues as mentioned above through the act of worshiping the Teacher, one should be constantly devoted to the worship of the Teacher.'

In this context, because the Teacher is primary, the act of worshiping the Dhamma and the Saṅgha should be understood as the act of worshiping the Teacher, both according to the Dispensation (Sāsana) and the world. Therefore, it is said:

'The Dhamma spoken by the Sugata is called the "Teacher"; at the time of Nibbāna, he (the Buddha) designated it as the Teacher. In the Suvatthi verses (Ratana Sutta), the Saṅgha is also called "Tathāgata"; thus, it is also the Teacher.'

Furthermore:
'Since the Dhamma-body (dhamma-kāya) is the Teacher, the Dhamma is therefore regarded as the Teacher. The Saṅgha, which is established in that Dhamma, also arrives at the designation of "Teacher".'

In the world, when people see a man holding a sword that is inside a sheath, they usually say 'This man is holding a sword' without separately mentioning the sheath. Therefore, the teacher (Dhammapāla) said:
'Homage to the Buddha-gem; homage to the Dhamma-gem; homage to the Saṅgha-gem, which brings together the Triple Gem.'

Furthermore, if 'Buddha' is designated based on the continuity of aggregates (khandha-santāna) characterized by the manifestation of the supreme liberation (vimokkha) caused by unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena, then what need is there to say that the Dhamma is worthy of homage? The Saṅgha is also shown to be the recipient (bhājana) of worship, as it was said: 'Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha; if it is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored, and the Saṅgha will be honored too.' Alternatively, the teacher pays homage with great reverence, saying 'I pay homage with my head,' reflecting: 'The Dhamma well-realized by the Blessed One has been brought down to this day by the succession of teachers without loss, like lion's oil placed in a golden vessel, and has thus reached the ear-doors of people like me.'
16:
In this way, teachers speak of the numerous benefits of paying homage. However, the specific purpose intended by the Teacher (the author) himself is stated in the fourth verse beginning with 'Iccev-accanta-namassaneyyaṃ'. In the word 'Iccevaṃ', the term 'iti' signifies the completion of the ritual of worshiping the Triple Gem. To prevent the undesirable implication that the Triple Gem deserves only the ritual of worship as prescribed and nothing more, he said 'Evam-accanta-namassaneyyaṃ'. In that verse, the word 'evaṃ' indicates the method already mentioned. It means that for one who pays homage continuously, without stopping even for a moment, either by the method mentioned or by any other such method, to the Triple Gem which is worthy of perpetual homage, it brings about great benefit and welfare.

Thus, I, paying homage to the Triple Gem which has attained the state of 'Gem' (ratana) in the sense of being rare and in the sense of having great fruit, have obtained a flood of merit (puññābhisanda). It is called 'puñña' (merit) because it cleanses the stain of unwholesome states through abandonment by substitution (tadaṅga-pahāna) and so forth. It is called 'abhisanda' (flood/outflow) because it moistens and cools the mind, being cool due to the subsiding of the fever of defilements. That which is merit and also a flood is 'puññābhisanda'; (I have obtained) that flood of merit. In the Ganthipadas (glossaries), they say 'puñña-mahatta' (greatness of merit), but the Teacher says that meaning is not suitable because of the word 'vipula' (abundant). Alternatively, the flow (or collection) of merits is 'puññābhisanda'; (I have obtained) that flood of merit. The root 'sanda' is used in the sense of flowing (savana). Therefore, the meaning 'stream of merit' or 'accumulation of merit' is appropriate. That flood of merit is shown to be extensive and not small by the word 'vipula'.

In the fifth verse: When the Vinaya Piṭaka exists in its entirety, both in text and meaning, through its occurrence among conscientious persons (lajjī), the whole of the threefold Dispensation (Sāsana) is established in those very persons. If one asks, 'Whose Dispensation is it?', it is the Dispensation of the Blessed One who is 'unestablished' (aṭṭhita). The Blessed One is called 'aṭṭhita' (not standing/fixed) because of the absence of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi), which is a cause for being 'fixed'. Indeed, one who holds annihilationism stands fixed only in the pursuit of sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga), being indifferent to the next world, and does not strive to perform merits for the benefit of the next world. Only one who holds eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) strives to perform those merits. The Blessed One, however, not standing (in those extremes) and not striving (in that way), practicing the Middle Way (Majjhima Paṭipadā), crossed the flood (ogha) himself and helped others to cross. As he said: 'Friend, being unestablished and unstriving, I crossed the flood.' Or he is called 'Susaṇṭhita' (well-established) because he is well and properly established toward beings by way of the four Brahma-vihāras. Because he is thus well-established, desiring solely to remove the suffering of beings, desiring to bring them welfare, rejoicing in their success, and being impartial, he teaches the Vinaya. Therefore...
17:
In this context of the explanation of the Vinaya commentary, wishing to praise with appropriate praise, he said 'Susaṇṭhitassa'. In the Ganthipada, the meaning of 'Susaṇṭhitassa' is explained by way of the suttas: 'Monks, when a pleasant kamma-vipāka is present...' and 'Good posture, good appearance...', but that meaning is not suitable to the intended context of this Vinaya commentary. In the word 'amissaṃ' (unmixed/pure), does it mean not mixing the Vinaya, or not mixing the power of former teachers? It is neither. Since the Vinaya commentary itself is unmixed (pure), it should be connected as: 'I shall explain that Vinaya commentary purely (amissaṃ),' by way of an adverbial neuter. 'The power of former teachers' refers to the power of those commentary teachers, as stated: 'In the past, they made the commentaries.' In the world, when one sees something extraordinary, people often say, 'Whose power (influence) is this?' Alternatively, the commentary is called 'anubhāva' (power/influence) because it follows the intention of the Blessed One and makes the meaning clear in various passages, or because of its clarification (vibhāvanā) of those various meanings.

To answer the question of why one should make an effort to explain again when the power (commentary) of former teachers already exists, the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth verses are spoken. In those verses, the connection should be understood as: those with pure knowledge (vijjā) because their stains have been washed away by the water of the knowledge of the Noble Path; those with pure analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) because their taints (āsava) have been washed away by that same water; and those skilled in explaining the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) because of their pure analytical insights. Some teachers say that when 'former teachers' is mentioned, it could include worldly teachers and teachers like Rāhula in the Dispensation; therefore, the verse beginning with 'Kāmañca' is spoken to exclude them. If it is asked whether saying 'I shall explain that commentary' implies the incompleteness of the former commentary, the answer is no. The verse beginning with 'Kāmañca' is spoken to show that it is explained through various wonderful methods. Those skilled in explaining the True Dhamma or those skilled in that explanation are called 'Saddhamma-saṃvaṇṇana-kovida'.

'Sallekhiye' means 'sallekha' because it scrapes away or thins out the mass of defilements or the abundance of the four requisites; the state of that sallekha is 'sallekhiya'; (it means) in that sallekhiya. 'Nosulabhūpamehi' means those who have comparisons that are hard to find. 'Mahāvihārassa' means belonging to the lineage of the Mahāvihāra monastery. Those who have a comparison to a banner (dhaja) because of the sense of being elevated by wisdom are called 'dhajūpamā'. Those who follow the intention of the Blessed One are called 'Sambuddha-varanvaya'. Here, the word 'vara' (excellent) is used because Paccekabuddhas are also included by the statement 'He is a Sambuddha because he realized the truths by himself'. Therefore, it is used to exclude them.
18:
After showing the deficiency of the [existing] commentaries, he now spoke the verse beginning with "Saṃvaṇṇanā" to show his own special manner of composing [the new commentary] and its benefits. The phrase "na kiñci atthaṃ abhisambhuṇāti" means it cannot achieve any purpose, result, or benefit. This is similar to the usage in the Pāḷi text (Pārājika, 538) such as "na taṃ tassa bhikkhuno kiñci atthaṃ anubhoti."

By the words "ajjhesanaṃ buddhasirivhayassa," he shows that just as the Blessed One taught the Dhamma because he was requested by Sahampati Brahmā, and the Vinaya was laid down based on the request of the Venerable Sāriputta, so too this teacher (Venerable Buddhaghosa), honoring the traditional custom of those teachers, composed this exposition (Saṃvaṇṇanā) based on the request of the Elder Buddhasiri. By the word "samanussaranto," he shows his recollection of that Elder's virtues (such as virtue, etc.) and his respect for him.

Following that [ninth verse], two verses were spoken to show the procedure to be followed. By showing this procedure, he dispels doubts concerning the reasons for the decisions mentioned in those commentaries. Alternatively, he prevents the rejection by a Vinaya expert skilled in only one commentary who might say, "This method is not in the commentary." By discarding unsuitable meanings, he causes those who are attached to such unsuitable meanings to relinquish their attachment. By presenting the Theravāda view, he shows the method of reasoning and analysis (uha-poha)—discarding what should be discarded and accepting what should be accepted according to logic—to the Vinaya experts regarding Vinaya decisions. By rejecting unsuitable Theravāda views, he rejects the practice of measuring by the person (puggala-pamāṇa). These benefits are thus shown by explaining the procedure to be followed.

"I, who am about to begin this exposition called Saṃvaṇṇanā, shall begin by taking the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā as the body (basis). There are decisions mentioned in the Mahāpaccariya, and likewise in the commentaries famous in the world such as the Kurundī. From those decisions, I shall begin by taking the meanings that are suitable, either by the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā or by Vinaya logic, like ornaments for that body." The word "Saṃvaṇṇanā" is used again to show whether he will begin only the exposition or something else. Alternatively, the construction (yojanā) should be understood as: "I shall begin by making an exposition that includes the Theravāda views within it." This is because the Theravāda views are spread outside the [main] commentary. Here, by the word "ādi," the Cūḷapaccari, Andhaka, Ariya-aṭṭhakathā, Pannavāra, and others are also included. Among them, "Paccari" is said to mean a raft in the Sinhala language; it acquired that name because it was composed while sitting on a raft. There is a monastery named Kurundivallivihāra; it was named "Kurundī" because it was composed while residing there.

"Samma samārabhis saṃ" means "I stand ready, having prepared the procedure to be followed; therefore, listen to this [exposition] of mine." In the verse, "me" means "of me," or "the exposition being spoken by me..."
19:
...is the remainder of the text. "Nisāmentu" means observe with the eye of wisdom, or listen. Listen to the Dhamma respectfully, honoring it by preparing it with the mental formations of faith, energy, joy, and gladness. Whose Dhamma do they honor? They honor the Dhamma of the Blessed One, who is the lamp of Dhamma (Dhammapappadīpa). What does this show? The Dhamma stands in the place of a lamp because it reveals what is beneficial and what is harmful. The Tathāgata, the bearer of the Dhamma, is like the one who carries the lamp. Therefore, even though the Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, he shows that one should listen to the Dhamma while honoring and respecting it without grieving over his passing. Alternatively, according to the word "The Tathāgatas have the Dhamma-body (Dhammakāya)," the Dhamma itself is the lamp that reveals benefits and faults; therefore, the Blessed One is called "Dhammapappadīpa."

Just as the Dhamma-Vinaya was taught by the Buddha, so too was that Dhamma-Vinaya known and fully realized by the disciples who are the sons of the Buddha. They [the ancient teachers] took it up in its entirety without overstepping the intention and purpose of those sons of the Buddha. "Purā" refers to the "Porāṇatthera" (Ancient Elders) of the past. "Aṭṭhakathā" is the accusative plural form meaning "the commentaries."

Excluding only the scribal errors (pamāda-lekha) of teachers who wrote erroneously, all the various meanings mentioned in the commentaries should be taken. Is the word of all teachers authoritative? No, it is not. Only the words of the wise who are respectful of the three trainings (sikkhā) and skilled in this Vinaya are authoritative. If something is stated as a dukkaṭa offense in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, whether it be true or false, that statement should be known as a scribal error. The connection should be made as: "Excluding scribal errors, it will be authoritative."

"Tato ca" refers to the sequence of the Pāḷi text from the various meanings mentioned in the commentaries. "Suttanta" refers to the parts of the Suttas. The word "anta" is found in contexts such as interior, part, or praise. The words occurring in the parts of the Suttas are called "Suttantika." It means the words that come in the Sutta texts. Alternatively, "anta" means completion or to bring to completion. By what is it completed? It is completed by the Sutta. The completion of the Sutta is called "Suttanta." What is that? It is the various distinctions of meaning. The words associated with those Suttantas are "Suttantika." I shall explain the meaning of those Suttantika words in accordance with the respective Āgama Suttas, Abhidhamma Suttas, and Vinaya Suttas. This is the brief clarification of the meaning in this context. I shall explain the meaning of the Suttantika words such as "Itipi so bhagavā" in accordance with the Āgama Suttas.
20:
"It may be wholesome, it may be unwholesome, it may be indeterminate" (Cūḷavagga, 220)—the meaning of such words associated with the Abhidhamma Suttantas should be understood as being presented in accordance with the Abhidhamma Suttantas, and so forth. "Hessati" means "bhavissati" (it will be) or "karīyissati" (it will be done). In the word "vaṇṇanāpi", the word "api" has the sense of conjunction and should be connected with the word "tasmā". How so? Because it is a standard for the wise, because the extensive sequence of words has been summarized, because the legal decisions (vinicchaya) are fully explained without remainder, because it does not deviate from the order of the Pāḷi text, and because it explains the meaning of words associated with the Suttantas in accordance with the Suttanta Commentaries—for these reasons, it should be studied respectfully. In this context, although the meaning is complete with the phrase "without deviating from the order of the Pāḷi," the Teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya) in sections such as the Verañjakaṇḍa passed over it, saying, "This is the burden (responsibility) of the Suttanta experts." However, to show that "we shall proceed only after explaining it," the word "suttantikānaṃ" is used.

## The Explanation of the Introduction to the Text is Finished.
21:
## Explanation of the External Introduction (Bāhiranidāna)

Since the Vinaya is manifold by way of divisions such as tadaṅgavinaya (discipline by substitution of opposites) and so forth, the Vinaya should first be defined. If it is asked: "Since it was stated previously that 'the Buddha taught the Dhamma and the Vinaya,' should it not be said now, 'By whom was it taught'?" The connection should be understood thus: the teacher spoke the meaning of the word "vuttaṃ" (taught) with reference to such statements as "At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling..." and so forth. The words "By whom was it borne? By whom was it brought? Where is this Vinaya established?" are spoken with reference to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "It is not a word from one's own direct perception" means it is not a word spoken directly (impinging on the Buddha's heart). In truth, for the Blessed One, there is no word of Dhamma that is not within his direct perception in times such as the past and so forth. If it is asked: "If it is not a word from one's own direct perception, would it not fail to cause a padasodhamma offense?" No, it would indeed cause it. Why? Because even a teaching spoken by a disciple can cause a padasodhamma offense. If it is asked: "Since there is no fixed rule, would there be an over-extension (atippasaṅga)?" No, there would not, because in the Commentary on the Padasodhamma training rule, it is specified as "words included in the three Councils (Saṅgīti)." Similarly, in the Commentary, because of being included in the Council, there are statements such as "The sequence of the aggregates... is called Saṃsāra," and whatever words follow the order established in the Council. The Venerable Upatissa says that all such words cause a padasodhamma offense.

## Explanation of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti)

In the phrase "Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma ca," the word "ca" has a redundant (atireka) meaning. By that word "ca," it indicates that there are other Councils as well. It is said that the name "Upavattana" became well-known because it was the place where [the Buddha], having gone to that Sāla grove and bid farewell to friends and kinsmen, turned back. In the phrase "yamakasālānaṃ," it is said that one Sāla tree trunk was at the head and one was at the feet. Among those Sāla trees, one young Sāla tree was near the head and one was near the feet. It is also said to be a pair of Sāla trees standing with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves intertwined with each other. In the phrase "anupādisesa nibbānadhātuyā," the instrumental case (in nibbānadhātuyā) has the sense of itthambhūtalakkhaṇa (characteristic of being such). It is like in the examples: "A man who has done his duty has a joyful mind due to rapture, with a face free from enmity and wearing adorned earrings," and so forth. Either because of the cause of Parinibbāna or in that place of Parinibbāna, because of the statement "Lamentation is called paridevana," do not grieve with the mind and do not weep with the voice. In the word "mahāsamanena," the instrumental case has the sense of the ablative (nissakka). It is like in the example: "The light that makes [things] clear from the sun's rays is the protection of the hermit." The teachers say: "Whatever favor of the Blessed One there is, it is mine (my authority) who has received that favor." Some teachers, however, say: "For whatever reason I have been favored." "Nibbasanāni" means those for which the act of wearing is finished, having been used by me...
22:
These are discarded hempen garments. Thinking, "If you can exert great effort, will you be able to bear it?" he asked. Garments woven from hemp are like armor. The nine successive abidings (anupubbavihāra) and so forth, entered in order, are like sovereignty. The eight attainments and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are called "successive abidings" (anupubbavihāra) according to the order of their attainment.

In the near future and likewise in the distant past, in both these times, the wise use the word "purā".

The teaching (sāsana) of the Buddha itself is called the learning (pariyatti). That learning has nine factors (aṅgas) by way of Sutta, Geyya, etc. Because they bear the entire variety of the learning, namely the Three Piṭakas, they are called "bearers of the entire variety of the learning of the Three Piṭakas" (tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadharā). Since it is said "bearers of the entire variety of the learning of the Three Piṭakas," it should not be said that it is impossible without the Venerable Ānanda. Even so, there is a distinction. Those Arahants learned in the presence of the Buddha and in his absence. However, for the Elder Ānanda, there is no word of the Buddha learned in his absence. In the phrase "na vāyanti," the word "vā" expresses the sense of option (vibhāsā). It means there is both knowing and not knowing. In that selection, the word "bahu" has the meaning of abundance. It is just like in the context "much should be known of the endless Three Piṭakas."

If it is asked, "Since it was previously said 'bearers of the entire variety of the learning of the Three Piṭakas,' is it not inappropriate to say 'this venerable one has learned much of the learning'?" No, it is because the Three Piṭakas are endless. Therefore, in comparison to us, it means that the venerable one has learned much. Otherwise, if taken differently, it would imply that the Venerable Ānanda had less learning than those Arahants. It would also contradict the statement "there is no word learned in the absence of the Buddha."

In the phrase "half a month has passed," one day is missing. That day is the first day of the waning moon. It is called the day of clamor (kolāhala). Therefore, that day is not included in the count here. Because of the celebration after hearing the grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu), it is called "auspicious play" (sādhukīḷana). In the phrase "tomorrow also," the word "api" is used in the sense of expectation or permission. If it is asked, "Since the Subha Sutta is said to have occurred 'not long after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna,' does it not fall within the 84,000 units of Dhamma?" No, because it follows the method obtained during the time of the Blessed One, it is included in the units of Dhamma, just like the Kathāvatthu.

Discarded and fallen rubbish is called "chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā." The command itself is called a "wheel" (cakka) because it is irresistible; hence it is called the "wheel of command" (āṇācakka). Because they fall together here, it is called "ekanipātana." Some teachers say, "He came through the air and sat down." The Venerable Upatissa says this refers to the second journey. Or else, having first gone through the air and reached the assembly, without disturbing the row of monks, he dived into the earth and manifested himself right at his seat. In both ways, he came into range. Therefore, both are suitable. Otherwise, one of the two would be untrue.
23:
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli... the Elder Upāli answered. It is written in the Gaṇṭhipada that this statement is a summary shown by the reciters (saṅgītikārakas) of the questions and answers previously mentioned starting with "First, friend Upāli." Let it be so. However, why is the sequence changed here to "He questioned the occasion (vatthu), he questioned the origin (nidāna), he questioned the person (puggala)," instead of the sequence shown previously, "He questioned the origin, he questioned the person, he questioned the occasion"? Some teachers say it is stated out of order because the occasion (vatthu) is the root of the laying down of the training rule (sikkhāpada). Regarding this sequence, it will be examined only when reaching the Verañjakaṇḍa. Rājāgāraka refers to the garden of that name. It is said that the royal pavilion (rājāgāra) is also very delightful. In that garden, it gets this name because of a certain pavilion.

Then, the group of masters who performed the rehearsal (saṅgီtikārakas) showed a summary of what was previously said starting with "Venerable Mahākassapa." If it is asked, "Why is the sequence of the Elder Ānanda's answers not shown, just as the sequence of questioning the origin and person was shown?" the answer is that it is to show that the five Nikāyas were not included in the rehearsal by this sequence. How then were they included? The Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the five Nikāyas in order. The Elder Ānanda, however, answered both what was questioned and what was not, inserting all appropriate words such as the nature of each sutta, the occasion that arose in between, the sequence of the brief and detailed expositions (uddesa-niddesa), and the sequence of the matrix and analysis (mātikā-vibhaṅga). Therefore, it is said, "By this method, he questioned the five Nikāyas." Or else, when it should be said "Ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ rājāgārake," by saying "rājāgārake ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ" in a reversed order, this meaning is also indicated. For is it not said in the Pali, "Ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ viharati rājāgārake"?

"House-builder" (gahakāra) means the carpenter of craving who builds this house of the self-existence (attabhāva). Seeking the knowledge by which he can be seen, for the sake of that knowledge, from the time of making the resolution at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, I have wandered for this long through many births in saṃsāra without finding that knowledge. The phrase "Birth is suffering again and again" is the statement of the reason for seeking the house-builder. "All your rafters" (sabbā te phāsukā) means "I have broken all your rafters of defilements without remainder." The ridge-pole of the house (gahakūṭa) is ignorance (avijjā). Knowledge accompanied by joy is called "somanassamaya." Because of the difference in the nature of the aggregates, there is no knowledge made of joy. It is said generally for the purpose of strengthening or loosening.
24:
We shall demonstrate the fact of being stated in such a general manner in those respective Pali passages. In the phrase "in the Dhamma and in the Vinaya, which are free from mutual confusion," among such statements as "killing living beings is unwholesome," only the intention (cetanā) that originates the effort (payoga) to cut off the life faculty (jīvitindriya) of one who desires death is unwholesome; the act of killing (atipāta), which is the cutting off of the life faculty known as a living being (pāṇa), is not unwholesome. Likewise, the intimation (viññatti) known as taking what is not given, which belongs to another, is an indeterminate (abyākata) state; only the intention to steal (theyya-cetanā) that originates that intimation is an unwholesome state. In this way, one is able to provide instruction in the Dhamma that is free from mutual confusion.

For a monk who takes gold and silver (jātarūpa-rajata) belonging to another with the intention to steal, one of the offenses among Pārājika, Thullaccaya, or Dukkaṭa is incurred according to the object. For a monk who receives an object given through the authority of a storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), a Pācittiya offense is incurred. For a monk who takes it for his own benefit, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. For a monk who handles it out of mere greed, an Anāmāsa Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. For a monk designated as a disposer of money (rūpiya-chaḍḍaka), there is no offense. In this way, it means one is able to provide instruction also in the Vinaya that is free from mutual confusion. "Bhāveti" means one develops or increases. By this term, the growth of the mind is shown by way of fruition (phala) and by way of impulsion (javana). In the reading "avisiṭṭha," it should be understood as having the meaning of "common" (sādharaṇa).

By virtue of the person who teaches these three Piṭakas, it is called "Desanā" (Teaching).
By virtue of the persons to be instructed, these three Piṭakas are also called "Sāsana" (Instruction).
By virtue of the meaning to be spoken, these three Piṭakas are also called "Kathā" (Discourse).
In this way, the distinction between Desanā, Sāsana, and Kathā should be manifested.

Because the word "Sāsana" is of the neuter gender, it is stated as "yathā... pe... dhamma-sāsanāni." That which is called the defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṅkilesa) is, in essence, intention (cetanā), or it is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) occurring in such a manner. Insight consciousnesses (vipassanā-citta) that occur after penetrating characteristics such as impermanence are called mundane realization (lokiya-abhisamaya) by way of the object, and supramundane realization (lokuttara-abhisamaya) by way of non-delusion. Or, some teachers say that only the supramundane is realization by way of the object known as Nibbāna, while the non-deluded knowing of objects other than Nibbāna, such as the Path, is realization. If it is asked how the knowledge called "penetration" (paṭivedha) here is profound (gambhīra)? Some teachers say that just as when the depth of deep water cannot be measured, a long measure is required, so too the word "idāni" (now) etc., is spoken to show the state of being unfathomable. For the sake of which Path and Fruit they learn, they do not experience that benefit; they do not attain any desired benefit of their own, nor the benefit of liberation from disputes. Why? Because it was learned without investigating and reflecting on the meaning. Because of the state of having attained the fruit, it is called "paṭividdha" (penetrated/unshakeable). Furthermore...
25:
By using the term "khīṇāsava" (one whose taints are destroyed), it intends to show only the Arahant, not the learner (sekkha). For just as a treasurer guards the king's bracelets, crowns, etc., and brings them forth at the desired moment, so too [the Arahant] teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the Path and Fruit to beings who possess the necessary conditions. Because those three knowledges (vijjā) are specifically mentioned in that Vinaya Piṭaka, teachers say that one attains only those three knowledges by making an effort.

For what purpose are only the three knowledges analyzed in that Vinaya Piṭaka? It is because the perfection of virtue (sīla-sampatti) is a powerful supporting condition (upanissaya) for those knowledges. The following Sutta is the evidence here: "A monk endowed with seven other factors is a bearer of the Vinaya. He knows an offense, he knows what is not an offense, he knows a light offense, he knows a heavy offense, he recollects many kinds of past lives... with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings... and through the destruction of the taints... he dwells having realized it." Having learned the Vinaya and depending on the perfection of virtue, one attains the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati) along with the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). Some teachers say that the phrase "only those knowledges" is used to show that there is no separate preliminary work (parikamma) required for these knowledges.

In the Abhidhamma, however, the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges (abhiññā), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and other special qualities such as the supreme efforts (sammappadhāna) are analyzed. Although they are analyzed, the word "eva" (only/certainly) is transposed to say "only those analytical insights in that very Abhidhamma" to show that one attains the four analytical insights because they are specifically of the nature of wisdom (paññā).

There is a remaining phrase "by the Dhamma poorly learned by oneself." Here, the word "attanā" (by oneself) is an instrumental case in the sense of the agent, and it also functions in the sense of cause (hetu); the meaning is "because of the cause of being poorly learned by oneself." By the word "Why?", the meaning of "anulomika" (conformable) is explained.

## The Method of the Commentary on the First Great Council ends.

## Commentary on the Second Council
"Pannabhārā" refers to the Arahants who have laid down the burden of the aggregates. For it is said: "The five aggregates are indeed the burden." "Those who say 'we shall be present' or 'we shall not be present'" refers to those who were young among them, namely the elders Siggava and Soṇa. "Jammi" means a low or mean sense.

## The Method of the Commentary on the Second Council ends.
26:
## Commentary on the Account of the Third Council

In this phrase 'brahmalokā cavitvā' (having passed away from the Brahma world), only these states—the four paths, the five heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma), and fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi)—are fixed (niyata). Since the lofty (mahaggata) states are not fixed, it is possible to be born in a lower realm by the power of aspiration (paṇidhi). 'Aticchatha' means to desire beyond, with the meaning: "Go and seek alms at another house."

The Keṭubha treatise is a work complete with the methods of composing poetry. Some teachers, however, say it is the Kiriyākappa treatise, which is complete with characteristics such as the agent (kattar) and the verb (ākhyāta).

Asandhimittā was the name of that queen. It is said that the joints in her body were not visible, and her body was like one made of beeswax. Therefore, they say, "She was born with such a name." By the Magadhan measure: four pattha make one āḷhaka, four āḷhaka make one doṇa, four doṇa make one mānikā, four mānikā make one khārī, and twenty khārī make one vāha. Ketumālā is said to be "a mass of radiance that arises and remains from the head."

This story is told in connection with the king's power and majesty, not in chronological order. To show the story of bringing the Buddha's Dispensation in order, it says "Rājā kira" (The king, it is said), etc. Tamed by subduing the defilements. Guarded in body and speech. There is also a variant reading 'Pācīnamukho'. Due to the habit of having been the elder brother in a previous life, he shows the gesture to take the bowl. 'Abhāsī' means the thought "I will preach." Other teachers say that although he said 'Aññātaṃ' (It is known), he preached everything.

'Amata' (Deathless) is an epithet for the quality of cessation called Nibbāna; the path to it is 'appamāda' (heedfulness). 'Maccu' (Death) is an epithet for the fault of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) which is occurring; the path to it is 'pamāda' (negligence). In this way, the Four Noble Truths are shown. Because of taking refuge in the Saṅgha, it is called ordination depending on the Saṅgha, or because the act of shaving the head is dependent on the Saṅgha.

Since this is the section praising the power of Elder Nigrodha, combining what was said before and what will be said later, it says: "Again, the king, having built the great monastery named Asokārāma... caused eighty-four thousand monasteries to be built." According to the saying "the use with reflection by a good worldling," only the trainees (sekha) are heirs of the Dispensation (dāyāda) in the ultimate sense.
