However, for the sake of Prince Mahinda's ordination, the Elder spoke in accordance with worldly and Dhamma custom: "Great King... your own breast-born son..." etc. As stated in the Vedas:
'You are born from limb to limb, you are born from the heart;
You are indeed the self called "son", may you live for a hundred autumns.'
27:
Therefore, by this means, if parents have their breast-born son ordained, those parents are, in effect, as if they themselves had ordained. Why do the Dhamma-preachers not inform [the king]? The king sent ministers saying, "Go and bring the Elder." The Dhamma-preachers were sent to be the retinue when the Elder arrived; therefore [they did not inform him]. Alternatively, that king speaks only in the manner mentioned because he is fierce. The fierce nature of King Asoka should be understood by the story of the minister who was told, "Cut down the mango tree and make a fence with bamboo." Why do the Dhamma-preachers obey the king's command? Because it is said, "He is able to uphold the Dispensation."

'Dīpakatittira' means a decoy partridge. Although this partridge was engaged in the work of a decoy, he had a pure mind; therefore, he questioned the ascetic. 'Sāṇipākāraṃ' means with a screen-wall. Because he teaches by analyzing, saying "Brahmin, there are various ways," etc., the Blessed One is called a 'Vibhajjavādī' (one who speaks analytically). Alternatively, because of the words "Monks, there is the unborn, the unbecome, the unconditioned (Nibbāna)," the Blessed One is also a 'Sassatavādī' (Eternalist). Because of the words "Conditioned states, unconditioned states," he is also an 'Ekaccasassatika' (Partial-eternalist). He is also an 'Antānantika' (Extensionist),

Because of the verse "The end of the world can never be reached by walking, yet without reaching the end of the world, there is no release from suffering," and because of the words "Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not evident," [he is an Antānantika]. Because of showing things that are undeclared (abyākata), such as "Is the world eternal? Is it not eternal?" and because of showing conventional truth (sammuti-sacca), the Blessed One slightly inclines towards the side of 'Amarāvikkhepika' (Eel-wriggler). That conventional truth should not be spoken of in terms of internal (ajjhatta) or external (bahiddha). As he said, "The sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) should not be called an internal object," etc.

Likewise, because of the words "Enjoying the peace obtained for nothing (mudhā)," he also inclines towards the side of 'Adhiccasamuppanna' (Fortuitous-originationist). In that verse, 'mudhā' (for nothing) is a synonym for 'adhiccasamuppanna'. By way of the existence with perception, existence without perception, and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the Blessed One is also a 'Saññīvādādika' (one who asserts perception). Because of the words "Brahmin, I preach the annihilation (uccheda) of lust," he is also an 'Ucchedavādī' (Annihilationist). Because of the words "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived," and "Now there is no more renewed existence," in this very life...
28:
Because he demonstrated the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and because he taught by analyzing according to the inclinations of those to be taught in various ways and through various methods, the Blessed One is called 'Vibhajjavādī' (the Teacher of Analysis).

## The Method of the Commentary on the Account of the Third Council.

The Elder named Puppha is the Elder Sumana. Some teachers say he is the Elder Mahāpaduma. They say Mahisaka-maṇḍala is the Andhra region. 'Dhamma-cakkhu' (the Eye of Dhamma) refers to the three lower paths. Some say it is the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). The five kingdoms are named the five China kingdoms. 'In Rājagaha' refers to the monastery built by the Queen. 'On Silakူṭa' means on the mountain peak. 'Vaḍḍhamāna' is decorative powder (scented powder). It is said that this powder is highly esteemed in the Ariya region. The Damilas (Tamils) take refuge with a single flavor. 'Sāra-pāmaṅga' is a noble sash or ornament. Having caused agitation (saṃvega) through the Peta-vatthu and so on, he also taught the Sacca-saṃyutta for the sake of the realization of the Truths. Meghavana Park is the site where the Mahāvihāra stands. There is also a reading 'Dvāsaṭṭhiyā leṇesu' (in sixty-two caves). 'Dasa-bhātika' refers to the ten brothers such as Prince Abhaya; they are not intended here. 'Having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā' refers to the Pavāraṇā performed at the end of the four months of rain. Alternatively, it means having performed the first Pavāraṇā, staying there for one month, and speaking on the full moon day of Kattika; otherwise, it would not be consistent with the statement 'On the full moon day, the Great Hero (Mahāvīra)...'. 'Mahāvīra' refers to the relics by way of a metaphorical usage for the Buddha. 'Jaṅghappamāṇa' is said to be the size of the stupa's pedestal. Cūḷodara and Mahodara are uncle and nephew. Just like the rays of the living Buddha, rays emerged from his body. The King presented a message on a gold leaf and also delivered this oral message. It is said that the relics, measuring a doṇa, would be about twelve nāḷis by the Magadhan measure. There is also a reading 'Paricchinnaṭṭhāne chijjitvā'. Although it is said that five rays emerged from five fruits from all directions, in reality, they are the six-colored rays. 'The first day of the bright fortnight of Kattika' means the first day of the waxing moon. There are clans of deities such as Nāgas and Yakkhas surrounding the site of the Mahābodhi. 'Gopakas' are those who perform the King's duties. Some say it is the name of those clans. Those who carry water and so on are the Kāliṅgas. Some say a family of noble birth in the Kāliṅga country is the Kāliṅga family.

The first 'pāṭipada' day means the day after the second Uposatha (the first day of the waxing moon). Because those standing there could see the ocean, that place is called Samudda-sāla-vatthu. There are sixteen families of noble birth, eight families of Brahmin ministers, and eight families of ministers. The Elder Mahā-ariṭṭha...
29:
He was ordained at Cetiyagiri. The phrase 'in the minister's dwelling' (amaccassa pariveṇe) is stated in terms of the present time. Elder Mahinda arrived at the island of Tambapaṇṇi when he was twelve years of vassa (seniority); having resided in that island of Tambapaṇṇi for two years and established the Vinaya, he attained parinibbāna when he was sixty-two years of vassa.

In the phrase 'Vinaya is for the sake of restraint' (vinayo saṃvaratthāya), it means either the Vinaya Piṭaka itself or the learning of that Vinaya Piṭaka is for the purpose of restraint (saṃvara). 'Knowledge and vision of things as they really are' (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana) is the discernment of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa-pariggaha) along with their causes. If there is no reflection (paccavekkhaṇā) on the Path and so forth, there is no such thing as attaining parinibbāna in the interval, nor is there the death of a trainee (sekha). It occurs only when there is such reflection. Therefore, it is said: 'knowledge and vision of liberation' (vimutti-ñāṇadassana). In the phrase 'for the sake of parinibbāna without clinging' (anupādā-parinibbānatthāya), it means for the sake of attaining parinibbāna without clinging to or grasping any state (dhamma) whatsoever, leaving nothing remaining. 'Upanisā' (proximate cause) refers to the sequence of causes beginning with 'Vinaya is for the sake of restraint'.

Having thus shown the accomplishment of one's own benefit, he now says 'lending an ear for this purpose' (etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ) to show the accomplishment of the benefit of others. The meaning of that Pali is: 'lending an ear' (sotāvadhānaṃ) is the attentive listening of others in order to learn the explanation of the Vinaya and the consultation of the Vinaya. It should be understood that for those persons who have the explanation and consultation of the Vinaya learned through such listening, the aforementioned sequence of causes is already established, and thus it is not shown again. Otherwise, if 'anupādā-parinibbāna' were already included by the words 'the proximate cause for this purpose', and since listening (sotāvadhāna) is impossible beyond 'anupādā-parinibbāna', then 'lending an ear for this purpose' at the end would be impossible and thus meaningless. However, it should be understood that it is not meaningless, as it is intended to show the root cause for the accomplishment of the benefit of others.

Thus, in whatever way and whichever word should be appropriate here,
The wise person should apply all of them in that very way and manner.

## The Commentary on the Narrative of the External Origin is finished.

## Verañjakaṇḍo
## Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

“At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. At that time also, not far from Vesālī, there was a village named Kalandagāma.” When the Vinaya Introduction is thus begun, if it is asked, “What is the purpose of beginning the Verañja Section?”—it is said that it is begun for the purpose of showing the Vinaya Introduction from its very origin. If it be so, if it is asked, “Does this not conflict with the statement, ‘Where, friend Upāli, was the first Pārājika promulgated? At Vesālī’?”—it does not conflict. Why? Because the question “Where was it promulgated?” is an inquiry into the specific occasion (nidāna). Even so, when it is asked, “What is the nidāna of the first Pārājika?”, if it is asked, “Is it not improper to answer with the Great Introduction (Mahānidāna) which pertains to all training rules?”—it is not improper; it is indeed appropriate. Because the nidāna of all training rules was asked individually, and because that nidāna must be answered, the Great Introduction common to all was spoken first. In fact, the Pārājikas and so forth were included in the Council (Saṅgāyanā) according to the sequence of questions and answers.

If it is asked, “How were they included?”—the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the entire Vinaya in sequence, and the Venerable Elder Upāli, being questioned, answered continuously as was appropriate. It should be understood that even unasked matters, such as the Vinītavatthu and other relevant cases, were included within the sequence of answers and the group recitation was performed. Otherwise, it would follow that the Verañja Section is only the nidāna of the first Pārājika, or that it was composed out of place, or that it is useless, or that only the specific answer should be given immediately after the inquiry into the nidāna of each training rule. Therefore, the passage beginning with “Tena samayena” (At that time) and so forth was undertaken for the purpose of showing the Vinaya Introduction from the beginning.

Now, we shall state the benefits of reciting the Introduction—since the Vinaya is a Teaching of Authority (āṇādesanā), the benefits of this Introduction are threefold: 1. To demonstrate the Blessed One's worthiness of authority. 2. To demonstrate that the Vinaya, which is the authority, is not within the domain of anyone else. 3. To demonstrate the great power of the disciples who abide by that authority. How? The Blessed One is worthy of disciplining by authority because he has abandoned defilements, because he has attained special qualities, because he is the eldest and foremost in the world, and because he has reached the state of “tādi” (steadfastness). The Blessed One's attainment of the state of “tādi” should be understood by his unshakability by the eight grounds of abuse (akkosavatthu), such as “tastelessness” (arasarūpatā) and so forth. By the Pali passage showing the possibility of those eight grounds of abuse occurring to himself, his abandonment of defilements...
31:
...should be understood. By the explanation of the attainment of the four jhānas and the three knowledges (vijjā), his attainment of special qualities should be understood. By the words, “Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas... whose head would split and fall off,” and by the words, “He is the eldest and foremost in the world,” his being the eldest and foremost should be understood. This is the purpose of demonstrating the Blessed One's worthiness of authority. The words, “Wait, Sāriputta; wait, Sāriputta; the Tathāgata alone will know the time for that,” demonstrate that it is not the domain of other disciples. The great power of the disciples who abide by the authority should be understood by these three lion's roars (sīhanāda) of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna: “Venerable Sir, I would turn the earth over,” “Venerable Sir, I will create a single palm [of land],” and “Venerable Sir, may the entire Saṅgha of monks go to Uttarakuru for alms.”

Why did the Blessed One stay only in Verañjā at that time, instead of staying in places like Sāvatthī? It was to generate joy for the Yakkha Naḷeru, to prevent the Saṅgha of monks from being fatigued in seeking alms, to generate faith in the Verañja Brahmin, because it was the place to demonstrate the power of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and because it was the place of reflection that caused the Elder Sāriputta to request the promulgation of the Vinaya. Among these reasons, the last one is the strongest. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: “‘Tena samayena’ means at the time when the Venerable... at that time.”

Among the first four secondary reasons: By the first, the Blessed One generates respect in the monks by protecting the minds of non-humans (amanussa) through the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) and so forth. By the second, he shows that a monk living in an assembly should support the assembly in this way, and should be of few desires and contented. By the third, he shows that support should be given to lay families without being attached to requisites. By the fourth, he shows that even with such great power, one should not be greedy for requisites, but should live solely depending on what is given by others. Because of the statement, “Of the text beginning with ‘Tena’... the explanation of the meaning of the Vinaya,” the text beginning with “Tena” is one thing, and the Vinaya is another.

If one objects: “What other Vinaya is there here besides the text beginning with ‘Tena’? Should the Vinaya Commentary be made only while showing the meaning of that Vinaya?” Has it not been said before: “This is not the Blessed One's own direct word,” and so forth? Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: “While showing in various ways the meaning of the text beginning with ‘Tena’ spoken by the Elder Upāli, I shall make the commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya, which is the Blessed One's own direct word.” If it be so...
32:
If it is asked: Does the statement 'Who maintained the Vinaya Piṭaka?', which has an introduction adorned with words such as 'At that time the Blessed One was staying at Verañjā', conflict with the phrase 'At that time' (tena samayena) because it shows that the phrase 'At that time' is included within the Vinaya Piṭaka? The answer is: No, it does not conflict. This is because such usage is established elsewhere as well, like the example 'A man whose dwelling is adorned with various kinds of wall-work'. Since it was authorized by the Council reciters as the beginning or introduction of the Vinaya, it is appropriate that those words are included in the Vinaya.

Here, the objector says: In the Suttanta, it is stated indefinitely as 'At one time' (ekaṃ samayaṃ), and in the Abhidhamma as 'At which time' (yasmiṃ samaye). Why is it stated here in the Vinaya first with the word 'taṃ' (that) as 'At that time' (tena samayena)?

The answer is: Because of the time of the enactment of each training rule, or because of the time that was the cause for the enactment of the training rule, the Blessed One stayed in various places; and that past time was well known to the Arahants who were the Council reciters. How? Because of statements such as 'Those monks who were of few desires complained...', 'Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One', 'Then the Blessed One, on account of this origin, had the Saṅgha assembled', 'For the sake of the excellence of the Saṅgha... based on the ten reasons...', and 'And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule'. Also, in the Khandhakas, because of the Vinaya procedures such as 'Monks, I allow ordination by the three refuges', the time of the enactment of the training rule and the time of those Vinaya procedures were well known to those five hundred monks who were bearers of the Dhamma (dhammadhara). This method is not possible in the Suttanta and Abhidhamma.

Therefore, because it was well known, and because the word 'At that time' (tena samayena) as the cause is directly connected with the word 'was staying' (viharati), and because an introduction with the word 'yaṃ' (which) is not possible at the beginning, only the designation with 'taṃ' (that) is stated first in the Vinaya Piṭaka. How? Because in this context, it is not possible to say 'At which time there is a village named Kalanda not far from Vesālī' or 'At which time Vesālī... exists'. Since the designation with 'yaṃ' is not possible and only the designation with 'taṃ' is possible, it is stated as 'At that time... there is a village named Kalanda'. Or simply, it is because it was well known.

Regarding the phrase 'aniyamaniiddesavacana' (indefinite designation): although this is actually a definite designation because it uses the word 'taṃ' according to the method mentioned, the commentator calls it 'indefinite designation' because it is not well known to other monks of the present time, unlike those Council reciters. The statement 'This logic is applicable to the entire Vinaya' should be understood as being said for the most part.
33:
If the word “Tena” (by that/at that) were an indefinite designation in all instances, then in the passage “Therefore (Tena hi), monks, the training rule for monks...”, this word “Tena,” which has a previously established meaning, would also be an indefinite designation. Also, the word “Tena” in passages such as “At that time (Tena samayena) the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Uruvelā” would be an indefinite designation, but it is not. Therefore, the commentator said, “This is an indefinite designation,” for the sake of those to whom the meaning indicated by the designation “Taṃ” is unknown.

Alternatively, it is called an “indefinite designation” because the definite meaning was not shown initially, and because later it is shown as a designation with “Yaṃ” (which) in connection with that “Taṃ”. Alternatively, because the word “Samaya” (time/occasion), which indicates time without specifying “such and such a time” among morning and so on, stands as a subordinate word (upapada), it is appropriate to say “This is an indefinite designation.” Alternatively, when “Tena” is said, the word “Samayena” (at the time) is added to establish a restriction (niyama) to prevent the implication of all other things like “by that pot” or “by that cloth.” At what time did he stay? He stayed at the time of Venerable Sāriputta’s reflection, which is established by the context later on.

Here, the objector says: If the “time of reflection” (vitakka-samaya) is intended here, then would it not contradict the statement to be made later: “Here, the causal sense (hetu-attha) and the instrumental sense (karaṇa-attha) are possible; that time of the promulgation of the training rule is difficult to know even for Sāriputta and others; by that time which is the cause and the instrument”? It does not contradict, because the commentator spoke according to the “majority method” (bāhullanya). Indeed, the objection is: Why is the designation made with the instrumental case in this Vinaya Piṭaka, unlike in the Suttanta and Abhidhamma? Therefore, in answering that objection, the commentator, wishing to state the purpose of the instrumental case according to the majority method, said: “That time of the promulgation of the training rule...”, and so on. He did not say this wishing to state the purpose of the instrumental case being mentioned right now; rather, for this [phrase “Tena samayena”], only the causal sense is appropriate, not the instrumental sense. Therefore, he said: “established by the context later on,” and so on.

“And the occasion” (Samayañca) means taking into account the concordance of conditions for the arrival [of the Buddha] and the time suitable for that. The intention is: “We shall know [the rule] having obtained the completeness of conditions and the time of arrival.”

Here, the objector says: Just as in the phrase “Monks, there is only one moment (khaṇa) and one occasion (samaya),” where ‘moment’ and ‘occasion’ have the same meaning, so too here in “taking into account the time (kāla) and the occasion (samaya),” ‘time’ and ‘occasion’ should have the same meaning. Furthermore, if ‘occasion’ here means the concordance of conditions for arrival, and since time is also a condition for arrival, time is already included by the term ‘occasion’. Why then is ‘time’ mentioned separately? To answer: Because time was first restricted by the phrase “perhaps even tomorrow,” ‘occasion’ is not...
34:
It means time (kāla). In that time designated as "tomorrow," it should be approached based on the concordance of other causes for arrival. Even in the designated time, based on the time divided into morning and so forth, which is in accordance with the aforementioned concordance, it shows the state of being fixed to times such as the morning on the day defined as "tomorrow." Therefore, because time (kāla) and occasion (samaya) do not have the same meaning, it should be understood that taking time (kāla) separately is also purposeful.

Because the word 'moment' (khaṇa) has many meanings, such as in "Monk, you are born, you age, and you die at every moment," or "He goes to the presence of the bhikkhunī constantly," or "They speak the Teacher's instruction at every moment," the word 'occasion' (samaya) likewise has many meanings. Therefore, defining one by the other, He said, "Monks, the moment (khaṇa) and the occasion (samaya) are one and the same." It is appropriate that the meanings of khaṇa and samaya are identical. Khaṇa means the obtaining of an opportunity. It means the ninth moment, excluding the eight inopportune moments (aṭṭhakkhana).

Because they speak of their respective views (samaya) such as annihilationism (uccheda) and so forth, it is called 'samayappavādaka' (one who propounds a view). That very place is called 'Tindukācīra' because it is surrounded by a row of Tinduka trees known as Tindukācīra. 'Ekasālaka' means a single Sāla tree. They also call it a "rest house" (kuṭi). 'Atthābhisamaya' means the attainment of one's own benefit. 'Dhīra' refers to a wise person, and no other. 'Sammā mānābhisamaya' means by the proper abandoning of pride, meaning the proper abandoning of pride by way of eradication (samuccheda).

In such phrases as "the sense of oppression of suffering (dukkha)," and "the penetration of the four truths in four ways," it is the sense of the nature of suffering of the five aggregates called dukkha. The sense of the 'conditioned' (saṅkhata) is the sense of arising from causes. There is the sense of burning through painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). There is the sense of change through pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). It should be understood that the sense of oppression and so forth is indeed the sense of realization (abhisamaya).

In instances such as 'the time of conception' (gabbhokkanti-samaya), it is manifest to devas and humans through earthquakes, the appearance of light, and so forth. The time of practicing austerities (dukkaracariya) is also manifest through such descriptions as "the ascetic Gotama is dark, or not dark." The seven-week periods and other ways of dwelling are called 'the time of dwelling in happiness in the present life' (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra-samaya).

"Accantameva taṃ samayaṃ" means from the beginning of the effort until the conclusion is reached, dwelling in that samaya through continuous association during that much time. "Karuṇā-vihārena vihāsi" means He dwelt in that samaya by dwelling in the task of compassion. This is because that samaya is the time for the task of compassion. The Blessed One has two tasks: the task of knowledge (ñāṇa-kicca) and the task of compassion (karuṇā-kicca). The knowledge that knows all things is called the task of knowledge. Having entered the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti)...
35:
...surveying the multitude of beings to be tamed (veneyya) and acting accordingly for their benefit is called the task of compassion. As it was said, "Monks, there are two things to be done by you who have assembled," the Blessed One also performs those two tasks. Or else, it refers to meeting with visiting (āgantuka) monks and so forth. In that context, wishing to show the dwelling that is the task of compassion, it is said, "He dwelt in compassion."

In the statement "The locus (adhikaraṇa) has the meaning of time," the syllable 'hi' has the meaning of cause (kāraṇa). In that Abhidhamma, the meaning of samaya should be understood in five ways: as time (kāla), assemblage (samūha), moment (khaṇa), concordance (samavāya), and cause (hetu).

How does samaya in the sense of time and assemblage become a locus (adhikaraṇa)? Just as when it is said, "He was born in the morning," the place of occurrence is called the locus; similarly, the word samaya in the sense of time should be understood as a locus. How is it in the sense of a mass (rāsi)? It is like saying, "It was produced in a heap of grain." Therefore, it means that at whatever time or in whatever mass the mind arises, at that time or in that mass, contact (phassa) and other states arise. In the phrase "the locus," the locus indicated in the Abhidhamma is both the sense of time and the sense of assemblage. It should be understood that it refers to the locus mentioned as "at whatever time" (yasmiṃ samaye).

Now, wishing to show the characterization of an occurrence by another occurrence (bhāvena-bhāvalakkhaṇa), the text says, "of those mentioned therein," and so forth. What is the 'state' (bhāva) of the things mentioned in that Abhidhamma? It is simply their arising and presence. That presence is the state of the dhammas such as contact (phassa) mentioned in that Abhidhamma. That presence, however, is marked and known by the presence of the samaya. Therefore, it means that the designation is made using the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti).

Among those five samayas, the 'moment' (khaṇa) is the ninth moment, which is free from the eight inopportune moments. When that moment exists, the Buddha appears. 'Concordance' (samavāya) is the harmony of causes such as the eye-faculty and so forth. When that concordance exists, the mind arises. 'Cause' (hetu) refers to the five objects such as visible forms. Therefore, it means that when those causes—the ninth moment, the concordance of causes, and the object—exist, the presence and existence of those dhammas like contact occur.

In this Vinaya, however, both the sense of cause (hetu) and the sense of instrument (karaṇa) are possible. This is because the word samaya mentioned in this Vinaya is said to take the instrumental case (tatiyā-vibhatti) in the sense of agent, instrument, and cause. That samaya is difficult to know. It means this is because it was said, "Only the Tathāgata will know the time for that." "Tena samayena" means because of that samaya as a cause. Just as when it is said, "He lives because of food, he lives because of knowledge," it means he lives for that purpose, wishing to obtain food or knowledge. Similarly, in the phrase "Tena samayena viharati," the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of cause. Therefore, it means He dwelt in various places while looking at the time for the prescription of training rules (sikkhāpada) and the transgressions. In the third Pārājika and others, "Monks, I desire..."
36:
It should be understood in the Pali passages such as "Addhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ" (Pārājika 162). Therefore, by the rule "Kāladdhāne accantasaṃyoge," the second case (accusative) can occur in the sense of continuous duration, as in "Māsamadhīte" (studies for a whole month) or "Divasamadhīte" (studies for a whole day).

In this context, however, both the sense of cause (hetu) and the sense of instrument (karaṇa) are possible. Among these two, where the sense of cause for the instrumental case is possible, the Blessed One dwelt in various places, reflecting on the reason for the laying down of the training rule (sikkhāpada), which is called the transgression of various objects or the time of transgression, due to that cause of "tena samayena" (at that time). Where the sense of instrument for the instrumental case is possible, the meaning is that the Blessed One dwelt in various places, laying down the training rules by means of that time which had arrived as the instrument.

In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: "The transgression of Sudinna and others is indeed the cause; the time which is the limit of that transgression is merely the instrument, because the training rule must be laid down without exceeding that time." This statement is faultless. As for the statement, "This instrumental case, although occurring earlier, is mentioned later because it belongs to the preceding part," that is poorly stated. For when the instrumental sense is joined after the causal sense, it follows the natural order; it is joined in that very manner. The teacher (Ācariya Ānanda) wrote that it should be understood that the commentator joined this instrumental sense, which was mentioned later, first, and joined the causal sense, which was mentioned first, later, for the sake of ease in interpretation. From here onwards, wherever it is said "Written by the teacher" (Ācariyena likhitaṃ) or "The teacher's reasoning" (Ācariyassa takko), the teacher should be understood as the teacher Ānanda who resided in Kalasapura.

Here, an objector says: Just as it is said in the Suttas, "Ekaṃ samayaṃ Bhagavā" (At one time the Blessed One), so should it be said, "Tena samayena Bhagavā Verañjāyaṃ" (At that time the Blessed One was at Verañjā). If the Elder wished to speak of the attributes along with synonyms, then terms like "Tathāgato Sugato" should also be mentioned. If there is any specific purpose in taking only these two words (Buddho Bhagavā), that purpose should be stated.

I shall state the answer: To some who do not know the sequence of the Blessed One's extremely profound intention, seeing the Vinaya scriptures such as the Pali "Apanyatte sikkhāpade anādīnavadasso... abhivinyāpesi" (Pārājika 36), "Atha kho Bhagavā āyasmantaṃ Sudinnaṃ paṭipucchi" (Pārājika 39), and "Sādiyi tvaṃ bhikkhu, nāhaṃ Bhagavā sādiyiṃ" (Pārājika 72), as well as the laying down of the second Pārājika rule by the measure spoken by a monk who was formerly a judge, and the permission for Devadatta's ordination, doubt might arise regarding the Buddha's perfect enlightenment. "Likewise, what benefit would there be for you, who roasts a human carcass?"...
37:
"Eater of spit" (Cūḷavagga, 336) and other such Vinaya scriptures connected with harsh words might cause doubt regarding the state of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). To dispel these two kinds of doubt, it should be understood that the Venerable Upāli Thera used these two words (Buddho Bhagavā) throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. By these words, he shows this meaning: Indeed, He is the 'Buddha' because He knows all things that should be known; He is 'Bhagavā' because He has destroyed all faults (defilements); and that Blessed One is the Teacher of gods and men. Later it is also said: "The Tathāgatas, though knowing, still ask... in speech not connected with benefit, the Tathāgatas destroy it as one destroys a bridge" (Pārājika 16). And in the Suttas it is said: "Kesī, I discipline with gentle words, and I also discipline with harsh words" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.111).

In the phrase "Asādhāraṇa-hetumhi" (in the uncommon cause), this method alone is obtained: wholesome roots are never the roots of unwholesome states; likewise, unwholesome roots are never the roots of wholesome states, and indeterminate (abyākata) roots are never the roots of wholesome states. Because wholesome causes are conditions by way of root-condition (hetu-paccaya) for the material phenomena produced by them, the method such as "wholesome states are conditions for wholesome states only" is not obtained. Evil things are called "pu"; because it destroys those evil things, it is called "pucimanda" (the Neem tree).

In the phrase "inclination towards producing the welfare and happiness of beings," the phrase "greatly helpful to humans" is stated to show the beings mentioned in general by dividing them into two. "Bahujanahitāya" means for the welfare of many people. Indeed, the Blessed One, through His perfection of wisdom, points out the welfare of the present life and the life to come. "Sukhāya" means for the sake of happiness. Indeed, through His perfection of generosity (cāga-sampatti), He grants the happiness that is helpful. Being endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, He always has compassion for the world of beings like a father and mother. This Blessed One is the protector and guardian of the world. In the phrase "devamanussānaṃ" (of gods and men), taking only the veneyya beings who are capable of realization, He shows His own arising for their attainment of Nibbāna, the Path, and the Fruition. When "atthāya" is said, it means for the sake of Nibbāna, the ultimate benefit; when "hitāya" is said, it means for the sake of the Path that leads to that Nibbāna, for there is no benefit (hita) superior to the Path. "Sukhāya" means for the sake of the happiness of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), for there is no happiness superior to that.

In the phrase "diṭṭhisīlasaṃghātena" (by the collection of view and virtue), the reason for taking only view and virtue without taking concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā) is that they are common to all trainees (sekkha) and non-trainees (asekkha). In the Kosambiya Sutta also, it is said: "He dwells possessed of common virtue; he dwells possessed of common view." If it is asked, "Is not wisdom also included by taking view?"—No, it is not, because even Stream-enterers and others are those who fulfill wisdom. Therefore, although they have the same characteristic, there is a difference in state between that wisdom and view, just as there is a difference between the faculty of persistence, concentration, and right concentration.
38:
Regarding the word 'Aññāsi', meanings known according to the sequence of the ear-door are called 'heard'. It is as in the passage: 'Venerable Gotama, it has been heard thus: evil conducts are both seen and heard,' and so forth. As in 'Upāli, a monk divides the Saṅgha,' etc., the word 'kho' is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). 'Verañjāyaṃ' means being present in the city of Verañjā. 'Itthambhūtassa' means to one who has become thus (the Buddha). 'How has he become?' It means the fame has spread and risen for the Great Buddha who, having gone forth from the Sakyan clan as a Sakyan son, remains in this state. Because of the association with the word 'abhi', the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used.

Regarding the statement, 'Because of clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna), one develops loving-kindness and is reborn in the Brahma world,' it is said that this rejects the view of those who say, 'Because of kāmupādāna as a cause, one performs kamma and is reborn only in the sense sphere (kāmabhava).' Some say: Having heard 'There are exquisite sensual pleasures in the Brahma world,' or having thought so, one later performs the practice (bhāvanā) leading to that Brahma world because of kāmupādāna, thinking 'I will enjoy prosperity there.' Therefore, even in the Brahma world, they are called 'sensual pleasures' (kāma) in the sense of being desired. They also say: 'Because of taking that Brahma world as an object, craving (taṇhā) is called kāmupādāna.' This point should be investigated.

Kamma is the productive cause (janaka-kāraṇa) of the eye; the root cause of kamma is craving. Therefore, craving is not the productive cause but only the root cause. Craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā) and so forth are called the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) because they are included in the five aggregates. This is also because of the word: 'Not getting what one wants is also suffering.' Because it is the root cause of those five aggregates, it is called 'the craving that gives rise' (samuṭṭhāpikā). It should be linked as 'the (past craving) that gives rise to these five aggregates which are the cause.' Because of the word 'With the arising of taints (āsava), ignorance (avijjā) arises,' it is also appropriate to say it is only the cause of that kamma.

Alternatively, because of the word 'Like forms, etc., craving is also the place of arising and abandoning of craving,' craving is also made the Truth of Suffering like forms, etc. For it is said: 'Craving for forms is a dear and pleasant thing in the world; here this craving, when arising, arises,' and 'here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned.' In the Visuddhimagga, it says: 'In every way, the five aggregates of clinging are both suffering and the Noble Truth, except for craving.' If one asks: 'Does the statement here that rūpa-taṇhā, etc., are the Truth of Suffering contradict that?' The answer is: No, it does not. This is because it is taught in various places to show them without mutual confusion. If craving were not included in the aggregates of clinging, it would have been said in the Sacca-vibhaṅga: 'Therein, what are the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering in brief?'
39:
In the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi (page 202), in the passage 'The aggregate of clinging to form... and so on... the aggregate of clinging to consciousness,' it should have said 'the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, excluding craving,' but it did not say so. Therefore, if one asks: 'Does this mean craving is included in the Truth of Suffering?' The answer is: No, because it would lead to the fault of confusing cause and effect. If one says there is no fault of confusion, in the Sacca-vibhaṅga Pāḷi, the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) is shown in five groups. 

How is it shown? 1. Craving is one section (vāra). 2. Craving and the remaining defilements are the second section. 3. Craving, remaining defilements, and remaining unwholesome states are the third section. 4. Craving, remaining defilements, remaining unwholesome states, and the three wholesome roots that are subject to taints (sāsava) are the fourth section. 5. Craving, remaining defilements, remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots subject to taints, and the remaining wholesome states subject to taints are the fifth section. While it is true that it is shown thus, it is only in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya and not elsewhere (Suttanta-bhājanīya). That method is not found in the Ariyasacca-niddesa. Because there it only says 'cattāri saccāni' (four truths), and not 'cattāri ariyasaccāni' (four noble truths) as in the Suttanta-bhājanīya and the question sections. Therefore, the Suttanta-bhājanīya is the standard, and craving is mentioned (separately) there. As it is said: 'Therein, what is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence... and so on... namely, craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), etc.' (Vibha. 203).

Because it is said by this method: 'That which is impermanent is suffering' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15), what is said there is also a standard. Because of the word 'He dwells having attained the first jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa,' 'kasiṇa' refers to the jhānas. Some say 'It is said with reference to the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta),' but that statement is not good. Because of the word 'Even in the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), one should discard the concept (paññatti) and establish mindfulness as "repulsive" (paṭikūla),' only forms, etc., which are the objects of mindfulness, should be known.

These seven: faith (saddhā), moral shame (hiri), moral dread (ottappa), great learning (bāhusacca), energy (vīriya), established mindfulness (upaṭṭhita-sati), and clear comprehension (sampajañña) are called the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). 'Sabhāvato' means by way of suffering (dukkha). 'Na cavati' is said with reference to the devas. 'Ñāteyya' means should be known. 'Daṭṭheyya' means should be seen. Or else, it means 'I do not say that the end of the world can be known by traveling.' 'Loka' (world) refers to the world of aggregates (khandha-loka). 'Cannot be reached by traveling' means it cannot be reached by physical travel or by going to wrong destinations (agati); it means only by reaching the end of the world through the traveling of the Noble Ones is there liberation from suffering. 'Samitāvī' is one whose defilements are stilled. 'Āhāraṭṭhitikā' refers to beings who subsist on causes (conditions/nutriment). Which...
40:
Some beings are established in causes; all those beings have the single name 'Loka' (world) in the sense of being subject to breaking and disintegration. Formations (saṅkhāra) are called 'Satta' (beings) because they arise in dependence on their respective causes and because they cling to objects such as forms. They wander about. The word 'Disā' is in the accusative plural. They shine. What are those shining things? They are the moon and the sun, which shine beautifully. The eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are merely formations. According to the words "around Mount Sineru," mountains such as Yugandhara stand surrounding Mount Sineru in a circular shape. This world-element stands very high, surrounding [it]. It is said that the letter 'ma' acts as a sandhi-maker (euphonic connector). Alternatively, He is called 'Lokavidū' (Knower of the World) because He knows the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) by way of characteristics and so forth; the world of beings (sattaloka) by way of inclinations and underlying tendencies; and the world of space (okāsaloka) by way of the dimensions of the universe, in every way.

How can the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana), which is of the sense sphere, limited, and mundane, overcome the entire world? It can overcome it like the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) because of its incomparable power. For that [knowledge] follows the course of the Blessed One's omniscience in its own domain, and it arises very rapidly, occurring immediately after two life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses. Such a very rapid mind does not arise for anyone else, even for the Venerable Sāriputta; it is said that even his mental process arises after fifteen life-continuum consciousnesses. It is said there were nāgas named Aggisikha and Dhūmasikha on the island of Ceylon. A word that clarifies the meaning is called 'atthapada'. The meaning is that this entire collection of words, being words that clarify a single meaning, is a sentence. The 'eight directions' refer to the eight liberations (vimokkha) or the eight attainments (samāpatti). The word 'satthavāha' is shortened to 'satthā', just as 'pisitāsa' is called 'pisāca'. "I was a frog living in the water, not a frog on land; the water alone was my range. While I was listening to your Dhamma, [someone] pressed my head with a staff..."—this is the remaining text. Or else, it is the genitive case in the sense of disregard (anādara). "Even with this much merit, there will be such power," he said, smiling. Here, 'vimokkha' refers to the Path (magga); the knowledge immediately following that Path is called the knowledge of the Fruit (phalañāṇa); at that moment, He is called 'Buddha'. He is called 'Buddha' in the active sense because He knows everything. He is called 'bodhetā' in the causative sense because He makes others know. A word that clarifies the most excellent meaning is called 'seṭṭha'; likewise, it is called 'uttama'. 'Sacchikā-paññatti' is the designation of being self-enlightened by way of realizing all phenomena; or it is called 'sacchikā-paññatti' because it is known and realized by Himself alone. He is called 'Bhagavā' because He shares (bhagī) robes, alms-food, and so forth. He is called 'bhajī' because He resorts to secluded forest dwellings and so forth. He is called 'bhāgī' because He possesses the essence of meaning, the essence of Dhamma, and the essence of liberation. He is called 'bhagga' because He has destroyed the group of defilements such as lust. He is called 'bhāvitatta' because He has a developed self. He is called 'bhavantago' because He has reached Nibbāna, the end of existence, through the attainment of the Path.
41:
“Monks, abandon one thing: greed.” Taking this as the method, the teachings found in the Ekakanipāta of the Itivuttaka and other texts are stated. Through the influence of defiling craving, views, and misconduct, perversions (vippallāsa) arise, such as perceiving the permanent in the impermanent, the pleasant in the painful, the self in the non-self, and the beautiful in the foul. Monks, craving arises in a monk because of robes, or because of alms-food, lodgings, or because of this or that state of becoming (bhavābhava). There are five mental barrennesses (cetokhila): doubting the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, or the training, and being angry with one's fellow practitioners.

There are five mental bondages (vinibandha): not being free from lust for sensual pleasures, for the body, or for forms; eating as much as one wants until the stomach is full, and practicing the holy life while aspiring for rebirth in a certain company of devas. The roots of dispute (vivādamūla) are: anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, stubbornness, impetuosity, clinging to one's own views, and being difficult to relinquish. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated as: “anger, contempt, envy, fraud, evil desire, and clinging to one's own views.”

Dependent on craving is pursuit; dependent on pursuit is gain; dependent on gain is decision-making; thus arise desire and lust, attachment, possession, stinginess, safeguarding, and because of safeguarding, unwholesome states such as the taking up of sticks and weapons occur. There are six types of craving: craving for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. These become eighteen through the influence of craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. These same eighteen, when applied to the internal and the external, become thirty-six. These thirty-six, when multiplied by the past, future, and present, result in the one hundred and eight modes of craving (taṇhā-vicarita).

He is called “Māra” because he kills. According to the saying, “Heedlessness is the path to death,” heedlessness is Māra. Also, defilements (kilesa) are called “Māra” because they destroy right livelihood. The aggregates (khandha) themselves are Māra because they are like executioners. Volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are Māra because they produce the suffering of birth and cause aging and so on to occur for the born being. Death (maccu) is Māra because it kills the life faculty (jīvitindriya) contained within a single existence.

Aṇimatā means reaching an invisible state like an atomic particle. Laghimatā means swift movement by means of the body or the mind. Mahimatā means being able to touch the moon, the sun, and so on with one's hand. Patti means reaching any desired place. Pākamma means manifestation or the accomplishment of a desired benefit. Īsatta means sovereignty over oneself. Vasitta means mastery, not being under the control of others. Yatthakāmāvasāyitā means the ability to accomplish a goal in whatever place, at whatever time, with whatever object, and to whatever extent one desires.
42:
In showing the Noble Truth of Suffering through the meanings of oppression (pīḷana), the conditioned (saṅkhata), burning (santāpa), and change (vipariṇāma), there is an answer preceded by this objection: "There are other meanings of the Truth of Suffering, such as the craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā), etc. Why then are only these four (oppression, etc.) mentioned?" If asked thus, the answer is: They are mentioned because they become manifest through the vision of the other truths.

Knowledge regarding the truths is stated by way of taking each truth as an object, in such ways as: "Therein, what is the knowledge of suffering? The wisdom that arises by taking the Truth of Suffering as an object is called the knowledge of suffering." It is also stated by way of the fulfillment of tasks in the remaining truths by taking one truth as an object, in such ways as: "Monks, he who sees the Truth of Suffering also sees the Origin of Suffering."

In that context, when one takes each truth as an object: by seeing the Truth of Origin, the conditioned meaning (saṅkhata) of the Truth of Suffering—which by nature has the characteristic of oppression—becomes manifest, because that suffering is conditioned and produced by the Truth of Origin, which has the characteristic of accumulation (āyūhana). Because the Path removes the heat of defilements and is exceedingly cool, the meaning of burning (santāpa) in suffering becomes manifest through the vision of the Path. This is like Prince Nanda seeing the celestial nymphs, whereby the lack of beauty of the princess Janapadakalyāṇī Sundarī became manifest. By seeing the Truth of Cessation, which is of a nature that does not change, it goes without saying that the meaning of change (vipariṇāma) in suffering becomes manifest.

By seeing the Truth of Suffering, the meaning of source (nidāna) in the Truth of Origin—which by nature has the characteristic of accumulation—becomes manifest. This is like seeing a disease caused by unsuitable food, whereby the fact that the food is the source (nidāna) of the disease becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of Cessation, which is the state of disjunction from the round of rebirths, the meaning of bond (saṃyoga) in the Truth of Origin becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of the Path, which is the means of escape from the round of rebirths, the meaning of impediment (palibodha) in the Truth of Origin should be understood to become manifest.

Similarly, by seeing the Truth of Origin, which is non-seclusion (aviveka), the meaning of seclusion (viveka) in the Truth of Cessation, which is the escape from the round of rebirths, becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of the Path, the meaning of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) becomes manifest. By seeing this Path, which has never been seen before in the beginningless Saṃsāra, and because that Path itself is conditioned (saṅkhata) due to having causes, the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna, which is a state without causes, becomes extremely clear. By seeing the Truth of Suffering, the meaning of the deathless (amata) in the Truth of Cessation becomes manifest. Suffering is like poison, and Nibbāna is like the deathless medicine.

Similarly, by seeing the Truth of Origin, the meaning of cause (hetu) in the Truth of the Path—which has the characteristic of escaping the round of rebirths—becomes manifest: "This Truth of Origin (craving) is not the cause for reaching Nibbāna; only this Truth of the Path (the Eightfold Path) is the cause for reaching Nibbāna." By seeing the Truth of Cessation, the meaning of vision (dassana) becomes manifest. This is like a person seeing extremely subtle forms and thinking, "Indeed, my eyes are very clear," whereby the clarity of the eyes becomes manifest. By seeing the Truth of Suffering, the meaning of dominance (adhipateyya) becomes manifest. This is like seeing many poor people oppressed by diseases, whereby the noble state of sovereign kings becomes manifest. Thus, in the analysis of these truths, by the power of characteristics and by the power of the manifestation of the other three truths through the vision of one truth...
43:
It is said that each truth has four meanings because, by seeing one truth, the other three truths become manifest. Because of being free from defilements, it is called upadhiviveka (seclusion from the basis of rebirth).

Because they desire the opposite (enemy), they are called paccatthika (enemies). Those who are opposing enemies are called paccāmitta (enemies). By the phrase "Having realized, He makes it known," the Buddha's omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is shown. Having shown the accomplishment of knowledge (ñāṇasampatti) with those words, now to show the accomplishment of compassion (karuṇāsampatti), it is said: "He taught the Dhamma," and so forth. Alternatively, what did the Blessed One make known? All the Dhamma that is known is solely for the benefit of the three worlds. What kind of Dhamma is meant by "He taught the Dhamma"? It is "good in the beginning," and so forth. By this statement, His worthiness to teach is shown.

Sāsanadhamma refers to ovādapariyatti (learning the instruction). Kiccasuddhi refers to the purity of the task of abandoning defilements and the task of taking Nibbāna as an object. Sāsanabrahmacariya refers to either the collection of the three trainings (sikkhā) or the mass of virtue (sīla) numbering nine thousand crores, etc. Because the Path itself is the noble practice, it is called maggabrahmacariya. The Piṭaka, which explains this maggabrahmacariya, is here called "sāttha" (with meaning) and "sabyañjana" (with phrasing).

Among the six terms of meaning (atthapada), explaining briefly is called saṅkāsana. Explaining from the beginning is called pakāsana. Teaching both of these in detail is called vivaraṇa. Further analysis and classification is called vibhajana. Making it clear through similes and so forth is called uttānīkaraṇa. Making it known by pleasing the hearts of the listeners and by sharpening the mind is to be understood as paññāpana.

Among the terms of phrasing (byañjanapada), it is called akkhara (syllable/letter) because it is inexhaustible; some teachers say, "A word with a single syllable is called akkhara." A word ending in an inflection is called pada. Because it makes the meaning clear, it is called byañjana (phrasing) or vākya (sentence). Alternatively, a collection of words is called vākya. Showing by analysis is called ākāra. The etymological definition (nirutti) such as "it is phassa (contact) because it touches" is called nirutti; the detailed explanation of the meaning expressed by nirutti is called niddesa. It is called phassa because it touches; that phassa is of three types: contact to be felt as pleasant, contact to be felt as painful, and contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

In these atthapada and byañjanapada, it should be understood by correlation thus: He explains briefly by syllables (akkhara), He explains at the beginning by words (pada), He reveals by phrasing (byañjana), He analyzes by modes (ākāra), He makes clear by etymologies (nirutti), and He makes known by descriptions (niddesa). Or, having explained briefly by syllables, He explains in order by words; having revealed by phrasing, He analyzes by modes; having made clear by etymologies, He makes known by descriptions. Or, it should be understood that He guides the person of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū) by opening with syllables and words; He guides the person of expanded intuition (vipañcitaññū) by revealing with phrasing and analyzing with modes; and He guides the person to be led (neyya) by conveying with etymologies and descriptions.

Attha (meaning) is the meaning of the Pali that is taught. The individual nature of that very meaning which is to be penetrated is called paṭivedha (penetration). Both of these are called attha. Therefore, it is said: "It is sāttha (with meaning) because of the profundity of meaning and the profundity of penetration." What is called Dhamma or desanā is only the phrasing (byañjana). The sāsanabrahmacariya, which is pure by being faultless, and...
44:
There is also the Path encompassed by the three trainings. Both the holy life of the teaching (sāsana-brahmacariya) and the holy life of the path (magga-brahmacariya) are included under the term 'brahmacariya'. 'Paṭipattiyā' means because of the cause of practice (paṭipatti). 'Āgamabyattito' means that through repeated study and recitation, the aggregates (khandhas) and so forth become clear. Studying poorly expounded scriptures only leads to confusion.

2-3. 'Kacci khamanīyaṃ' is asking whether one can endure cold, heat, and so forth. 'Kacci yāpanīyaṃ' is asking whether one can sustain life with the requisites obtained for livelihood. 'Appābādhaṃ' means having few afflictions. 'Appātaṅkaṃ' means being free from illness. 'Kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ' is asking whether one can rise quickly for bodily duties. 'Kacci balaṃ' is asking whether one has strength for the duties of a recluse (samaṇa). 'Kacci phāsuvihāro' is asking whether one lives comfortably, either due to the absence of afflictions as mentioned before, or through the power of non-dissatisfaction and so forth. From the age of sixty-seven onwards is the last stage of life (pacchimavaya). 'Uttarāmukho' means facing north. When the power of 'opening the world' (lokavivaraṇa) arose, what did he look at in this world system? Since there is no one like you in this world, he said, "You are the supreme in the world including the devas," and so forth. 'Āsabbiṃ' means noble speech. Devas arise by way of spontaneous rebirth (upapatti). Because they arise in accordance with the pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā) associated with lust (rāga) that arises through the enjoyment of forms or through aspiration, and because they satisfy the heart, they are called 'tastes of forms' (rūparasa), like the taste of a mango and so forth.

It is stated by the power of his authority that these 'tastes of forms' (rūparasa) have been abandoned by the Blessed One. The abandonment of these 'tastes of forms' by the Blessed One is like a palm tree with its top cut off. How so? By the term 'tastes of forms', the resultant phenomena (vipākadhamma) are taken. Although these resultant phenomena exist, because craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), which are like the top, have been cut off by the sword of the Path, they are no longer able to produce resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandha) in the future, which are like a row of palm trees. Therefore, it means they have been made like a palm stump (tālāvatthukata). It is said, "Wholesome joy (kusala-somanassa) is also included here." Those 'tastes of forms' abandoned by the first Path stand in the place of the course of action (kammapatha). By the second Path, the coarse roots are cut off. By the third Path, the 'tastes of forms' residing in sensual lust (kāmarāga) are made like a palm stump. By the fourth Path, the 'tastes of forms' residing in lust for form (rūparāga) and lust for the formless (arūparāga) are brought to non-existence. To show the nature of non-decline, he said, "They are of a nature not to arise in the future."

Alternatively, they are abandoned by abandonment through substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna) at the moment of insight (vipassanā) or at the moment of the preliminary stage of absorption (jhāna). At the moment of absorption, the roots are cut off by abandonment through suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna). Was it not taught, "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures"? At the moment of attaining the third knowledge (vijjā), they are made like a palm stump by abandonment through eradication (samucchedapahāna). These 'tastes of forms' and so forth, having reached non-existence and being of a nature not to arise in the future—this statement has only one meaning. Or else, they are abandoned by the first knowledge, the roots are cut off by the second knowledge, and they are made like a palm stump by the third knowledge. Because they are thus, they are said to have reached non-existence; therefore, they should be known as being of a nature not to arise in the future. Alternatively, they are abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (dukkha-ñāṇa), the roots are cut off by the knowledge of the origin (samudaya-ñāṇa), they are made like a palm stump by the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-ñāṇa), they reach non-existence by the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa), and they are known as being of a nature not to arise in the future by the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Or else, they are abandoned by the mundane path (lokiya-magga), the roots are cut off by the path of seeing (dassana-magga), and they are made like a palm stump by the three paths of development (bhāvanā-magga), and so forth. Since it was not the domain of the brahmin Verañja, the 'tastes of the Dhamma' (dhammarasa) were not revealed.

11. In this term 'dhammadhātu', omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is called the dhammadhātu. In accordance with the words of compassion for beings, he said, "Like the light of the full moon." The word 'suppaṭividdhattā' is the speech of the Noble Ones (ariyas). Having a mind like the earth and dwelling with compassion is called 'dwelling in compassion' (karuṇā-vihāra). Although his own virtues were concealed, because he showed them by saying, "I have exerted energy," and so forth, it is like the speech of the sun.
45:
They should be understood as having their roots cut off by the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-ñāṇa), like a palmyra stump; having reached the state of non-existence by path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa); and having the nature of not arising in the future by reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). Alternatively, they are abandoned by the mundane path, their roots are severed by the path of seeing (dassana-magga), and they are made like a palmyra stump by the three paths of cultivation (bhāvanā-magga), and so on. Because it is not the domain of the Brahmin Verañja, the flavors of the Dhamma (dhamma-rasa) are not extracted and shown.

## In this term 'Dhamma-dhātu', Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is called the Dhamma-element.

In accordance with the words of compassion for beings, it is said, 'Like the full moon.' The statement 'Because of being well-penetrated' is a statement comparable to the sun. The cause of having a mind like the earth is called 'the diffusion of compassion.' When revealing his own hidden virtues by saying 'Indeed, my energy has been aroused' and so on, it should be understood that he is revealing the diffusion of his compassion. 'Vara-bhūrimedhasa' means the Buddha who possesses noble and extensive wisdom. Alternatively, 'Bhūrī' means the earth; it means the Buddha who possesses noble wisdom as expansive as the earth. By the sense of the location where he awakened (adhikaraṇa-sādhana), the tree is called 'Bodhi'. He himself awakens, or those endowed with it awaken by means of it; therefore, the Path is called 'Bodhi'. Likewise, Omniscience is also called 'Bodhi'. Because it is the truth to be known, Nibbāna is called 'Bodhi'. Due to being the basis for the three knowledges (vijjā), the three knowledges should be understood as they occur. Sharpness is understood by the power of one-pointedness (ekaggatā). Some sharp arrows become blunt upon hitting the target, but this insight-knowledge is not like that. Its hardness should be understood by the power of the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), its clarity by the power of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), and its courage by the power of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), because it thoroughly overcomes the enemies of defilements without retreating in the middle. The time of 'taking the womb' for the sake of giving birth to the Path is because it is 'conformity' (anuloma) immediately following the 'equanimity towards formations' (saṅkhārupekkhā).

Desire (chanda) and intention (saṅkappa) are merely lust (rāga) distinguished by different stages. As in:
'A man with a lustful heart approaches the limbs of a woman with affection;
With a heart stained by lust, he approaches with a desire for union;
In this world, a woman fallen into sensual desire is like a mother without limit,' and so on.

Even if the meaning is stated in the Vibhaṅga itself, this is the intention in this commentary: even if it were stated here in detail by bringing the Vibhaṅga Pali, it would not be helpful to everyone; therefore, I shall explain that meaning only by the method of the Commentary. 'From this' means from sensual pleasures (kāma).
46:
Among physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) and others, seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka) is the third. Therefore, excluding the third upadhi-viveka and taking the two (physical and mental seclusion), and from among the types of seclusion like temporary seclusion (tadaṅga-viveka), taking seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), it is said "only three." If so, since mental seclusion (citta-viveka) and seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka) have the same meaning, would there be no distinction? This should not be regarded so, because this is the section on attainment (appanā-vāra). By taking physical seclusion, the preliminary stage (of jhāna) is understood. Therefore, mental seclusion refers to temporary seclusion (tadaṅga-viveka), and seclusion by suppression should be understood as the seclusion occurring at the time of attainment (appanā), thus avoiding confusion. Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that both temporary and suppression seclusion are included in mental seclusion, while the other (physical seclusion) includes only suppression seclusion. Otherwise, it would be like a man involved in two tasks because of sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma). Just as in the world, something non-existent is called "a fruit-bearing tree" by way of a non-existent designation, so too in the Sasana, something existent is called "jhāna with initial and sustained thought" by way of an existent designation.

In the word "vūpasamā" (through the subsiding), through the subsiding of which states? Is it through the subsiding of initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) belonging to the first jhāna, or those belonging to the second jhāna? In this question, if it is said to be the subsiding of those in the first jhāna, their subsiding is not possible. For there is no first jhāna devoid of initial and sustained thought. If it is said to be the subsiding of those in the second jhāna, there is no subsiding because they do not exist there. Because of such possible questions, the word "samatikkamā" (through transcending) is said. If it is said that transcending is not only of those initial and sustained thoughts, but indeed of the entire group of states of the first jhāna, then because of such a question, it is said "through transcending the gross states," and so on. If it is said that all states of the first jhāna are grosser than the second jhāna, and not only the pair of initial and sustained thought, that is not so. Because of the gross nature of the states associated with initial and sustained thought, only initial and sustained thought are gross. By seeing the disadvantage in those initial and sustained thoughts alone, their absence occurs at the moment of the second jhāna. Therefore, it is said "because of their non-appearance at the moment of the second jhāna." To show the state by whose power or association this jhāna is called "inner tranquility" (sampasādana) and "unification of mind" (ekodibhāva), faith and concentration are mentioned in the Vibhaṅga. When it is said "like ghee etc." in the Paṇီtabhojana training rule, this explanation of the meaning is not contradictory.

"He looks on with equanimity" means that, having abandoned sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca), for an Arahant, when the six desirable and undesirable sense objects appear at the six doors, the equanimity that is the mode of not abandoning the pure natural state is called "six-factored equanimity" (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). The equanimity that is the middle state in well-established grasping by reflecting on the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) etc., is called "equanimity towards formations" (saṅkhārupekkhā). The equanimity that is the middle state in investigation is called "insight equanimity" (vipassanūpekkhā). Among those types of equanimity: six-factored equanimity, equanimity of the divine abodes (brahmavihārupekkhā), equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgupekkhā), specific neutrality (tatramajjhattupekkhā), jhāna equanimity...
47:
Pārisuddhi-upekkhā is also essentially just tatramajjhattupekkhā; the distinction between these equanimities is only due to the difference in states (occasions). Although saṅkhārupekkhā and vipassanūpekkhā are one by way of wisdom, they should be understood as twofold by way of function.

Chaḷaṅgupekkhā occurs in the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), while brahmavihārūpekkhā occurs in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara); thus it should be understood by way of sphere. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā occurs only for the Arahant (khīṇāsava), while brahmavihārūpekkhā occurs for the three types of persons: worldlings (puthujjana), trainees (sekha), and non-trainees (asekha); thus it should be understood by way of person. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā is associated with minds accompanied by joy (somanassa) and equanimity (upekkhā), while brahmavihārūpekkhā is associated only with minds accompanied by equanimity; thus it should be understood by way of consciousness. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā has six objects, while brahmavihārūpekkhā has the object of dhammas (beings); thus it should be understood by way of object. Vedanūpekkhā is included in the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha), while the remaining nine equanimities are included in the formations aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha); thus it should be understood by way of aggregate classification. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā, brahmavihārūpekkhā, bojjhaṅgupekkhā, jhānūpekkhā, pārisuddhi-upekkhā, and tatramajjhattupekkhā are essentially one; therefore, at a single moment, only one can occur, not the others. Similarly, saṅkhārupekkhā and vipassanūpekkhā are also one. The occurrence of vedanūpekkhā and vīriyūpekkhā at a single moment is possible. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā is an indeterminate (abyākata) state; brahmavihārūpekkhā is a wholesome (kusala) or indeterminate state; the remaining equanimities are likewise. However, vedanūpekkhā can also be unwholesome (akusala). Thus it should be understood by way of the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-ttika). These ten equanimities are, in brief, only four states: energy (vīriya), feeling (vedanā), neutrality (tatramajjhattatā), and wisdom (paññā/ñāṇa).

If it is asked, 'Why is it stated in the manner mentioned in the Vibhaṅga, rather than in the order of abandoning as "pain, grief, pleasure, and joy"?' It is stated for the purpose of preserving the Sutta teaching. Regarding the phrase 'iṭṭhāniṭṭha-viparīta' (perversion of the desirable and undesirable), it is said that it should be understood as experiencing by way of the perverted mode of the desirable and undesirable, without taking it by way of the object. Why? Because all jhānas occur by taking a single kasina as an object. Since it comes as being helpful starting from the third jhāna, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the foremost. Even when there is the gloom of clouds etc. in a clear night due to the absence of clouds etc., the night is not unhelpful as in the day; therefore, it is said, 'also because of being helpful to oneself.' It is said that 'these two reasons—oppression by sunlight and not obtaining the companion of the night—are the causes of impurity. These two reasons—having a clear nature and being helpful to oneself—are the causes of similarity (sabhāgatā).' This means the cause of that impure birth; therefore, some teachers say it is a statement of cause.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Jhāna is finished.
48:
## Explanation of the Talk on Recollection of Past Lives

Because jhānas share the nature of one-pointedness of mind (cittēkaggatā), it is said, 'Some jhānas have one-pointedness of mind as their benefit.' Because wholesome states share the nature of entering into existence (bhavokkamana), it is said, 'Some jhānas have entering into existence as their benefit.' Because they do not share the same nature, in other cases, instead of saying 'pādakatthāni' (benefits of the basis), it says 'pādakāni' (bases). By saying so, it shows how even the jhānas that serve as a basis bring about one-pointedness of mind and entering into existence as far as possible, and how the remaining jhānas bring about the nature of being a basis as far as possible. Because they do not share the same nature, it also shows that the basis for impulsions (javana) and the basis for insight (vipassanā) can be the same as the basis for higher powers (abhiññā), and the basis for higher powers can also be the basis for insight. Likewise, it shows the state of being a basis. For higher power, only the fourth jhāna is the basis, not the others. Among those jhānas, it should be understood that the basis for the fourth is the third, the basis for the third is the second, and the basis for the second is the first. Alternatively, the phrase 'four jhānas' is stated according to what is attained.

Because the Buddha's residence in the city of Verañjā was the origin of the Vinaya Nidāna, the Blessed One taught the three knowledges (vijjā) in Verañjā.

It is stated (in the First Great Council Talk): 'A monk well-practiced in the Vinaya, relying on the perfection of virtue (sīla)...' and so on. For one possessed of virtue, sitting in places for the night and day to reflect on his virtue, starting from the sitting, because of the abundance of recollecting his past activities, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussativijjā) is accomplished without difficulty. Similarly, because of the habit of perceiving the passing away of beings based on oneself, the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (cutūpapātañāṇa) is accomplished without difficulty. Because of the habit of seeing subtle things in water etc., the divine-eye knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) is accomplished. Because the holy life (brahmacariya) reaches the state of being unbroken etc. by avoiding the seven types of sexual bonds or by avoiding the taints of sensual desire etc., the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is accomplished without difficulty for him. Thus, only the three knowledges are shown in the Vinaya Nidāna. Therefore, it is said, 'desiring to show a portion of those qualities which he was the giver of.' Otherwise, it would imply the mere attainment of the three knowledges.

With the words 'So evaṃ' (He thus...), although the preliminary practice of the four jhānas is also included, and not only the first triad of jhānas, the commentator, taking only the first triad of jhānas, says: 'Evaṃ indicates the method of ascending to the fourth jhāna; it means after having obtained the fourth jhāna in the order starting with the attainment of the first jhāna.' That...
49:
Why? Because it is the preparatory ground (sambhārabhūmi). For this is said in the Commentary (Visuddhimagga 2, 381): "In this teaching, because the first three jhānas are pervaded by rapture and happiness, one enters into the perception of happiness and the perception of lightness; having a body that is light, soft, and wieldy, one attains psychic power (iddhi). Therefore, because they lead to the attainment of psychic power in this manner, they should be known as preparatory grounds (sambhārabhūmi). The fourth jhāna, however, is the natural ground (pakatibhūmi) for the attainment of psychic power." Or, referring to this very meaning, it is said: "Previously, these four jhānas were the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññāpādaka) for some."

If so, why is it not said "thus" by including the fourth jhāna as well? If one asks whether it is because that fourth jhāna is the natural ground? It should not be said so, because of the existence of the mind that has reached the state of being concentrated (samāhita), etc., after the fourth jhāna. When it is said, "Previously, he directed his mind toward the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa)," therefore, when that fourth jhāna mind has become the basis for higher knowledge, reaching the state of the natural ground, it says of the preparatory mind (parikammasitta), "he directed it toward the knowledge of recollection of past lives." In the phrase "it becomes fit for directing" (abhinīhārakkhamam), he directs the preparatory mind for the purpose of attaining the various psychic powers (iddhividha). He removes it from the kasina object and sends it toward the various psychic powers. In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, because it is said "for the purpose of drawing out the various psychic powers, etc., from the jhāna which is the basis for higher knowledge," the meaning of "fit for directing" is conceived.

The construction "when he is thus concentrated, thus reached imperturbability (āneñja)" should be understood in the second alternative, because it encompasses the functions of the first jhāna, etc., by being far from the hindrances and by transcending initial thought (vitakka), etc. This construction is not possible in the first alternative, because the word "thus" (evaṃ) is prevented from following by the statement "but in the words such as pure (parisuddha), etc." For that very reason, it says "pure by way of the purity of mindfulness through equanimity," etc.

"Moving in the sphere of desire" (icchāvacara) means "Anangaṇa" (without blemish) because of the absence of anger (kopa) and lack of faith (apaccayā) which arise by the power of desire produced in the manner of "O, would that I had committed an offense and the monks did not know about me," etc. And here, even the desire of the kind mentioned is an obstacle to the attainment of the first jhāna, etc., because it is said "deliberate lying, friends, is an obstructive state"; how much more so the anger and lack of faith moving in the sphere of desire. Therefore, it is said "of the evil ones moving in the sphere of desire who are opponents to the attainment of jhāna," etc. In some books, however, there is the reading "of those moving in the sphere of desire who are the cause (paccaya) for the attainment of jhāna"; that reading is merely a scribal error (pamādalekha). In the Gaṇṭhipada also, "O, would that the Teacher would question only me and teach the Dhamma..."
50:
"...teach [the Dhamma]"—that meaning which is written there is poorly written (an error). For in the Anangaṇa Sutta, anger, etc., are not taught as causes for the attainment of jhāna. The Teacher says that it is not even logically possible because those who have attained jhāna lack such [anger, etc.]; that statement should be investigated. Here, it should be understood that the eight factors are shown repeatedly with "when the mind is thus concentrated," etc., to show the progressive excellence of the three knowledges (tevijjā). And the progressive excellence should be understood by showing the vision of one's own suffering, the suffering of others, and the cessation of those two.
