The Blessed One, having seen his own infinite suffering in Saṃsāra through the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), and having seen the suffering of the world of others through the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa), and having seen the cessation of both through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa), he teaches that Dhamma. Or else, by the first knowledge, because of seeing one's own suffering, he shows the abandonment of self-love. By the second knowledge, because of seeing the suffering of others, he shows the abandonment of anger toward others; and by the third knowledge, because of seeing the Noble Path, he shows the abandonment of delusion. Thus, because of showing various special qualities, it should be understood that these two mundane higher knowledges are taken here.

If it is said that because only a past birth is a "dwelling" (nivāsa), one should not say "in past births"—no, because the usage of the term "dwelling" is seen to be established even in a portion of a birth. Although in the Pali, by the words "one birth, two births," etc., it seems as if the recollection of the entire birth is pubbenivāsānussati, it should not be regarded so. The locative case (bhumma vacana) is used to show that even the recollection of a portion of that birth is indeed pubbenivāsānussati, and for the purpose of including the place (okāsa), etc. In the phrase "in the recollection of those who have cut the round [of rebirth], etc.", by the word "ādi" (etc.), it should be understood as taking the world-systems, islands, countries, cities, and villages where one has not lived before.

In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "The supramundane virtue (lokuttara-sīla), etc., of those Arahants who have cut the round were not known by the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta." By implication, it follows that mundane things were known; that statement seems to agree with the words "revilers of the Noble Ones" in the section on the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Indeed, such [accusation] is not possible for one who does not see the Noble Ones. If it is asked, "Why is it called anussati (recollection) here? Is this not the section on knowledge (vijjā)?" [The answer is] because it is produced by the power of mindfulness for the beginner, and because mindfulness is especially dominant in regard to past phenomena. For is it not taught, "I recollect"?

Regarding present things, there is knowledge (vijjā);
Regarding past things, one recollects (sarati);
Regarding future phenomena, there is the distinction of recollection and knowledge (aspiration/resolve) (paṇidhi).

Teacher Kumārita also spoke this verse.
51:
At that time [of world destruction], if lust is excessive, there is destruction by fire (tejosaṃvaṭṭa). If hatred is excessive, there is destruction by water (āposaṃvaṭṭa). If delusion is excessive, there is destruction by wind (vāyosaṃvaṭṭa). Some teachers say: "If hatred is excessive, there is destruction by fire; if lust is excessive, there is destruction by water; if delusion is excessive, there is destruction by wind." Because the mind or speech occurs with the determination of existence, etc., as "in that [life]" (amutra), therefore He said "or in existence" (bhave vā), and so on. By the two words "of such a name, of such a clan" (evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto), He shows the range of residence (gocaranivāsa) known as designation, which has internal and external as its basis. "One who eats fallen fruit" (pavattaphalabhojana) means one whose food consists of fruits that have fallen by themselves. The statement "having a lifespan of eighty-four thousand aeons" refers to the time before the aspiration for Buddhahood. Reflection while regressing is not the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). It is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada that "this is a demonstration of the power of those who have attained the knowledge of recollection of past lives." In this first connection regarding "amutra", recollection is stated according to the lion's stride (sīhokkanta), and that is indeed in the forward order (anuloma). Some also write "in the reverse order" (paṭiloma), but that is difficult to understand. To show the lion's stride, He said "in many crores of aeons," and so on. By the illustration "as that" (yathā taṃ), He shows the commonality of the fruit through the commonality of practice, thereby generating respect in the Brahmin and preventing the statement that "He only exalts Himself." He encourages the Brahmin only with the thoughts that previously arose in him, saying, "Indeed, the sight of such Arahants is excellent." By the words "the first breaking out" (paṭhamā abhinibbhidā), He shows the state of having many layers in the shell of ignorance (avijjāṇḍakosa); by showing that, He shows the state of being unbreakable by the eightfold power, etc.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Recollection of Past Lives is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Talk on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

The phrase "for the sake of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth" (cutūpapātañāṇāya) is spoken by way of metonymy of the fruit (phalūpacāra). Indeed, this knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa), because it has visible form as its object, takes as its object the limited (paritta), the present, and the internal and external. It does not take passing away (cuti) or rebirth (paṭisandhi) as its object. Therefore, it should be understood that this statement is spoken only by way of metonymy of the fruit, like the statement "I know beings passing away according to their kamma." It is called "divine" (dibba) by way of metonymy of the cause (kāraṇūpacāra) because it is based on the divine abiding (dibbavihāra). By this, the views of some teachers who say, "The eyes that are wholesome and unwholesome are the divine eye, and they belong to the sense sphere," are refuted. For here, the wisdom of the fourth absorption (jhāna) is intended. Regarding the terms "being of great splendor" (mahājutika) and "being of great destiny" (mahāgatika), it is said "according to the science of grammar." Of the eleven...
52:
The sequence of the arising of the defilements (upakkilesa) and their nature as defilements should be understood thus: When the Bodhisatta, having increased the light, saw various forms with the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), doubt (vicikicchā) arose: "What indeed is this?" This is a defilement. Because it is said in the Upakkilesa Sutta: "My concentration fell away due to doubt; when concentration fell away, the light disappeared and the vision of forms [disappeared]."

Then, thinking, "Doubt has arisen in me while looking at forms; now I will not attend to anything," inattention (amanasikāra) arose. Then, while remaining without attending to anything, sloth and torpor (thinamiddha) arose. Then, to abandon that sloth and torpor, he increased the light and looked at forms; when he saw Dānavarakkhasa (ogres) and others in places like the Himālaya, fear (chambhitatta) arose. Then, to abandon that fear, he thought, "When I look at the danger I have seen as it is, it does not exist; what indeed is there to fear in what is not seen?" When he thought thus, elation (uppilāvitatta) arose.

In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "Elation arose due to seeing divine forms." That is poorly stated, because that meaning is established by the later word "longing" (abhijappā), so says the Teacher [Ānanda]. Then, to abandon fear, he thought, "I have exerted energy too strongly; therefore, this elation has arisen in me." When he relaxed his energy, bodily grossness, bodily distress, and bodily laziness arose. Then, when he gave up that laziness, excessive energy (accāraddhavīriya) arose. Seeing the fault in that excessive energy, sluggish energy (atilīnavīriya) arose.

Then, having abandoned that sluggish energy and with energy balanced with concentration, he abandoned places like the Himālaya due to the danger of fear, and increased the light towards the celestial realms. When he looked at the host of devas, longing (abhijappā), which is called craving (taṇhā), arose. Then he thought, "Longing has arisen in me while attending to a form of a single kind; therefore, now I will attend to various forms." Thus, sometimes towards the celestial realms and sometimes towards the human realm, he increased the light and attended to various forms; then the perception of diversity (nānattasaññā) arose.

Then he thought, "The perception of diversity has arisen in me while attending to various forms; therefore, now, due to the danger of longing and so on, I will give up grasping the signs of pleasant objects and attend only to a form of a single kind." When he did so, excessive gazing at forms (abhinijjhāyitatta) arose. Even though he abandoned the defilements in this way, because there was no determination (anadhiṭṭhitatta), it happened that "I know the light, but I do not see forms," and so on.

The meaning of that is: When I attend only to the light of the preliminary work (parikamma), then I perceive the light, but I do not see forms with the divine eye. But at the time of seeing forms...
53:
It means one does not even know the light and radiance. For what purpose is this word 'visuddhaṃ' (purified) spoken? Is it not that this (the Buddha's Knowledge of the Divine Eye) does not reach the state of defilement? In this Knowledge of the Divine Eye, it is not only the abandoning of defilements (upakkilesa) that should be done; it is intended to show that there is another further task to be performed by which this (vision) becomes purified.

In passages such as 'Doubt is a defilement of the mind,' some say, 'I abandoned these states by seeing their danger as defiling states, because at that time (craving) did not arise in me.' By this word 'mānusakaṃ vā' (or human), it shows the transcending of the nature of ordinary humans. By this phrase 'as if with the fleshly eye,' it compares the acquisition of learning (pariyatti) and the state of having only color as an object. In this phrase (satte passāmi), the word 'satta' (being) refers only to color. It is not like in the Pali 'sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā' (all beings are sustained by nutriment), where it refers to all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata). Having a low caste and so forth are the consequences and results (vipāka) of delusion (moha). It should be understood in connection with the rest of the Pali text that those endowed with bodily misconduct existed in the past life and have now reached hell.

'The Knowledge of Passing Away and Reappearance according to Kamma (Yathākammūpagata-ñāṇa) certainly has a past object, while the Divine Eye has a present object'—this is spoken by way of the functions of the two knowledges. In the word 'mahallaka' (elderly), it should be understood as a reproach by destroying virtues, spoken with the intention that one does not know what is suitable or unsuitable for monks, or worldly etiquette. If a Noble Person (ariya-puggala), who is described as 'one who is certain and destined for enlightenment,' were to speak harsh words capable of obstructing the Path, he might also perform an unwholesome deed leading to the lower realms; if he did so, he would be one who goes to the lower realms; therefore, it should be reflected upon—so say some. Others say, 'Because the Elder said, "Do not make an effort," he causes an obstruction to the Path.'

Since the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) has already closed the door to the lower realms even before the offense, there is no 'obstruction to heaven' (saggāvaraṇa) for him. 'Pākatika' (natural) means that it became a resultant process (pavatti-vipāka), so they say. Some say it became natural because of the words: 'Bhikkhus, this is growth in the discipline of the Noble Ones, when one sees an offense as an offense and makes amends according to the Dhamma.' The phrase 'If he does not endure' is spoken either because of the weakness of the quality of patience (khanti) in Stream-enterers and others, or with reference to non-endurance for the sake of his better restraint in the future. Kālakañjika Asuras exist because of the absence of objects that are causes of happiness. Because of the words 'Go from here to a happy destination,' the human destination (manussa-gati) is also included. 'Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa-vijjā' means 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of seeing the Divine Eye itself, and 'wisdom' (vijjā) in the sense of knowing various meanings.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye is finished.
54:
## Explanation of the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints

In this Pali text 'so evaṃ samāhite citte' (with the mind thus concentrated), is the mind concentrated only in the previous jhāna, or is it concentrated in another fourth jhāna mind? In the Commentary also, it is said, 'In this context, the fourth jhāna mind which is the basis for insight (vipassanā-pādaka) should be understood,' in order to show that the very jhāna from which one emerged and attained the two previous types of higher knowledge is performed anew and repeatedly by way of re-attainment.

Here, an objector asks: If that very jhāna is made new by way of re-attainment, then why is it not said as before, 'In this context, the fourth jhāna mind which is the basis for insight, the basis for higher knowledge, the basis for the attainment of cessation, the achiever of all tasks, and the giver of all mundane and supramundane virtues should be understood,' but instead only 'In this context, the fourth jhāna mind which is the basis for insight should be understood' is said? Is it not that in this stage of the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints, the fourth jhāna of such a nature is the appropriate thing to be mentioned, because it achieves all virtues together with the Path of Arahantship, and not just the achievement of the two previous types of higher knowledge?

It is replied: It should be understood that the term 'vipassanā-pādaka' (basis for insight) is used here to show that the determination of the Enlightenment Factors, Path Factors, Jhāna Factors, Practice, and Liberations of the Noble Path occurs by the determination of the preceding 'insight leading to emergence' (vuṭṭhāna-gāminī-vipassanā), known as the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa). This Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship arises because it is included in the destruction of those taints (āsava), and not merely by taking that fourth jhāna as an object. 'Pariyāyato' (indirectly) means by another way (by way of being a taint other than the truth of the origin of suffering).

For what purpose is this section beginning with 'Ime āsavā' (These are the taints) undertaken? It is for the purpose of making it conform to the heading 'Knowledge for the destruction of taints.' This is spoken by way of the method of unity (ekatta-naya): that the mind is being liberated at the moment of the Path, and is liberated at the moment of the Fruit. That which is being liberated is the very thing that is called liberated in the subsequent stage. And that which is liberated is the very thing that is called 'being liberated' in the preceding stage. Just as one who is eating is called 'one who has eaten' at the conclusion of the meal.

In the context of 'By this, he shows the Reviewing Knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa),' the sequence of occurrence (uppatti-kkama) is stated in the Paṭṭhāna Pali: 'Having emerged from the Path, he reviews the Path, reviews the Fruit, reviews Nibbāna, and reviews the defilements that have been abandoned.' However, in this context of Reviewing Knowledge, the sequence of process (pavatti-kkama) is stated in two ways: by way of specific form (sarūpa) and by way of meaning (attha). Among them, 'The knowledge arose: It is liberated' is the illustration of the sequence of process for the fourfold Reviewing Knowledge by way of specific form. 'Birth is destroyed' and so forth is the illustration by way of meaning. Therefore, at the end, he gave the teaching in terms of a person (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna) saying 'abbhaññāsiṃ' (I directly knew), because Reviewing Knowledge does not occur in that (other) way. One who knows 'I will not undergo rebirth again' is said to know 'Birth is destroyed.' 'By the Divine Eye, the knowledge of the present and the future' is said because the Knowledge of the Future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) is dependent on the Divine Eye.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints is finished.
55:
## Explanation of the Declaration of Lay Discipleship

"Pleasant to the ear and touching to the heart" is said only with reference to the words. "Absence of self-exaltation" etc. is said by way of the person. "Pleasant to the ear" refers to the ear-faculty (sotindriya). "Delightful in the object" means delightful in the object of knowledge (ñāṇa). Whether it is naturally facing downwards or not, the Path is without sorrow, because sorrow is abandoned at that time. It is not contradictory because it conforms to conduct and so forth. Because it is said, "This word is sweet," the phrase "this Dhamma" seems redundant. Therefore, one should connect them separately as "this Dhamma of the fading of passion," and then combine them as "approach this Dhamma." It shows that they recite, "He approaches the Dhamma alone for the sake of refuge."

The Triple Gem is called "Refuge" (saraṇa) because it destroys fear, dread, bad destinations, anxiety, and suffering for those who have gone for refuge through that very act of going for refuge. The arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that has defilements destroyed through faith, respect, etc., and which proceeds in the manner of relying on those [gems], is called "Going for Refuge" (saraṇagamana). The being endowed with that refuge-going "goes to the refuge." In terms of classification, going for refuge is of two kinds: supramundane (lokuttara) and mundane (lokiya).

Among them, supramundane going for refuge is accomplished in all three gems by way of function, taking Nibbāna as the object, through the absolute cutting off of the defilements of going for refuge at the moment of the Path for the Noble Ones (ariyas) who have seen the Truths. Mundane going for refuge is accomplished by taking the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as the object, through the temporary suppression of the defilements of going for refuge for worldlings (puthujjanas). In essence, it is the acquisition of faith in the Triple Gem and Right View rooted in faith.

The benefit of supramundane going for refuge is the four fruits of recluseship as the resultant fruit, and the end of all suffering as the blessing fruit. For has it not been said: "He who [goes for refuge] to the Buddha, the Dhamma... is released from all suffering"? The benefit of mundane going for refuge is the attainment of success in existence and wealth. For has it not been said: "Whoever have gone to the Buddha for refuge..."?

Mundane going for refuge can be defiled by ignorance, doubt, and wrong knowledge regarding the three objects; it is not of great majesty or great influence. There is no defilement in supramundane going for refuge. In mundane going for refuge, there are two kinds of breach: blameworthy and blameless. Among them, the blameworthy breach occurs through dedicating oneself to other teachers and so forth; such a breach yields undesirable results. The breach through death is blameless; it has no result because there is no [kammic] result to be given. There is no breach at all in supramundane going for refuge. Even in another life, a Noble Disciple does not point to another teacher. Any householder who has gone for refuge is called a lay disciple (upāsaka). He is called an upāsaka because he attends to (upāsana) the Triple Gem. The five
56:
abstinences are Virtue (sīla). Right Livelihood (ājīva) is living righteously, being free from trading in weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants, and poisons. Failure in the aforementioned virtue and livelihood is called "failure" (vipatti). The opposite of such failure is "attainment" (sampatti).

The words "Will we get it?" are spoken with reference to poor people. The words "Will we be able?" are spoken with reference to wealthy people. It happened there in Verañjā. "Paggayhati" means holding the bowl; the meaning is "with the bowl thus held." The word "samādāya" (having taken up) is an illustration (nidassana). "Not allowable" refers to cooking again. Even if it were allowable, it is said so because it is not well-cooked [and thus discarded]. The commentary statement, "Even if one obtains undercooked rice, it is not allowable to cover it [for recooking]," is the evidence here. By the words "I will prescribe training rules for disciples," the "Virtue afterwards" is said with reference to the Virtue of Purity of Livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla). Elder Upāli also shows that there are many training rules prescribed by the Blessed One based on various incidents.

If it is asked, "If so, does it not disagree with the words 'It is time, Blessed One [to prescribe rules]' in Verañjā?", the answer is no. This is because of the absence of training rules prior to that [in Verañjā]. The Elder, setting aside those already prescribed, spoke with reference to those to be prescribed now which are sufficient for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. The Blessed One also, as in the Bhaddāli Sutta ("Sāriputta, the Teacher does not yet prescribe training rules for disciples"), spoke with reference to rules to be prescribed thereafter, even though some had already been prescribed.

In this very commentary, there are statements such as "Cooking for oneself is not suitable for recluses and is not allowable," and "breaking the night or breaking the rains," etc. In another way, the teacher analyzed that this placement of the Pali "Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, question monks in two ways" is contradictory. That analysis is good, because of the existence of training rules prescribed even earlier. However, the analysis of the contradiction in the Pali placement here seems to me to be useless. Why? Because it is the Pali text recited by Elder Upāli at the time of the Council (saṅgīti).

"Ratticcheda" (breaking the night) is said with reference to the seven-day business (sattāhakicca). It is said in the Mahā-Aṭṭhakathā: "Not even a single monk, having gone on seven-day business, broke the night or the rains." Therefore, some say that if there is a reason for breaking the rains, it is allowable to perform the seven-day business. However, the Vinaya experts do not accept this. Therefore, the intention of the commentary should be investigated. In this Verañjā, they were inspired by the practice of fewness of wishes and so forth. A variety of fine rice is called "sālivikati."

17-8. "Upappannaphala" means having much fruit. There is also the reading "khuddaṃ madhuṃ" (small honey). By asking the Elder to roar the lion's roar, the teacher [refers to] what was previously in the command...
57:
The demonstration of the great majesty of the disciples who are present is what we meant by "the benefit of residing in Verañjā"; it fulfills that statement. Wishing to show the arising of thought in both places—Rājagaha and Verañjā—together in one place, he said: "Then to the Venerable Sāriputta..." and so on. The grammatical analysis (viggraha) is "ciraṃ" with reference to time, and "cirā" with reference to stability.

Indeed, it is called "hetu" (cause) in the active sense (kattu-sādhana) because it leads to the production of its own fruit. However, here it should be called "hetu" because the fruit arises by means of that cause. Similarly, it is called "ghaṭa" because it occurs in conjunction with that cause. "Kilāsuno" refers to those who are inactive due to a lack of purpose. "Abbokiṇṇāni" means not mixing with incompatible monks. "Āgāminiyā" means that which will occur in the future. To show that it is not only for these Buddhas, it is said "for all the Buddhas". "Until the end of the Sasana" means as long as the Buddhas are alive. Only the Khattiyas and Brahmins are noble; to show the distinction among them, it is said "high, low, and of great wealth". There is also a variant reading "manasi katvā". These two words "upasampādya upasampādya" are called "upasampajja" in the Māgadha language. "Anupādāya" means without clinging by way of taking as an object. In the word "āsavehi", the third case (instrumental) is in the sense of the agent (kattā). "Cittāni" is the nominative plural. "Vimucciṃsu" is in the passive voice (kamma-kāraka). The teacher says it means "they were liberated". In the Gaṇṭhipada, the meaning of "āsavehi" is explained as an instrumental case used in the sense of the nominative.

If being "anāsava" (free from cankers) is due to the cankers being ceased by the Noble Path, then the minds in the world would also be "anāsava". If it is argued that because ceased minds cannot take objects, those minds are "sāsava" (with cankers) due to unceased cankers—would the path-mind of a Stream-enterer be "sāsava" due to the cankers to be abandoned by higher paths? Or would the fruit-minds be "sāsava" because they have the power to eradicate the remaining cankers? No, because the fruit comes from the path which has the power to eradicate the cankers. Doing something terrifying is called "bhiṃsanakata"; in that "bhiṃsanakata", it means "because of doing something terrifying". It is used by changing the feminine gender to neuter or masculine. Regarding the sense of cause (nimittattha), here:
"They kill the leopard for its skin, the elephant for its tusks, the yak for its hair, and the sarabha is killed for its horns"—this is the locative case (adhikaraṇa).
58:
20-21. When the cause for not lasting long was stated, although the cause for lasting long was established by implication as the opposite of the stated cause, the Elder Sāriputta, with the intention of creating an opportunity to request the prescription of the Vinaya, asked the Blessed One again: "Venerable Sir, what is the cause?" to bring it to the point where he could request the Vinaya prescription. The Blessed One, wishing to accept the request, explained. In saying "things that are bases for cankers appear in the Sangha", it is said so because an individual is included within the Sangha. Here, it is said twice out of respect. This is because the Elder had requested twice—first in Rājagaha and now in Verañjā. Seeing him requesting repeatedly with respect, the Blessed One himself said with respect: "Wait, Sāriputta."

By saying this, He shows: "Do not request repeatedly; your request has already been accepted by Me. Because I accepted your request previously, I have prescribed this many training rules during this much time. The time has not yet arrived to authorize the recitation of the Āṇāpātimokkha for My disciples. Although you are repeatedly pointing out through inference that 'Blessed One, this is the time,' it is not yet that time. Indeed, only the Tathāgata will know the proper time for that." Since it is said that "from the time of prescribing the training rules, only the Āṇāpātimokkha is to be recited," He spoke referring only to the training rules sufficient for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. The use of the locative case (bhūmmavacana) "in that" (tattha) referring to the request for prescribing training rules is because when one thing is accomplished, the other is also accomplished. "Being the domain (visaya) of the disciples"—this statement in the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, which rejects the view of the Elder Mahāpaduma, is very good. Reproaching in one's presence is "garahā". Blaming behind one's back is "upavāda".

"Bhikkhus, a monk with less than ten years... commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)." The Blessed One prescribed this training rule when He had been a Buddha for ten years. This is because there was no such prescription for a monk with less than ten years at that time. At that time, there were no monks with more than ten years, and only those with ten years had reached the greatness of seniority (rattaññu-mahatta). Therefore, it is established that this training rule was prescribed in Rājagaha before the rains-retreat in Verañjā. Since this is established, it is also clear that the statement "as long as the Sangha has not reached the greatness of seniority" was spoken during the first request before this Verañjā period. In the Commentary (Atthakathā), the mention of the number "two training rules" at the time of reaching the greatness of seniority refers to what was said during the first request. Otherwise, it would imply that there were only two and no others when the greatness of seniority was reached.
59:
It was also mentioned in the first request in the ancient city of Rājagaha. Therefore, this point is indeed concluded. In the Commentary, when the Sangha had become senior and mature, the word "sikkhāpadāni," which defines the number of rules, was spoken with reference to the words used in the first request. If the meaning is taken in another way, it would imply that when the Sangha was senior and mature, there were only two training rules and no others.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Atha kho āyasmato Sāriputtassa," the following explanation is intended to clarify the meaning from this point onward. It is said that this Venerable Sāriputta, having analyzed and reflected upon the Dhamma teaching consisting of only a single verse received from Elder Assaji through hundreds of thousands of methods, attained Arahatship and became established in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). He thought, "How wonderful and great is the power of this True Dhamma! Even without the presence of the Lord of Dhamma, and merely by hearing it in His absence, it has produced such great and special qualities in me. May this True Dhamma endure for a long time; how good it would be if it remained so!" He then penetrated with his knowledge as a Chief Disciple the meaning and the reasons behind the question, "The teaching of which Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, does not endure for a long time?" Having concluded that "the prescription of training rules for the disciples is the cause for the long endurance of the Sasana," he questioned the Blessed One to create an opportunity to request the prescription of the Vinaya.

Subsequently, when the opportunity to request the Vinaya prescription arose during the answering of the question, he requested: "Blessed One, now is the time; Sugata, now is the time for the prescription of the Vinaya." Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show His acceptance of that request, while also indicating that the time mentioned by Venerable Sāriputta was not yet the right time and that knowing the proper time for prescribing the Vinaya is the exclusive domain of the Buddhas, said: "Wait, Sāriputta," and so forth. Thereafter, based on Venerable Sāriputta's request and His own compassion for all beings, and following the method starting with "At that time, the monks were without preceptors, without teachers, and without being exhorted..." (Mahāvagga, 64), the Teacher prescribed the Vinaya duties such as the duties toward the preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta) and the training rules appropriate to those circumstances, as the Sasana grew in abundance and greatness.

Following that, in due course, He stayed in the city of Verañjā during the twelfth rainy season. At that time, when the causes for the long endurance of the Sasana as pointed out by the Teacher had arisen, Venerable Sāriputta thought: "Now the nine-fold Sasana of the Teacher has become vast and great, and the Vinaya prescriptions have become numerous. Only the recitation of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhuddesa) has not yet been authorized for the disciples. That Pātimokkha recitation should be performed only by a pure Sangha. Now the Sangha is pure, for even the most junior monk is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna)." Wishing to have the Pātimokkha recitation authorized, and placing the request for the prescription of as many training rules as are necessary for the Pātimokkha recitation first, Venerable Sāriputta—intending to make known his previous thought for the long endurance of the Sasana—requested the Pātimokkha recitation through the sequence of questioning and answering. When the opportunity for the request arrived, he said: "Blessed One, now is the time," and so forth.

In that passage, the words "the Blessed One should prescribe training rules for the disciples" were said with reference to the training rules sufficient for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. This meaning is shown by the Bhaddāli Sutta.
60:
This meaning is shown by the Bhaddāli Sutta. In that Bhaddāli Sutta, although many training rules had been prescribed and were being prescribed, it was said, "Bhaddāli, the Teacher has not yet prescribed training rules for the disciples," and so forth, with reference to the training rules that had not yet been prescribed. Similarly, it should be understood here that the statement refers to the training rules not yet prescribed. Wishing to show that He would not yet authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha of Authority (āṇā-pātimokkhuddesa) for the disciples because of the purity of the Sangha, He said, "Nirabbuda" (free from strife), and so forth. Indeed, in a pure Sangha, there is no reason not to recite the Pātimokkha of Exhortation (ovāda-pātimokkhuddesa); the reason for not reciting it is the intention to authorize the Pātimokkha of Authority. Thus, that Pātimokkha was authorized eight years after that time. As it is said in the Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka (Cūḷavagga, 386): "Monks, from this day forward, I will no longer perform the Uposatha... you yourselves shall recite the Pātimokkha."

Regarding the story in the Upasampadakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga, 129) which says, "At that time, the monks, having ordained a certain monk, left him alone and departed... that monk, having engaged in sexual misconduct, returned after a long time," although this event occurred after the story of Sudinna, it was mentioned in that Upasampadakkhandhaka to be placed together according to its relevance. Similarly, in that same section, the factors should be understood through passages such as, "Both Pātimokkhas come to him in detail and are well-transmitted." This is because both Pātimokkhas were not yet completed from the very beginning.

Furthermore, this sequence should be understood from the beginning, namely: when Prince Rāhula was born, the Bodhisatta went forth, practiced austerities for six years, and attained Enlightenment in the seventh year. In that same year of His Enlightenment, He went to Kapilavatthu and ordained Prince Rāhula as a novice. In the Commentary to the Ambalaṭṭhikā-rāhulovāda Sutta, it is said: "This Venerable Rāhula, at the age of seven, held the corner of the Blessed One's robe and requested his inheritance, saying, 'Samaṇa, give me my inheritance; Samaṇa, give me my inheritance.' Therefore, the Blessed One handed him over to the General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāriputta, and had him ordained." Thus, because it was said with reference to Prince Rāhula, "Monks, I authorize the novice ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) by the Three Refuges" (Mahāvagga, 105), it is clear that ordination as a monk by the Refuges was abolished within the first rainy season, and ordination by a formal motion with four proclamations (ñatticatuttha kamma) was authorized. Furthermore, in the story of Rāhula, the training rule was prescribed: "Monks, a son who does not have the permission of his parents should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." Therefore, it is evident that training rules had already been prescribed even before the residence during the rainy season at Verañjā.
61:
That Venerable Sāriputta, having heard the path leading to the fruit which is the cessation of causes (Nibbāna), quickly and penetratingly understood the cause of cessation. Being the Chief Disciple of the Great Buddha and a seer of the arising and passing away of phenomena, that Elder contemplated this world entirely with the knowledge of insight.

Being the Chief Disciple and the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) of the Tathāgata, the King of Dhamma, that Elder attained unparalleled fame in the Dispensation, having been praised by the Lord of Sages himself in sixteen ways repeatedly.

For that reason, even knowing the time when a training rule (sikkhāpada) was prescribed in the world is extremely difficult. What then need be said about knowing the specific distinctions in the nature of the training rules? What then need be said about knowing other distinctions in both of those matters?

Even Paccekabuddhas are unable to know both of those; what then need be said about making others know them? In this matter, only the Tathāgata will know without doubt—thus said Venerable Upāli.

In this Dispensation, a monk, having understood this meaning and realizing that he himself cannot know the sequential order and the distinction in nature of the training rules, nor can he make others know them, should search only for the appropriate path of logic (yuttimagga) in this matter.

In that regard, the distinction in sequence (kama-bheda) of the training rules will become clear later. As for the distinction in nature (bhāva-bheda)—on account of following a monk who has been expelled (ukkhittaka), a monk does not incur an offense (anāpattika), but a bhikkhunī, having been exhorted up to the third time (by formal act), incurs a Pārājika. In the case of concealing a Pārājika offense, a monk incurs a Dukkaṭa offense, while a bhikkhunī incurs a Pārājika offense. For one who speaks of a gross offense (duṭṭhullā) and for one who conceals it, a Pācittiya offense is incurred. For a monk who speaks of a Pārājika offense, which is of great blame, and for a monk who conceals it, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Searching for the logical reason through such distinctions in nature, even in training rules that have no such distinction in nature, would be a part of being free from confusion and weariness.

By this sequence of words, Venerable Upāli has shown the introduction (Nidāna) of the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, adorned with seven factors: Vitakka (thought), Yācanā (request), Kāla (time), Kālaññū (knower of time), Kāraṇa (cause), Phala (result), and Payojana (purpose). Among those factors, the Elder's
62:
The thought which is the cause for requesting the prescription of Vinaya rules is called Vitakka. The request made by that Venerable Sāriputta with the words, "Blessed One, now is the time (to prescribe training rules)," and so forth, is called Yācanā. The time when greatness of seniority (rattannū-mahatta), greatness of abundance (vepulla-mahatta), greatness of gain (lābha-mahatta), and greatness of great learning (bāhusacca-mahatta) have been reached is called Kāla. Only the Buddha, who knows all things, is called Kālaññū (the knower of time). The manifestation of things that are the basis for taints (āsava-ṭṭhānīya) is called Kāraṇa (cause). In accordance with the words, "For the sake of warding off those very things that are the basis for taints," the warding off of those things is called Phala (result). In accordance with the words, "So that this holy life may be long-lasting," the long-term endurance of the holy life of the Dispensation is to be understood as Payojana (purpose). In this regard, it is said in a verse:

"Thought, request, time, the knower of time, cause, result, and purpose—these seven factors are the introduction to the Vinaya here."

'Antima-maṇḍala' means the inner circle (antara-maṇḍala). It is so called either because it is in the midst of other circles or because it is the small circle (khuddaka-maṇḍala). Having given permission to those monks, there are beings to be tamed (veneyya-satta) who are disciplined by the travels of those Buddhas. "As if gathering" means that just as florists gather flowers for a long time from a bush with many flowers, similarly, the Buddhas stay for a long time in villages and so forth where there are many beings to be tamed, carrying out the merit of those beings while wandering. Peaceful happiness (santa-sukha) does not mean a happiness that involves agitation like the happiness of feeling (vedanā-sukha), but refers to the happiness of Nibbāna. "In the ten thousand world-systems" is said with reference to the devas and brahmās. As for humans, those capable of being enlightened arise only in this world-system. He constantly surveys beings with great compassion. "When descending" means when arriving in the midst of the assembly or when being addressed. "For what reason can we give offerings to the Venerable ones? Where can we obtain those offerings? The household life is full of many duties," it is said. According to the second method, "that" (taṃ) refers to the offering. "Where did you obtain that offering?" is stated in the Anu-gaṇṭhi. Some say, "The first interpretation regards the action (kiriyā), the second regards the offering." The Teacher (Venerable Ānanda), however, says, "According to the first method, where can the merit of giving be obtained? The household life is full of obstacles to merit. According to the second method, it shows: 'Since the time has passed for what I should have given within the three months, where can I give it now?'" Thus, he caused the great rain of the Dhamma-gem to fall, showing the wholesome states such as virtue.

In the region of Pattuṇṇa, the Pattuṇṇa cloth is an excellent cloth. 'Mahāyāga' means a great offering. 'Paripuṇṇa-saṅkappa' means, "I have heard today the Dhamma that was to be heard throughout the three months."

'Tatridam' means this cause.
63:
Venerable Upāli, Venerable Dāsaka, and so on, according to the lineage of teachers. Regarding the phrase "by showing the varieties of the nidāna," it refers to the external nidāna, the internal nidāna, and the specific nidāna known as the place of enactment (paññattiṭṭhāna) of the training rules. The Theravāda and others are the varieties of the stories (vatthu). The phrase "by avoiding the views of others" refers to instances such as "By one's own admission, expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya," and so forth. The phrase "by showing the varieties of the Vibhaṅga method" refers to "The three types of women: those dwelling on the ground, those dwelling on land," and so forth.

In this matter, a question may arise: "Does the Blessed One not have the power to prevent the deception of Māra?" He does have the power; however, he endured it because it would be a cause for devotion later during the time of Venerable Upagutta. Here, the resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) of Venerable Upagutta should be mentioned. If asked, "What is the benefit of the Buddhas making the Brahmin see?" the benefit is to make known the danger to the Brahmin's merit caused by Māra's deception.

That Brahmin, too, while ruining the desire of Māra,
gave various kinds of allowable goods (kappiya-bhaṇḍa)
without remainder as an offering to the Excellent Conqueror
and the community of disciples.

A question may arise: "Did the Blessed One, together with his disciples, depart carrying such a large amount of allowable goods as bundles?" He did not. However, the Teacher did not reject the mass of merit, the gifts collected over three months, but gave them back to the Brahmin through skillful means (upāya).

Otherwise, only Māra's desire would be fulfilled,
and the Brahmin's desire would not be fulfilled;
moreover, that Brahmin would reach a great demerit
through false pride toward the Tathāgata.

Therefore, it is said that the Blessed One, without taking delight in those gifts and yet without rejecting them, increased the Brahmin's merit through skillful means, and having thwarted Māra's desire, he departed. It is said, "This method is established in accordance with the Pāḷi method even without the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā)." How?

If the Teacher, together with his disciples,
had accepted the robes of that Brahmin from the beginning,
during the twentieth year of our Protector's monkhood,
even Jīvaka's request would be contradicted.
Nevertheless, having well-considered everything,
it is proper to think only of the appropriate method.
64:
Now, the Venerable Elder Upāli, having shown the general origin (sādhāraṇa-nidāna) of the Vinaya regulations, begins with the origin known as the place of enactment for each training rule. To clearly demonstrate the various procedures such as the designation of individuals (puggalapaññatti), supplementary regulations (anupaññatti), the analysis of offenses, and the different types of offenses without confusion, he spoke the words beginning with: "Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Verañjā as long as he liked..." Standing at this point:

One should show the sequence of all training rules. Only when that sequence is established can the sequence of the origins (nidāna) be established.

In that sequence, four types of order are found according to the possibility for all training rules: the order of teaching (desanākkama), the order of abandoning (pahānakkama), the order of practice (paṭipattikkama), and the order of arising (uppattikkama). Among these four, following the order of teaching regarding the recitation of the Pātimokkha that the Blessed One allowed for the monks in Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahākassapa first asked about the Pārājika section. After that, he asked about the Saṅghādisesa section, then the Aniyata section and the detailed (vitthāra) section, and then he asked about the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga in that same order. To ask about the training rules that are included in the introduction (nidānuddesa) but not yet explicitly shown, he also asked about the Khandhakas. In this way, the thullaccaya offenses enacted in the Khandhakas are also included. Following the order of the questions, the Venerable Elder Upāli, while teaching all those various offenses, taught by including the training rules that show the origins (samuṭṭhāna) of the thullaccaya and dubbhāsita offenses. This is the order of teaching (desanākkama) here. Selecting from the two Vibhaṅgas and the Khandhakas, the Parivāra Pāḷi was made separate at that time. Referring to this method, it is said in the Commentary: "By this very means, they also presented the Khandhaka and Parivāra," etc. Alternatively, in the Pāḷi text, it is only stated: "By this very means, he asked about both Vinayas. Being asked again and again, the Venerable Upāli answered." Therefore, Mahākassapa asked only about the two Vibhaṅgas. However, when answering, the Venerable Upāli, wishing to teach without leaving anything out, taught by including the Khandhaka and Parivāra. At that time, the Khandhaka and Parivāra Pāḷi were made separate; this is the order of teaching. If it is asked, "Should the nidānuddesa (introduction) not be taught first?" No, because that is not possible. For that nidānuddesa proceeds by the method "If there should be an offense for a monk," etc., and it is not possible if the offenses included in the training rules have not been shown first. According to the words, "Whatever training rules I have enacted for the monks, I allow the recitation of the Pātimokkha of those rules," only the training rules should be taught first, and thus the order of the Pārājika recitation is appropriate.
65:
Since the unwholesome offenses included in the Pārājika recitation and others are to be abandoned according to their grossness, the order of abandonment (pahānakkhama) is possible here. Because of the word, "Immediately after becoming a monk, the four things not to be done (akaraṇīya) should be told," and the word, "Having undertaken them, he trains in the training rules," the order of practice (paṭipattikkhama) is also possible here, in accordance with hearing the heavy offenses. Thus, the order of arising (uppattikkhama) of these training rules taught through these three orders is also possible as far as it can occur.

This is true: when a common training rule arises concerning a monk, it is also prescribed for bhikkhunīs, saying, "Whatever bhikkhunī should indulge in sexual intercourse with consent." If considered otherwise, that training rule would be a rule not yet promulgated (anuppannapaññatti) for bhikkhunīs. If that were so, the statement in the Parivāra, "There is no rule not yet promulgated among those bhikkhunīs," would be contradictory. Since it reached the state of being taught first through these three previously mentioned orders, and because it arose first in the Pārājika recitation, the Elder Upāli, wishing to teach the Pārājika on sexual intercourse first of all, placed it by bringing it to Vesālī, saying, "At that time, the Blessed One was in the city of Vesālī..." Otherwise, if there were an intention to teach training rules such as "Monks, human flesh should not be consumed," which were prescribed in the city of Bārāṇasī, he would have placed it by bringing it to Bārāṇasī.

## The Discussion on the Internal Introduction is finished.
## The Commentary on the Verañja Section is finished.
66:
## 1. Pārājikakaṇḍo
## 1. Paṭhamapārājikaṃ
## Sudinnabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā

Standing at the introduction (nidāna) of the first Pārājika, which is the beginning of this Vinaya Pali, the method of objection (codanānaya) and the method of resolution (parihāranaya) should be understood only in the explanation of the person and the story.

In that regard, after the Blessed One had spent the rains retreat in the city of Verañjā, while traveling in stages, he arrived at the city of Vesālī during the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika. From then until the first Pārājika training rule was prescribed, although it appears in the order of the Pali as if he stayed only in Vesālī for eight years, the Blessed One did not stay only in that Vesālī for such a long time. In fact, after the Blessed One had allowed the going forth and higher ordination for Sudinna's disciples and stayed in that city of Vesālī as long as he pleased, while traveling he reached the Bhesakaḷā forest and spent the thirteenth rains retreat in that forest. Following that order, he reached the city of Sāvatthī and spent the fourteenth rains retreat; the fifteenth in Kapilavatthu; and the sixteenth in Āḷavī. After the rains retreat in Āḷavī, while traveling he reached the city of Rājagaha and spent the seventeenth rains retreat, and in this order, he spent three more rains retreats in that same city of Rājagaha. By this sequence of rains retreats, when the Blessed One had completed twenty years of rains retreats, he arrived at Vesālī in stages from Rājagaha. At that time, Sudinna, who had been a monk for eight years, committed the act of sexual intercourse in Vesālī itself. It should be understood that because of that act of sexual intercourse, the Blessed One prescribed the first Pārājika in that story.

In that regard, because the Elder Upāli did not wish to show the training rules prescribed at an earlier time than this or in that Vesālī, but wished to show only the first Pārājika immediately after the Vinaya introduction, he combined the first residence in Vesālī and the residence at the time of prescribing this training rule later, and said, "At that time, the Blessed One was in Vesālī," and so on. Therefore, it is said, "Standing at the introduction of the first... in the explanation."

Therefore, standing at this introduction, which is called the place of prescribing the first Pārājika, in the explanation of the person of this training rule, "At that time, not far from the city of Vesālī, there was a village named Kalandagāma... he lived depending on a certain Vajji village," and in the explanation of this story, "At that time, there was a famine in the Vajji country... he committed the act of sexual intercourse three times," the method of objection and the method of resolution occur.
67: It means it should be understood. Herein, this is the explanation: If it is asked, "For what purpose did the Elder Upāli, unlike how he briefly stated the personal accounts (puggala-vatthu) of other training rules, state the personal accounts in detail without leaving anything out—where this Sudinna was born, how he gained faith in the Dhamma, how he went forth, and how he caused this incident of engaging in sexual intercourse?" The answer is stated as follows: Even for those who, with such faith and difficulty, having renounced great wealth and relatives, have gone forth and are entirely lovers of virtue (pesala), if this most base of all things, sexual intercourse, should occur, then the cessation (virati) is not accomplished entirely by the preaching of the Dhamma alone. Therefore, even though the Nine-fold Sublime Dhamma has been taught by the Teacher, the Vinaya must be laid down; only then is there the purity of the Dhamma. Due to the absence of Vinaya, such transgression (ajjhācāra) will occur; therefore, the laying down of Vinaya is beneficial even for the lover of virtue. Since one who does not see the danger commits this evil, the Vinaya alone makes the danger clear to those with faith. Therefore, this Vinaya is beneficial to those who follow by faith (saddhānusārī), and the Dhamma is always beneficial to those who follow by Dhamma (dhammānusārī); thus, both teachings were given. Furthermore, it is intended to show the manifestation of the transgression to show that: if even for one who has not yet committed a transgression of the regulation, ill-repute spreads as far as the Brahma world, how much more so for others? How so? — Sudinna is not fit for Arahantship; the mother and father of Bījaka are fit for Arahantship. For that purpose, this regulation for what has not yet arisen (anuppanna-paññatti) was made. Is it not that [the Buddha] taught the Dhamma for the benefit of Māgaṇḍiya's parents, disregarding Māgaṇḍiya? To show this meaning, the Elder Upāli showed the attainment of Arahantship by the mother and father of Bījaka. The statement "At that time, there was a village named Kalandagāma not far from Vesālī, at which time Sudinna engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife" or "At which time the Blessed One laid down the first Pārājika" is not appropriate here. Why? Because the words of the Commentary stating "Here, there is the sense of cause and the sense of action" are not obtained here. Indeed, that Kalandagāma is long-established...
68: The village did not exist only at that time. Indeed, although that Kalandagāma was a long-established village, because it is worthy of being said to exist at all times since the time it was established, for that reason it is said: "At that time, there was a village named Kalandagāma not far from Vesālī." 25-6. "But have you been permitted (by your parents)?" The Blessed One asked this to show the conduct of a recluse (samaṇa-vatta). In the phrase "not permitted by parents," it is said that He asked to show that only the parents had not permitted him. "Sudinna, the Tathāgatas do not (act in this way)..." This was said by way of the request "May the Blessed One let me go forth." The Blessed One did not personally give the refuges and ordain him. In the word "dukkhassa" (of suffering), it should be understood that there is a remaining text "even a part (of it) [he does not know]." "In both alternatives" means in the second and third alternatives. "Of the preceding word" means of the word "kiñci". "By the following word" means by the word "dukkhassa". "The case is the same" means the possessive case (genitive). How so? It should be understood that although it should be said "kassaci dukkhassa", it is stated as "kiñci dukkhassa". "We shall be separated against our will" means "We shall live against our will without dying with you." Even if we do not die, we shall reach separation from you against our will; let our death occur even while you are alive, and even by death, we shall reach separation from you against our will. "Taking strength for a few days"—In this phrase: Why did this Sudinna, who had such a strong desire for going forth, delay for two or three days at home and take physical strength even though he had received permission? It was because he was joyful that his parents and friends had given permission, and it was to satisfy their hearts. In some Commentary manuscripts, some teachers write: "This Sudinna became a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika) by virtue of the rag-robe dhutaṅga after the Jīvaka incident," and "Having rejected the robes offered by householders, he became a rag-robe wearer by virtue of the rag-robe dhutaṅga." This writing contradicts the statement "not long after being ordained (acirūpasampanno)." Likewise, it contradicts the statement: "Sudinna went forth in the 12th year of the Blessed One, and in the 20th year, having been eight years since his going forth, he entered his relatives' house for alms," and the Commentary statement: "From the time the Blessed One attained Buddhahood until this incident, during these 20 years, no one accepted householder robes; all were rag-robe wearers." He was eight years by going forth (pabbajjā), not by full ordination (upasampadā). As for full ordination, [he received it] after the Jīvaka incident...
69:
If it is asked: "He obtained it later; therefore, being one of no seniority (avassika), could it be that he entered his relatives' house for alms?" the answer is: "No." This is because it is stated immediately after: "Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, obtained the going forth (pabbajjā) in the presence of the Blessed One; he obtained the higher ordination (upasampadā)." In truth, immediately after going forth, that Sudinna became a fully ordained monk, and while undertaking and practicing the thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga), he lived in the Vajjī country for eight years. Having become one released from dependence (nissayamuttaka) and capable of living according to his own will, he arrived at Vesālī with the thought: "At present, there is a famine in the Vajjī country," and so forth. Therefore, in those manuscripts where only the text "By virtue of the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes, he is a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika)" is found, that alone should be taken as the standard. By the text "He is a forest-dweller (āraññika)," the five ascetic practices related to lodgings and the practice of the sitter (nesajjika) are included, as they share the same nature of dwelling. By the text "He is an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika)," the five ascetic practices related to alms-food are included. By the text "He is a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika)," the two ascetic practices related to robes are included. It should be understood that the practice of walking for alms from house to house (sapadānacārika) is mentioned separately to explain the reason for approaching the relatives' house. The phrase "Mā atiharāpesuṃ" is spoken by way of a change in tense. Because it causes an obstacle to the Dhamma, although it is called "this way (naya)," it is in fact a wrong way (anaya).

Generally, for beings,
When destruction is imminent,
A wrong way appears in the guise of a right way
To their intellect.

Regarding the phrase "When the training rule was not yet laid down," there are two ways of laying down training rules (sikkhāpada-paññatti). How? There are two types: Sa-uddesa (with recitation) and Anuddesa (without recitation), as in "And thus, monks, you should recite (uddiseyyātha) this training rule." Among them, the five groups of offenses that appear in the Pātimokkha in their own form are called Sa-uddesa-paññatti. That Sa-uddesa-paññatti is again of two types: Sapuggala-niddesa (specifying the person) and Apuggala-niddesa (not specifying the person). A rule in which the person is shown, either with or without the offense, is called Sapuggala-niddesa. The other is known as Apuggala-niddesa. Sapuggala-niddesa is also of two types: showing the offense (dassitāpatti) and not showing the offense (adassitāpatti). Among them, the rules that do not show the offense are the eight Pārājika rules. For it is said, "He becomes one defeated (pārājika), not in communion (asaṃvāsa)"; thus only the person is shown, not the offense. The rules that show the offense are found in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha: "Seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules; the Saṅghādisesa offense should be disclosed"; here the offense is shown along with the person. Similarly, Apuggala-niddesa is of two types: showing the offense and not showing it. Among them, the rules that do not show the offense are the Sekhiya rules; the rest should be understood as showing the offense. That [showing the offense] is also of two types: specifying the doer (niddiṭṭhakāraka) and not specifying the doer (aniddiṭṭhakāraka). Among them, the rules that do not specify the doer are Sukkavissaṭṭhi, Musāvāda...
70:
There are fifteen types [of aniddiṭṭhakāraka rules] by way of the training rules: Omasavāda, Pesuñña, Bhūtagāma, Aññavādaka, Ujjhāpanaka, Gaṇabhojana, Paramparabhojana, Surāmeraya, Aṅgulipatodaka, Hasadhamma, Anādariya, Talaghātaka, and Jatumṭṭhaka. The remaining training rules and those that specify the person should be understood as Niddiṭṭhakāraka (specifying the doer).

Anuddesa-paññatti is also of six types: Padabhājana, Antarāpatti, Vinītavatthu, Paṭikkhepa, Paññatti, and Avuttasiddhi. Among those six, an offense that is evident in the word-by-word commentary (padabhājaniya), such as "For what is mostly eaten, there is a Thullaccaya offense," is called a Padabhājana training rule. Rules such as "One should not come naked; for one who comes [naked], there is a Dukkhaṭa offense" are called Antarāpatti training rules. Rules such as "Monks, I allow a monk who wishes to seclude himself during the day to do so after closing the door" are called Vinītavatthu training rules. Rules such as "Monks, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, if not yet ordained, should not be ordained; if already ordained, should be expelled" are called Paṭikkhepa training rules. The Dukkhaṭa and Thullaccaya offenses laid down in the Khandhakas are called Paññatti training rules. By the statement "Whatever bhikkhunī should go to see dancing, singing, or music, there is a Pācittiya offense," any group of offenses or Vinaya acts evident in the commentaries, such as "Whatever bhikkhunī should dance, sing, or play music, there is a Pācittiya offense," is called an Avuttasiddhi training rule.

These six types of training rules are called Anuddesa training rules because they are not fit to be recited [in the Pātimokkha] for six reasons. Those reasons are: because Thullaccaya and Dubbhāsita offenses are incompatible with the five recitations (uddesa) as far as possible; because the two offenses of Dukkhaṭa and Thullaccaya, even if they share the same object (sabhāgavatthu), are dissimilar offenses (asabhāgāpatti); because Antarāpatti and Paññatti training rules have various objects and offenses; because some Paṭikkhepa and Vinītavatthu-paññatti rules do not show the offense; because the Thullaccaya offense for following a schism does not show the object; and because Avuttasiddhi training rules do not show the offense or the object. By this much, the statement "The laying down of training rules is of two types: Sa-uddesa and Anuddesa" has been explained in brief.

In that context, it should be understood that the phrase "When the training rule was not yet laid down" refers to the Sa-uddesa training rules. Some teachers explain it thus: "Having asked questions such as 'In which year after the Enlightenment did the Blessed One lay down the four Pārājika rules?' among those Pārājikas..."
71:
## The First Pārājika

Some explain: "The Buddha laid down the first Pārājika training rule in the fifth year after his enlightenment, in the first month of the winter season, during the second fortnight, on the tenth day, at a time when the shadow was two and a half (or three and a half) man-lengths, while seated facing the East in the midst of one thousand two hundred and fifty monks, concerning Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, in the city of Vesālī." Such an explanation is not appropriate. Why?

Because the Victorious One (Jina) resided in the city of Verañjā during the twelfth rainy season. In that year, the Saṅgha was still pure; thus, the Pārājika training rule had not yet been laid down. The request of the Elder Sāriputta for the laying down of training rules is well-known to have occurred in that year. It is indeed an established fact that heavy offenses (garukāpatti) were not yet laid down during that year of the residence in Verañjā.

Did the Teacher reject the Ovāda Pātimokkha when he had reached four years [of Buddhahood]? Did he allow the Āṇā Pātimokkha in its entirety? (It was not so.)

Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṅgha by relying on King Ajātasattu during the later period of enlightenment (pacchimabodhi). The Sage (Muni) declared, "Monks, in the past, you have delighted my heart." For us, only the Sutta (the Pali text) is the standard. The period during which he was thus delighted was not short.

As for the statement made by the commentator, "At that time, the Blessed One, seeing no transgression, did not lay down either a Pārājika or a Saṅghādisesa," this was said in reference to the entire set of training rules (sakala-sikkhāpada). It does not refer merely to the training rules with a recitation (sa-uddesa); rather, it means it refers to the entire Pārājika, which has various classifications of primary and subsequent injunctions (sa-uddesa and anu-uddesa).

Although touching the navel is also considered bodily contact (kāyasaṃsaggi), it is mentioned separately because of its specific definition and because it involves sensual desire (kāmarāga). Here, only the bodily contact of one who is affected by sensual lust (chandarāga) is intended. Regarding the drinking of semen, it is said that a son named Valakābya (or Valābya) was born because a female elephant drank the urine of a hermit. The story of Valakābya should be told. It is also said that Maṇḍabya was born merely from the touching of the navel. Regarding the sight of a form, doctors say:

"Sometimes, due to seeing women, semen may move within the chamber. By reaching mutual sexual conduct, conception and so forth can occur." In this same manner, it should be understood by comparison that this can also happen to women due to seeing men.
72:
Furthermore, it is said:
"When a woman is pure during her flowering (menstrual) season, she can conceive a child just by looking at that man; thus says the teacher Kāsave."

It is said that such an event (conception by sight) once happened to a woman in Sri Lanka (Sīhaḷadīpa), just as it might occur among the women of a king's harem. Therefore, this was said. Although [Sudinna's] voice spread as far as the Brahma world, it was not within the sensory range (auditory range) of humans. Just as the form of Brahmas is not within the range of human eyes, so it was with his voice. That is why the monks asked, "Friend Sudinna, are you dissatisfied (in the Dispensation)?"

'Kali' means anger; the instruction of that anger is 'Kali-sāsana' (quarreling). 'Gāma-dhamma' (village dharma) here refers to the custom of country folk (sexual intercourse). 'Atta' refers to the mind and the body. 'Asuttanta-vinibaddha' means that which is not included in the Vinaya Pali, nor in the Sutta or Abhidhamma; it means it is outside of the Pali text. 'Kusuma-mālā' (flower garland) is said in reference to various qualities of virtue. 'Ratana-dāma' (jewel string) is said in reference to the perfection of meaning. There is an intention to reject, as in the case of the Elder Bhaddāli. 'Pada-nirutti-byañjanāni' are merely synonyms for a name, as in "name, naming, designation, definition," and so forth.

In the primary sense, abstinence (virati) is called a training rule (sikkhāpada). On the unwholesome side, immorality (dussīlya) is indeed volition (cetanā). On the wholesome side as well, in the Vibhaṅga, volition is figuratively called a 'training rule'. In the phrase 'saṅghasuṭṭhutāya' (for the excellence of the Saṅgha), the excellence of the Saṅgha becomes clear when laying down a rule that is a worldly fault (lokavajja) because the fault is obvious. When laying down a rule that is a prescribed fault (paṇṇattivajja), the comfort of the Saṅgha (saṅghaphāsutā) occurs because the benefit is obvious.

Between those two, by the first point, the ill-behaved (dummaṅkū) persons are restrained; by the second point, the well-behaved (pesala) persons live in comfort. By the first point, the taints (āsava) that would occur in the future life are prevented; by the second point, those of the present life are prevented. Likewise, by the first point, those who are not yet inspired are inspired; by the second point, those who are already inspired increase in their inspiration. It is said, "Because he was a son of good family urged by past merits, Sudinna dispelled that remorse (kukkucca) and realized Arahantship; for that very reason, his ordination was allowed." This point should be carefully examined. Likewise, it should be understood that by the first point, the True Dhamma (saddhamma) is made to endure, and by the second point, it serves as a support for the Vinaya.

In another way, among these training rules, where there is a transgression of the object that is purely unwholesome, it is laid down as a worldly fault (lokavajja) for the excellence of the Saṅgha. Those rules where an offense occurs only if the injunction is known, and not otherwise, which are connected to the teaching of Dhamma for the endurance of the True Dhamma or for the production of inspiration, and the other Sekhiya rules—these are called worldly faults (lokavajja). Even in the absence of the intention to transgress the object or the injunction, by performing what is prohibited or by not performing what is required...
73:
Alternatively, in a training rule where there is no intention to transgress either the object or the regulation, but an offense may be incurred due to performing an act that should be avoided or failing to perform an act that should be done; all such training rules, with the exception of the rule on drinking intoxicants (surāpāna), should be understood as paṇṇatti-vajja (fault by regulation). The duties of a guest (āgantuka-vatta), a resident (āvāsika), one departing (gamika), appreciation (anumodana), the refectory (bhattagga), the alms-collector (piṇډacārika), a forest-dweller (āraññaka), lodgings (senāsana), the sauna (jantāghara), the toilet (vaccakuṭi), a co-resident (saddhivihārika), a preceptor (upajjhāya), a pupil (antevāsika), and a teacher (ācariya-vatta)—these, when counted by the method of taking only what has not been taken, are fourteen. In detail, they are known as the eighty-two great duties (mahāvatta). Restraint through the seven classes of offenses is called saṃvara-vinaya (discipline of restraint); it is indeed the promulgated training rule itself. Among these disciplines, the connection should be understood thus: the discipline of regulation (paṇṇatti-vinaya) is for the sake of the discipline of settling (samatha-vinaya), the discipline of settling is for the sake of the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya), and the discipline of restraint is for the sake of the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya). The statement that the excellence of the Saṅgha is the comfort of the Saṅgha is made as if they were one, to show that if there is excellence in the Saṅgha, there will be comfort in the Saṅgha. Here, because they are performed for various special purposes called atthavasa, atthavasa is called 'pakaraṇa'. In the ten terms, by making each one the root and combining them ten times, one hundred terms are spoken. In such combinations, by the power of the subsequent terms, there are one hundred meanings (attha); by the power of the preceding terms, one hundred teachings (dhamma); by the power of the expressions (nirutti) that illuminate the meaning, one hundred expressions; and by the power of the expressions that are the teachings, one hundred expressions—thus there are two hundred expressions. In the hundred meanings, there are one hundred knowledges (ñāṇa); in the hundred teachings, one hundred knowledges; and in the two hundred expressions, two hundred knowledges—thus four hundred knowledges should be understood. Here, saṅghasuṭṭhutā means the excellent state of the Dhamma-abiding Saṅgha. It is said, 'Atthapada refers to the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), and Dhammapada refers to the Pāḷi Canon.'

Regarding the act of sexual intercourse, which is commonly named methuna-dhamma, whether by one's own effort or another's effort, if one indulges with enjoyment in any single moment—be it the insertion, the state of being inserted, the staying, or the withdrawal of one's own organ into one's own or another's path, or another's organ into one's own path—one becomes a pārājika and is one who is no longer in communion (asaṃvāsa). Some teachers, however, say that if one indulges in four, three, two, or even one of these—insertion, etc.—one becomes a pārājika. This is because it is stated: 'If he enjoys the insertion, the state of being inserted, the staying, or the withdrawal, it is an offense of pārājika,' and so on. According to their view, one would incur four pārājika offenses in the four instances. These same teachers say, 'Let the pārājika offense of sexual intercourse be incurred because it is of the same nature as the pārājika offense of sexual intercourse.' Because a person who, due to his own transgression, has reached pārājika and saṅghādisesa offenses, then disrobes and becomes a layman, indulges in sexual intercourse and incurs pārājika, then ordains again, receives higher ordination, and after rehabilitating one or many saṅghādisesa offenses, becomes free of offenses, therefore he...
74:
...is one who had offenses while a layman; even for one who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu), there is indeed rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna) from the offense. However, because one cannot be purified through the declaration of rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna-desanā), and because there is no purpose in counting, it is not said, 'For every effort, there is a pārājika offense.' Even if it is not said, they state a reasonable argument that this meaning is established by the words 'an offense of pārājika' in the word-by-word commentary (padabhājana). If that were so, it should also be stated in the Matrix (mātikā), 'Whatever monk should indulge in sexual intercourse, there is an offense of pārājika'; and the word 'without remainder' (anavasesa) for pārājika would not be appropriate.

Since it is called 'anavasesa' because it stands without leaving out any class of offenses or the count of monks, the offense is incurred only at the moment of entry, not after entry, etc. Intending only that one moment of entry, the statement in the recital of the introduction (nidānuddesa), 'to whomsoever there may be an offense,' should be understood as including the pārājika offense. Therefore, in the mātikā, not saying 'pārājika' but using the designation of the person, 'he becomes a pārājika,' is to show that by that physical connection, he is no longer fit for higher ordination. The statement 'an offense of pārājika' in the padabhājana is to show that even for a person who has committed an ultimate offense and is a pārājika not in communion, he is not a communion-thief (theyyasaṃvāsaka).

Even if he enjoys the communion, he does not become a communion-thief; therefore, he is simply called 'a monk who has received higher ordination.' For this very reason, it was said: 'A person is impure, having committed a certain pārājika offense; if a person of pure view, without asking permission, speaks with the intention to abuse him, he incurs an offense of dukkaṭa for abusive speech (omasavāda).' Since this does not apply to one not higher ordained (anupasampanna), it is clear that he is simply called 'a monk who has received higher ordination.' Because of this, it should be understood that he does not give rise to offenses of padasodhamma and sahaseyya, but he does give rise to offenses such as slandering among monks (bhikkhupesuñña).

In the saṅghādisesa offenses of bhikkhunīs, however, to show the difference in the procedure for rehabilitation from the saṅghādisesa of monks, although the person is designated by 'this bhikkhunī also... has incurred an offense,' the name of the offense is mentioned as 'a saṅghādisesa involving expulsion' (nissāraṇīyaṃ saṅghādisesaṃ) to show a different intention from pārājika. By this much, the dyad of showing and not showing the offense in the designation of the person has been explained in detail. The reason for not showing the offense in the sekhiya rules, which do not designate the person, is stated only in the Sekhiya Commentary. Because there is no such reason as in those sekhiya rules, the offense is shown in the remaining training rules. Thus, the dyad of showing and not showing the offense in rules that do not designate the person has also been explained in detail.

## The Explanation of the First Promulgation is finished.
## The Recitation Section on Sudinna is finished.
75:
## Commentary on the Story of the Female Monkey

40-1. In the second prescription, the present tense 'indulges' is used to denote frequent indulgence, as in the phrase 'here the Mallas fight.' Although the meaning was already complete in the first prescription—that 'it is only with a human woman, not with a female animal'—this [second rule] was stated either due to one's own wrong view or with the intent of seeking a pretext. To confirm that very completeness of meaning, it was said, 'Is it not so, venerable friends?' For this reason, the Makkaṭī-vatthu (Story of the Female Monkey) is included among the Vinīta-vatthu (Decided Cases) because there is no distinction. The Vajjiputtaka-vatthu is the same. The analysis of this case will become clear in the third prescription.

When it is said, 'Venerable friends, the Blessed One has in many ways...', it is stated to show that the matter is settled not only by the Sa-uddesa-sikkhāpada (the rule with the preamble) but also by the Anu-uddesa-sikkhāpada (the subsequent rule) which states, 'There is a Pārājika even with female animals and so forth.' Alternatively, it is stated to show that if the Sa-uddesa-sikkhāpada was prescribed as having a remainder, why would it not be settled by this Anu-uddesa-sikkhāpada?

In saying, 'Monks, therefore I shall prescribe a training rule for the monks,' it means that the very same training rule first prescribed will be re-prescribed with an emphasized meaning to leave no opportunity for those seeking a pretext. Otherwise, as in the Aññavādaka Vihesaka training rule, two offenses would be incurred due to two cases; however, two offenses are not incurred. The meaning is that the same original meaning is well-illustrated by another statement and made firmer by making it more distinct. This is clear in the third prescription and in other decisions.

Regarding the phrase 'For one who, on the side of the intentional (sacittaka)...' and so forth, the method of the Gaṇṭhipada (Glossary) is stated first. The term 'side of the intentional' (sacittaka-pakkha) is said in reference to unintentional (acittaka) training rules such as drinking intoxicants (surāpāna). Among intentional training rules, those that are strictly produced by unwholesome states, or those that are both intentional and unintentional, are called Lokavajja (worldly faults). In the training rule on drinking intoxicants, drinking while knowing it is 'liquor' or that 'it is not proper to drink' is indeed unwholesome.
