Similarly, for Bhikkhunīs, anointing for the sake of fragrance and complexion is unwholesome, but it is said to be 'not to be analyzed' because there is no fault when anointing for medicinal purposes. In that training rule on fragrance and complexion, the words 'knowing it is improper' or 'knowingly' are not appropriate. This is because a Paṇṇattivajja (fault by regulation) training rule could then fall into the category of being a Lokavajja.

To avoid this undesirable consequence, it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada of the teacher Vajirabuddhi: 'In this Dispensation, the analysis of intentional (sacittaka) and unintentional (acittaka) occurs only in the recognition of the object (vatthu), not in the recognition of the regulation (panyat). If it occurred in the recognition of the regulation, all training rules would be Lokavajja, and not all training rules...'
76:
...are Lokavajja. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that [the analysis] occurs only in the recognition of the object.' Why? Because in the Sekhiya training rules, the recognition of the regulation is the standard, not the mere recognition of the object.

In that same Gaṇṭhipada text, it is said: 'If someone should pour liquor into the mouth of a sleeping monk, and it enters inside, there is an offense.' In that training rule, it is like when a Bhikkhunī, while a man touches her body below the collarbone and above the knees, does not move her body but consents only with her mind, it is said an offense is incurred. Because it mostly arises from action (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna), it is said 'it is only an action (kiriya).' Similarly, this offense of drinking intoxicants is said to be 'only an action' when liquor enters while sleeping. This statement is well-analyzed because it does not definitely establish an unwholesome state. However, the strictly unwholesome nature of the surāpāna offense is stated by considering that an offense is incurred by a monk who drinks with a single effort (payoga), even if he perceives it as not being liquor.

The meaning in this decision regarding intentional (sacittaka), unintentional (acittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), and fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja) is as follows: Taking the offense by the head of the training rule, any intentional training rule whose mind is strictly unwholesome is a Lokavajja. Also, for an unintentional training rule categorized among the intentional and unintentional, if the mind is strictly unwholesome on the intentional side, that unintentional training rule such as drinking intoxicants is also a Lokavajja. Combining these meanings, it is said: 'Any training rule whose mind is strictly unwholesome on the intentional side is a Lokavajja.' This phrase 'on the intentional side' is said in reference to unintentional training rules. For there is no special purpose in qualifying a strictly intentional training rule with 'on the intentional side.'

In this decision, although the mind is strictly unwholesome on the intentional side through the mind that recognizes the regulation of a Paṇṇattivajja training rule, the mind on the intentional side through the mind that recognizes the object may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate (abyākata). Therefore, it cannot be said that 'the mind of that training rule is strictly unwholesome on the intentional side.' Thus, the commentator said, 'The rest are Paṇṇattivajja.' In the case of overestimation (adhimāna), there is no intention to transgress; and in dreams, it is inconsequential (abbhohārika). This means that even if there are shadows of transgression in dreams, they are inconsequential. This statement is also made for the purpose of strengthening the former prescription and relaxing the latter prescription. Therefore, it should be understood that my statement in the section on the External Introduction (Bāhiranidāna-kathā), 'It is mostly stated for the purpose of strengthening and relaxing,' is indeed well-said.

## The Commentary on the Story of the Female Monkey is finished.
77:
## Explanation of the Case of the Vajjiputtaka Monks

43-4. Those who live in the Vajji country are called the Vajjis; their sons are meant by the term 'Vajjiputtakas'. 'Yāvadatthaṃ' means as much as desired (according to one's intention). In this supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) of the third case, the phrase 'without disavowing the training, without revealing weakness' would indeed be appropriate if the disavowal of training and the revealing of weakness—which is equivalent to disavowing the training—had already been prescribed; if not yet prescribed, it would not be appropriate.

Nevertheless, this is spoken in reference to the training rule that is about to be prescribed. How so? It should be understood as being similar to the training rules such as: 'Why do the group-of-six (chabbaggiya) monks carry extra robes?' (Pārājika 459), 'The Āḷavaka monks are having huts built that are without measure' (Pārājika 342), 'Bhikkhunīs ordain a probationer (sikkhamānā) who has not trained for two years in the six rules' (Pācittiya 1077), and 'They ordain one not authorized by the Saṅgha' (Pācittiya 1084). Indeed, before those rules, formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā) was not yet permitted. Because of the absence of determination or assignment, it is called 'an extra robe' (atirekacīvara). Because the measure was not yet prescribed, it is called 'a hut without measure'. In this same way, the completeness of this example should be understood.

After requesting higher ordination (upasampadā) with the words, 'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha raise me up out of compassion,' and having become a monk, immediately after ordination, the training rule is prescribed: 'A monk who has been ordained must not engage in sexual intercourse; one who does so is no longer a son of the Sakyans (asakyaputtiya).' Is it not true that a monk who wishes to enter the state of a non-monk (asamaṇa) by means of that prescribed rule must first disavow the training he has undertaken? Or should he reveal his weakness in that training rule? However, it should be understood that the statement 'they engaged in sexual intercourse without disavowing the training and without revealing weakness' was made for the purpose of providing an occasion for the supplementary regulation.

Although the statement 'If he comes back, he should not be ordained' is mentioned only at the end of this third regulation, it should be understood as applying to the other Pārājikas as well, as the case may be. Indeed, one who, without disavowing the training and without revealing weakness, commits a Pārājika offense—such as taking what is not given with the intent to steal, or depriving a human being of life, or claiming a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to one who understands—should not be ordained if he returns.

A supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) serves the purpose of either strengthening or relaxing the original regulation. This is because a supplementary regulation has the characteristic of serving the purpose of showing the definitive rule for that offense, whether it be a Pārājika or another offense. It is like the supplementary regulation 'whether in a village or in a forest' (Pārājika 91), which is mentioned at the beginning rather than at the end. In this complete training rule:

'The Origin (Nidāna), the division of the Matrix (Mātikā), the Analysis (Vibhaṅga) which determines it,
Then the division of the Offense (Āpatti), and the Non-offense (Anāpatti) which is otherwise.'
78:
This method should be understood. In that division of the Vinaya, the three types of cases called the case of Sudinna, the case of the monkey (makkaṭī), and the case of the Vajjiputtakas constitute the Origin (Nidāna) of this training rule. From that Origin, the division of this Matrix (Mātikā) arose: 'Whatever monk, possessed of the training and the system of life of the monks... is one who is defeated (asāṃvāsa).' In that first Pārājika training rule, because of the use of the feminine gender in the phrase 'even down to a female animal', another person might be able to set up a pretext (lesa), like the monkey Pārājika case, saying: 'True, venerable sirs, the Blessed One has prescribed the training rule, but that prescription applies only to a woman, not to a man, not to a eunuch (paṇḍaka), and not to a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka).'

Therefore, to show that there is no opportunity for such a pretext for such a monk, this phrase 'even down to a female animal' is spoken. The specific wording of the Matrix 'even down to a female animal' due to the Origin called the monkey case was not made to show that the accomplishment of sexual intercourse occurs only with a woman. Therefore, the Analysis (Vibhaṅga) is the determiner of that Matrix; it is the Vibhaṅga that determines the intended meaning in that Matrix. For in the Vibhaṅga, the determination is made by closing every opportunity for a pretext in this manner: 'Three types of women, three types of hermaphrodites, three types of eunuchs, three types of men; the three paths of a human woman... the two paths of a male animal' (Pārājika 56), and so on.

On this point, an objector might say: 'If it is so, whether by virtue of being a common (sādhāraṇa) training rule or by virtue of a change of sex (liṅgapariivattana), it should be stated in the Vibhaṅga "possessed of the training and the system of life" not only for monks but also for bhikkhunīs.' If it is not so stated, a bhikkhunī who, upon the appearance of the male sex, stands in the state of a monk, might say: 'At the time of my ordination, I was not possessed of the training and system of life of the monks; therefore, even without disavowing the training, I do not become one defeated (pārājika) by engaging in sexual intercourse.'

It is replied: It should not be said so, because it would lead to an undesirable conclusion. If it were said 'possessed of the training and system of life' for bhikkhunīs as well, it would imply that there is disavowal of training for bhikkhunīs too, and that is undesirable. This is another undesirable conclusion: that 'all training rules are only common (sādhāraṇa), and there are no specific (asādhāraṇa) ones.' Furthermore, to show that this monk who has changed sex is indeed possessed of the training and system of life of the monks, it is said: 'Monks, I authorize that very preceptor (upajjhāya)' (Pārājika 69), and so on. Alternatively, any monk who engages in sexual intercourse by setting up such a pretext becomes defeated like the Vajjiputtaka monks. For even in the absence of the phrase 'possessed of the training and system of life of the monks', those monks of the Vajji country were told by the Blessed One: 'Monks, you have fallen into an offense of defeat (pārājika).'

In this context, because of the address 'Monks', some remained in the state of monks. 'Venerable Ānanda, if we could now receive from the Blessed One...'
79: Because it is said, "We wish to receive the novice ordination and the higher ordination in your presence," it should be understood that some have returned to the lay life. Furthermore, the differentiation of offenses means that, according to the Vibhaṅga teaching, "a Pārājika offense is incurred for a body not yet consumed [by animals], and a Thullaccaya offense is incurred for a body mostly consumed," and so on; this is the differentiation of offenses. "Non-offense is otherwise" means that from that same Vibhaṅga, the variety of non-offense occurs in a manner other than how the offense is stated. Indeed, without the Vibhaṅga, it would not be clear that "If one consents, there is a Pārājika offense; if one does not consent, there is no offense." With this much, the meaning of the verse has been briefly stated. In this context—"The differentiation of the origin (Nidāna) and the matrix (Mātikā), the purpose of the Vibhaṅga, the types of non-offense, and the first [part] being purposeful or purposeless"—the meaning of all training rules should be explained by showing this method. How? The origin is twofold: whether the manner in which the Blessed One laid down a training rule is complete or incomplete; this is the differentiation of the origin. The matrix is also twofold: dependent on the origin and independent of the origin. Among them, training rules such as the fourth Pārājika are dependent on the origin. Indeed, the monks living by the banks of the Vaggumudā River did not themselves speak of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) that did not exist in them, which would be characterized by false speech. They spoke to laypeople of each other's superhuman qualities, and that alone does not constitute a Pārājika case. Regarding those monks, the Blessed One, making that case the origin, laid down the Pārājika; therefore, it is called "dependent on the origin." By this method, knowing the training rules dependent on the origin, it should be understood that the opposite training rules are independent of the origin; this is the differentiation of the matrix. It should be understood that the Vibhaṅga, which is the analysis of the matrix, is undertaken based on three purposes in all training rules: to show the nature of the analysis of the matrix by showing the determination of the basis (vatthu), effort (payoga), and mind (citta) sufficient for the root offense through various ways; or to show the differentiation of offenses when there is a transgression due to the insufficiency of those bases etc., or due to the deficiency of one of them; and to show non-offense when there is no transgression. In this [first Pārājika], the Vibhaṅga proceeds by showing the literal meanings: "He is a monk (bhikkhu) because he begs; he is a monk because he has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering; he is a monk because he wears rags." Or it proceeds by showing the designation of the name "monk" without regard for the possibility of being a monk: "He is a monk by common designation." Or it proceeds by showing the attainment of monkhood through the types of ordination: "He is a monk by the call 'Come, monk'; he is a monk by being ordained through the three refuges; he is a monk by being ordained through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations"...
80: ...or it proceeds by showing the monk endowed with the qualities that make one a monk, such as "an excellent monk, a monk of essence, a monk in training (sekha), a monk beyond training (asekha)." This Vibhaṅga should be regarded as a general term connected to all training rules, and as proceeding through the doors [of action] and through the showing of legal issues (adhikaraṇa) in other related training rules. It should be understood thus because such a Vibhaṅga does not exist elsewhere. In that Vibhaṅga (Padabhājanī), it proceeds by showing the determination of the basis, such as "three kinds of women." It proceeds by showing the determination of effort, such as "For a monk who indulges in sexual intercourse in the three paths with a human woman, there is a Pārājika offense." It proceeds by showing the determination of the mind, such as "The mind to indulge arises in the monk." It proceeds to show offense and non-offense based on the presence or absence of the determination of the mind, even when the determination of the basis and effort exists, such as "If he consents, there is a Pārājika offense; if he does not consent, there is no offense." It proceeds to show the differentiation of offenses in transgression due to the insufficiency of the basis, such as "If a corpse is mostly eaten, there is a Thullaccaya offense." It proceeds to show non-offense because there is no transgression due to the deficiency in the determination of the mind, such as "If he does not consent, there is no offense." In this way, the method should be understood as it applies to other training rules. This is the purpose of the Vibhaṅga. The section on non-offense (Anāpattivāra) is of three kinds by way of showing non-offense: from the root offense, from a portion of other offenses, and from all offenses. Among those three, the first non-offense section proceeds based on three special purposes, just like the Vibhaṅga. What are the three? To show the nature of being purposeful or purposeless through the extraction (uddharaṇa) or non-extraction (anuddharaṇa) of the matrix terms—whether they are meaningful or meaningless—in a different way; to show the sequence of practice in a different way; and to grant exemption from an offense even in a situation where an offense could occur. How? In the Sheep's Wool Training Rule (Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada), the words "Sheep's wool may arise for a monk who has set out on a long journey; the monk who desires them should accept them" are words that merely show the basis and are thus "meaningless" (in terms of offense), and there is no offense for such acceptance. By the method "There is no offense if sheep's wool arises for a monk who has not set out on a long journey and he accepts them if he desires," the nature of being purposeless is shown by non-extraction in a different way. In the matrix, the phrase "should he indulge in sexual intercourse" is a meaningful statement.
81:
To demonstrate the beneficial nature of that [Pali text], it is stated: "There is no offense for one who is unaware or for one who does not consent." Since an offense occurs through the state of knowing and consenting, and there is no offense for a monk who does not indulge (is unaware), it should be understood that it is stated in the Mātikā: "Whatever monk should indulge in sexual intercourse is defeated (pārājika) and no longer in communion (asaṃvāsa)." In order to clarify the exemption from offense regarding property possessed by Petas or animals when the five factors are fulfilled—namely, "property possessed by another, the perception of it being possessed by another, a requisite worth five māsakas, the intention to steal, and the act of taking"—it is stated: "There is no offense in property possessed by Petas," and so forth (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, Commentary on the Second Pārājika). It should be understood that instructions such as "Know this, give this, bring this, there is a need for this, make this allowable (kappiya)," etc., are stated to show the procedure for other types of conduct. By this much, the meaning of the verse beginning with "Nidānamātikābhedo" is explained.

In this context, the first regulation (paññatti) was laid down when the greatness of seniority (rattannu-mahatta) was reached, because it was laid down after the first period of enlightenment and during the eighth vassa of the Venerable Sudinna. The second supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) arose when the greatness of much learning (bāhusacca-mahatta) was reached. That venerable monk involved in the Monkey Pārājika (makkaṭi-pārājika) thought that just as female animals are not intended in the training rules concerning women, it would be the same here; thus he said, "Friends, it is true that the Blessed One has laid down a training rule, but that training rule concerns human women, not female animals." The third supplementary regulation arose when the greatness of peak gains (lābhagga-mahatta) was reached. For those Vajjiputtaka monks, having reached the greatness of peak gains, ate as much as they liked, bathed, and slept on noble beds, thereby causing the occasion for the third supplementary regulation. Because those monks appeared when the Saṅgha had reached the greatness of abundance (vepulla-mahatta) and they themselves had reached the greatness of abundance, it is said, "The greatness of abundance is also found here." It should be understood that this first Pārājika training rule was laid down based on three types of subject matter and upon reaching four types of periods.

In that Pali, the phrase "Yo pana" (Whatever [monk]) is a term that encompasses all without exception. The word "Bhikkhu" is a term that limits the over-extensiveness of that "Yo pana." The phrase "Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno" (endowed with the monks' training and way of life) is a qualifying description of that "Bhikkhu." For not everyone called a "monk" is necessarily endowed with both: the training (sikkhā) prescribed by the Blessed One to be practiced as the minimum requirement for monks ordained by any kind of ordination, and the way of life (ājīva) described as "herein they live together." When is one so endowed? By any kind of ordination,
82: Immediately after reaching the status of a monk, whether one knows those two—the training and the way of life—or not, one is called "endowed" (samāpanna) because of having entered into them. Because of the meaning "they live together" (saha jīvanti) as long as one does not renounce the training and does not reach the state of defeat (pārājika), one is endowed with the way of life (sājīva). The statement in the Andhaka Commentary, "One who fulfills the training is endowed with the training (sikkhā-samāpanna); one who does not transgress the way of life is endowed with the way of life (sājīva-samāpanna)," is spoken according to the highest standard (ukkaṭṭha-pariccheda). In truth, it is not that one who does not fulfill the training, or who is full of sensual thoughts and the like, or who transgresses some minor way of life (training rule), is not called "endowed with the training and way of life"; (rather, he is indeed so called). However, by way of the excellent definition, a fourfold classification (catukka) can be obtained: (1) There is a monk who is endowed with the training by reflecting on the virtues (sīla), but is not endowed with the way of life because of transgressing an unintentional (acittaka) training rule. (2) There is a monk who is not endowed with the training because of being full of sensual thoughts and the like, but is endowed with the way of life because he is free from offenses. (3) There is a monk who is neither endowed with the training nor endowed with the way of life because he has committed a terminal offense (pārājika). (4) There is a monk who is both endowed with the training and endowed with the way of life because he fulfills the training and does not transgress the way of life. Only this fourth monk is intended here as the "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha) one. If it is argued, "It is not proper for the Blessed One to speak of one who is not excellent," it is not so; because that would contradict the statement: "Among those, that which is the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is the training intended in this context." If the intention were to take only the excellent, it should have been stated only as "Training means the three trainings," because only one endowed with the three trainings is the most excellent of all. If it is argued that only the training in higher virtue is meant, in view of the subsequent words "should indulge in sexual intercourse," it is not so; because even one endowed with that higher virtue is not fit (to indulge in sexual intercourse). Indeed, a monk who fulfills the training in higher virtue and does not transgress the way of life is not fit to indulge in sexual intercourse; it is only one who does not fulfill that training and transgresses the way of life who would indulge in it—this is the meaning. Therefore, the meaning should be taken here in this way: Since the way of life (sājīva) known as the code of training rules (sikkhāpada) encompasses only the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), and not the other training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) or training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā), therefore it was said: "Among those, that which is the training in higher virtue is the training intended in this context." Thus, the way of life that encompasses the training in higher virtue is called "sikkhāsājīva." In this way, the word "sikkhā" is included to qualify "sājīva." To clarify that meaning, the Vibhaṅga, without separately analyzing "sikkhā," stated: "He trains in that; therefore he is called 'endowed with the way of life' (sājīva-samāpanna)."
83:
Because it is said so, this shows that this training rule (sikkhāpada) is a term with a single meaning. Since the state of being a monk is something to be practiced and strived for immediately after attaining ordination (upasampadā), it is said "he trains" (sikkhati) and "he is endowed" (samāpanno). For such a monk, who is designated as "one endowed with the training and the shared livelihood" (sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno), if he, based on such a reason, later engages in sexual intercourse (methuna dhamma) without renouncing the training known as sājīva and without declaring his weakness in that sājīva, this meaning is appropriate. However, it would result in rejecting the method of the Commentary (Atthakathā). That method of the Commentary is not worthy of rejection; therefore, it should be followed accordingly.

The intention here should be sought; that intention will now be stated: In all training rules, this characteristic of a monk is common, namely, "one endowed with the training and the shared livelihood of monks." Even a disciple who is an Arahant (khīṇāsava) may incur an offense (āpatti) without intention (acittaka); likewise a Sekha. A worldling (puthujjana), however, may incur an offense even with intention (sacittaka). Therefore, because this characteristic of a monk is common to Sekha, Asekha, and Puthujjana monks, the term "sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno" is compounded using the sarūpekadesekasesa method—representing one endowed only with training, one endowed only with livelihood, and one endowed with both. By taking the highest (ukkaṭṭha), the inclusion of the lower ones is accomplished; thus, only the highest is mentioned in the Commentary.

To fulfill that meaning, in the explanation of why "sikkhāpada" is not mentioned in the phrase "he trains in that, therefore he is called one endowed with the shared livelihood (sājīvasamāpanno)," it is stated that since he is also endowed with the training (sikkhā), he should be understood by meaning as "sikkhāsamāpanno." Thus, the intention of the Commentary should be understood as: "without renouncing the training with which he is endowed, and without declaring weakness in the shared livelihood with which he is endowed." In this intention, it should be understood that only the training in higher morality (adhisīla-sikkhā) is to be taken, because it is required in all training rules and because the Vinaya is preceded by morality (sīla). Just as it is said that one who undertakes a training rule undertakes morality, so it is appropriate to say that one who renounces a training rule renounces the training known as morality. Therefore, it is said in that Commentary: "without renouncing the training with which he is endowed." The Blessed One, in allowing ordination for one who engages in sexual intercourse after renouncing the training, does not revoke [the original rule]. This is because that person did not engage in it while being a monk, as the rule is prescribed only as "whatever monk..." By this much, what should be said regarding the term "sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno" has been stated in brief.

What is the purpose of this specific statement? Should it not simply be said: "Whatever monk, without renouncing the training and without declaring weakness... becomes one not in communion (asaṃvāsa)"?
84:
If [it is asked], it should not be said so because of the consequence of an undesirable meaning (aniṭṭhappasaṅga). If a person who has not reached the state of sikkhāsājīva becomes a monk merely by name or by claim, such as a "theft-consort" (theyyasaṃvāsaka) and so on, for him too, there is the renouncing of the training. If such a person engages in sexual intercourse without renouncing the training, he would incur a Pārājika offense. Or, if a person later incurs a Pārājika offense and thus does not reach the state of sikkhāsājīva, or if a person, being a pakkha-paṇḍaka (half-month eunuch), reaches the state of a eunuch and thus does not reach the state of sikkhāsājīva, for him also, both the renouncing of training and the declaration of weakness would [wrongly] exist.

It is said, "In the phase of being a eunuch, a pakkha-paṇḍaka is not a valid subject for ordination"; therefore, it is established that in the other phase, he is a valid subject. A person who becomes a monk in that [valid] phase is said not to reach the state of sikkhāsājīva during the eunuch phase because of his eunuch status. Since he has no training to be renounced, if he were to engage in sexual intercourse, such as taking another's male organ with his mouth, without renouncing the training, how could he incur a Pārājika offense? This is the meaning. This method is appropriate only for one who does not obtain the non-eunuch phase later. For one who does obtain it, however, just as there is no death for formless beings (arūpa-satta) even when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted at the moment of wholesome attainment (kusalasamāpatti), the state of being a monk exists even during the eunuch phase. For one who consents to communion, there is no state of being a "theft-consort" (theyyasaṃvāsaka), just like one who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu). Nor does it give rise to [offenses like] sleeping in the same room (sahaseyya) and so on. Like one who has committed an ultimate offense, he is not a quorum-filler (gaṇapūraka). Such a person does not reach the state of sikkhāsājīva [in the eunuch phase], but he does in the other phase. This is his distinction from that [Pārājika] person.

Is this person sahetuka (with roots) or ahetuka (without roots)? He is not ahetuka. This is because ordination was allowed for him in the non-eunuch phase due to having a sahetuka rebirth-linking. If it is asked why it was not allowed in the eunuch phase, it is because he is a eunuch, like a eunuch by assault (opakkamikapaṇḍaka).

Furthermore, by this term "sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno," the undertaking of training by that person is shown; thus, it is appropriate to say "without renouncing that undertaken training and without declaring weakness therein." Because it is not appropriate otherwise, and due to the aforementioned consequence of an undesirable meaning, it is said: "Whatever monk, having reached the state of the monks' sikkhāsājīva, without renouncing the training..." and so on. Just as in this case, so too in all training rules, it should be applied according to the method: "Whatever monk, having reached the state of the monks' sikkhāsājīva, without renouncing the training and without declaring weakness, takes what is not given, known as theft, from a village or from a forest... or causes a robe to be made to the measurement of a Sugata-robe or larger, there is a Pācittiya offense involving cutting..." and so on.
85: (In all training rules), it should be applied. The statement "even down to a female animal" is said with reference to a human woman. It is not appropriate to say "not to mention a paṇḍaka or a man." The rest of the sequence of words follows the method already stated in various places. ## Ayaṃ paṭhamapārājikassa mātikāya tāva vinicchayo. ## Catubbidhavinayakathāvaṇṇanā "Nīharitvā" in this context means extracting from the Dispensation (Sāsana). From the Pariyatti Sāsana, such as "Upāli, a monk endowed with five factors... does not know the Sutta, does not know what conforms to the Sutta," they extracted and explained the Sutta and the Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa) that conform to the Sutta. From the Pariyatti Sāsana, such as "There is no offense in learning and questioning like this for our teachers," they extracted and explained the Teacher's Tradition (Ācariyavāda). In the Bhārukaccha case, from the Pariyatti Sāsana itself, such as "Venerable Upāli said: Friends, there is no offense in a dream," they extracted and explained their personal opinion (attanomati). Indeed, through such personal opinion, the Elder attained the foremost position (etadagga). Furthermore, the Blessed One taught: "If one is spoken to by a non-ordained person about what is prescribed or what is not prescribed... and acts with disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)." In that Pali text, "prescribed" (paññatta) refers to the Sutta (the Pali text), and the remaining three are called "not prescribed" (apaññatta). Therefore, this verse is well-said: "O Great Elders, the Vinaya is fourfold." Venerable Nāgasena spoke with that point in mind. "Āhaccapada" means a collection of words spoken by striking the eight places of articulation, or a group of words uttered from the throat. "Rasa" means the essence of that spoken word, the decision extracted from it. Because it is like the shadow of the Sutta, it is called "Suttānuloma." "Ācariyavāda" is called "Ācariyavaṃsa" to show that the tradition handed down through the lineage of teachers mentioned in the Pali is the authority. "Adhippāya" (Intention) means the purpose established by logic and reasoning, involving the rejection or acceptance of views, and resembling the means of knowledge such as direct perception. In this context, some teachers define "adhippāya" as "attanomati" (personal opinion).
86:
Although it is stated in the Parivāra Commentary and in this commentary as "the four Great Authorities in accordance with the Sutta," in essence, it refers to what is rejected or not rejected, what is allowed or not allowed, and what is suitable or unsuitable, as established by the method of the Great Authorities. In the term "Mahāpadesa," the words "ṭhāna" (place), "okāsa" (opportunity/room), and "padesa" (region/point) are synonyms for "cause" (kāraṇa). Because in the Dispensation it is used as "Ananda, there is no cause (aṭṭhāna), no opportunity (anavakāsa) for this to happen," and in the world as "place of suppression" (niggahaṭṭhāna), "obscure place" (asandiṭṭhiṭṭhāna), and "obscure point" (asandiṭṭhi padesa), therefore "Mahāpadesa" means "Great Causes." Here, "cause" (kāraṇa) refers to the indicative cause (ñāpaka-hetu). Their greatness is due to their vast scope, like the four great elements (mahābhūta).

Those Great Authorities are of two kinds: Vinaya Great Authorities and Suttanta Great Authorities. Among them, the Vinaya Great Authorities apply only to the Vinaya, while the other Suttanta Great Authorities apply to both. Therefore, in the Anuyogavatta of the Parivāra, it is said: "He does not know the Dhamma, he does not know what is in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānuloma)." In that context, "Dhamma" refers to the other two Pitakas, excluding the Vinaya Pitaka. "Dhammānuloma" refers to the four Great Authorities found in the Suttanta. Among them, if a person knows only the Dhamma and the Dhammānuloma but does not know the Vinaya and the Vinayānuloma, he, while saying "I will protect the Dhamma," turns the Vinaya into non-Vinaya. Another person, while saying "I will protect the Vinaya," turns the Dhamma into non-Dhamma. Only one who knows both can fulfill both.

To explain this briefly: Among them, the first person who knows only the Suttanta behaves wrongly in the following matter: "If he consents to the insertion (of the male organ), or consents to it when inserted, or when it is staying, or when it is being withdrawn, there is an offense; if he does not consent, there is no offense." When that venerable one experiences the contact of the derived matter (upādā-rūpa) which is to be felt as pleasant, and the body-faculty (kāyindriya) meets it, he defines it as "consenting" merely by the arising of the bodily pleasant feeling, and thus he causes a Pārājika offense to be incurred even by one who has no intention to indulge. Similarly, for one who has an unpleasant, disagreeable feeling due to a fish-cloth being spread or due to a genital defect, or for one who has no bodily feeling because of being struck by paralysis, he shows the Suttanta "there is no offense for one who does not consent" and thus causes no offense to be incurred even by one who has the intention to indulge. Likewise, if an offense of Saṅghādisesa is incurred by one who makes an effort with the lust for emission (of semen), he takes the case of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and makes it a Saṅghādisesa case, saying "how much more so for one with the lust for sexual intercourse?" In this way, he turns the Vinaya into non-Vinaya. The other one, who is a Vinaya-holder, because it is said "there is no offense for one who does not know," for one who knows...
87:
Saying, "Whether pleasant feeling arises or not, there is enjoyment while knowing," he makes an offense out of what is not an offense for one who knows but has no intention to indulge; he makes what is faultless faulty. Thus, he makes the Dhamma into non-Dhamma. However, one who knows both the Sutta and Vinaya says, "Because of the statement 'the monk's intention to indulge is present,' the intention to indulge is the only standard here; if that intention exists, it is a Pārājika offense; if it does not exist, there is no offense." Thus, he protects and fulfills both. In this manner, the full application (yojanā) should be made as far as possible in all training rules.

It means the sequence of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) which, being set apart from the Pali text established in the Councils, proceeds by way of decision-making that enters into the Pali method, by way of meaning, method, and conformity. Even though the Blessed One knew, "The Saṅgha will not abolish [the rules]," He said at the time of His Parinibbāna, "Ānanda, if the Saṅgha so desires, let them abolish the minor and lesser training rules after my passing," solely to show that "the later generations should regard the views of those [disciples like Mahākassapa] as authoritative as my own words." Therefore, this is established: "If the Blessed One permitted the Saṅgha to abolish even a prescribed training rule, what need is there to mention showing what is in conformity with the prescription? Much less what is already permitted by the Blessed One?" Furthermore, He spoke to show that there should be no mutual dispute among the lineages of teachers regarding deficient or excessive training rules. Why did the Saṅgha not abolish them? Because they saw the risk of mutual dispute. The Blessed One also said, "All should train in harmony, with joy, and without dispute." In that matter, by showing other views like "Some elders said this," it became a case of training while disputing. To prevent such dispute, he made them train without dispute by reciting the motion and second proclamation (ñattidutiya-kammavācā).

"Api ca" is an introduction to clarify one's own opinion. In that context, because of the words "in the Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya Commentaries," it should be understood that this discussion applies to all three Piṭakas. However, words like "Atha panāyaṃ kappiyaṃ" apply only to the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Kārakasaṅghasadisaṃ" means similar to the Saṅgha that conducted the Council. In Dhamma-siri Thera's Gaṇṭhipada, it is said, "It is similar to the Saṅgha that performs an act without rejecting the four [criteria] such as the Sutta and without contradicting them." That statement is inappropriate because it is inconsistent with these words: "The Sutta itself is the strongest. For the Sutta is similar to the irreversible Saṅgha that performs an act."
88:
In the ordinary Gaṇṭhipada manual, it is said, "Having decided that meaning, it is similar to the Saṅgha that makes that decision." "Paravādī" refers to a person from another sect who understands our doctrine. How does a Paravādī speak in conformity with the Sutta (suttānuloma)? "Except for water and tooth-sticks..." is a Sutta of the Sakavādī. In conformity with that Sutta, the Paravādī says that the water of a coconut is also just water.

"The water of a coconut, when old, binds the essence (pitta-bandhana).
That same water, when young, destroys the essence and builds strength."

When the Paravādī says this, the Sakavādī rejects it, saying, "That coconut water is only yāvakālika (temporary)," because the coconut is similar to a grain (dhanyaphala) and because it fulfills the purpose of nutriment. "Paravādī speaks the teacher's tradition (ācariyavāda)" means: according to the Commentary statement, "In evading tax, if one crosses the boundary and takes it away, it is indeed theft," the Paravādī says, "One who does so commits a Pārājika." Then the Sakavādī refutes this by showing the Sutta "If one evades tax, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)" along with the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā statement found in that same place, saying, "For one who does so, it is only a wrongdoing." "Paravādī speaks his own opinion (attanomati)" means: here, the Paravādī says, "If one who is commanded to steal another's property in the morning makes an effort to steal only in the morning but happens to steal in the evening, that effort is still a morning effort. Therefore, because it is your Theravāda that the instigator (mūlaṭṭha) is not released from the offense, it is a Pārājika for the instigator." Then the Sakavādī refutes this by showing the Sutta, "If one steals that property earlier or later than the appointed time, there is no offense for the instigator."

"Paravādī speaks the Sutta" means: showing the Sutta written in the Paṭṭhāna, "A state of undetermined cause is a condition for a state of determined cause by way of object-condition," the Paravādī says, "The object of the Noble Path is not Nibbāna alone." Then the Sakavādī refutes this, saying, "It does not enter into conformity with the Suttas such as the Object-Triad (Ārammaṇa-ttika)." For only that which enters into conformity with the Suttas is called a Sutta, not otherwise. Therefore, although it could be established by the mere words "it is known as appearing in the Pali," it is said, "it is known as appearing in the Pali established in the three Councils," etc. The teacher says such Pali is a "pamādalekha" (scribal error). According to the words "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless, heedlessness is the path to death," one who lives establishing mindfulness, avoiding dangers after consuming the offered food, is one who is steadfast.
89:
A Sutta presented by virtue of such a meaning should also not be accepted. Therefore, although it would suffice to say, "If it does not so appear," it is said, "If it does not so appear, does not enter into the Sutta, and does not conform to the Vinaya." Because it is said, "Whether it be an external Sutta," even if it is one's own Sutta, if it does not agree with the meaning, it should not be accepted. In the two methods beginning with "paro ācariyavādaṃ," the words of the commentaries found here and there due to clerical errors (pamādalekha) should be understood by reconciling them with the Theravāda.

Furthermore, in this matter, I shall speak of the ācariyavāda (teacher's view). If an opponent (paravādī) says, "What is called a root-seed (mūlabīja) includes turmeric, ginger, orris root... etc. One who perceives a seed as a seed, if he cuts it or causes it to be cut... incurs a Pācittiya offense, as stated in your Pali text; therefore, one who cuts a piece of turmeric incurs a Pācittiya," the proponent (sakavādī) rejects this by showing the Pali beginning with "Whatever other things are produced in the root" and using the teacher's view known as the commentary on that Pali. For a knot does not arise from a knot. If the opponent says, "There is no offense; thus is the learning of our teachers in accordance with the Word. Our ancient monks, having locked a room in a single mansion, slept with a non-ordained person, saying it is allowable, and they acted accordingly; therefore, it is allowable for us. Since some among you even say so, you cannot say anything," the proponent forbids this by showing the commentary words such as "The learning of the teachers who have learned the Sutta and what conforms to the Sutta is the standard (pamāṇa)." When the opponent states his own opinion (attanomati), asking, "Among those who sleep without asking permission after opening the door, who are exempt?" and says, "Since it is stated in your Theravāda that these two people—one possessed by a yakkha and one who is bound and made to lie down—are exempt, all others who lie down in whatever manner are also exempt," [the proponent] rejects it.

Furthermore, in this matter, I shall speak of the attanomati. If the opponent shows a Sutta and says, "They incur an offense," the proponent forbids it by showing the commentary words such as "For one who, being tired during the day, sits on a couch and falls asleep without lifting his feet from the ground, there is no offense," and says that those who lie on one side, etc., are also exempt. Furthermore, in this matter, I shall speak of the attanomati. Because it conforms with the words of the Buddha such as "O King of Devas, I say that distress (domanassa) is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated," there is no fault for you in supporting your wife and children...
90:
Therefore, it was said, "The support of son and wife" (in the Khuddakapāṭha and Suttanipāta). When the opponent says this, the proponent, even if he is not highly learned, rejects it, saying, "It must be an unwholesome state (akusala) accompanied by lust (rāga)." In other cases as well, it should be applied accordingly by this method or by other suitable methods. All this was said by Upatissa Thera and others. However, Dhamma-siri Thera says, "In this context, the one called 'para' (other) is a member of another sect; he brings only his own Suttas and so forth. The proponent, having compared those Suttas with his own Suttas, etc., accepts them if they agree, and rejects them if they do not."

## The Explanation of the Fourfold Vinaya Discourse is finished.

## Explanation of the Word Analysis (Padabhājanīya)

In the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, although the term "yo pana" is a term that includes all without exception, because it has the same grammatical relation (samānādhikaraṇa) with the subsequent term "bhikkhū," only the Vibhaṅga terms conforming to that are spoken. Although the three types of definitions for the word "bhikkhu" are common to any renunciant (pabbajita), whether they possess the state of a monk or not, it is said to show that only a person endowed with the meaning of the definition is the basis (vatthu) in this context, and not another who is a layman, in such Suttas as: "A person who has committed a certain Pārājika offense is impure; if a person of pure view, without asking permission, speaks with the intention of making him fall from the monkhood, he incurs a Saṅghādisesa or a Dukkaṭa offense." For the Blessed One began with the basis characterized as a monk, which is common to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.

The meaning shown is this: A person who, while being pure, remains in the guise of a layman for some reason, is a basis because of his own state of being a monk; and an impure person is also a basis because of remaining in the guise of a monk. It is meant that even an impure person who, due to relatives, enemies, or fear of the king, etc., has the effort to wear the saffron robes but has had the robes removed, is indeed a basis. This is because, by taking up the saffron robes again, he does not fall into the state of one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka), and because he has not laid down the burden (given up) the meaning of the definition of a monk. One who is a thief of the guise, having himself entered into the meaning of the definition of a monk and stealing the communion—if a person of pure view, without asking permission, speaks with the intention of making him fall from the monkhood...
91:
The meaning that it constitutes a Saṅghādisesa offense and a Dukkaṭa offense has also been shown.

The two phrases "bhikkhu by designation" (samaññāya bhikkhu) and "bhikkhu by claim" (paṭiññāya bhikkhu) support the aforementioned meaning. It shows the special meaning that one whose roots of merit are severed due to fixed wrong view (niyata micchādiṭṭhi) arising in the interim is called a "bhikkhu" merely by name or by claim, but not in the ultimate sense (paramattha). What is meant is this: "Monks, I do not see any other single thing so very blameworthy as this, monks, namely, wrong view. Monks, wrong views are the most blameworthy of all." This is found in the Suttas of the three Councils, directly spoken by the Buddha himself. In the commentary of that Sutta, it is also stated: "Among these things, wrong view is the most blameworthy, thus it is called micchādiṭṭhiparama." The five heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) are very blameworthy, but wrong view is even more blameworthy.

Why is that? Because those heinous crimes have a limit; even the most powerful of them lasts only for the duration of an aeon (kappa). However, for fixed wrong view, there is no limit; for one possessed of that view, there is no way out of saṃsāra. Therefore, it cannot be said, "This person still has wholesome states (kusala dhamma) resulting from being a monk," or "This person is pure." Because it is stated that "two offenses are committed due to the failure of view," it cannot be said "This person is impure" or "He has committed one of the Pārājika offenses." He does not belong to either side; therefore, it is said, "He is a bhikkhu by designation and by claim, but not in the ultimate sense."

Why did the Blessed One not prescribe a Pārājika for fixed wrong view, which is so blameworthy? Because it is difficult to discern. By nature, it is difficult to distinguish whether a view is "right" or "wrong," let alone whether it is "fixed" (niyata) or "not fixed" (aniyata). If it were prescribed as a Pārājika, monks might think those with different views have fallen into Pārājika and, without performing the Uposatha and other acts, the Sāsana would soon perish. They would also accumulate demerit themselves by acting wrongly toward pure monks.

Therefore, being skillful in means (upāyakusala), the Blessed One did not prescribe it as a Pārājika but prescribed the act of suspension (ukkhhepaniya-kamma) and the proper conduct (sammāvatta) to be observed, making him one with whom the Saṅgha does not associate or live. If his view was not fixed, he could fulfill the proper conduct, receive reinstatement (osāraṇā), and become a monk of normal status again. If it was fixed, it is impossible for that person with fixed wrong view to fulfill the proper conduct, receive reinstatement, and become a monk of normal status. Merely...
92:
...bearing the name "bhikkhu by designation, bhikkhu by claim," after death, like the monk Ariṭṭha, he will be like a stump in saṃsāra—this was the vision the Buddha saw.

Among the eight types of ordination (upasampadā), only three are mentioned here in the word-analysis (padabhājanīya) of the word "bhikkhu": Ehi bhikkhu ordination, ordination by going for refuge (saraṇagamana), and ordination by a motion with three proclamations (ñatticatuttha). The remaining five types are not mentioned here because they apply only to specific individuals or do not concern monks. Among those five, ordination by accepting advice (ovādapaṭiggahena) and ordination by answering questions (pañhābyākaraṇa) were only for the two Elders [Mahākassapa and Sopāka]. The remaining three concern only bhikkhunīs and are not intended here. In the midst of those three types of ordination, the four terms beginning with "a good bhikkhu" (bhadro bhikkhu) are mentioned because they are common to all three ordinations. One who has become a monk through Ehi bhikkhu, or by going for refuge, or by the ñatticatuttha act, can be one of good qualities, one of essential qualities, a trainee (sekkha), or one beyond training (asekkha). The word "ordination" (upasampadā) is used to indicate their status as disciples (sāvakabhāva). Only these monks can commit an offense; the Fully Enlightened Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas do not commit offenses.

Regarding the phrase "In this sense, a bhikkhu is intended," Elder Dhammasiri said that only those ordained by the ñatticatuttha act are capable of committing an offense. Those ordained by Ehi bhikkhu, going for refuge, accepting advice, or answering questions are not capable of committing an offense; therefore, excluding them, only the last one (ordained by ñatticatuttha) is meant by "In this sense, a bhikkhu is intended." That statement is improper. It was only taught that "Two persons are incapable of committing an offense: Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas." Otherwise, monks ordained by Ehi bhikkhu and others should also have been mentioned as those who do not commit offenses. Furthermore, it is taught generally that "Two persons are capable of committing an offense: monks and nuns," and also because the fear of offenses is seen. How? The Venerable Sāriputta, fearing an offense, did not accept a meal intended for guests. The Venerable Mahākassapa, fearing being separated from his robes, took all his triple robes while crossing a river and was nearly swept away. Moreover, Dukkaṭa offenses are seen to be prescribed for those ordained by going for refuge who do not properly observe the duties of a co-resident (saddhivihārika-vatta), etc. Therefore, this analysis is incorrect.

Elder Upatissa, however, said that the phrase "In this sense, a bhikkhu is intended" was said for fear that it might be thought that the previously abolished ordination by going for refuge was being re-allowed. If that ordination by going for refuge were included with reference to the capability of committing an offense, even though it was abolished before, monks might have a wrong grasp or doubt, thinking the Buddha had re-allowed it by speaking this way now. Therefore, it is said that it was not mentioned. This agrees with the text: "A bhikkhunī is one ordained by both Saṅghas." This was said for fear that the ordination allowed for the Sakyan princesses and others might be continuously practiced.
93:
Here, our view (inclination) is this: since it is a definition of the term 'bhikkhu' (bhikkhu-pada-niddesa), after showing all those who are included by that term 'bhikkhu'—whether they are seen in various places in the Vinaya Piṭaka as incurring an offense themselves or as causing others to incur an offense in matters such as announcing or concealing a grave offense (duṭṭhullāpatti)—now, in order to show the specific meaning of that term 'bhikkhu', by the power of the subsequent term "endowed with the training and livelihood" (sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno), it is said: "In this sense, such a bhikkhu is intended." For only he becomes endowed with the training and livelihood immediately after the formal act (kammavācā). From that time on, the arising of the training rules with their recitations is seen, and only in him is the renunciation of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhāna) seen, not in others. Only in him is the renunciation of the training possible, because it was undertaken after saying, "Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha lift me up out of compassion." Only in him is the announcement of the things not to be done (akaraṇီya) and the supports (nissaya) seen immediately after becoming a monk. And because he is fulfilled with the characteristics of renouncing the training, such as "I renounce the Vinaya, I renounce the Pātimokkha, I renounce the recitation (uddesa)," it is meant that only he is intended here with reference to the renunciation of the training.

Since (yasmā pana) the renunciation of the training is suitable for that monk in every way, it is appropriate to say: "For one who renounces the training and transgresses various matters, there is freedom from those respective offenses; for another, there is an offense." Therefore, it should be understood that it is appropriate to say: "Wherever there is a regulation concerning what is blameworthy (sāvajja-paññatti) or what is blameless (anavajja-paññatti), and it is said 'In this sense, this bhikkhu is intended,' there, for the purpose of that transgression, only the one ordained by the formal act with the motion as the fourth (ñatticatuttha-kamma) is intended." This being so, the statement "A bhikkhu ordained by any kind of ordination is intended in the sense of 'having practiced sexual intercourse, he becomes one defeated (pārājika)'" should not be said. If so, what happens? The fault of contradiction (virodha-dosa) is also avoided. How? If only the one ordained by the motion as the fourth were intended here by the terms "bhikkhu" and "ordained" (upasampanna), then considering those not ordained by the motion as the fourth as "unordained" (anupasampanna), the Elder Mahākassapa and others who were ordained by methods other than the motion as the fourth would, while standing in the position of unordained persons towards others, incur offenses of sleeping in the same place (sahaseyya) and reciting the Dhamma word by word (padasodhamma); and in matters like insulting (omasana), they would only incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The teacher says that such contradictions are avoided. "Maṅguracchavi" means a person with dark-brown skin.
94:
Because an exceedingly great pride of birth (jātimada) overwhelms your minds, you should train yourselves in my Dispensation in this way: 'Accompanied by pleasure, accompanied by the bliss of the first jhāna, in both foulness (asubha) and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna)'—so it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada. 'Perception of a bloated corpse' (uddhumātakasaññā) refers to the perception of the first jhāna obtained through the sign of a bloated corpse. 'Fine-material perception' (rūpasaññā) refers to the fine-material sphere jhāna perceptions such as the earth kasina. That novice Sopāka answered the question: 'Venerable sir, the perception of a bloated corpse is not clear because the foulness was not developed; venerable sir, the fine-material perception is clear because the kasinas were developed.' The fivefold sequence of ordination is taken from the Mahāvagga.

In the phrase 'by the motion and fourth proclamation' (ñatticatutthena), although the motion (ñatti) is spoken first of all, because there is no difference in the meaning or phrasing of the three proclamations (anussāvanā), the motion, which differs in meaning and phrasing, is considered the fourth relative to them; thus it is called 'motion-fourth.' In accordance with the phrasing, it is stated in the Commentary as 'by three proclamations and one motion,' but according to the sequence of the occurrence of meaning, it should be stated as 'by one motion and three proclamations.' In this context of formal acts, because of the words 'Bhikkhus, these acts are four; bhikkhus, these acts are six; an unrighteous act, an act by a faction,' even a flawed act (kuppakamma) is called an 'act' (kamma) in some places; therefore, it is specified as 'by an unshakable act' (akuppena).

Since even some unshakable acts are not fit for the occasion—as in the Campeyyakkhandhaka where it is said 'he is well-admitted' regarding one who has not reached admission (osāraṇa)—therefore, it is said 'by an act fit for the occasion' (ṭhānārahena). If it is argued: 'This term "ṭhānārahena" alone should be said, and not the preceding term "akuppena," because the meaning of unshakable is established by it'? That is not so; because one ordained by an unshakable act that is not fit for the occasion is not intended in this sense, there would be the fault of including an undesired meaning. However, when these two terms are spoken together, this meaning becomes clear: 'This person ordained by a merely unshakable act is also intended as a "bhikkhu" in this sense; and this person ordained by an act fit for the occasion is also intended as a "bhikkhu" in this sense; but one ordained by a flawed act is not intended.' By that term (akuppa), this meaning is also accomplished: 'Whatever monk knowingly ordains a person under twenty years of age, that person is unordained (anupasampanna).' According to this statement, as long as it is not known, even if he has reached the state of a monk by designation (samaññā-bhikkhu) or a monk by claim (paṭiññā-bhikkhu), he does not become the basis for offenses such as insulting (omasavāda pācittiya) by standing in the position of an ordained monk like the previously shown monks by designation or claim; he stands merely in the position of the unordained (anupasampanna), and 'in the case of one who is not a monk...'
95:
"If one who perceives another as ordained teaches the Dhamma word by word, he commits a Pācittiya offense," and so forth; such a case stands merely as the basis (vatthu) for an offense. However, a person who has attained the status of a monk through an unshakeable act (akuppa-kamma), even if he later falls into a Pārājika offense, still stands in the place of a monk in terms of his initial ordination. Therefore, among those persons to be avoided, as taught in the manner of "Monks, a paṇḍaka should not be ordained; if ordained, he should be expelled" (Mahāvagga 109), it should be understood that some persons are called "ordained" but do not stand in the place of the ordained, while some do stand there.

In this context, this fourfold set (catukka) should be understood: (1) an act that is unshakeable and suitable to the situation (akuppa and ṭhānāraha), (2) an act that is suitable but not unshakeable, (3) an act that is unshakeable but not suitable, and (4) an act that is neither unshakeable nor suitable. Among these four, the first has already been mentioned. The third and fourth are obvious. The second case is obtained by way of a figurative explanation (pariyāya) when a sex change occurs in a bhikkhunī who was ordained by only one side (ekato-upasampannā) from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. For that person, the ordination through the act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma) obtained previously during the time as a sikkhamānā was indeed unshakeable and suitable; however, when the male sex appears, because it does not fall within the scope of the Pali text "Monks, I allow that same preceptor, that same ordination" (Pārājika 69), it is said that the act [of ordination as a nun] has now become "shaken" (kuppa) merely by the person's transition to the status of a sāmaṇera. It should be understood that just as the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of a robe is lost through a sex change, the ordination performed by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha for that person also reaches destruction. Otherwise, it would follow that such a person is an ordained monk (bhikkhu).

Alternatively, even if there is no sex change, that one-sided ordination act is shaken; it does not stand in its original place. Therefore, such a person cannot yet be reckoned as a "bhikkhunī." This is because a person who, whether having fallen into a Pārājika or not, desires to disrobe and adopts the guise of a layperson, must receive ordination again from both Saṅghas; for that reason, it is called "shaken (kuppa) because it is destroyed." However, because there is no defect in the act (kamma-dosa) as previously mentioned, it is called "suitable to the situation" (ṭhānāraha). When a bhikkhunī adopts the guise of a layperson, if the male sex appears, no supporting reason is found to show that she can obtain ordination among the monks. Some teachers say that if she disrobes by renouncing the training (sikkha-paccakkhāna), she can obtain it; however, the Teacher says, "That is not proper, because there is no renunciation of the training for a bhikkhunī; this is our view (khanti)." It is stated in the Ganthipada: "To perform an act with the thought that 'if it is not done as it was said it should be done, it will be shaken (invalid),' is the teaching of the Master." Wherever "Ganthipada" is mentioned, it should be understood as the "Ganthipada of Elder Dhammasiri."
96:
## Commentary on the Sājīvapada-bhājanīya

It is stated in the Anu-ganthipada: "Great Bodhisattas are assured (niyata) [of attaining Buddhahood]." Wherever "Anu-ganthipada" is mentioned, it should be understood as the "Anu-ganthipada of Elder Vajirabuddhi." Among the three types of Bodhi—Sāvaka-bodhi, Pacceka-bodhi, and Sammāsambodhi—those beings who are devoted to Sammāsambodhi are called Bodhisattas or Great Bodhisattas. It is stated in another Ganthipada that [this virtue] is primary (adhika) because of the abundance of Pātimokkha virtue, because it is the virtue of monks, because it functions by way of closing off the defilements, and because it was prescribed by the Most Exalted Blessed One. It is supreme (uttama) because it occurs only during the appearance of a Buddha.

Although Pacceka-buddhas are also naturally endowed with the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla), for that reason it is restricted as "occurring only during the appearance of a Buddha" by way of that figurative explanation. Therefore, he said: "For one cannot remove that regulation," and so forth. Even compared to Pātimokkha restraint, the virtue associated with the Path and Fruit is indeed Higher Virtue (adhisīla), but that is not intended here. For that is not included within the Pātimokkha recitation (pātimokkhuddesa).

Since the reasoning called Samantabhadra has the characteristic of being common to all training rules, it is established in this supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) that even Noble Persons (ariya-puggala) fall into certain offenses. Therefore, does the statement in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), "One who is endowed with that Higher Virtue does not indulge in sexual intercourse," seem inadequate? It is not inadequate; it is indeed adequate. This is because such an investigation exists for each specific training rule, and the Commentary proceeds by the power of each respective training rule.

For this very reason, in the section on the water-splashing boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, it is stated: "For a bhikkhunī who, having covered the three circles (ti-maṇḍala) and not lifting her inner robe (antaravāsaka), emerges [from the water]," because this appears in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga. In other such matters, the same method should be understood. If it is asked, "For what purpose is this said?" it is for the purpose of showing the sequence of the Pali by following the sequence of the Pali. To clarify the meaning in brief in showing that Pali sequence: in the threefold classification (tika-pariccheda) of the training rule on teaching Dhamma word by word (padasodhamma), if one perceives an ordained person as ordained, there is no offense; by the power of the training rule on false accusation (akatanudhamma), there may be an offense regarding an ordained person who has been expelled (ukkhittaka); likewise in the training rule on sleeping in the same place (sahaseyya), and so forth. The meaning of this will become clear further on.

In the Commentary, it is stated: "Beyond that, only the mind of the Path and Fruit is Higher Mind (adhicitta), but that Higher Mind is not intended here," and "Beyond that, only the wisdom of the Path and Fruit is Higher Wisdom (adhipaññā), but that Higher Wisdom is not intended here. For a monk endowed with that wisdom does not indulge in sexual intercourse." This statement seems to contradict the Pali: "Among those three trainings, that which is the training in Higher Virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is the training intended in this sense." For this Pali shows that only the training in Higher Virtue is intended here.
97:
This Pali passage beginning with "Tatrāyaṃ" indicates that only the training in higher morality (adhisīla-sikkhā) is intended. It does not refer to higher concentration (adhicitta) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā). However, the words of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) show that all three mundane (lokiya) trainings are indeed intended. In this context, the intention of the Commentary is as follows: in this first Pārājika, all three mundane trainings can occur. There is the possibility that a monk who has acquired higher concentration and higher wisdom may, at times, depending on unsuitable circumstances, decline from that higher concentration and higher wisdom and reach the destruction of his virtue (sīla). However, a monk who has attained supramundane (lokuttara) mind and wisdom cannot reach the destruction of virtue. This principle applies not only to the first Pārājika but also to all other training rules involving intention (sacittaka), such as taking what is not given (adinnādāna). In training rules that do not involve intention (acittaka), however, a different principle applies. Nevertheless, because the Vinaya Piṭaka and Pātimokkha virtue are comprehensively included, it should be understood that in this subsequent phrase "sikkhāṃ appaccakkhāya" (without renouncing the training), the Pali states, "Among those three trainings, this training in higher morality is the training intended in this context," in order to show only the mundane training in higher morality which is capable of being renounced.

In this context, "training" (sikkhā) refers to abstinence (virati) from bodily and verbal misconduct and the volition (cetanā) which constitutes that abstinence. In other places, it should be understood as volition alone. "Training rule" (sikkhāpada) refers to the rules included in the recitation (sa-uddesa-sikkhāpada) and some rules not included in the recitation (anu-uddesa-sikkhāpada). The phrase "cittassa adhikaraṇaṃ katvā" is stated to show that the locative case is used in the sense of the basis (adhikaraṇa), meaning "one trains in that [training]." "Yathāsikkhāpadaṃ" is stated by way of reflection (paccavekkhaṇā) on virtue. This is because the reflection on virtue is itself virtue. Therefore, even one who produces a volition dissociated from abstinence regarding the training rules of conduct (cāritta-sikkhāpada) such as being well-covered (suppaṭicchanna), etc., is still reckoned as one who fulfills the training. One who does not transgress the limit stated as "In a deliberate lie, there is a pācittiya" is said to be "training in that training rule." In another Ganthipada (glossary), it is stated: "Sikkhā is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that occurs as the state of training in that training rule. Sājīva is the regulation (paññatti). To show that meaning, it was previously a designation for the restraint regarding sexual intercourse (methuna-saṃvara)." Since there is no lineage of training that is esteemed as a quality or as merit, the manifestation of weakness (dubbalya-āvikamma) among the laity is not possible in that training. This is because that training is something to be desired. Therefore, it is stated: "having attained whatever sājīva, without manifesting weakness therein." The Venerable Upatissa said that weakness can only occur in the command (āṇā/sikkhāpada).
98:
## Explanation of the Discussion on Renouncing the Training
Regarding this renunciation of the training, "I will go" means "I will go to the monastery of such-and-such heretics, or to a house, etc." "Bhāvavikappākārena" (by way of a specific state of mind) means that because the expression "I would be" occurs, it refers to the specific manner of intending to become whatever name or status one desires, specifically a manner of intending a state other than that of a monk.

The word "Handa" (Well then) indicates only verbal utterance. Through the words beginning with "desiring the state of a layman," the mental requirement (citta-niyama) is shown. It should be understood that the renunciation of the training occurs only with that specific mind, and not in its absence.

Through the words beginning with "the Buddha, the Dhamma," the objective requirement (khetta-niyama) is shown. In that renunciation, the first fourteen terms show the abandonment of the nature of a monk, and the last eight terms show the taking up of another state. Through the terms "paccakkhāmi" (I renounce) and "dhārehi" (consider me), the temporal requirement (kāla-niyama) is shown. By the word "vadati" (he speaks), the requirement of effort (payoga-niyama) is shown. By the word "viññāpeti" (he makes [another] understand), the requirement of understanding (vijānana-niyama) is shown. By the words "a madman renounces the training" and "one renounces the training in the presence of a madman," etc., the personal requirement (puggala-niyama) is shown.

By the words "one renounces the training in the presence of a Milakkha (barbarian/foreigner) using the Ariyaka (Aryan/Pali) language," etc., it is shown that even if there is a personal requirement, etc., the renunciation is invalid because the requirement of understanding (vijānana-niyama) cannot be met. Among those requirements, the Teacher (Ācariya) says: "It is our opinion that even in a Milakkha language where there is no temporal requirement, if that language can express the meaning of the temporal requirement, the renunciation of the training is successful." By the words beginning with "desiring to play," it is shown that even if there is an objective requirement (khetta-niyama), etc., the renunciation is unsuccessful because of the absence of the mental requirement (citta-niyama). By the words "he desires to make [another] hear but does not make [him] hear," it is shown that even if there is a mental requirement, the renunciation is unsuccessful because of the absence of the requirement of effort (payoga-niyama).

"He makes one who is incapable of understanding hear, but does not make one who is capable of understanding hear" is stated to show that even if the requirements of mind, field, time, effort, person, and understanding are present, the renunciation is successful only if the specific person intended to hear actually hears it; it is not successful just because someone else hears it. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary: "If he informs a single person, determining 'Let only this person know,' and if that person indeed knows, the training is renounced. But if that person does not know... [pe]... the training is not renounced." Or, if he does not make anyone hear at all, the training is not renounced. This is stated to show that the renunciation of the training is successful only through the requirements of mind, etc., and not otherwise. By this much of the Pali sequence, the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanīya) of the phrase "sikkhā... [pe]... dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā" is given in three ways...
99:
By this sequence of the Pali text, the renunciation of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhāna) has been shown in three modes. Among those three, it should be understood that the first two are unmixed, while the last one is mixed. Regarding the phrase "by that utterance alone," it means that by merely hearing the words that express the meaning of renouncing the training, one is made to understand by that very utterance. "Associated with the mind" refers to the utterance associated with the mind that desires to renounce the training. "One who knows the time (samayaññū)" means one who merely understands the intention of that person.

The Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna Sutta is a discourse that illustrates the virtues of the Buddha. The verses recited by the householder Upāli are called the Upāli Gāthā. The terms "paññāṇa" and "saññāṇa" are identical in meaning; therefore, "bodhipaññāṇa" means the recognition of enlightenment (bodhisaññāṇa) or the seed of enlightenment (bodhibīja).

Regarding the phrase "restricting both," it is stated in another Ganthipada (glossary) that "when it is said with the intention 'I renounce the training' only when both parties understand, if only one of them understands, he is not one who has renounced the training." This statement does not agree with the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). When one says "I am a layman" or "In a layman," although it is in the present tense, it does not constitute renunciation because it lacks the meaning of "please take note," and even if one says "please take note," it rests only upon the other person. "The Dhamma that is visible (sandiṭṭhikaṃ dhammaṃ)" is said to clarify the word "Dhamma" which is referred to as "sandiṭṭhika" in all contexts. Otherwise, if one says "I renounce the victory of the conquered," the word "Buddha" might also have to be mentioned at the end in connection with that word "vijaya" (victory) in the case of Cakkavatti kings and so on. In the synonyms used by teachers, such as "the one who ordained me," it is said with reference to the person who performed the ordination, referring to another person without taking the preceptor (upajjhāya).

"Okallaka" is a term for a poor or lonely person. "Moḷibaddha" means one who has tied a top-knot or one who has removed a crown. "Cellaka" is a young novice, "Ceṭaka" is a middle-aged novice, and "Moḷigalla" is a great novice (mahāsāmaṇera). Renunciation can occur in the presence of Nagas in human form, or in their Naga form, or in the presence of Kinnaras and others who understand human language. It is said that there is a reading, "Deities are of great wisdom." "Davāya" means speaking hastily or playfully. "Ravābhaññena" means speaking with a faulty voice. A faulty voice occurs either due to ignorance of the determination of letters or due to the lack of clarity in the places of articulation (karaṇa). Due to the inability to control the faculties, it is said "to one who is like a statue (potthakarūpa)"; such a person is one of dull wisdom (garumedha) or weak wisdom. If it is asked, to what extent is one considered dull-witted? It is because of lack of skill in the convention of letters (samaya).

## The Explanation of the Renunciation of the Training is finished.
100:
## Explanation of the Original Regulation (Mūlapaññatti)

The term "paṭisevatināma" is not in the Matika (Matrix); therefore, the text says "paṭisevetyāti ettha" and so forth. The phrase "this is called sexual intercourse (eso methunadhammo nāma)" exists in all Pali books; however, in the Commentary, it is extracted as "this is said to be sexual intercourse (eso vuccati methunadhammo nāma)." This connection of "one's own organ with a woman's organ" is shown because it is difficult to understand. The connection of "a woman's organ with one's own organ" is not shown because it is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "except for the four places," it is said with reference only to touching the internal and external parts. For a monk who extracts it without touching, there is no offense. "Majjha" refers to the tip. "Upari-bhāga-majjha" refers to the tip of the upper part. In the case of "one with destroyed bodily sensitivity (naṭṭhakāyappasāda)," if it is asked whether an offense occurs here as well because an offense is possible for one with impaired faculties? To show that it does not, the text says "or dead skin (matacammaṃ vā)" and so forth. Dead skin is matter not grasped by karma (anupādinna); a Pārājika offense occurs only in the case of matter grasped by karma (upādinna). "Apidhāya" means without covering. The intention is that one should sit with the mouth closed so that the teeth are not visible.

"Gonasa" is a snake with markings like an ox's back (a python or viper), which has distinct red circles on its back. By the inclusion of fish that dwell in mud and fish that move in water, although there are large-mouthed fish in the ocean capable of swallowing an elephant's body in one gulp, and even larger creatures can be caught, some teachers say there is no classification of "location" (thāna) for those fish because sexual intercourse is not possible in their mouths and so on; this point should be accepted after investigation. The phrase "etameva hi" is said with reference to the immediately following verse. It is a conjunction of letters (sandhi) through grammatical connection. Because it is said, "The training rule that is laid down is called 'equality of training' (samasikkhatā) because it must be trained in equally by all persons who possess shame," all training rules must be trained in by all monks.
