There is no deficiency or excess for anyone; so it is stated in that Ganthipada. In the Parivāra, however, it is said:

"One who is not suspended, nor on probation,
Not a schismatic, nor one who has gone over to a faction,
Standing on the ground of common communion,
How could he be uncommon (asādhāraṇa) in the training?" (Pari. 479)

In that Commentary, it is also said, "This question is asked with reference to a monk who was formerly a barber. This monk is not allowed to carry barber's tools, while others are. Therefore, he is uncommon in the training." All these statements should be understood as being consistent and in agreement. A monk also trains in the training rules that are specific only to bhikkhunīs. In this way, even another monk who is not a barber trains to become skillful in those training rules. For this reason, the statement is made that all training rules are called "equality of training." "Three types of women" and so forth is the Vibhaṅga Pali for defining the objects. A doll made of gold or silver in the form of a non-human woman...
101: A monk who is not a suspended monk (ukkhittaka), not one on probation (parivāsika), does not cause a schism, and does not join a sect of titthiyas, but remains in the common communion (samānasaṃvāsaka). It is asked: "Why is he unshared (asādhāraṇa) in the training?" That question is asked with reference to a monk who was formerly a barber. Because this former barber is not permitted to carry barber's tools, he does not receive them, while other monks do. Therefore, all those words stating that he is unshared in the training with reference to the former barber are understood by how they harmonize. A monk also trains in training rules that are shared only with bhikkhunīs. Thus, because other monks who were not formerly barbers also train in those rules to become proficient in their meaning, the statement that all training rules are called "common training" (samasikkhā) is the connection. The Vibhaṅga text beginning with "tisso itthiyo" (three types of women) is stated to define the basis (vatthu), as it serves as the marker for that Pārājika case. By that Vibhaṅga text, dolls made of gold, silver, etc., which are used through attachment to non-human women, are excluded. Starting from this text "tisso itthiyo," the three special benefits previously mentioned for the existence of the Vibhaṅga should be understood by applying them accordingly. ## Paṭhamacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā In the phrase "āpatti pārājikā assa hoti," because that unwholesome offense overcomes the monk's possession of virtue (sīla), and when virtue is overcome by lust, it is named Pārājika; it overcomes and destroys preliminary offenses such as dukkhaṭa and thullaccaya that occurred before, and it alone becomes his sole offense. Some teachers say that it is not overcome by other offenses of the same class as Pārājika, whether similar or dissimilar in basis. That matter has already been analyzed before. However, when all four Pārājika offenses occur together, they overcome the monkhood of that monk, making him a non-monk, a layman, or a novice; he is not a monk even by name. Some say it does not produce an omasavāda pācittiya offense. By the second alternative meaning, the sense that "attaining or fulfilling the Pārājika state is an offense (āpatti)" is included. Thus, the view of teachers who speak of being "endowed with an offense" is included. This latter method is also appropriate and depends on other terms. Such a monk is called "one with an offense." Otherwise, by the momentary dissolution (khaṇabhaṅga), he would be "without offense," but it should be understood that he is not without offense. If one asks, "When is he without offense?" It is when he dies, or when he renounces the training and remains in the stage of a novice or similar. In that case, by renouncing the training, the Pārājika offense is renounced, and the training is also renounced. Thus, both the offense and the training exist together for him. Is a saṅghādisesa or other offense not renounced by renouncing the training? Must it not be confessed again by one who has been re-ordained? Renouncing the training is an "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna) from the offense. He emerges from the offense by becoming a non-monk, he emerges by becoming a layman, he emerges by becoming a novice. Such an emergence...
102:
...in that case, it would not be called 'rising' [from an offense] because it would be contrary to the Vinaya. If it were said that one rises from an offense [simply by disrobing], then a layman or a novice who is endowed with virtue could be an attainer of jhāna, or an attainer of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) or the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala). A person with an offense who is guilty of a Pārājika would be an Arahant. A suspended person (ukkhittaka), or one who has left the monkhood, or one deserving probation (parivāsa) or penance (mānatta) who has left the monkhood, could be endowed with virtue and be an attainer of jhāna, or an attainer of the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of arahantship. He would be an Arahant who has an offense and an obstruction. If that person re-ordains, he must be rehabilitated (abbhāna) after being given probation or penance; if he is a suspended person, he must be reinstated (osāraṇa). This point is found to be the same.

The decision in this matter is as follows: As long as a person who has committed a Pārājika offense still claims to be a monk and enjoys communion (saṃvāsa), because of the obstructive nature (antarāyikatā), even if he undertakes virtue by himself like a layman on Uposatha days, etc., the undertaking of virtue does not succeed, let alone jhāna and so forth. If that person does not claim to be a monk, does not enjoy communion, and clearly reveals the offense to the monks, but does not give up the yellow robes only because of fear of kings, enemies, or thieves, etc., then although he is an unordained person (anupasampanna), even if he commits [offenses like] sleeping in the same place, he is one who shares in the portion of virtue, jhāna, and so forth. For this was said by the Blessed One: 

'By one who has committed an offense and desires purification, an existing offense (santī āpatti) should be revealed; for when it is revealed, there is comfort for him for the attainment of the first jhāna,' and so forth.

In that passage, 'existing offense' means all offenses committed, classified as those with a remainder (sāvasesa) and those without a remainder (anavasesa). This being so, one who remains in the state of a layman, etc., can be a sharer in jhāna and so forth because he stands on the side of purity. However, if a suspended person who has not yet been reinstated, or one who has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) and has not yet risen from it, renounces the training and remains in the state of a layman, etc., he cannot be a sharer in jhāna and so forth, both because he does not stand on the side of purity and because he still has duties to perform (sakaraṇīyatā). For that very reason, the Blessed One said, 'If he re-ordains, he should be reinstated.' Therefore, those obstructive states (offenses) committed during his time as a monk produce remorse (vippaṭisāra) in that person and prevent the arising of joy (pāmojja), etc., which have non-remorse as their root. It is not that they prevent it only while he is wearing the robes. If they do not prevent it, [joy, etc.] can arise. If one has committed a heavy offense, revealed it to the monks, and then left the monkhood, because he left the monkhood as one of natural status (pakatatta)...
103:
One who has disrobed may become an attainer of jhāna and so forth. This is because it is said: "For him, making [the offense] manifest leads to comfort." Some teachers say that one can [attain them] even during the time of being a bhikkhu; however, a suspended (ukkittaka) monk cannot, because he still has duties to perform.

A follower of that [suspended monk] who abandons that view may become an attainer [of jhāna and so forth]. In the passage, "Monks, for the assembly including laypeople... for one who has renounced the training, for one who has reached the ultimate matter (antimavatthu), for the seated assembly...", a layperson (gahaṭṭha) refers to one who remains in the natural lay form. One who renounces the training but still remains in the monk's form is called "one who has renounced the training" (sikkhāpaccakkhātaka). If such a person, having regard for his own dyed robes, desires the status of a novice (sāmaṇera), he becomes a novice in that same form through the three refuges.

One who has reached the ultimate matter (antimavatthu/pārājika), even if he enjoyed the [sexual] association, if he later desires the status of a novice without enjoying it according to the previously mentioned sequence, he becomes a novice through the three refuges just like one who has renounced the training. Bhikkhus should not have him receive the dyed robes again, because he remains in the form originally given. If a monk who has committed a pārājika is accused and, having lost, says, "Venerable sir, I will now become a novice; please give me the refuges," one should not say, "Very well, take them." He should be placed in lay form, made to receive the dyed robes again, and then ordained as a novice. "All of this, being stated according to one's own opinion (mati), should be accepted after consideration," says the Teacher (Elder Ānanda).

Insertion (pavesana) means the contact of the organ for one who is inserting the organ. Entered (paviṭṭha) means the time of effort during the process (vippakata) for one who inserts up to the base. Staying (ṭhita) means the organ remaining at the time of emission. Withdrawal (uddharaṇa) means the time of taking out. In the Ganthipada (of Elder Dhammasiri), however, it is said: "Staying (ṭhita) means remaining after ceasing effort." That was said to show the distinction without confusion. Emission of semen indeed occurs during the times of insertion, entry, and withdrawal.

## The Explanation of the First Group of Four is Finished.
## The Explanation of the Two Hundred and Sixty-Ninth Group of Four

59–60. Because of the statement "A dead [carcass] is mostly not chewed (not eaten)," it shows that even if a living [carcass] is mostly chewed, it is still a pārājika case. It shows that a [carcass] that is entirely chewed or skinless is only a thullaccaya case. Similarly, "Mostly..."
104:
##

...chewed," because of this statement, it shows that a dead [carcass] that is entirely chewed or pulled out is a dukkaṭa case. They do not legislate regarding what remains. Why? Because this training rule is a worldly fault (lokavajja), not a prescribed fault (paṇṇattivajja). In that [statement regarding lokavajja], "training rule" means pārājika. The thullaccaya offense included in that pārājika is also a worldly fault, not a prescribed fault.

Alternatively, both are legislated without remainder. For in the field of pārājika, having established it down to the lowest limit, beyond that pārājika case, it is legislated as thullaccaya. In this regard, the field of thullaccaya should be understood as being taught with a lower limit, just like the field of pārājika. In the statement "a thullaccaya for a half-chewed [carcass]," in whatever object the mark (organ) is chewed, that chewed object should be known as a dukkaṭa case. Here, if it is asked, "Does the Blessed One legislate the paṇṇattivajja training rule only with a remainder?" the answer is "No." Indeed, we shall explain it in various places as it may occur. As for the question "Why did the Blessed One not legislate a pārājika for a half-chewed [carcass]?", this is a question that should not be asked in the first place, as the legislation of the Vinaya is the domain of the Buddhas (Buddhavisaya). However, a plausible reason here is "because the state of being half is difficult to determine." "Mostly chewed" (yebuyyena khāyita) means chewing that passes two out of four parts of the rectum, urethra, or mouth, up to the end of the third part. Passing the third part up to the end of the fourth part is a dukkaṭa case.

If it is said that the statement "the mark is entirely chewed" refers only to a living body, that statement should be accepted after consideration. "Moist body" (alla-sarīra) means a fresh or non-decayed living human body; [offenses] in the eyes, nose, and so forth are only thullaccaya. The statement in the Commentary that there is a thullaccaya in the nose and bladder of animals such as elephants and horses is taught here by the specific meaning of the Pali: "He inserts the non-path into the non-path; there is an offense of thullaccaya." In the armpits and so forth, there is a dukkaṭa. In the eyes, ears, and scars of all animals, there is a dukkaṭa. In the remaining parts of the body, it is also a dukkaṭa. This decision is shown in the Vinītavatthu [in the case where a woman says]: "Come, venerable sir, let us indulge in the sexual act." By the words "Enough, sister, this is not proper," the absence of sexual lust is first shown. By the words "Come, venerable sir, rub between my thighs... pe... that monk did so," the enjoyment of emission is first shown; therefore, the Blessed One said, "There is an offense of saṅghādisesa." This was taught with the understanding that "If a monk rubs between the thighs with sexual lust, there is an offense of dukkaṭa for him" is established.
105:
In the case of human eyes, ears, wounds (scars), etc., it is a matter of a thullaccaya (grave offense); in the case of animals, it is a matter of a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing)—in this context, the subtle nuance of the Pali (pāḷi-lesa) is difficult to understand. Therefore, according to the word: "Bhikkhus, the genital organ should not be touched with a lustful mind; for one who touches it, there is an offense of thullaccaya," it is concluded that for a bhikkhu who touches the eyes, ears, or a wound with a lustful mind, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. This should be understood as the subtle nuance of the Pali (pāḷi-lesa) appearing in the Cammakkhandhaka. Regarding the phrase "for a living man," it is said that the word "living" is mentioned to indicate that there is no need to speak of a dead body.

As for the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, although it is said, "Taking the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā as the body (basis)," because the phrase "in the mouth with sexual desire" does not exist in the other commentaries but exists only in that Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated for the purpose of showing that word in conjunction with the words of the Pali. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, regarding "all that also," it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā itself: "If one touches the female organ with sexual desire without inserting it, there is an offense of thullaccaya." In some Pali versions, it is also stated as "in the mouth with sexual desire." Since it is stated in the Pali without distinction, "Bhikkhus, the genital organ should not be touched with a lustful mind," it is thus said "all that also."

Regarding "they praise the former meaning," it is because it accords with the words of the commentaries such as: thullaccaya offense according to the method already stated starting with animals... etc., and dukkaṭa offense for lustful bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga-rāga). This statement, "All that also... they praise the former meaning," is said to be the decision made by the teachers of the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) after the Council, by comparing the words stated in the Pali and the Commentaries.

In this context, "by another method" means by the natural mouth. If it is asked, "Why is it a dukkaṭa offense?" It is appropriate because it is stated that "for one who inserts fingers, testicles, etc., there is a dukkaṭa offense." In this context of "the urinary tract of a female animal," since the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā previously said "organ (nimitta)" and here says "urinary tract (passāvamagga)," it appears appropriate to say dukkaṭa for the remaining parts of the organ. "According to the method already stated" means with sexual desire. As for thullaccaya, since it appears in the Khandhaka only by way of the urinary organ, it should be accepted after careful investigation.

## Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion (Pakiṇṇaka-kathā)

In the Miscellaneous Section (Pakiṇṇaka-kaṇḍa), those training rules which are called "kiriya" (action) should be understood by way of the body and speech together with intimation (viññatti). By way of "akiriya" (non-action) training rules, they should be understood without intimation. In this matter of kiriya and akiriya, the mind (perception/saññā) is not the measure, because the origin (samuṭṭhāna) of the training rule on announcing superhuman states (bhūtārocana) is kiriya and because it is acittaka (independent of specific intent). In that training rule of bhūtārocana, the action (kiriya) should be understood as having its origin in the mind immediately preceding the offense. Some training rules that do not produce intimation are also generally called "kiriya," as in the case of this first pārājika; for even in the absence of intimation, it is stated: "If he consents, there is an offense of pārājika," and "If he does not consent, there is no offense."

Action (kiriya) known as intimation (viññatti) also cannot occur without the mind of indulgence (sevana-citta), because it is mind-produced (cittaja), because it is a form of variation (vikāra-rūpa), and because it follows the mind. Therefore, this form of intimation called kiriya, like other mind-produced matter, cannot remain without the producing mind; whereas the other, the sound-base (saddāyatana), remains. Therefore, when there is kiriya, since the sevana-citta that produces that kiriya definitely exists, the statement "If he does not consent, there is no offense" seems inappropriate. Because even though it is a mind that produces intimation, the sevana-citta does not produce intimation at all times; therefore, since it can arise by itself even without intimation, it is stated: "If he consents, there is an offense of pārājika."

If that mind does not arise spontaneously, it is called "not consenting," and there is no offense for that bhikkhu. For that very reason, the Blessed One defines the offense only by the mind, asking, "Bhikkhu, what was your mind?" and not by the action (kiriya). By this sequence of words, the six origins of offenses (āpatti-samuṭṭhāna) come to be; and those six alone are called the factors that produce offenses. One incurs an offense through four modes: by body, by speech, by body and speech, or by formal act (kamma-vācā). Thus, these scriptural terms are not contradictory; otherwise, they would be contradictory. How? For whatever offense one incurs by formal act, it would follow that the body and so forth do not occur in that offense.
107:
Because of this, the factors that produce an offense along with the kammavācā (formal act) reach the number of seven. In the presence of these factors that produce an offense, if body and so forth are obtained either collectively or individually, the statement "by four ways" would be inappropriate, and it should be said "one falls into an offense by seven ways." Thus, contradictions arise. How are they not contradictory? It is because body and so forth are distinguished by being saviññattika (with intimation) and aviññattika (without intimation). There is an offense that is an act (kiriya); some such offenses are committed by the body with intimation. Some are committed by speech with intimation. Some are committed by both body and speech with intimation. There is an offense that is a non-act (akiriya); some such offenses are committed by the kammavācā, and specifically only by the remaining aviññattika body and speech, not without them. This is because of the word: "If he does not renounce it by body or speech, at the conclusion of the kammavācā, he falls into a saṅghādisesa offense." Or, without distinction, some offenses are committed by the body, some by speech, and some by both body and speech. Here, regarding the commission by body and speech, it should be understood that some are committed by body and speech alone, while some are committed by the kammavācā. Thus, they are not contradictory.

To clarify the meaning in brief: regarding "falling into an offense by the body," some offenses are committed by doing what should not be done with the body with intimation, and some are committed by not doing what should be done with the body without intimation. Both of these are called bodily action (kāyakamma). In the world, even what is not done is called "done," as in "I have done wrong (dukkaṭa) in that I did not do the merit." In the Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, it is said: "Friend Ānanda, this is a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for you, that you did not ask the Blessed One." Thus, in this sequence of Vinaya teaching, even what is not done by the body is called "bodily action." The same method should be understood for "falling into an offense by speech," etc. The inclusion of "origin" (samuṭṭhāna) is to show that one falls into an offense only by considering the distinctions of body and so forth, whether by an act or a non-act, and not otherwise. The inclusion of the word "act" (kiriya) is to show the distinction between saviññattika and aviññattika of the body and so forth. The inclusion of the word "perception" (saññā) is to show the distinction between the mind that is a factor of the offense and the mind that is not. Therefore, the mind that is present in the characteristic of an act or a non-act, or from which an act or non-act arises, is not indiscriminately a factor (aṅga) or a non-factor (anaṅga) of the offense. Rather, the mind associated with the perception called "saññāvimokkha" (release through perception) is the factor, and the remaining mind is not the factor.
108:
Now, the mind by which a training rule is "with mind" (sacittaka), and the absence of which makes it "without mind" (acittaka); because of the blameworthiness of that training rule without distinction by that mind, it is called only lokavajja (worldly fault). However, to show that among blameworthy training rules, some are called lokavajja and some are called paṇṇattivajja (fault by regulation), the concept of lokavajja is presented. Since the mind itself is called "lokavajja," the term "action" (kamma) is used to prevent the undesirable conclusion that mental action (manokamma) could also be an offense. In discussing this action, the term "wholesome triad" (kusala-tika) is used to prevent the undesirable conclusion that an action characterized by non-act (akiriya) might be exempt from the wholesome triad. Among these triads, there is the indeterminate (avyākata) offense; some teachers say that even a monk who has entered the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha-samāpatti), which is without feeling, falls into an offense. To prevent the undesirable conclusion that the feeling triad (vedanā-tika) is not obtained in such a person, the term "feeling triad" is used. Indeed, because a training rule is designated as "three minds, three feelings" (ticitta tivedana) by virtue of a person with mind, even when an offense is committed by one without mind, it is still called "three minds, three feelings." Regarding falling into an offense without mind being called "three minds, three feelings," there is this scripture: "One falls into an offense without mind; one emerges from an offense without mind. One falls into an offense with a wholesome mind; one emerges from an offense with a wholesome mind," and so forth. In the Anuganthipada, it is said: "Perception (saññā) always produces only non-offense; the mind (citta) produces only offense. What is called 'without mind' (acittaka) is the non-cognition of the object; it is not the release through perception (saññāvimokkha) but the cognition of the transgression; this is the distinction between that perception and mind."

"By way of all-inclusiveness" (sabbasaṅgāhakavasena) means by way of including all training rules. Giving a robe to a bhikkhunī and so forth occurs due to act (kiriya) and non-act (akiriya). Accepting gold and silver and so forth sometimes occurs due to act. Not rejecting gold and silver placed nearby sometimes occurs due to non-act. Building a hut exceeding the measurement on a site that has been marked out sometimes occurs due to act; building a hut exceeding the measurement on a site that has not been marked out sometimes occurs due to act and non-act. In the phrase "only the mental factor that is obtained," it refers to the bodily mind and the vocal mind. In the phrase "even without mind," it means both without mind and with mind. The body that is said to be both saviññattika and aviññattika, the action of that body is called bodily action (kāyakamma); likewise for vocal action (vacīkamma). Among those saviññattika and aviññattika bodies, the saviññattika body accomplishes the action by occurrence (uppatti), and the other aviññattika body accomplishes the action by non-occurrence (anuppatti). It should be understood that vocal action is the same. A training rule is said to be associated with transgression because of the statement: "Whatever name-group (nāmakāya) or word-group (padakāya) is there." In the Anuganthipada, it is said: "The hasituppāda (smile-producing) and votthabbana (determining) minds are also minds that originate an offense. When one laughs and sees, thinking 'I have not delimited this matter,' then the votthabbana follows the course of impulsion (javana)." Minds of direct knowledge (abhiññā) should be taken at the time of performing supernormal powers and so forth without knowing the regulation.
109:
In this miscellaneous collection: regarding a monk who is endowed with the training and livelihood of monks, by indulging in sexual intercourse, some become defeated (pārājika) and are in non-communion (asaṃvāsa), while some are in non-communion without being defeated. There are also those who are not defeated because they indulge in matters involving wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) or grave offenses (thullaccaya).

A half-month eunuch (pakkha-paṇḍaka) who receives higher ordination during the non-eunuch half-month and then indulges in sexual intercourse during the eunuch half-month does not incur a pārājika offense; thus, he is called one who is not defeated. This is because there is no such thing as an offense for one who is not a monk. A question may arise: when he returns to the non-eunuch half-month, being free from offense, is he in non-communion or not? He is in non-communion. This is because it was said, "He is unfit for monkhood with such a physical constitution." If it is argued that since it was said, "A monk who... is in non-communion," only one who indulges in sexual intercourse while being a monk is unfit (abhabba), and this pakkha-paṇḍaka is not unfit because he is not defeated—that is not so. In the context where it was said, "The Saṅgha should be informed by a competent and capable monk," just as a formal act (kamma) does not succeed even if the ritual text (kammavācā) is recited by a non-monk because of the failure of the act (kammavipatti), the fulfillment of this higher ordination (upasampadā) should be understood in the same way.

In this matter, there is this logic: our teacher holds that the kamma succeeds only if the kammavācā is recited by one who was previously ordained and the Saṅgha perceives him as ordained; it does not succeed otherwise. If a householder, a titthiya (member of another sect), or a paṇḍaka recites the kammavācā while being perceived as not ordained, it is not considered as the Saṅgha reciting the kammavācā. According to the words, "The Saṅgha should ordain, the Saṅgha ordains, one is ordained by the Saṅgha," it should be understood that the kammavācā is considered recited by the Saṅgha only if it is recited by one who belongs to the Saṅgha or by one who is perceived as belonging to the Saṅgha. This is the appropriate logic for all formal acts.

Likewise, there is a person who must be expelled (nāsetabba) for indulging in sexual intercourse. Because it was said, "One who violates a nun (bhikkhunī-dūsaka) should be expelled," such a person must be expelled even if he is not ordained. He causes offenses such as sleeping in the same place (sahaseyya), and a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) offense is incurred for reviling (omasana) him. However, one who indulges in sexual intercourse with a woman who is not a nun does not need to be expelled, as there is no Pali text stating, "A non-monk who commits an ultimate offense (antimavatthu) should be expelled." Therefore, he remains in the status of a monk and does not cause offenses like sahaseyya. However, because he is in non-communion (asaṃvāsa), he cannot be a quorum-filler (gaṇapūraka). This is because performing a single formal act or a single recitation (of the Pātimokkha) is also called communion (saṃvāsa). Having the same training is also called communion. Therefore, since he no longer has communion with a monk who has fallen into defeat, there is an indication of the reason that he does not cause a padasodhamma offense. With a nun, the Bhikkhu Saṅgha's...
110:
Because there is no communion (saṃvāsa) such as performing a single formal act, a nun is in non-communion (asaṃvāsa) with a monk; likewise, a monk is in non-communion with a nun. Due to this non-communion, there is an indication of the reason that it does not cause a padasodhamma offense. Similarly, since it is not stated that "even one who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu) should be expelled by another monk," this indication of the reason is not accepted through this example.

Furthermore, according to the statements, "A monk offends against a sleeping monk; if the latter consents upon waking, both should be expelled," and "Therefore, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā," it should be understood that if a person enters the midst of the Saṅgha and is found defeated after being questioned by an examiner, he is also a non-monk (anupasampanna) and does not cause an omasavāda pācittiya offense. Although there is no Pali text saying, "desiring to revile an ordained person while perceiving him as ordained," and although the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary states, "The four factors here are: the ordained status of the person reviled, reviling by mentioning birth etc. without referring to another, the knowledge that 'he is reviling me', and the absence of a beneficial purpose etc.," nevertheless, according to the Dhuṭṭhadosa Sikkhāpada, which states, "A person is impure (having committed a pārājika); if one who sees him as pure, having asked for permission, speaks with the intention to revile, he incurs an omasavāda offense," a monk who reviles an impure monk while perceiving him as ordained incurs a pācittiya. For a monk who perceives him as impure, it is a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Because of the statement, "A person is pure (not having committed a pārājika)...", the fact that Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī does not mention "his ordained status and the perception of him as ordained" should be understood as being because that factor is not constant.

Furthermore, the fourfold set regarding the renunciation of training should be understood here: there is a person who has renounced the training but is not endowed with the training and livelihood; there is one who is endowed with the training and livelihood but has not renounced the training; there is one who has both renounced the training and is endowed with the training and livelihood; and there is one who has neither renounced the training nor is endowed with the training and livelihood. Among these four, the third type should be understood as the nun's renunciation of training. Indeed, as long as she does not give up the mark (liṅga), even if she renounces the training while still being attached to the saffron robes and wishing to fall away from the state of a female recluse, she is still a nun and is still endowed with the training and livelihood. For it was said by the Blessed One, "Monks, there is no renunciation of training for a nun." When, then, does that nun become a non-nun?...
111:
When does that bhikkhunī cease to be a bhikkhunī and become a layperson? When she desires to leave the state of a recluse and wears lay clothing, she is reckoned as "disrobed" (vibbhamitā). The Blessed One also said: "At the very moment she is disrobed, at that moment she is [no longer] a bhikkhunī." By how much is one called "disrobed"? Desiring to leave the state of a recluse, without attachment to the saffron robes, she discards the robes, or goes naked, or goes covered with grass and leaves, or wears the saffron robes in the manner of lay clothing, or wears white clothing, or while still in her own form, enters among heretics (titthiya) and undertakes their practices such as plucking out hair, or adopts the appearance of a heretic; then she is called "disrobed." In that disrobing, a bhikkhunī who, while remaining in the form of a bhikkhunī, undertakes the practices of heretics, like a monk who has gone over to heretics, cannot later receive even the lower ordination (pabbajjā). The rest of the disrobed bhikkhunīs can receive only the lower ordination, but not the higher ordination (upasampadā). Although in the Pali it says, "Monks, a bhikkhunī who has gone over to a heretical fold while still wearing saffron robes, should not be given the higher ordination upon her return," it seems to allow that one who first disrobes and then goes to a heretical fold may be given the higher ordination upon return. However, because the teachers of the Council stated there are "twenty-four Pārājikas," she should not be given the higher ordination again. For this reason, the Blessed One did not allow the formal relinquishing of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhāna) [for nuns]. A bhikkhunī who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu) is still a bhikkhunī. A pakkapaṇḍukī is also a bhikkhunī. "Kinti" is a question.

## Explanation of the Decided Cases (Vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā)
Cases that have been decided are called Vinītavatthu. Because they extract the names and numbers of various cases such as "At that time, a certain monk..." and purify the faults of deficiency or excess, they are called Uddāna. Because they are verses marked by the characteristics of prosody (chandoviciti) completed with meters such as makkaṭa, they are called "Uddāna-gāthā." The word "de" is in the sense of purifying; through the power of that root, the form "uddāna" should be understood. These Uddāna-gāthā were placed by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma at the time of the Council. Where were they placed? At the end of the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanīya). It is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada (Word-Glossary) that "Vatthu-gāthā are the introductions to these decided cases such as 'At that time, a certain monk...'". Therefore, it should be understood that the decided cases themselves are called "Vatthu-gāthā" according to the method stated in that Gaṇṭhipada. This is the summary of the meaning here.
112:
The demonstration of the meaning is as follows: either by way of showing the root offense, "Monk, you have fallen into a Pārājika"; or by way of showing the distinction of offenses, "Monk, there is no Pārājika, but there is a Saṅghādisesa or a Dukkaṭa offense"; or by way of showing the absence of offense, "Monk, there is no offense for one who does not consent"—those cases which have been decided are called Vinītavatthu. The scriptural text that illuminates the introductory story of those decided cases is called Vatthu-gāthā. Some teachers say that the Uddāna-gāthā themselves are the "Vatthu-gāthā." Their view contradicts the statement [in the Commentary], "By this characteristic, Vinaya-holders will decide the Vinaya in the future." For in the Uddāna-gāthā, no characteristic for decision is apparent. A separate purpose for the Uddāna-gāthā is stated: "Vinaya-holders will learn them easily." Therefore, because of the difference in purpose, the distinction [between these terms] should be understood.

In this context, the word-analysis (viggaha) for Vatthu-gāthā is: the cases (vatthu) themselves are the verses (gāthā), thus Vatthu-gāthā. The word gāthā is used here to distinguish them from the Vinītavatthu (decided cases in prose). The word vatthu is used to distinguish them from the Uddāna-gāthā. Some teachers, however, say: "Though they should be called 'cases of the verses,' they are called Vatthu-gāthā." In the case of the female monkey, other monks reported it; in this decided case, he reported it himself. Because it is said in that case of the supplementary regulation, "The Blessed One laid down the training rule," the Vajjiputtaka monks were also different monks. It is stated in another Gaṇṭhipada: "In that supplementary regulation, the Elder Ānanda reported; in this decided case, only those local monks reported." The teacher's intention was stated previously; therefore, it should be investigated.

67-8. Ñatvā means knowing by oneself without asking. Pokkhara means the body, like the surface of a drum. People in the world call one with a complete body "beautiful." Therefore, by the first sense of vaṇṇa-pokkharatā, it means having an excellent bodily complexion; by the second sense, it means beauty of appearance. It is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada: "Because her complexion was like the heart of a lotus, she was golden-colored; therefore, she received the name Uppalavaṇṇā." The phrase "complexion like a blue lotus" indicates a golden complexion. In the world, because it is said, "Fair like a lotus is praised," and because it is said, "That golden-colored woman, with a complexion like a lotus and a golden waist, lives in heaven as my attendant," a golden complexion is praised among women. There is also a variant reading: "yāvassā naṃ andhakāraṃ." One who is not smeared by the defilement of sensual desires (kilesa-kāma) in the objects of sensual desire (vatthu-kāma) [him I call a Brahmin].

69. Itthilingaṃ pātubhūtaṃ means the appearance of the female form. This occurs through the disappearance of the male faculty (purisindriya) and the appearance of the female faculty (itthindriya). The same applies to the appearance of the male faculty. By this, just as the male faculty does not arise for Brahmas, but only...
113:
Only the appearance of a man arises. Just as for some eunuchs (paṇḍaka), a male appearance arises even without the male faculty (purisindriya), it is shown that it is not like that for them (those whose sex changes). That female faculty (itthindriya) or male faculty (purisindriya), when disappearing, vanishes starting from the 17th thought-moment in reverse order, like those who are dying. When the current faculty has ceased, the other dissimilar faculty (visabhāgaindriya) appears. Since it is said that the dissimilar faculty appears only when one has fallen into a deep sleep, it is stated: "while fallen asleep during the night part."

According to the words, "Monks, I allow that very preceptor, that very ordination," the preceptors and teachers of ordination who have arisen are indeed bhikkhunīs. Therefore, a question arises: should this [transformed] monk always go to the bhikkhunīs' quarters in the evening and morning to perform the duties toward the preceptor and the teacher? And should those bhikkhunīs come to this monk's monastery to perform the duties of a co-resident (saddhivihārika), etc.? By the words, "Monks, I allow [him] to associate with bhikkhunīs," it is intended to show the separation [from monks]. It should be understood that the statement "Monks, I allow that very preceptor," etc., is meant only to show that there is no need to take a preceptor again, nor to undergo ordination again.

In that context, "to associate with bhikkhunīs" means I allow being together with bhikkhunīs only, while being apart from male monks. Therefore, by this Pali implication, the commentary statement "there is no offense for her due to [traveling] between villages, etc." is established. One can come and associate. Based on the traveling allowed by the Blessed One, how could there be an offense due to reasons such as [traveling] between villages? Since the Blessed One does not urge one toward an offense, that statement is quite appropriate.

Otherwise, according to the Pali statement "those offenses of monks which are not common to bhikkhunīs, by those offenses there is no offense," it would follow that there is no exemption from offenses for [traveling] between villages, etc. If it is argued: "Since it is not stated: 'those offenses of monks which are not common to bhikkhunīs, and those offenses of traveling between villages, crossing a river, staying away for a night, or being left behind by the group while associating with bhikkhunīs, by those offenses there is no offense,' then it must be a common offense and thus an offense is incurred"—[the answer is:] it was not stated so because of the risk of an undesirable implication (aniṭṭhappasaṅga). The meaning is that it was not stated that way because it might lead to the undesirable conclusion that even for her who has moved with the bhikkhunīs, if she leaves them and associates with others, there would always be no offense for [traveling] between villages, etc.

In the case of offenses such as [traveling] between villages, even if one transgresses intentionally at that time, there is no offense (anāpatti) because of the reason of the appearance of the [new] gender. It should be understood that one is said to "emerge" (vuṭṭhāti) precisely because of not incurring the offense. Similarly, a practitioner (yogī)...
114:
...just as a practitioner (yogāvacara) extinguishes defilements that have not yet arisen; or just as a bowl without a binding is called "a bowl with fewer than five bindings"; or just as the training is not renounced if one does not announce it at all; in the same way here, even an offense not yet reached is said to be "emerged from" (vuṭṭhita).

However, since that [transformed] bhikkhunī, although not incurring the offense of lying down together (sahaseyya) with a man, is able to associate with bhikkhunīs, the commentary says "the offense of sahaseyya occurs for both" considering it as no offense [in the other sense]. It is said in the Parivāra: "In four other ways also, one incurs an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual, due to the appearance of the [new] gender." The statement in the Parivāra, "one who is incurring an offense emerges, and one who is emerging incurs an offense," should be understood as referring to both: incurring [offenses like] sahaseyya and emerging from uncommon offenses.

A monastery four or five hundred [bow-lengths] away from a village is called a distant monastery. For a bhikkhunī entering a village starting from the outermost monastery, it means there is an offense of traveling between villages (gāmantara). "Saṃvidahanaṃ parimocetvā" means without making an arrangement for a long-distance journey. "Tā kopetvā" means having abandoned those bhikkhunīs. According to the statement "even by a novice of full years [twenty]," it seems there is no taking of a preceptor for a novice who is not of full years. "Placed after performing a Vinaya act" means placed after performing a formal assignment (vikappanā). It should be understood that items placed without vikappanā become forfeitable (nissaggiya) after ten days have passed.

The statement "it is allowable for seven days after receiving again" is said according to the word: "Monks, I allow monks to consume [provisions] after having them received by bhikkhunīs." "By relinquishing without expectation" means either by relinquishing the object without expectation or by receiving it with the thought "I will consume it after receiving it again." If the gender changes again while practicing the half-month penance (pakkhamānatta), only the six-day penance (mānatta) should be given. If it is due to an offense not concealed during the time of being a monk, the teacher's view is that mānatta is given; if it is not due to a concealed offense, it is not given.

The statement that there is no granting of probation (parivāsa) should be understood as being said because concealment of an offense is not possible for a bhikkhunī. If a bhikkhunī incurs an uncommon Pārājika offense and then obtains the male gender, she does not receive ordination (upasampadā) among monks, but she receives the going-forth (pabbajjā). That person, remaining in the state of a monk without re-ordaining, does not produce the offense of sahaseyya. If the male gender appears to a bhikkhunī who has disrobed, she does not receive ordination among monks; it is a Pārājika. If the female gender appears to a layman who has not disrobed but is a defiler of a bhikkhunī, she never receives ordination among bhikkhunīs.
115:
Furthermore, it should be understood that if a change of gender occurs, the status of a monk is not obtained [in the context of a nun becoming a man then disrobing]. When a nun undergoes a change of gender, she becomes a monk. If that monk, after disrobing and returning to lay life, regains the female gender, she can receive ordination among the nuns again, because she did not reach the state of pārājika in either previous state (as a nun or as a monk). A nun who has completed twelve years of seniority and regains the male gender is indeed an ordained monk. If he disrobes and returns, he should not be ordained [as a monk] because he has not completed twenty years of age [as a male]. If the gender changes again to female, she can receive ordination among the nuns.

In this way, it is said that a twelve-year-old girl who changes gender to a male and then back to a female should be ordained as a nun since she has completed twelve years. If a nun reaches the state of a pakkha-paṇḍaka (half-month neuter) due to the disappearance of the female gender, or a monk due to the disappearance of the male gender, that nun should not be expelled (nāsana) by the nuns, nor the monk by the monks, because of the possibility of returning to their original state. The statement 'a paṇḍaka should be expelled' refers to a natural (pakati) paṇḍaka. A pakkha-paṇḍaka should only be expelled from communal living (saṃvāsa-nāsana), whereas the other [natural paṇḍaka] should be expelled by both types of expulsion (ubhaya-nāsana) [from the Saṅgha and communal living].

If they return to their original state, the legal procedure 'Monks, I allow her to associate with the nuns with that same preceptor, that same ordination, and those same years of seniority' is applicable. If another gender appears, the rule that offenses shared by monks and nuns can be rehabilitated in the presence of nuns, while unshared offenses do not constitute an offense, is also applicable. Regarding the statement in the Parivāra: 'With the acquisition [of the new gender], one abandons the former and stands in the latter; intimations (viññatti) subside, and designations (paññatti) cease,' our teacher holds that this refers to the aforementioned procedure.

When the female or male gender disappears, does it disappear taking the whole body with it, or does only the gender itself disappear? Here, if it disappears taking the whole body, that person would have passed away (cuta). Therefore, they would fall from their status, and if ordained again, they would be an opapātika (spontaneously born) monk. If only the gender itself disappears, that would contradict the nature (bhāva) of the person. In reality, the female faculty (itthindriya) and so on pervade the entire body. Therefore, their disappearance should be understood like momentary cessation (khaṇa-nirodha). Thus, it should be understood that the aforementioned faults do not apply. Just as when the light of one of several intermingled lamps is extinguished, the light of the others remains in that place, so too the rest of the body remains in that place.
116:
71-2. Whether [semen] is emitted or not, it is only a dukkaṭa (offense of wrongdoing) because of the absence of lust for emission. 'Beyond one's scope' (avisaya) means that in such a situation, it is difficult not to take pleasure. What is called sexual intercourse (methuna-dhamma) is accomplished by the effort of both parties, as it is said, 'it is the union of a pair.' Therefore, do not make an effort; if you do not make an effort, there will be no offense for you. This means this training rule is one of action (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna). Because of the words, 'Monk, you have fallen into a pārājika offense,' although this training rule is also one of non-action (akiriya), it is generally established as being called 'action' (kiriya).

73-4. It is said: 'For one who, out of fear of a pārājika offense, performs insertion etc. only in open space, if the organ accidentally touches the palate or the side, it is only a dukkaṭa.' Why? Because it is not due to sexual lust; this point should be investigated. The exterior of the teeth is like the exterior of the lips, being a basis for a thullaccaya (grave offense), as it is said: 'There is a thullaccaya for the tongue and the teeth protruding outside.' By the words 'having made that person unconscious,' it is shown that the person is one with a distracted mind (khittacitta). If a person who is not unconscious takes pleasure in the perception of the movement of elements in their own organ, they belong to the side of the unconscious because of the absence of the perception of intercourse (methuna-saññā); thus, a semblance of no offense is seen for them. If one takes pleasure while knowing, 'I think this is the intercourse of some non-human,' there is indeed an offense. 'The sexual intercourse of a paṇḍaka' means in the anus or the mouth of a paṇḍaka; the genitive case here has the sense of location (locative). Even for one who does not feel [pleasure], there is an offense by virtue of the intent to associate, just as in associating on a rug.

In the case of the 'impaired faculty' (upahatindriya), there are two readings: 'They informed [the Buddha] of this matter' and 'He informed.' Among them, the reading 'They informed' is better because of the statement, 'Monks, did he feel [pleasure]?' Otherwise, it should have been said, 'Monk, you have committed an offense.' It is said that the island-dwellers [of Sri Lanka] read it as 'vediyā vā.' The preliminary efforts (pubba-payoga) of sexual intercourse are grabbing the hand and so on; therefore, it should be connected with the preceding phrase, 'there is only a dukkaṭa for him.' Since there is only a dukkaṭa for him, it should be understood that as long as the person does not reach the 'head' (sīsaṃ), they remain in the dukkaṭa. 'Head' means the insertion into the tract. In another gaṇṭhipada (glossary), it is said: 'As long as one does not reach the head, a pārājika does not occur, and one remains in the dukkaṭa of preliminary effort.'
117:
It is written (in another Gaṇṭhipada): In the phrase "uccālingapāṇaka-daṭṭhena," it should be understood that the suffix 'ta' is used in the sense of 'bhāva' (state). The three words 'daṭṭha', 'daṃsa', and 'khādana' are identical in meaning.

76-7. This monk is like a brave man fighting on the front line of a battlefield; therefore, he is called "a monk who is like a warrior on the battlefield." A door closed with a wooden pin is called 'rukkhasūcidvāra'. A door closed with one or many thorns is called 'kaṇṭakadvāra' (thorn-door). A cloth door and a curtain door are called 'dussasāṇidvāra'. Everything mentioned as "kilañjasāṇī" etc., is also included under 'dussasāṇiya' (cloth curtain). Because it is similar to one, it is called "eka". 'Ākāsatala' means 'hammiyatala' (open space/terrace).

The phrase "This is the summary here" is said with reference to what is about to be explained. Because it is said, "They are sitting while doing something," it is said that asking permission from those who are lying down is not proper. Although it is said without distinction that "the monk who does not rise according to the designated time incurs an offense," what is intended there is only the dukkhaṭa offense of disrespect (anādariya-dukkhaṭa). How is this known? It is known because it is said, "A monk who sleeps with the door open at night and rises when the dawn breaks incurs no offense," and because it is specifically stated in the Mahāpaccariya that "he is not exempt even from the anādariya-dukkhaṭa." By saying this, it implies that he is exempt from other dukkhaṭa offenses (resulting from sleeping during the day).

In the statement "the monk who does not rise according to the designated time incurs an offense," it does not refer to the anādariya-dukkhaṭa. By using the restrictive term "yathāparicchedam-eva" (only according to the designated time), it means that no offense is incurred within the designated time. Again, it is stated as a final decision, as in the case of "one who is asleep." The phrase "one who sleeps in this way" refers only to the dukkhaṭa offense incurred at the time of lying down; therefore, it means that two dukkhaṭa offenses are incurred by a monk who does not rise according to the designated time.

In the Andhaka Commentary (Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā) also, it is said: "If one lies down at night without closing the door, thinking 'I will rise during the day,' he incurs a dukkhaṭa offense due to disrespect." Here too, it should be understood because it says "lies down" and does not say "rise when the dawn breaks." Some teachers say, "In the Mahāpaccariya, it is said with reference only to the anādariya-dukkhaṭa, not the dukkhaṭa mentioned in the Commentary."

The statement "that monk incurs no offense" is said because, in essence, he is not lying down. They say: "If one is sleeping at night with the door closed, and someone opens the door at dawn, the monk who sleeps without attending to the door etc., certainly incurs an offense. Why? Because it is the field of offense (āpatti-khetta)."

Because a person possessed by a yakkha is like an unconscious person and is called one with a deranged mind (khittacitta), he has no offense (anāpatti) even for a pārājika offense, let alone for others. Therefore, the statement in the Mahāpaccariya that "even a monk who is unconscious like one possessed by a yakkha is not exempt"...
118:
...is said with the meaning that if one previously lies down during the day with the intention to sleep and later becomes possessed by a yakkha or becomes unconscious, he is not exempt because the offense was already incurred at the moment of the preliminary effort (payoga) of lying down. In the statement "Only one who is tied up and made to lie down is exempt," it does not apply only to those possessed by a yakkha etc.; even a monk who is tied up and made to lie down is exempt as long as he himself does not have the desire to sleep.

When he becomes weary and has the desire to sleep, he should sleep only after having the door closed, or having someone guard it, or by applying mindfulness (ābhoga). Otherwise, he incurs an offense. If there is no compatible person (sabhāga), or if he does not see anyone nearby, or if he is unable to go, and after enduring for a long time, he eventually falls asleep without mindfulness because he is oppressed by pain (vedanāṭṭa), then according to the word "There is no offense for one oppressed by pain," he incurs no offense. For him, an offense is not apparent because it is beyond his control (avisaya). For one who sleeps only in a state of unconsciousness, an offense is not apparent according to the word "There is no offense for one with a deranged mind."

However, the teachers do not say this; they do not say "no offense is apparent" without distinction. If one sleeps without regaining consciousness (sati-saññā), no offense is apparent because he is not under his own control (avasa-vatta). If he regains consciousness but sleeps while consenting to the sleep because his body is weary, the teachers say that he certainly incurs an offense because the state of not being under his own control is not apparent. This is the meaning.

In the view of Elder Mahāpaduma (Mahāpaduma-ttheravāda), one possessed by a yakkha and one with a deranged mind are exempt. The meaning is that one who is tied up and made to lie down is also exempt because of the lack of desire to sleep and because of being oppressed by pain. In this way, the Pāḷi, the Commentaries, and the Theravāda are in agreement. Therefore, the Teacher says, "It is our view that only this meaning of various decisions is appropriate."

In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said that neither one possessed by a yakkha nor one who is unconscious is exempt. The meaning is that such a monk is capable of falling into a pārājika offense because he regains consciousness at intervals.

If it is asked, "According to the words of the Kurundī, 'or one who is tied up and made to lie down,' does even one who lies on one side not get exempt?" He is indeed exempt. Why? Because in essence, he is not sleeping. The Kurundī view and the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā view are in agreement. Why? Because of the commonality of not being under one's own control. Even if they agree, the teachers do not say so. To show that not only those teachers but also Elder Mahāpaduma does not say so, it is stated "by Elder Mahāpaduma" (Mahāpadumattherena). In the view of Elder Mahāpaduma, it is also said, "One who is possessed by a yakkha is incapable of falling into a pārājika offense."

In that view, the teachers say: "Because it is said, 'If one who is falling asleep, even without knowing, places his feet on the couch, he certainly incurs an offense,' for a monk who falls down and sleeps in that very place without rising, whether he knows at intervals or not, the offense..."
119:
In order to show the combined statements mentioned in all the commentaries, it is said: "In this Dispensation, who is released from an offense and who is not?" Whether one is possessed by a yakkha or has become unconscious, it is not only that they are capable of falling into a Pārājika; every monk [in such states] falls into an offense. Thus, regarding the statement "Only a monk who is tied up and made to lie down is released," they do not say "no offense is apparent" for that monk (who is tied up with creepers and made to lie down) because he is also unable to follow his own will. Since he is not one of those who are insane, mentally deranged, or oppressed by pain, they say "it is indeed an offense." All these words, it is said, were not included in the Council (Saṅgīti). Because it is said, "He consents to the insertion [of the organ]," etc., some say it is also a non-action (akiriya); that statement should not be accepted. It is stated in the Anu-gaṇṭhipada that whenever he consents, at that moment even a subtle intimation (viññatti) indeed occurs; therefore, in this [first Pārājika], it is only an action (kiriya).

## The Commentary on the First Pārājika is Finished.

## 2. Second Pārājika

## Explanation of the Dhaniya Story

In the second Pārājika, the name "Rājagaha" is acquired because it is possessed only by kings. The meaning is that [the Buddha] was dwelling in the four residences on the Gijjhakūṭa mountain near the city of Rājagaha, which has the locative case ending obtained in the sense of proximity and location. The connection of that word "Rājagahe" should be understood with the words "vassaṃ upagacchiṃsu" (entered the rains retreat). Only three monks, having set aside the motion (ñatti), perform a group act (gaṇakamma); those fewer than three or more than three (i.e., four monks) do not perform it because it would not be a valid act. In this regard, this miscellaneous method should be understood for the sake of proficiency in the acts of the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual according to the Vinaya method. There is an act of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma) that only the Saṅgha performs, not the group or the individual; setting aside a portion of the characteristics of the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma), the other four types of acts should be understood as such. There is an act of the Saṅgha that the Saṅgha performs, the group performs, and the individual performs. What is it? It is the act previously established. For it is said in the Parivāra Commentary: "In whatever monastery two or three persons dwell, the act performed by them sitting in harmony is just like an act performed by the Saṅgha itself. However, in whatever monastery there is only one monk, the agreement (katikavatta) made by that monk who is seated after performing the preliminary duties and preliminary works on the Uposatha day is also just like an act performed by the Saṅgha itself." Again, it is said, "In a monastery with a single monk..."
120:
...even if it is made known by a single person, the previously made agreement is indeed settled. There is a group act (gaṇakamma) that is performed by the Saṅgha, performed by the group, and performed by the individual. That act is performed by three types of Pārisuddhi-uposatha in the presence of others; it should be understood by way of that. There is a group act that only the group performs, not the Saṅgha or the individual; that act is performed by way of mutual announcement (ārocana) of the Pārisuddhi-uposatha; it should be understood by way of that. There is an individual act (puggalakamma) that only the individual performs, not the Saṅgha or the group; that should be understood by way of the Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha. There is a group act that only a certain group performs and another does not; therein, two persons perform the act without a motion (aññattika), not three. Only three persons perform the act with a motion (saññattika), not fewer or more than that. Therefore, it is said: "Only three persons, having set aside the motion, perform a group act; because if fewer or more than that, the act is not valid (akiriya)." Therefore, by the Vinaya method, only three persons are called "Sambahula" (a group); it should be understood that it does not refer to more than that.

In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "Although only three persons perform the characteristics of the act, because it is said that the act performed by them is like one performed by the Saṅgha, by one method, three persons are also called Saṅgha by the Vinaya method." All this is said with reference to Vinaya acts. But with reference to gains (lābha), even at minimum one person or even an unordained person (novice) is counted as "Saṅgha," it is said. Immediately after the dawn of the Pavāraṇā day, they are called "those who have completed the rains retreat" (vutthavassa). By the method of excellence (ukkaṃsa), it is said "starting from the first day of the waning moon (paṭipada)." For that reason, it is said "those who have performed Pavāraṇā with the Mahāpavāraṇā." Otherwise, those who could not perform Pavāraṇā due to an obstacle would not be called "vutthavassa."

Pillars and such should be understood as woodwork (kaṭṭhakamma). Some people place a small wooden pillar inside and make a pillar made of clay. This Venerable Dhaniya, however, did not do so; therefore, it is said "having made a hut entirely of clay." He made it with red clay mixed with oil.

"May the later generations not fall into the killing of living beings"—by this secondary rule (Anuddesa-sikkhāpada), it is shown that a monk, knowing that living beings will die, must not even speak unallowable speech (akappiya-vacana) in such matters as baking bricks, baking bowls, making a hut, having a monastery built, undertaking new construction, repairing broken or dilapidated parts, sweeping the monastery, providing fire, or having wells and ponds dug. For that very reason, without speaking in a roundabout way (pariyāya), it is said in the section on non-offenses (anāpatti-vāra) of those training rules: "There is no offense for one who is unmindful or for one who does not know." This training rule is also named "Antarāpatti-sikkhāpada." By this statement, "Go, monks, and destroy that hut," it is also established that there is indeed a dukkaṭa offense for those who, having obtained a clay hut made by another, dwell therein. Otherwise...
121:
If the Blessed One had permitted [living in a mud hut made by another], he would not have ordered it to be demolished. This principle applies to breaking, cutting, and uprooting; there is only a difference in the type of offense. For this reason, in the training rules concerning breaking and so forth, it is not stated: "If one obtains and uses that which was made by another [exceeding the measurement], there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)." Likewise, it is clear that making it for another or for the sake of a shrine (cetiya) and so forth is merely an offense of wrongdoing. Otherwise, as in the Kuṭikāra training rule and others, he would have stated the method: "Except for a dwelling for another, there is no offense in all cases," and he would not have ordered it to be demolished.

However, if one removes the state of being entirely made of mud and uses it after mixing it with wood, stone, and so forth, there is no offense. Indeed, in the Chedanaka training rule and others, the Blessed One gave the method: "Having obtained that which exceeds the measurement made by another, one uses it after cutting it down," and so forth.

Some teachers, however, say: "By the word 'vayakamman' (expenditure of labor/cost), it includes that which is caused to be made by giving payment; therefore, it is clear that it is not allowable even if made by another." This statement is not sound. Why? Because even for one who buys the building materials and builds it himself, there is the possibility of expenditure. Or else, if there is a hint in the Pali, the method of the commentary's hint should be followed.

In the passage "A hut made in the form of a brick house (giñjakāvasatha) is allowable," a dwelling built by laying natural bricks is called a giñjakāvasatha. Such a dwelling is not called "mud-made" but is called a "brick hut" (iṭṭhaka-kuṭi). Therefore, the teacher [Ānanda] does not hold the view that a hut made of mud mixed with chaff, cow dung, grass, or dry leaves, or a hut made of unbaked bricks, should be called "entirely mud-made." This is because chaff and such are added only for the purpose of strengthening the mud. A hut made of unbaked bricks also does not fall under the category of a brick house (giñjakāvasatha). Moreover, the Venerable Dhaniya did not finish that hut all at once as a potter finishes a pot; rather, he finished it by laying mud lumps after drying them step by step. Like a hut made of unbaked bricks, an entirely mud-made hut is monolithic (joined as one). A hut made of baked bricks is not like that. Therefore, some say that [the brick hut] is allowable.

If one builds a grass hut or similar outside an entirely mud-made hut and lives inside, it is still an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If one makes holes here and there and ties them to make it one piece, it is allowable. If one builds a grass hut or similar inside and lives inside, it is allowable. If the builder himself lives there, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing due to the act of making, not due to the act of living. If it is plastered with lime (sudhā) inside, outside, or on both sides, it is allowable. Since an entirely mud-made hut is easy to break, the bowl, robes, and other items placed there are not secure and can be stolen by thieves. Therefore, it was said [in the commentary], "for the purpose of securing the bowl and robe."
122:
## Commentary on the Decisions not found in the Pali

At that time, the group of six monks (Chabbaggiya) carried various types of bowls and various types of bowl-stands. Based on these incidents, the Buddha laid down a rule: "O monks, various types of bowls should not be carried. For the monk who carries them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." In this manner, the offense of wrong-doing was also prescribed for unallowable requisites. Why? Because they are similar to those unallowable bowls. Even in cases where it is not explicitly prescribed, such as "O monks, various types of umbrellas should not be carried; for the monk who carries them, there is an offense of wrong-doing," an offense of wrong-doing can occur. Therefore, starting with the phrase "This is a decision not found in the Pali (Pāḷimuttaka)," it should be understood that the commentator stated "it is not allowable" to indicate that making any requisite smooth and ornate (vaṇṇamaṭṭha) or modified with special designs (savikāra) entails an offense of wrong-doing.

In this matter, an objector asks: "The Buddha allowed all ironware except weapons; all woodenware except long chairs, couches, wooden bowls, and wooden sandals; and all earthenware except the polished bronze-colored ones and those made by potters. Therefore, except for those excluded items, are not all iron, wood, and earthenware allowable without distinction, whether they are smooth and ornate or modified with designs?" This statement is not appropriate because it contradicts the aforementioned Pali. Therefore, the Pali starting with "except weapons" is an allowance based on the type of material (jāti), while the aforementioned Pali is a prohibition based on the modification (vikāra) such as being smooth and ornate. Thus, both do not contradict each other. Therefore, it should be noted only as stated. 'Āraggena' means with the tip of a lathe-chisel. According to the method stated in the phrase "as a mustard seed on the tip of a needle (āragge)," it refers to a mark made with the tip of a needle or a lathe-chisel.

'Paṭṭamukhe' means at the edge or border of the robe. 'Pariyante' means at the end of the robe. 'Veṇimutuṅgiyaṃ' refers to sewing in a tube-like pattern. 'Agghiyaṃ' (or Akkhiyaṃ) refers to sewing in the shape of a cetiya (pagoda). 'Gayamuggaraṃ' refers to sewing in the shape of a balance-beam or a mallet. A 'gayā' is a bamboo stick that is thin at the base and thick at the tip. 'Ukkiranti' means they take out, they make, or they place. 'Koṇasuttapiḷakā' refers to thread-knots or beads made of thread at the corners, such as the corners of a waistband. In this context, for whichever robe or bowl is said to be "not allowable," it should be understood that the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and the formal sharing (vikappanā) of those items are not valid.

'Deḍḍubho' refers to a water snake. 'Acchi' refers to the elephant's eye pattern. 'Gomuttakaṃ' refers to zigzag lines in the shape of a cow's urine path. Since a key (kuñcikā) is a requisite for the monastery, there is a view that it is allowable even if made of gold or silver; however, because of the statement "making a key smooth and ornate is not allowable," only keys made of other allowable metals are permitted, as they are portable requisites. 'Ārakaṇṭako' is a type of curved knife used for piercing palm leaves and such. 'Āmaṇဍakasārako' is said to be a container made from the jujube fruit.

It is stated that making palm-leaf fans and similar items smooth and ornate is allowable. Although they are portable items like keys, they are not included in the Pali prohibition of "not carrying various items." Specifically, the Buddha allowed them with the phrase, "O monks, I allow a fan made of palm leaf." In the Ganthipada, it is said that making oil tubes smooth and ornate is allowable because they are monastery requisites. 'Rājapallabhā' refers to monks who are favorites of the king. Here, it refers to the land and the Sīmā (consecrated boundary). In the Anu-ganthipada, it is stated that others should not establish a Sīmā on land owned by certain people. Only the monks who own the land or the Sīmā should be the ones to prohibit it. It is said that monks who establish a Sīmā on another's land have no authority to prohibit others. However, the Commentary states that they should be prohibited from doing so to prevent potential schisms in the Sangha (saṅghabheda).

The Commentary on the Decisions not found in the Pali is finished.
123:
Some teachers say: "In the case of palm-leaf fans and the like, making them smooth and polished is allowable." Although these fans are to be carried like keys (kuñcikā), it is stated so because there is no prohibition saying "various (high-grade) fans should not be carried." Specifically, regarding those fans, the Buddha said: "Monks, I allow a fan and a palm-leaf fan," and so forth (in the Cūḷavagga). In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: "In oil containers, making them smooth and polished is allowable because they are requisites for the lodging (senāsanaparikkhāra)."

Rājavallabha refers to those who are close to the royal household (confidants of the king). Here, sīmā refers to the desired ground and the bound boundary (baddhasīmā). "The boundary belongs to those whose property the land is; others should not perform [acts] there," is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada. Some say: "If the land and the boundary are the property of certain people, only they have the right to prohibit [others]; those who have established a boundary on another's land have no authority to prohibit." It is known that the Andhakaṭṭhakathā says: "Because it is a cause for a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda) and so forth, it should certainly be prohibited, saying 'Do not do it.'"

86-7. Regarding the meaning of "to build a small wooden hut," there are variant readings as 'kātuṃ' and 'kattuṃ'. 'Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ' should be understood like large and small fruits (phalāphala). Considering that the word "command" is usually used in undesirable matters, he commanded the binding. 'Issariyamattāya' is intended to show that the word 'mattā' exists in the sense of fulfillment (samiddhi).

There is also a reading: "Having spoken such words." Does this speech, "You have escaped by a single hair; do not do such a thing again," indicate anger (byāpāda)? Would this speech, which indicates a mass of greed even toward wood, be appropriate for that king who is a Sotāpanna? One might argue: "Should he not have invited them, saying, 'Venerable sir, what was done before was well done; please speak again of what you need,' and thereby generated great joy and rapture (pītipāmojja)?" This is true; being a Sotāpanna, he is one who dearly loves the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Therefore, being unable to tolerate the monks doing what is unallowable, and wishing to provide an occasion for the laying down of a training rule (sikkhāpada), he spoke thus even though he was pleased in his heart, thinking, "My wood has been well utilized." In such a context, "in accordance with the words that have arrived" means that when other words, or fewer words than these, arrive, they should be applied accordingly; so it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada. The Anugaṇṭhipada states: "Not only in this training rule, but they also appear in other training rules; therefore, the application should be understood in accordance with the words that have arrived in those respective places." The meaning of the reproach is solely due to taking what was not given; they reproached.

The Rudradāmaka coin is a coin produced by King Rudradāmaka and others. In cities like Vārāṇasī, the Nīlakahāpaṇas are those produced by various kings in accordance with ancient treatises and endowed with proper characteristics. It is said that a Rudradāmaka is worth about one-third of those Nīlakahāpaṇas; therefore...
124:
One pāda (a quarter) of that coin is the basis for a grave offense (thullaccaya). Here, the māsaka is not the standard. At certain times, a kahāpaṇa is less than twenty māsakas; at other times, it is more than twenty māsakas. Therefore, a portion of about five māsakas, or more than five māsakas, or less than five māsakas, which is one-fourth of that kahāpaṇa, should be understood as a pāda. To clarify this meaning, it was said: "At that time in Rājagaha, one kahāpaṇa was twenty māsakas," and so forth. That kahāpaṇa may be made of silver, gold, or copper. As in Suvaṇṇabhūmi, where the pāda is also made only of copper, the teachers say that very copper pāda is indeed a pāda. Some say that since a pāda is worth one-fourth of one Nīlakahāpaṇa, only one-fourth of that pāda should be [the measure of] a pāda. This statement is not appropriate. If only one-fourth of the goods worth a pāda were the basis for a Pārājika offense (it would be too little). If the goods worth a pāda are the basis for a Pārājika offense, then the statement "That pāda itself is the final basis for a Pārājika offense" is established. In all places, they do not take goods and value them only by the Nīlakahāpaṇa standard. Since they value them only by the standard of the kahāpaṇa of each respective region, it should be noted that the pāda of each respective region is indeed the pāda, and goods equal to that value are goods worth a pāda. Some say: "That pāda is only by the power of the ancient Nīlakahāpaṇa, not by the power of other coins, and only in places where Nīlakahāpaṇas are used," but this should be accepted only after careful investigation.

## Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā
The phrase "from a village or from a forest" is mentioned at the beginning of the first primary regulation because it is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) that marks the location of the basis for a Pārājika offense. A village from which people have departed is called an uninhabited village (amanussagāma). It is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: "It is allowable to enter an uninhabited village without wearing the outer robe and without asking permission to enter the village." Some say: "If people have departed from a village while intending to return, it is not allowable to enter that village in this manner." Other teachers say: "Even if it is a village possessed by yakkhas, it is called a 'village' only if shops and so forth are clearly present; if they are not clearly present, there is no offense in entering." They say that if "gāmūpacāra" is taken as a kammadhāraya compound, meaning "the village itself is the precinct (upacāra)," then what is said in the Kurundī-aṭṭhakathā and other commentaries is also well-said. It rejects the statement: "His house-precinct is called a village." The view of the teachers who say "The village precinct and the village are called gāmūpacāra" does not conflict with that kammadhāraya compound. They also say: "We do not reject the statement in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, 'The house is the house-precinct,' and so forth, which was said with reference to the characteristics of these gains and so on."
125:
In the word 'kataparikkhepo ca', it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada that the area of such extent around a house is called the precincts (upacāra). In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: 'Whichever Commentary-view (Aṭṭhakathāvāda) or Theravāda-view is mentioned later, this is said with reference to what follows from here, not with reference to what has passed. If it were said with reference to the past as well, it would follow that only the view of Elder Mahāpaduma is the standard; therefore, the teachers say it is said only with reference to what follows.' The word 'sesampi' means that the characteristics of the village precincts (gāmūpacāra) should also be taken.

In the phrase 'tatrāyaṃ nayo', this following method is the way to understand that village precinct. Regarding the phrase 'vikāle gāmāpavesanādīsu', it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada: 'Entering a village [at the wrong time] should be requested only outside.' It is said that this statement does not agree with the Commentary. My opinion is that if it is taken as referring to the precinct reckoned as the village, it can be consistent.
