By the word 'ādi', the Gaṇṭhipada states it means taking vessels and such that are containers for gains given to those staying in the house. The Anugaṇṭhipada states that a Pārājika offense is incurred by monks who, knowing of the gains that should be received by those in the village precincts, intentionally do not give them. Although it should not be called a 'pamādalekhā' (clerical error) because it was stated in the Kurundī and other commentaries in accordance with the words spoken in the Pāḷi, the decision stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā has come down since the time of the Council. The teachers of the Commentaries in the island of Sīhaḷa called the passage 'That which is in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā' etc., as the 'viniścayanaya' (method of decision). By the phrase 'should be demarcated only by a stone's throw', only the area worthy of being enclosed is shown, not the precincts. Indeed, that village is demarcated by a stone's throw other than that [actual] form. By the specification 'in this Adinnādāna training rule', it means that in other training rules, it is otherwise. Or, by that specification, the meaning according to the literal word is also suitable here. By the words 'Abhidhamme pana' etc., it shows how the completion of the offense is achieved in other ways as well.

In the Gaṇṭhipada, it is stated: 'Even if one does not know "this is my property" when abandonment etc. has not been made, it is still property possessed by another, just like property that becomes the children's upon the death of the father; that property is included in what is not yet abandoned in meaning.' The ancient Gaṇṭhipada (Porāṇagaṇṭhipada) states: 'The act of a thief is theft (theyya); the goods that should be taken by a thief are theft (theyya); therefore, it is reckoned as theft (theyyasaṅkhāta).' Since that act of 'theyya' is the act of a thief, and that thief has the intent to steal (avaharaṇacitta), it is also suitable according to the method of those ancient teachers to extract the word 'theyyasaṅkhāta' and explain it as 'theyyacitta avaharaṇacitta' in the Padabhājanīya. Nevertheless, it should be taken only according to the method stated in the Commentary. The mind that arises in the preliminary stage as 'I will steal', and the mind that accomplishes going or touching etc. in the middle stage, and...
126:
...there is also the mind that accomplishes the effort of moving [an object] from its place (ṭhānācāvana-payoga). Among those three types of mind, the Anugaṇṭhipada states: 'Only this last portion of the mind is intended here; others say "theno" (the thief).' Regarding the intents to steal property worth less than a māsaka, a māsaka, a pāda, etc., it is stated that teachers say it is a single portion of the mind among the intents to steal.

## Pañcavīsatiavahārakathāvaṇṇanā

The so-called twenty-five ways of theft are different only by the distinction of words (grammar); in meaning, however, they are not different. In the phrase 'confusing and difficult to know the decision', they are difficult to know for those monks who have not fully grasped the decisions in the presence of teachers. They are confusing and difficult to know the decision like the Paṭṭhāna Pāḷi such as the Dukatikapaṭṭhāna. In fact, the teachers explain all those meanings and decisions of the Pāḷi without creating contradictions between the preceding and following, and without destroying the method that has come down since the Council; therefore, others also say, 'It is like the Paṭṭhāna Pāḷi.' 'Porāṇa' refers to the teachers of the Council. In this training rule, giving in this way is merely an act of respect. If one does not give, there is no offense; however, just as a monk who desires the training gives out of fear of Pārājika, so it should indeed be given. As for the cases (vatthu) found in these five groups, they were inserted into the Commentaries by the teachers in the island of Sīhaḷa with the consent of the Saṅgha and others. It is stated: 'For the benefit of fellow practitioners in the future, they were inserted even after the time they were committed to writing.' The effort by command (āṇattika-payoga) incurs the offense at the very moment of commanding. The effort that accomplishes the purpose (atthasādhaka-payoga) accomplishes the result even after a long time. With reference to the difference in time, this is the distinction between these two. 'Bhaṭṭha' means separated. 'Antarasamudde' means in the Aturumuhutta island in the middle of the ocean. 'Pharati' means accomplishes. 'Navadhota' means a newly made vessel. 'Pāsāṇasakkhara' refers to stone and gravel.

## Bhūmaṭṭhakathādivaṇṇanā

In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is stated as only a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) whether it is true or false. It should be understood that this statement is a clerical error (pamādalikhita), and it should be taken with logic at the present time. In taking it so, it should be understood that while it should have been said, 'Setting aside the four groups, it is allowable to perform all Saṅgha acts such as Upasampadā, Pavāraṇā, and Abbhāna,' they wrote 'Upasampadā, Pavāraṇā, Kathina, Abbhāna, etc.' The teachers explain such writing only as a 'pamādalekhā' (slip of the pen); therefore, it is called 'pamādalikhita'. It is stated that whichever word is false (musā), in that case, a Pācittiya offense occurs. Because there is no purpose in stating a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa), it is said 'in the preliminary effort of Adinnādāna'. In other training rules as well, if it is a case for Pācittiya in the preliminary effort, it is indeed a Pācittiya. In the word 'pamādalikhita'...
127:
In this context, if one takes only the intended meaning in this Bhūmaṭṭhakathā and considers it as "stated in the Commentary," it would seem consistent. However, the teachers say that after stating "a Pācittiya in a case of Pācittiya," although the Dukkaṭa should have been mentioned separately, it was stated generally as "whether it is true or not"; therefore, it should be understood as a "clerical error" (pamādalekha). Since it is stated that "there is no offense in going with a wholesome mind," it is like there being no offense through the words "I will also give alms."

In saying that one is not free from a Dukkaṭa in a case of Pācittiya, one incurs a Dukkaṭa offense along with the Pācittiya. When it is said that "offenses are many," a monk who incurs offenses by doing ten each of digging, scratching, and extracting is freed from those offenses by confessing ten Pācittiyas in the case of extraction. In terms of category (jāti), it is stated in the Kurundī that "one is freed by confessing only one," which is consistent with the earlier statement. Because "Dukkaṭa" is mentioned in the combined effort (payoga), it makes it known that many Dukkaṭa offenses occur due to the same effort. In the case of digging, when it is said "they are many," the offense does not subside because the effort is the same. Regarding the phrase "by taking the Commentary teacher as the standard," it means that just as in this second Pārājika, in other training rules as well, such statements found in the Commentaries should be accepted because they have been handed down since the time of the Council (Saṅgāyanā). The Elder Dhammasiri, however, reportedly said, "They should be taken only in this second Pārājika, not in other training rules." In the Gaṇṭhipada, it is stated, "The initial digging subsides when it reaches the subsequent digging; therefore, one is freed by confessing only one." Furthermore, it is stated, "When it reaches a different action, the preceding action subsides."

In this way, the displacement of a pot (kumbhi) situated in one place should also be understood through six aspects in this Bhūmaṭṭhakathā; this is how the connection should be understood. The word "kumbhiyā" is in the locative case (signifying place). When it is said that a person who lifts it upwards incurs a Pārājika if they release it from the ground even by a hair's breadth, this is consistent with the statement "displacement from a place should be understood through six aspects" if the part touching the rim of the pot is released from the opening. Without saying that, they firmly assert, "When it is released from the ground, if it passes even by a hair's breadth, it is said to be released from the ground." This point should be accepted after careful investigation. In this matter, some teachers state the meaning thus: "The one who digs first causes the remaining parts to be detached (from the earth); when that pot is released from the earth, a Pārājika occurs." The statement in the Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā, Mahāpaccarī-aṭṭhakathā, etc., is shown to be a clerical error (pamādalekha) by the words "making it reach into one's own vessel or cutting the handful."

Regarding the statement "a Pārājika occurs just by drinking," at the present time, in the phrase "the five types of consciousness have a basis that has arisen and an object that has arisen," it means "having a basis that has arisen and..."
128:
The commentary statement "rejecting the future" should be changed to "rejecting the past and the future" in consideration of the statement "having a non-confused basis, having a non-confused object, having a pre-arisen basis, having a pre-arisen object"; it should be understood that it is changed in such a manner. Indeed, the Commentary teachers do not speak words that are contradictory from beginning to end. That statement which the teachers have removed and rejected, saying "this is a clerical error" (pamādalikhita), and then speak and teach—that very statement is also rejected as a "clerical error" by this teacher (Venerable Buddhaghosa). And the Sutta which those teachers showed to reject it, this teacher also rejects it by showing that same Sutta; therefore, it is said, "That statement is in that very place..." and so on.

"It is stated only as no offense" means that it is neither theft nor grasping the neck, but simply that no offense occurs; this is said to show that the difference is only in phrasing (vyañjana) and not in meaning (attha). If one asks, "By whom were such clerical errors made?", the answer is that they were made by the scribes or authors of the various types of books mentioned previously; this method is the same in all cases. It is stated in the Anu-gaṇṭhipada that "it is not the case that the same mind, which by reason is not a Pārājika in many places, becomes a Pārājika in some specific place." In the case of "placing what is poorly placed," it is a Pārājika because it is done with the intention that "it will leak from there," thus referring to displacement from its place; whether one takes it or not, it should be understood from the words "breaks it," etc., in that very place. In another Gaṇṭhipada, it is stated, "In that very place, without moving it from its position and without the desire to move it, it should be known simply from the commentary word 'breaks'."

Likewise, others say, "One can take the moist earth from the leaking place, put it in water, cook it, and take it; therefore, it is said with reference only to the taking." The statement "one acts upon an empty pot, the goods must be compensated" contradicts the nature of a command (āṇatti); at the very time of the command which fulfills the meaning "whenever you are able, steal those goods," a Pārājika is incurred. Furthermore, stationary efforts (thāvara-payoga) such as digging a pit are also evidence here. Some teachers say that there are no Pārājika objects involving time-bound efforts (kālakata-payoga), and therefore it should be investigated. Wherever it is said "others" or "some," one should investigate thoroughly and accept what is appropriate, and discard the other. "They say" means the teachers say. "No, because the meaning should not be taken otherwise" is said for the purpose of explaining the Pali. The statement "thus some say" should not be accepted. Why? Because "discarding urine" and "making it unusable" are identical in meaning, and also because it is stated in the Commentary, "one strikes and breaks it with a hammer."
129:
Regarding the passage beginning with "Ayaṃ panettha sāro" (This is the essence here), Elder Dhammasiri said, "It is the command of our teacher." Some say, "It is the view of the Saṅgahācariyas (Compendium teachers)." The teachers mentioned previously are indeed those same teachers. Therefore, by the power of convention (vohāra), even if one does not wish to discard it, one who acts in such a way is called "one who discards." Thus, the meaning of these words should be understood. 

In this case, it aligns very well with the Commentary's statement: "Because there is no displacement from the place, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." In that Commentary statement, because there is no intention to displace from the place (ṭhānācāvana-citta), even if it moves from the place, it should be understood as "not displaced from the place." Alternatively, because there is no intention to steal (theyyacitta), even if one wishes to displace it from its place, the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is appropriate. 

For a monk who moves a naturally fallen peacock feather here and there, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). In the determination of objects situated in the air (ākāsaṭṭha-vinicchaya), it is said that this should be understood in order to avoid confusion regarding objects in the sky (vehāsa) and so on. The Ganthipada says, "Similarly, it should be understood in other matters connected with material things (āmisa)." By the statement "moving it without displacing it from its place," it means there is no grave offense (thullaccaya) in displacement. Some teachers say there are offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and grave offense (thullaccaya) for displacement or non-displacement even without causing movement. Some say, "Those teachers should be refuted by showing this Commentary statement: 'without displacing it from its place.'" This point should be investigated.

Cutting, releasing, etc., are said with reference to the upper part. It certainly causes it to reach the open space from its place. Here, some say, "It is said with reference to making an object reach the open space while it is on a bamboo pole with one end protruding." However, those teachers should be refuted by showing the Commentary statement: "If one moves the remainder here and there to protect it without cutting the base, [it is not a defeat]. But if one holds it with the hand and makes it reach the open space without removing it from the base, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika)."

"An object leaning against a wall" (bhittinissita): some say it refers to being supported by a wall. "Depending on a wall" refers to being placed on a wall-peg (nāgadanta) and so on. "Just upon cutting" refers to it rising and staying above. 

In the phrase "on the back of an object situated above," it refers to sliding it downwards. For one who slides it downwards, as soon as it passes the space situated below from the back of the upper object, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika). For one who lifts it upwards, as soon as it is free from the water, [there is an offense of defeat]. "In this way...
130:
It is said that if one takes it just as it is free from the water, it aligns with the statement in the Bhūma-aṭṭhakathā. The place where dead fish are situated is indeed their "place" (ṭhāna). For a monk who kills and takes [fish] with the intention to steal, if the value is less than a quarter-māsa, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); some teachers say there is no pācittiya offense because it is a simultaneous effort (sahappayoga). In the phrase "madanaphala-vasa" etc., the word "vasa" is in the Sinhalese language and means "poison"; or it refers to a fish kept in a basket made in the shape of a garuda.

It is just as previously stated in the example of a pig caught in a snare. There is also a variant reading: "In a boat placed on land, just the part not touching [the ground]." Because of the statement "because the wind comes," if the effort is made when there is no wind, it does not constitute theft (avahāra); if it is done when there is wind, it is indeed theft. If one asks, "To whom should the compensation for the goods be given?", the Anuganthipada says, "It should be given to those from whose hands the kahāpaṇas were taken, or to the boat owner if the boat owner has not yet taken the boat."

"Stepping on it from above" or "establishing a new one" means bringing about something new.

In the section on "situated in a village" (gāmaṭṭha), the definition "a village is..." is not stated because the characteristics of a village have already been fully described at the beginning. 

In the section on "situated in a forest" (araññaṭṭha), the definition "a forest is..." is stated again not because only the forest with previously mentioned characteristics is intended here, but to show that this forest is indeed possessed by others, and that such a forest is intended here. Therefore, the word "forest" is also taken in the sense. In the phrase "cut at the tip and at the base," it is said that they are not standing entwined, but it refers to a tree that will fall just upon being cut. "Carved and placed" refers to a tree carved and placed by others who obtained it from the forest owners. "Addhagata" means a tree that has been there for a long time. The Ganthipada says, "It should not be taken" means it should not be taken even by a monk who has been given permission by the forest owners. The phrase "it is covered with bark" shows the lack of concern (nirapekkhatā) of the owners. Therefore, it is said, "It is allowable to take it." If the owners still have concern (sāpekkhatā), it is not allowable. 

In that Water-section (Udaka-kathā), the Anuganthipada says, "Starting from 'in vessels, lotus ponds, and reservoirs,' the three or ten rounds are summarized by showing only the beginning."
131:
In the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is stated as 'saṅkhittā' (abbreviated). 'Nibbahana water' refers to the water that exits through an overflow gate for the purpose of protecting the tank. It is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada that 'because one does not have the right to take it, it is not a proper act (sāmīcikamma) of the owner.' From this point onwards, when 'vuttaṃ' (it is said) is mentioned, it should be understood as being stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada. 'Before the water comes out' is a textual ellipsis. The meaning is that because the effort (payoga) occurs in a dry canal, there is no liability for restitution (bhaṇḍadeyya). Since it was first stated that 'the tank is common to all' because the field was cultivated depending on the tank, this refers to that statement. Others say: 'Although the water in the tank is common to all, if there is a canal, it is not proper to take it by bypassing that canal; therefore, with reference to that canal water, it is stated in the Kurundī and other texts that there is theft (avahāra).' The teacher says that the statement in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is appropriate because the place common to all is that very tank, and because it is common to all and there is no agreement, it does not fit this characteristic.

It is said: 'From then on, even if one takes it with the intention to steal, there is no theft (avahāra).' Therefore, it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada that this tooth-stick belonging to the Saṅgha is neither the property of others nor the property of the Saṅgha, because it is something used by shaven-headed monks, there is no guardian, and it is common to all.

In the phrase 'stands straight,' it is said: 'If it slips slightly but stands straight because it is supported by nearby tree branches etc., it is theft (avahāra). If it falls like a cut bamboo, there is no offense.' This is well-said because in the decision regarding crops, it is stated: 'If they are guarding those things.' 'Not otherwise' means that if one clears the wind-path when the wind comes, it constitutes a pārājika offense.

The statement that there is no 'investigation' (vicāraṇā) in other texts means that since it is not rejected in those texts, this decision alone is final. It is said: 'By this decision, it is shown that there is no offense for a monk who, even after laying down the burden (dhuranikkhepa), demands and takes the goods brought by thieves.'

'In this same way' means a pārājika is incurred just by lifting it from its original place. Why? Because a mark common to other bowls is mentioned. 'According to the footstep' refers to a monk who goes taking the goods brought out by a thief. 'Village gate' is just a figure of speech; it means 'village' because it should be known according to the command. For both, a pārājika is incurred just by lifting it from its original place.
132:
By the words 'having gone to such-and-such a village,' this entire area up to the vicinity (upacāra) outside that village is the area commanded (by oneself). It is written: 'Whether standing, sitting, or resting, if one has calmed the previous intention to steal and does not put down the goods taken for the purpose of going, but carries them as they were taken, the decision is made according to the footsteps. If the goods are put down, the decision is made by lifting them.' When it is simply said 'it is written,' it should be taken from the Gaṇṭhipada. 'One who uses with the intention to steal' refers to one who, without moving it from its place, uses it by wearing or wrapping it with the thought, 'I took this robe previously.' It is written: 'If it is lost, there is liability for restitution (bhaṇḍadeyya).'

By the words 'or another person,' it is shown that if the person who placed it gives it, there is no offense, just like a garden-keeper giving it. In fact, other teachers say that in this case, there is only liability for restitution (bhaṇḍadeyya). Because of the words 'or another person,' it should be understood that the person who placed it can also get it. By the word 'or' (vā), if the person in whose hands it was placed gives it, it is like the accountant in Rājagaha giving to Venerable Dhaniya. Therefore, a pārājika is appropriate. At the moment of saying 'You have obtained a thick cloth,' a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to false speech (musāvāda). In the phrase 'having written his name,' it is said: 'Because he was commanded "Take and keep it," there is no offense at the time of writing the name; it is not like transferring a label (kusa-saṅkamana).'

'They do not know' means 'they do not hear.' If they know but do not accept it in their mind, it is the same way. If the one who knows does not wish to guard it, he must reject it; this duty (vatta) should be known. 'Ummaggena' means by a path made by digging an old hole.

Fellow monks give food to the attendant monk (nissitavārika). Therefore, it is said that it should be done just as the sequence in the monastery; they cannot fail to take the turn that has arrived. It is said: 'His fellow monks also cannot fail to give.' In the phrase 'to one who is with a second person,' the food brought by one person is not enough for two; to show that if it is enough, it should be provided, the words 'or to whom' etc. are said. It is written: '"Giving an interrogation" (paripucchā) means providing the answer to a question asked.' The burden of the Saṅgha is said to be 'only the teaching of the True Dhamma.' It is also said: 'One who manages new works (navakammika) is also meant.' It is written: 'The meaning of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā phrase "it rolls from this bundle and enters inside again" is explained by the Kurundī and Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā.'

In the phrase 'or in a moving vehicle,' Elder Upatissa reportedly says: 'This is said with reference to what is standing outside the customs house.' 'Or in a moving vehicle' etc...
133:
It is said, "It should be taken within the customs station." There is nothing to be said for one standing outside, because it is stated in the context (adhikāra) as "standing inside." This is appropriate: if goods placed on a vehicle etc. are carried away without his effort (payoga), it is not a Pārājika. If it is asked why compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya) is not required? It is because it is outside the customs station. For goods in the forest, it is said in the Commentary: "Even for one who passes by through lack of mindfulness, compensation is required," because those goods have an owner. But here (at the customs station), because of the words "of one who has entered here," it does not refer to one standing outside; for that is the customs boundary (suṅkasaṅketa). If one has another carry it, there is no offense because of the words "with one's own hand" in that context. Although the Commentary says "they become Nissaggiya," it is a Pācittiya; in carrying it past the precinct (upacāra), there is a Dukkaṭa offense because of the fault.

"One should go only after paying the tax at the customs station"—this is the basis (mātikā) of what is to be said now, says Elder Dhammasiri. "At the four gates of Anurādhapura, they collect taxes. Among them, the road in front of the South Gate, having circumambulated the Ānanda Cetiya from Thūpārāma, is situated near the inner wall of Jetavana Monastery; one who does not enter the village but enters the precinct (upacāra). One who goes to Rājavihāra having circumambulated the Mahācetiya from Thūpārāma does not enter (the precinct)"—so it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In this (evading customs), it is written: "By two clod-throws (leḍḍupāta), as brought down by the lineage of teachers." The phrase "two clod-throws" is appropriate if the boundary of the customs station is not fixed; if fixed, even if it exceeds a league (yojana), it is the customs station. Beyond that, the distance of two clod-throws should be taken as the precinct (upacāra). That precinct here is of two types: external and internal. Regarding that, referring to the external precinct called the second clod-throw, a Dukkaṭa is mentioned in the Pāḷi and the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Referring to the internal precinct, the Kurundī Commentary says [it is theft/Pārājika], which is not our preference (khanti). The teacher says: "The place designated as 'take the tax of one who enters here' is definitely the Pārājika field. If that place is enclosed, the distance of one clod-throw is the Dukkaṭa field. If it is not enclosed, the distance of the second clod-throw is [the Dukkaṭa field]—this is our meaning."

In the phrase "wealth increases at the place it has gone," it is written: "Compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya) is required for the thief along with the increase (vaḍḍhi)." If he promised "I will give that increase," it is said regarding one who does not perform the task as promised that it increases. In an undesignated area, it does not increase. They say: "Whatever wealth increases, for the thief who gives that wealth, not giving the increase results in a Pārājika."
134:
By name means calling by the name of a snake or by a name given by the owner.

In the inner grounds (antovatthu) of the royal house, "inner grounds" means the enclosed royal courtyard. For an elephant standing in an unenclosed royal courtyard, the "station" (ṭhāna) is the entire city. For an ox, it is said: "For one standing in an unenclosed place, the very spot stepped upon is the station." Thus, "khaṇḍadvāra" means a hole or breach broken by oneself. Regarding killing in that very place: "Since the object is the life-faculty, does a Pācittiya occur due to the intent to kill?" The answer is "No." Why? Because it is an act of theft (adinnādāna-payoga). That theft-intent also has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object. Here, both are obtained along with the preceding and succeeding stages, as stated in the Gaṇṭhipada.

Regarding "if the one commanded to remove that property lifts it, all incur Pārājika": this means if the person commanded definitely carries that property, the Pārājika occurs at the very moment of command. "Why do all three incur Pārājika here? Is it not a Thullaccaya because of saying 'Venerable sirs, you three carry it,' and since the others were commanded individually in sequence, should it not be a Dukkaṭa for each? How is it? For example, if one person steals a water-filter worth one māsaka, confesses, and loses the effort (ussāha) to steal, then again steals a needle worth one māsaka in the same way, and again steals something worth one māsaka—is it like that?" No, it is not. Just as the lotus-thief (Uppalathenaka) incurred Pārājika because his effort remained until the value reached five māsakas, so these people also have ongoing effort and have not yet confessed—so it is written. In the Pāḷi and Commentaries, it seems as if it is said that among those who go after consulting together, if one lifts it, all incur Pārājika without a specific command (āဏatti). However, saying "this is its meaning," in later decisions and regarding "one item, one place," etc., it is stated by restricting it to the command: "many people command one person." Therefore, the command should be desired and investigated. They say: "The reading 'one item, one place' is because of the phrase 'property of one family.'"

119-120. In the case of a scout (ocaraka), it is the same as the method mentioned for property that must be carried away. "That agreement" (taṃ saṅketaṃ) means the time of that agreement. Or, it is stealing after exceeding that agreed time or before reaching it. This method also applies to "that sign" (taṃ nimittaṃ). Acts like blinking the eye are swift and of short duration; it is impossible to steal property at that very moment. Some property may be distant or heavy; by the time one goes to take it and lifts it, it may be after the time of the sign. If that property...
135:
Because it is close as if already obtained, and light, it is possible to steal at the very moment the sign (nimitta) is given. Is it said with reference only to such goods? No, even if it was stated previously, it is said that one steals by that very sign from that time onwards because the effort is ongoing (āraddha). If that were the case, the view that "this is the effort (payoga) before the meal" would be the standard (pamāṇa). However, because the view of Mahāpaduma Thera is stated later, that view is not the standard. Action by sign (nimittakamma) should not be regarded like action by agreement (saṅketakamma). For in that action by agreement, there is a limitation of time, but in this action by sign, there is no limitation of time. This itself is the difference between the two.

"To avoid confusion in that matter" means: one person says, "Take it either before the meal or when you see [me] blinking, etc."; another says, based on the goods to be taken, "Take the goods of such color and shape before the meal." This is meant to show such various types of agreement (saṅketa) and sign (nimitta) to avoid confusion. "According to intention" means the second person tells the third, the third tells the fourth, and so on in succession. If the second person tells the fourth directly, it is known not to be "according to intention."

In the phrase "merely by accepting," if one certainly accepts, it is written that a thullaccaya (grave offense) is incurred from the start. The dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) for the monks who accept is not mentioned here because there is no opportunity in all cases. It is said that they reach this dukkaṭa offense before reaching pārājika.

It means the pārājika offense occurs at the very moment the intention of command (āṇatti-cetanā) that accomplishes the purpose arises. In that case, if it is asked which intention stands in the Path (magga) and which stands in the Fruit (phala), it is clear that it is the intention standing in the Fruit, because it is said, "The intention that accomplishes the purpose is like the Fruit immediately following the Path." If the command (āṇatti) were to stand in the Path, it would not be possible because it is conascent with the intention. Likewise, the certain taking of the goods would not be possible. For if it is said that the goods must certainly be taken at the moment of command, the acceptance by the thief would also not be possible as it is a future event. If the intention stands in the Path and either one of the commands, etc., or the certain taking of the goods stands in the Fruit, the meaning is not possible. Because only the pārājika offense is worthy of standing in the Fruit and nothing else, the comparison is possible here. The intention stands in the Path, and the pārājika offense arising from that intention stands in the Fruit.

As for what the example is: in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said, "Knowledge of faith is dhammapaṭisambhidā; knowledge of the meaning of faith is atthapaṭisambhidā." Here it is clear that faith is one thing and the meaning of faith is another. Just as a single state called non-delusion (amoha) [assists] associated states by way of root-condition (hetu-paccaya)...
136:
...by way of predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, faculty, path, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. In this Pali, it is clear that the state of non-delusion (amoha) is one thing, and its root-conditionality, etc., are another. Just as the six originations of offenses (āpatti-samuṭṭhāna) are mentioned in the Vinaya Piṭaka, likewise, the "seven groups of offenses" (āpattikkhandha) are mentioned as applicable. Among those offenses, the state of being an origination of an offense is one thing, and the state of being a group of offenses is another.

By this method of groups of offenses, if asked, "How many bases (ṭhāna) of the legal issue of offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa) are there?" one should answer, "The seven groups of offenses are the bases." If asked, "How many objects (vatthu)?" "The seven groups of offenses are the objects." If asked, "How many planes (bhūmi)?" "The seven groups of offenses are the planes." Such Pali passages should also be shown. Similarly, there is the pārājika offense standing in the Fruit, which is distinct from that intention of command (āṇatti-cetanā) that accomplishes the purpose and stands in the Path—being non-different [in essence] but designated as a specific mode and occurring without interval. Therefore, it should be understood that "the intention that accomplishes the purpose is like the Fruit immediately following the Path." Alternatively, the Teacher (Commentator) said this merely as a metaphor for the natural law of things (dhammaniyāma). Therefore, one should not look for a correspondence between the illustration and the illustrated in that statement. "All this should be accepted after investigating by the power of reasoning," says the teacher Ānanda.

## The explanation of the Bhūmaṭṭhakathā, etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the Classification of Offenses

Because it is said "by showing the method of the Vibhaṅga," the [text] "Now, in various places," etc., is begun to complete that method. In that commentary, "by way of the classification of factors (aṅga) and objects (vatthu)" means by way of the classification of knowing the factors of theft, and by way of the classification of the heavy or light nature of the goods to be stolen. Alternatively, it means showing the factors and the classification of offenses by way of the classification of objects.

In this Pali, "more than one māsaka, less than five māsakas," the word "or" (vā) is not mentioned. It should be understood that even with three phrases, only a single limit is stated. Anajjhāvuṭṭha means property that is not cherished (not taken possession of) by anyone, such as a forest guardian. Chaḍḍita (discarded) means property discarded by a wealthy owner, etc., due to lack of desire for it. A lost object where the search has ceased and the attachment (ālaya) is broken is called "that which has the root of broken attachment." Ownerless object means property for which there is no owner even if attachment is not yet broken, or it is abandoned without regard, or it is abandoned to deities, etc. All this is called ownerless property. Property abandoned to deities or to the Buddha and Dhamma is also...
137:
If it is held by other guardians, it is indeed property possessed by others (parappatiggahita). Indeed, in such cases of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), kings would seize the thief and carry out punishments such as execution. Regarding the property of the Buddha or the Dhamma in a monastery without a resident monk, or in a place that is not a park, etc., it is seen as being counted as property possessed by others, similar to the property of the Saṅgha in a monastery with resident monks, because of the statement: "It should be guarded, protected, and cherished by monks who come and go." If any monk in authority is able to prevent such requisites from being taken even by thieves, he may take them back by force and restore them to their original place. Although it seems as if there is no offense for one who perceives property as belonging to others even when there are six factors in unpossessed property, and although the factor "it must also be property possessed by others" is present, it should be understood that this is stated with reference to those who act in such a manner toward the property of others.

If thieves steal one's own property, it becomes property possessed by others because it is held by the thieves. Therefore, if another person takes it with the intention to steal (theyyacitta), he commits a pārājika offense. If the owner himself takes it, he does not commit a pārājika, because he is entitled to take it by accusing or by seizing it, saying, "I am taking my own property." If he first relinquishes the burden of ownership and later takes it with the intention to steal, this is the same principle. If that thief dies while the owner has relinquished the burden, and another person takes it with the intention to steal, he does not commit a pārājika. If the thief dies only before the burden is relinquished, a monk who takes that property with the intention to steal commits a pārājika, because it remains the property of the original monk. When the thief-monk dies, if the Saṅgha distributes and takes it as "the requisites of the deceased," the original owner is still entitled to take it, saying, "This is my property."

Here, a question arises: Are the varieties of theft only those beginning with bhūmaṭṭha (situated on the ground) and ending with nimittakamma (theft by sign), or are there others? If there are others, they should also be mentioned. For the Blessed One does not lay down the pārājika with anything remaining. If there are no others, how do cheating with scales (tulākūṭa), cheating with substitutes (kaṃsakūṭa), cheating with measures (mānakūṭa), bribery (ukkoṭana), deception (vañcana), fraud (nikati), stealing by taking cover in a snowy forest (sāciyoga), plundering (viparāmosa), robbery (ālopa), and acts of violence (sāhasākāra), which are found in the Suttas, fall into the types of theft mentioned here in the Vinaya? The answer is: They are already established by the characteristics of theft. How? By way of the factors and the objects, according to the method beginning with "by five aspects." The varieties of offenses are already stated in the Pali text. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) also, it is stated: "He takes by deceiving with cheating measures, cheating scales, counterfeit coins, etc.; for one who takes in such a manner, the theft is..."
138:
...theft by stealing (theyyāvahāra)." Since this is mentioned (in the Samantapāsādikā, Vol. 1, p. 138, and the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary on the second pārājika), it is evident that cheating with scales and so on are included in theyyāvahāra. Viparāmosa (stealing by picking), ālopa (plundering), and sāhasākāra (acts of violence) are included in pasayhāvahāra (theft by force) mentioned in the Commentary. To demonstrate this pasayhāvahāra, the matrix (mātikā) "property situated in a village, property situated in a forest" was laid down, and the classification was taught in the manner: "Property situated in a village is placed in four locations," and so on. Therefore, this means: it was made separate to show the different modes of taking. This is because there is no property situated in a village or forest other than those on the ground and so on.

Among those types of theft, cheating with scales (tulākūṭa) is included in vehāsaṭṭha (property situated in the air) through the fourfold classification: rūpakūṭa, aṅgakūṭa, gahaṇakūṭa, and paṭicchannakūṭa. Among the three types of cheating with measures (mānakūṭa)—hadayabheda, sikhābheda, and rajjubheda—it is included here: "This hadayabheda breaks the limit." Indeed, hadayabheda (breaking the center) is found when measuring ghee, oil, etc. Sikhābheda (breaking the peak) is also found in the context: "He causes it to move, he makes it enter his own vessel." It is said that this sikhābheda is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. Rajjubheda (breaking the rope) is included when measuring fields. Ukkoṭana (bribery/perverting justice) is included in the phrase: "Practicing the legal process, he causes the owner to lose." Similarly, deception (vañcana) and fraud (nikati) are also included.

## The Explanation of the Classification of Offenses is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Classification of Non-Offenses

If one takes another's property on trust (vissāsaggāha) without the owner being pleased, but with the intention of returning it, it seems to disagree with the Pali: "At that time, there were two monks who were friends. One monk entered the village for alms... Monk, there is no offense in taking on trust (vissāsaggāha)." For in this Pali, the owner's displeasure is indicated by the statement: "That monk, having known, accused him, saying, 'You are no longer a recluse.'" If it is asked whether taking on trust is valid even when there is displeasure, as indicated by the statement: "Monk, there is no offense in taking on trust"? It is not so, because it should be understood with a different meaning. The meaning here is: if there is a taking with the perception of trust, one is free from the pārājika offense. That owner-monk, being a friend, did not accuse out of anger, but being a dear friend, he meant: "Are you no longer a recluse? Go, go to the assembly for a decision and purify yourself." ... As for the Elder...
139:
He reprimands him, saying, "Remain pure." Even if that person reprimands him out of anger, the statement "there is no offense" (anāpatti) merely indicates the absence of a pārājika offense; it does not establish that the taking was by trust (vissāsaggāha). One who remains silent in the midst of an assembly due to shame means he says nothing. It is said that if he later has the desire to speak, he is entitled to have the item returned.

If a thief wishes to take something by force, but says, "Venerable sir, please accept my robes here," and the Elder gives the robes, or if the thief takes them himself without them being given, the Elder is entitled to demand them back if he later finds companions. The previous acceptance is not considered as true acceptance because he remained silent out of fear. It is said, "The owner is entitled to have the robe returned here." One must restore it to the owner as it was; it is said, "This is indeed the duty."

If a certain monk has taken property belonging to the Saṅgha, and if that property is used to benefit the Saṅgha or the Dhamma, he should give it back after informing the Saṅgha of the amount taken. By restoring it to its original state as it was taken, that monk becomes free of debt; it is said that this same method applies to the sick and so forth.

## The Word-by-Word Commentary is finished.

## Commentary on Miscellaneous Matters

Sāhatthika (by one's own hand) and āṇattika (by command) occur only in relation to a single object. If two people consult and move an object from its place through the effort of both, saying, "This is very heavy; you lift one side, and I will lift the other," an offense is committed through body, speech, and mind. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement: "The sāhatthika is not a factor of the āṇattika, nor is the āṇattika a factor of the sāhatthika."

However, the Elder Dhammasiri said: "This method is not obtained only in the case of a heavy object. If two people consult and take an object worth even five māsakas, it is called sāhatthika for both of them individually. Because it is a sāhatthika effort regarding a single object, the statement 'the sāhatthika is not a factor of the āṇattika' does not prohibit this method. What is meant in that Gaṇṭhipada is that it is not a factor of a sāhatthika object. But here, since it is said with reference to the effort (payoga), it is appropriate." This statement is inappropriate because there is no traditional saying of "bodily action and verbal action." Therefore, an offense is incurred through either one of the efforts among sāhatthika and āṇattika.
140:
It arises; even so, occurring very rapidly, this (bodily and verbal action, etc.) is stated by way of taking by oneself or causing another to take in acts such as plundering. Just as "internal and external objects" (ajjhatta-bahiddhā-rammaṇa) are spoken of with reference to the rapid arising of objects, sometimes taking one's own phenomena as the object and sometimes taking another's phenomena as the object, the fulfillment of this analogy should be understood in the same way.

In that term (ajjhatta-bahiddhā-rammaṇa), those phenomena such as the supramundane states have exclusively external objects; those phenomena such as the sphere of infinite consciousness have exclusively internal objects; the remaining phenomena are called "internal and external objects" because their objects are not fixed. They are not so called because of having both objects in a single moment. This offense, however, is indeed both sāhatthika and āṇattika according to the method already stated. Therefore, it is inappropriate to say that this (ajjhatta-bahiddhā-rammaṇa) statement is not a fitting illustration. Some teachers say: "Just as they are called ajjhatta-bahiddhā-rammaṇa because the object is not fixed, so too this offense is called sāhatthika-āṇattika because the effort is not fixed; thus, this is indeed an illustration."

"These teachers [think] there is no taking of both (internal and external) as an object together. If there were, there should be a text in the Paṭṭhāna such as: 'Dependent on a phenomenon with internal and external objects, a phenomenon with internal and external objects arises through the root-condition,' and so on. In their view, the statement 'it might be internal and external objects' would be meaningless. But it is not meaningless. Therefore, there certainly is a phenomenon that takes internal and external objects together. Furthermore, because there is no Pali text that specifically points out 'this is it' like the internal and external objects, it might not have been explicitly extracted (in the Paṭṭhāna). Precisely because it was not extracted there, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā, it is not stated as 'internal and external objects' by way of a phenomenon that takes both internal and external phenomena as an object together, but it is said to be 'internal and external objects' when it occurs in the internal and external continuity at different times. Therefore, we think that the method stated in the Gaṇṭhipada is the essence," says the Teacher. In that commentary, the reason for not mentioning "bodily and verbal action" is that it is a sāhatthika effort, and because there are many actions in a single effort. If it were mentioned, mental action should also be mentioned. Just as mental action, though present in that effort, is considered negligible (abbhohārika), so too in that sāhatthika-āṇattika effort, verbal action should be understood as negligible. That verbal action is merely a decisive support (upanissaya) for the bodily action. Just as the mind is merely a factor in that effort, so it is said "because it is a sāhatthika effort." We think it is called sāhatthika-āṇattika with reference only to its status as a factor; this should be accepted after careful consideration.
141:
For whatever offense there are origins of body and speech, in that offense, the action (kamma) is not merely that [stealing] thought; the action perishes [but the offense occurs].

For whatever origin such as action (kiriya) or non-action (akiriya) should become action (kamma) or non-action (akamma), such an occurrence is not appropriate because it is contradictory [to action etc.]; only a single action is appropriate.

## Explanation of the Vinīta Cases

In this Pāḷi passage, "There is no offense for a monk in the arising of a thought," it refers to the mere thought of stealing (without mixing with touching etc.); it means that there is no offense from the offenses just by the arising of that thought. Here, the objector asks: "In cases such as consenting to what is laid down (upanikkhittasādiyana) and in all precepts of non-action (akiriya-sikkhāpada), an offense occurs even without movement of the body or movement of the speech; why is there no offense only in this precept, and why is it not that there is no offense in all offenses?" (The answer is:) It is not that there is no offense; it indeed occurs. As to why there is no offense [in this specific case]:

Training should be practiced exceedingly,
Without making an intimation (viññatti) of body or speech,
How can one reach that offense with body and speech that are devoid of intimation?

Because it is a mere hint (lesa) of the nature of a thought-intention to steal, it cannot reach the state of an offense. Because it does not stay on a suitable object and has acquired repetition (āsevana), and thereafter runs along excessively, it is called "sandhāvati" (runs along). Thereafter, whether it occurs together with covetousness (abhijjhā) or together with ill-will (byāpāda) and runs specifically, it is called "vidhāvati" (runs specifically).

Regarding "making a wound to take," some teachers say that although there is no offense by this precept, a dukkaṭa offense occurs for a monk who touches a woman's form in whatever place. Others say, "Taking an object connected to the body is appropriate; it is said to be 'allowable' (vaṭṭati) with reference to taking that object connected to the body." One should consider both statements before accepting.

## Explanation of the Case of Shifting the Grass Marker

In the Mahāpaccari Commentary and others, the statement "It should be decided only by the lifting of the foot" is well-said. However, this statement is made to show that the mere premeditated theft (parikappāvahāra) of that stealing is not evident. At the very moment of lifting the foot, this monk reaches an offense; therefore, the statement "It should be decided only by the lifting of the foot" while going after seeing [the object] is said to be ill-stated in that Mahāpaccari etc. How is this? A person desiring a cloth takes only the cloth-bag and goes outside, and after knowing it is a cloth, thinks "I will take it later"; a monk who takes with such premeditation does not yet reach an offense at the time of lifting [the bag]. When outside...
142:
...standing outside and seeing "This object is a cloth," if he goes, is it not that it should be said that it is decided only by the lifting of the foot? In fact, although the premeditation (parikappa) is evident, it is evident only in the preceding part; it is not evident at the moment of stealing. Therefore, that stealing is not premeditated theft (parikappāvahāra). This meaning has already been stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā; therefore, they say, "It is only the appropriate method." "Kammantasālā" refers to the houses of farmers and the houses of woodsmen.

Regarding "Ayam tāva," from "Sace upacārasīmaṃ" onwards, as far as the Theravāda exists, it is the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In that method, because it is Theravāda and because there is no logical reason (yutti), the statement beginning with "Keci pana" (but some) should not be accepted. The reason is that in personal manual effort (sāhatthika-payoga), such an intention that achieves the purpose (atthasādhaka-cetanā) does not exist. Only in effort by command (āṇattika-payoga) does the intention that achieves the purpose exist. It is said, "The remaining words agree with the meaning stated in the Mahāpaccari."

In shifting a boundary marker, if another person knows "This pile is not mine," just by being released from the other monk's hand, a Pārajika offense occurs, as in shifting a stake. They say, "If he knows it as his own property, a Pārajika does not occur." If this is the case, the groups of five (pañcaka) become confused; therefore, it should be carefully investigated.

Regarding the term "Parānuddayatāya" (out of compassion for others), if it is asked why the Blessed One, who has reached the pinnacle of compassion for others, taught "There is no offense in the property of Petas or the property of animals," it is solely out of compassion for others. The reason is that for the taking of such requisites, kings would not arrest and kill a thief; if the Ascetic Gotama were to prescribe a Pārajika for such requisites and make a monk a non-monk, the masses would lose faith in the Blessed One and become those bound for the states of deprivation (apāya).

Trees and such that are not possessed by Petas are very rare, and it is not possible to know. Therefore, the community of lay devotees (upāsaka) who fear evil regarding trees etc., would not build image houses, cetiyas, Bodhi-tree houses, monasteries, etc., and would fall away from a great mass of merit. The supports (nissaya) taught as "The monkhood depends on the dwelling at the foot of a tree and robes made of rags (paṃsukūla)" would not be true supports. This is because monks who perceive them as property possessed by others would not accept the foot of a tree or rag-robes. Thus, the monkhood would not be possible. When bitten by a snake, they might reach death because they do not dare to take a tree for ash [medicine]. In times when robes are snatched away, they would not take branches or broken wood, and being naked, they would wander around showing the views of the sectarians (titthiya) as if they were good views. If that happened, the world would have faith only in the sectarians, and reaching wrong views, they would become like stumps in Saṃsāra. Therefore, the Blessed One...
143:
It should be understood that [the Buddha] spoke the words "There is no offense in [taking] the belongings of hungry ghosts (peta)" and so forth, solely out of compassion for others.

It is written that regarding goods taken after saying, "Give me another portion (of one who has no owner)," because it is similar to making a request, there is no compensation to be paid (bhaṇḍadeyya), nor is there an offense of defeat (pārājika). This statement is appropriate for ordinary people. However, they say, "If the owner or one commissioned by the owner gives another portion, thinking, 'This monk is taking or requesting a portion for an absent companion monk,' then compensation must be paid for that portion."

148-9. Regarding the phrase "compensation for one who eats," it is said that giving to a thief who has arrived or to the original owner is considered a valid gift. "Without distinction" means it was stated without specifically saying "to those who have made an effort to go." This is because the property of the Saṅgha does not cease to be communal property (saṅghika) just because some individuals do not make an effort. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā as well, it is stated: "If they go with effort, there is a theft for one who consumes with the intention to steal." Thus, both statements are identical. In an abandoned monastery, it is impossible to know the extent of the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā). If this monk stands outside the precinct boundary and consumes or eats after ringing a bell, etc., it means that such eating is "well-eaten" (validly consumed). It is said, "In other monasteries, one should proceed according to the aforementioned procedure." It is written, "It is well-eaten because it is within the monastery." Because it is the property of all monks yet to come, it is said because it was offered with the words, "I give to the Saṅgha of the four quarters." Even if one does not say this but says, "I give to the Saṅgha," it is the same. Therefore, it should be understood that a monk standing outside does not receive the gain, according to the words of the Blessed One.

Because of the word "dead pig," one cannot give that same pig while it is alive as compensation. It is shown that it is proper to give it because it has been killed (or a pig killed by another).

Regarding the phrase "they go trampling, compensation," how much is the compensation? Because it is impossible to know, "This many pigs have trampled and gone, or will go." Whatever amount is given to the owners such that they are satisfied, thinking, "My goods have been given to me," that amount should be given. If they are not satisfied, should one pay the price of the past pigs and dig a pit? No, one should not. In that case, if the accused monk lays down his burden to both parties, does he incur a pārājika? No, he does not. He should simply satisfy the owner by giving allowable requisites (kappiyaparikkhāra). The teacher says, "In other such cases, this same method applies; this is not my mere conjecture." It is said, "He goes trampling on that day or the second day." He throws it into a thicket.
144:
The phrase "only compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya)" is spoken with reference to what will inevitably enter. At a time when one must flee to another place due to danger from kings, etc., danger from another king's army arrives at a certain monastery. "Severance of the original property" (mūlavatthuccheda) means that because of the statement "The monks residing in this monastery are the masters of all lodgings," it implies that the remaining monks are not the masters.

"Park-keeper" (ārāmarakkhaka) refers to what is taken by way of relinquishment. Regarding the phrase "knowing the intention" (adhippāyaṃ ñatvā), there is a decision here: if the owners do not forbid or prevent a monk from receiving a gift or a portion, it is allowable to take that person's gift without concealing it. Even that decision is stated as "not allowable in the case of communal property (saṅghika)." "Only this monk is the master" means that the monk wishes to stay in a certain place, and he obtains it because of the reason of knowing his own benefit. Alternatively, some say "it should not be forbidden." "With the object" (savatthuka) means together with the land. After saying "it is heavy property (garubhaṇḍa)," it is stated "even a mere blade of grass should not be given." If one asks, "Is that grass not heavy property?" it is said with reference to grass in an unprotected or insecure place that is about to be destroyed. Whether it is called an allowable object or not, even regarding the property of one's mother and so forth which is fit to be taken, [a pārājika] can occur through the arising of the intention to steal. This training rule was established at a time when gains reached their peak and became abundant, as evidenced by the words, "Even kings have great faith in these monks."

## The Explanation of the Second Pārājika is Finished.

## 3. The Third Pārājika

## Explanation of the Origin of the First Injunction

Regarding the phrase "pure by three" (tīhi suddhena), the word "tīhi" can be either in the ablative case (nissakka) or the instrumental case (karaṇa). In the case of the ablative, it should be construed as: [the Buddha] who is pure from the doors of body, speech, and mind; likewise, who is pure at the very seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) from all triads of defilements, such as the stains of misconduct, the uneven states (visama), and the impediments (papañca), and so forth. In the case of the instrumental, it should be construed as: [the Buddha] who is pure by means of the three doors of body, speech, and mind; likewise, who is pure by means of all triads of virtues, such as the three right conducts (sucarita), the three liberations (vimokkha), the three meditations (bhāvanā), and the three [trainings] of virtue, concentration, and wisdom (sīla-samādhi-paññā). "Clarified" (vibhāvita) means expanded by the teaching, or made clear, or arranged, or laid down. "Commentary" (saṃvaṇṇanā) refers to the use of the present tense in the proximity of the present time.
145:
Not only is the city of Rājagaha limited; this city (Vesālī) is also limited. 'Sapari-ccheda' means having a limit or boundary. Some say 'sapari-kkhepa' (having a circumference). In the phrase 'haṃsavaṭṭakacchadanena,' it is written as 'in a circular shape like a swan.'

'Kāyavicchin-danīyakathā' refers to the preaching of the Dhamma that causes the abandoning or cutting off of desire and lust (chandarāga) for one's own body or the bodies of others. It is 'asubha' (unattractive/foul) because it is devoid of beautiful aspects. It is 'asuci' (impure) because it originates as a result of impurities. It is 'paṭikūla' (repulsive) because it is loathsome and is the locus of bile, phlegm, and so forth.

'Asubhāya vaṇṇaṃ' means preaching the details of the foul aspect or the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna). Here, the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive. It means preaching the 'vaṇṇa' (praise/description), which is the detailed talk for the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of the sign of foulness (asubha-nimitta). The meditative mind (jhāna-citta) is called 'mañjūsā' (a casket) because it is endowed with the ten characteristics of the beginning, middle, and end, and cannot be overcome by the thieves of defilements (kilesa).

'Tatrīmāni': The collective meaning here is—in whichever impulsion process (javana-vāra) the first jhāna arises for a single mind-moment, taking that entire impulsion process—including the preliminary (anuloma), preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and absorption (appanā)—as 'first jhāna' by the method of unity (ekatta-naya). Based on the accomplishment of the task through the direct knowledge (abhiññā) such as 'quick direct knowledge' (khippābhiññā) which leads to the absorption of that first jhāna, 'purification of the way' (paṭipadā-visuddhi) etc., should be understood by way of its arrival. The intensification of equanimity (upekkhā-nubrūhanā) through the accomplishment of the task of 'equanimity in the middle' (tatramajjhattū-pekkhā) should be understood as the 'middle' (majjha). The gladdening (sampahaṃsanā) through the accomplishment of the task of the knowledge that purifies (pariyodāpaka-ñāṇa) should be understood as the 'end' (pariyosāna).

Among those three, from the initial mind until the moment of arising (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of the first jhāna, the interval is to be known as 'purification of the way' (paṭipadā-visuddhi). The intensification of equanimity occurs at the moments of arising (uppāda) and presence (ṭhiti); gladdening occurs at the moments of presence (ṭhiti) and dissolution (bhaṅga). Because it is marked by this nature, it is called 'lakkhana' (characteristic). The initial part is marked by 'plunging into the practice of purification' (visuddhi-paṭipatti-pakkhandana) etc. The middle is marked by the three types of looking on with equanimity (ajjhupekkhana). The end is marked by the four types of gladdening (sampahaṃsanā). Therefore, it is said 'ten characteristics.'

The impulsion mind (javana-citta) of the initial stage ending with change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) is called 'purification of mind' (citta-visuddhi) because it is pure from the obstacles known as hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Because it is thus pure, that impulsion mind, for the sake of that absorption, approaches the absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) known as the 'sign of concentration' (samādhi-nimitta) which is the middle, and is said to practice by inclining through a single continuity. For one who practices thus...
146:
The mind's plunging into the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) is its arrival at that state of serenity; thus it is called 'the mind's plunging into that sign of serenity.' In this way, at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna, 'purification of the way' (paṭipadā-visuddhi) should be understood by way of its arrival. For the mind that is thus purified and has reached absorption (appanā), there is 'looking on with equanimity' (ajjhupekkhana) because there is no further effort in purification. Because serenity has been attained, there is no further effort in establishing the mind; thus there is 'looking on with equanimity' for one who has attained serenity. Having abandoned association with defilements and being established solely in a single object, there is no possibility of effort to establish it again in that single object; thus there is 'looking on with equanimity' for one whose mind is established in a single object.

'Born in that mind' means the concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā) born in that jhāna mind are pure because they do not overstep each other in the sense of being yoked together (yuganaddha), and because they are liberated from various defilements. The faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) etc., have a single taste in the sense of the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa). The yogi causes the mind and the energy (vīriya) appropriate to those states to proceed, which have the nature of not overstepping each other and have approached those two (concentration and wisdom). Because of the sense of producing energy that approaches those states, because of being a 'partaker of distinction' (visesabhāgiya), and because of the sense of repeated cultivation (āsevana), it should be understood that 'gladdening' (sampahaṃsanā) occurs.

Alternatively, it is written here: 'The change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) mind that has just passed away arrives by inclining through a single continuity.' In that statement, the words 'arrives by inclining' are not possible for a mind that has passed. Furthermore, it is written: 'The change-of-lineage mind approaching the absorption concentration mind plunges into that absorption.' The teacher (Ācariya Ānanda) says that the previous statement is also inconsistent with this, because it was said 'it is already past at the moment of practice,' so the statement 'the change-of-lineage mind plunges into that absorption' is contradictory. Because it is said 'Even though it is only for a single mind-moment, one cultivates, develops, and frequently practices the supramundane mind,' it is said 'Even for a jhāna of a single mind-moment, there are these ten characteristics.' It is also said, 'From then on, cultivation is indeed development (bhāvanā).'

'Adhiṭṭhāna-sampanna' is written as 'endowed with a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna).' The meaning is: that jhāna which is called 'consisting of beginning, middle, and end' is also 'possessed of the three types of goodness' because it is endowed with the excellence of those three. Thus, the jhāna mind of the three stages is the 'foundation' (adhiṭṭhāna) in the sense of being the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the qualities rooted in the attainment of that jhāna, or for the attainment of higher jhānas. Therefore, because it is endowed with the state of being a foundation for the mind, it is called 'adhiṭṭhāna-sampanna.'

'To dwell in seclusion for half a month': In this regard, the teachers said: 'While the Buddha is present, if the monks were to see or hear each other killing one another, and because they do not know the means to prevent that danger, they might say "This ascetic Gotama is not omniscient," taking a non-cause as a cause. Not understanding the lack of sovereignty over kamma even for the Lord of Dhamma, many people, being foolish due to not seeing all, would be headed for the Avīci hell. Therefore, that Blessed One...'
147:
The Blessed One, having known beforehand that those monks would kill one another, and having well-determined that there was no means to prevent it, desired to perform the sole benefit of attaining a happy destination for the worldlings among them. Through the teaching on foulness (asubha-desanā), and by causing them to refrain from the useless sights of forms and sounds, and because of seeing the emergence of the basis for the third Pārājika rule which must inevitably be prescribed—as if manifesting His Omniscience to the wise who investigate—He wished to dwell for that half-month in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) which fulfills the welfare of those to be tamed (veneyya). Thus, He said: "Monks, I wish to go into seclusion for half a month," and so forth.

"Teachers" refers to the group leaders such as the Elders Buddhamitta, Dhammasiri, and Upatissa, and those who had previously heard and learned from the Commentator. It should be understood that there are other teachers besides these.

If it is asked: "Does this statement 'They were disgusted and loathed their own bodies... it will be' not disagree with the later statement 'At that time, for those monks who were not yet free from lust, there was indeed fear, horripilation, and trembling'? Furthermore, does this statement not conflict with the purpose of the Blessed One's focus on the talk on foulness?" No, it does not. This is said because of not understanding the meaning of that Pali text. Even though they were disgusted and loathed their own bodies, because those worldling monks still had attachment (sineha) not yet abandoned by the Noble Path, they could not remain without fear regarding death like the Arahants; fear indeed occurred. However, that fear was diminished by the power of practicing the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā). It did not become great enough to delude the mind as it does in those who are not disgusted with the body, and it did not lead those beings to the lower realms (apāya). This is how the meaning should be understood.

Alternatively, this is a statement of cause for what was said before. Since fear, trembling, and horripilation indeed occurred to those monks at that time, it was said: "At that time, the Blessed One was giving a talk on foulness," and so forth.

Or else, by the statement that fear occurred even to those who were disgusted with their own bodies, He shows the great distinction of the Arahants who possess great power and are free from lust. He also shows that this fear of death is extremely difficult to endure, since fear occurs even in such individuals because they are not yet free from lust. "Others besides them" (tadannye) refers to any individuals among those five hundred monks. By this, He shows: "Seeing that executioner coming with a sword in hand, fear indeed occurred to the others; what need is there to speak of those monks? Having considered this, the Blessed One taught the talk on foulness to those monks beforehand, so that later, fear did not occur to them. In this way, the talk on foulness was of great benefit to them." Among these methods, the last one...
148:
...is the method that agrees with the commentary statement: "Among those monks, not a single monk showed any bodily or vocal disturbance; all of them, being mindful and clearly comprehending, lay down on their right sides."

The phrase "But others say" (apare panāhu) is stated for the purpose of refuting a wrong view. If it is asked: "Does the statement 'This is indeed a view' conflict with the statement 'He will not transcend the realm of Māra'?" No, it does not. How? If this Migalaṇḍika were to refrain from killing the monks, they would transcend the realm of Māra; but by committing an unwholesome act, he himself remains in Māra's realm. If he kills the monks, they would not transcend the realm of Māra because of the power of that unwholesome kamma—thinking thus as a partisan of Māra, he held his own view that "Those who do not die are not liberated from Saṃsāra." Therefore, being urged on both paths in killing those monks, he spoke thus. For this reason, they are not called "partisans of Māra who hold the same view as Māra," but are called "followers of Māra's will." Some write: "What is meant by this? Because he followed Māra's will, even though he thought thus, he spoke according to his own view." They come to me to attend together; they receive instructions and so forth in the presence of their own teachers and preceptors.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing Concentration

What is shown by the words: "Monks, this mindfulness of breathing concentration also..."? It refutes the wrong view of those who think: "The death of those monks was due to the practice of the meditation subject taught by the Blessed One." The death of those monks was solely due to unwholesome kamma performed in the past. This meditation on foulness, however, served as a strong support (upanissaya) for some of those monks to reach the fruition of Arahantship; for some to reach the fruition of Non-returning, Once-returning, or Stream-entry; for some to attain the first absorption; for some to exhaust the craving that is self-love through abandoning by suppression and abandoning by substitution of opposites; and for some to be reborn in a happy destination. Thus, my talk on foulness was indeed beneficial. However, because I was requested by the Venerable Ānanda, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach another method," I shall teach another method. The connection should be understood as: "Monks, just as you practiced the meditation on foulness taught previously, so too should this mindfulness of breathing be practiced." It is said: "Mindfulness is established by means of inhalation." That mindfulness is established in the preliminary stage by taking the inhalation or exhalation as the object; in the later stage, it is established by taking the sign (nimitta) arising from the inhalation and exhalation as the object.
149:
The meditative work that occurs in the foul (asubha) or is called foul is called 'asubha-kamma' (foul work). That very foul work is called 'asubha-kammaṭṭhāna' (subject of foul meditation) because it is the cause for the repeated arising of another [meditative knowledge]. Or, because the object which is the proximate cause of the foul work is called a 'base' (ṭhāna), here the foul absorption (asubha-jhāna) is intended by the term 'asubha-kammaṭṭhāna'. Therefore, it is said, "Because of having a gross object."

"By way of penetration" means by way of attaining the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) such as initial application (vitakka), etc. "Because of the tranquility of the object" refers to the tranquility by way of the subsiding of bodily distress, starting from the time of sequential tranquility.

"Preliminary work" (parikamma) means that the preliminary work for a kasiṇa ends with the arising of the sign (nimitta). At the time of performing that preliminary work, because of the lack of gratification, there is lack of tranquility and lack of aspiration (appaṇihita). Just as in access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) there is tranquility due to the disappearance of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the manifestation of absorption factors, it is not so here [in the preliminary stage]; rather, in this context, it means it is tranquil and perfect "due to attention from the beginning."

In the second interpretation, "asecanaka" means being so excellent that one cannot be satiated; therefore, it is said to be "full of essence" (ojavanta). Mental happiness (cetasika-sukha) exists even at the moment of absorption; even so, it is said that "both [bodily and mental happiness] should be taken only for one who has emerged from absorption." If [unwholesome states] are not suppressed in one's own continuity by tranquility (samatha), and if one considers them suppressed only by absorption and not by tranquility, then base unwholesome states would arise together with absorption.

Aggregates (khandha) and so on are called "nibbedha-bhāgiya" (leading to penetration) because they are the basis for the supramundane (lokuttara); or it refers specifically to the person for whom it becomes nibbedha-bhāgiya. "By the power of the tetrad beginning with 'contemplating impermanence' (aniccānupassī), one reaches the Noble Path in sequence and cuts off [defilements] at the root; this does not exist for others," so it is written.

"Prohibiting such a state" is said because the sixteen-based [mindfulness of breathing] does not exist for sectarians (titthiya). By the power of the first four phrases, sectarians have only mundane absorption (lokiya-jhāna); in that mundane absorption, the basis for the supramundane is simply non-existent. "Phalamuttama" means the most excellent among the fruits. "Suitability with the three seasons" means going to the forest in the hot season, to the foot of a tree in the cold season, and to an empty place in the rainy season. The forest is suitable for one of phlegmatic temperament (semha-dhātu), the foot of a tree for one of bilious temperament (pitta-dhātu), and an empty place for one of windy temperament (vāta-dhātu). The forest is suitable for one of deluded temperament (moha-carita); in a great forest, the mind does not shrink. The foot of a tree is suitable for one of hateful temperament (dosa-carita), and an empty place for one of lustful temperament (rāga-carita).

Standing and walking are on the side of restlessness (uddhacca); sleeping is on the side of sloth (līna). Sitting cross-legged brings firmness, and by keeping the body erect, one gains the happiness of the occurrence of in-breaths and out-breaths. By the phrase "setting up mindfulness in front" (parimukhaṃ satiṃ), the means of grasping the object is shown. "Kārī" means one who acts habitually. In the Vibhaṅga of this, it is not said "he breathes in, he breathes out," but "acting with mindfulness" (sato kārī). Therefore, "he breathes...
150:
In saying "he breathes out" (passasati), it is written: "Only the first tetrad is obtained, not the remaining ones"; and in the term "by way of long breathing" (dīghaṃ-assāsa-vasena), it is done as an unelided compound (alopa-samāsa); and "non-distraction due to one-pointedness of object"; and "of one who knows by way of non-delusion"; and "by that knowledge"; and "by the knowledge called 'one who knows' (pajānato)"; and "sato-kārī means one who acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension"; and "the out-breaths of one contemplating relinquishment are themselves the out-breaths of contemplating relinquishment." Even if it comes out of sequence, it is still appropriate; for that reason, it is rejected [as an objection]. It is said that because it touches the palate and is extinguished, a newborn infant makes a sneezing sound; by the power of desire (chanda) and joy (pāmojja), the previous three and the [other] six make nine. "By a single mode" means either by way of in-breathing or by way of out-breathing; for one who develops mindfulness of breathing in this way, the development of the subject of mindfulness of body (kāyānupassanā) in the body is fulfilled.

"Body" (kāya) refers to the in-breaths and out-breaths. "Setting up" (upaṭṭhāna) is mindfulness (sati). "Long" (dīghaṃ) refers to the in-breaths and out-breaths that have gone quickly. "Addhāna-saṅkhāta" means a portion of time, as in a collection of time; or it means a long time. One person notes only the in-breath, one the out-breath, and one both; therefore, it is said "without making a division." "Desire" (chanda) means that from breathing in and out in this way, gratification (assāda) arises; by the power of that gratification, the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) arises. From that, joy (pāmojja) arises.
