Because the in-breaths and out-breaths are difficult objects to know, the mind turns away (or shifts); for one who gives up counting and attends only to the point of contact, pure equanimity (upekkhā) alone remains. "Four colors/marks" (cattāro vaṇṇā) means four shapes, as in "the three colors of the bowl," etc.

"Tathābhūtassa" means "of one who develops mindfulness of breathing." "Restraint" (saṃvara) is restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara). Or else, it is the abandoning of hindrances by the first absorption, of initial and sustained application by the second, of rapture by the third, of pleasure and pain by the fourth, and of the perception of form, perception of resistance, or perception of diversity by the attainment of the sphere of infinite space. "Virtue (sīla) is virtue as abstinence (virati), virtue as volition (cetanā), virtue as restraint (saṃvara), and virtue as non-transgression (avītikkama)"—the meaning should be understood here in this manner. "States that occur in such and such ways are called virtue (sīla) in the sense of 'virtuousness' (sīlana), which is defined as upholding and composing," so it is said. Similarly, in the phrase "this training is the intended training in this context," it refers only to virtue as volition; in some places, it should be understood as referring to virtue as abstinence as well. Otherwise, there would be the implication of abstinence even in training rules that are merely matters of social convention (paṇṇatti-vajja).
151:
Because of the reason that one dwells restrained by the power of abstinence even in the training rules involving offenses born of transgressing the injunctions, the inclusion of abstinence in those training rules involving offenses born of transgressing the injunctions has occurred. 'Tasmiṃ ārammaṇe' means in the object of in-and-out breathing (ānāpāna). 'Tāya satiyā' means by the mindfulness arisen in that object of ānāpāna. In the phrase 'tena manasikārena', it is written as 'by reflection'. By this phrase 'tena manasikārena', since it shows the occurrence of various advertings (āvajjana), it amounts to showing that one is said to practice through various impulsion processes (javanavāra). Or, one practices with whatever attention (manasikāra).

In the phrase 'ñāṇuppādanādīsu', by the word 'ādi', it should be understood up to the end. 'Tatra' means in that object of ānāpāna. In the word 'evaṃ', it is written as 'by the method to be mentioned now'. Or, in the word 'tatra', it refers to the grossness of those inhalations and exhalations (assāsa-passāsa). That previous method agrees well with this statement: 'pubbe apariggahitakāle' (in the time before being grasped). The first view is the opinion of the Dīghabhāṇaka (Reciters of the Long Discourses). In detail, those Dīghabhāṇaka teachers say: "For a meditator who, after attaining the first jhāna, sits in a place and strives to attain the second jhāna, the inhalations and exhalations that occur at the time of the occurrence of the gross mind by the power of initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) in the access concentration (upacāra) are gross." The Majjhimabhāṇaka (Reciters of the Middle-length Discourses) say that because of the peaceful state of the occurrence of the mind higher and higher, both at the time of attainment for a person who has attained jhāna and upon regaining a single seat, there is subtlety in the access concentration of the second jhāna compared to the first; so it is written.

In insight (vipassanā), however, in the phrase 'vipassanāyaṃ pana', it should be understood that this sequence occurs for a meditator who applies his mind beginning with the definition of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna), and it also occurs for a meditator who applies his mind to other meditation subjects. Aiming at this vision of knowledge that "matter is only this much, there is no matter other than this," it is said 'sakalarūpapariggahe' (in the grasping of all matter). In the phrase 'rūpārūpapariggahe', it should be understood in the same way. Strong insight occurs starting from the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa) which takes the characteristics such as impermanence (anicca) as its object. 'Pubbe vuttanayena' means by the view of all those Reciters (bhāṇaka), starting with 'apariggahitakāle' and so on. 'Sodhanā' means explaining or resolving. 'Assa' is the meaning of the phrase 'passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ' (calming the bodily formation).

Bending forward is called 'ānamanā'. Bending sideways is called 'vinamanā'. Bending well (completely) is called 'sannamanā'. Bending backward is called 'paṇamanā'. It should be understood that these terms like 'ānamanā' are mentioned to make clear the shaking, such as standing while holding the knees. In whatever manner bending forward etc., or shaking etc., occurs, it should be understood in connection with 'passambhayaṃ' as 'calming such a manner'. In the phrase 'iti kira', it means 'if it is said so'. In the phrase 'evaṃ sante', it means 'if it is calmed even though it is peaceful and subtle'. 'Pabhāvanā' means producing or developing. Because the inhalations and exhalations have become calmed, the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-samādhi) no longer occurs. Since that development of concentration does not exist, one cannot enter into attainment; because of the absence of entering into attainment, one does not emerge. By this statement 'iti kira', it means 'one shall practice in this manner'.
152:
He answers that objection. The sound 'santa' itself is called the sound-sign (sadda-nimitta). Based on the words "mindful he breathes out, mindful he breathes in," the thirty-two phrases and the four tetrads (catukka) should be understood.

'Appaṭipīḷana' means not giving rise to those various defilements (kilesa). Although duties such as the shrine terrace duty (cetiyangaṇa-vatta) are included in the virtue of restraint of the Patimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) according to the meaning of the statement "if there should be an offense for someone," yet, because it is not intended in this Pali passage: "Sāriputta, the Teacher does not yet appoint the training rule for the disciples or recite the Patimokkha as long as certain taint-producing states (āsavaṭṭhāniyā dhammā) do not manifest in the Sangha," it is called 'ābhisamācārika' (pertaining to good conduct). In these ābhisamācārika training rules, that which is not a ground for an offense is indeed unmixed; so it is said.

'Yathāvuttena' is because it is the proximate cause for the task of devotion to yoga (meditation). 'Sallahukavutti' refers to a monk who carries only the eight requisites (parikkhāra). 'Pañcasandhika kammaṭṭhāna' (meditation subject with five connections) means in this context the jhāna, the sign (nimitta), and the scriptural study (pariyatti) that clarifies that jhāna and sign are called the meditation subject. Lodgings etc. that are endowed with proper going and coming are called 'senāsana'. Washing soiled robes and so on are minor obstacles (khuddaka-palibodha). The mind wavers, thinking, "Has it fallen in between?"

It means with a mind that has reached distraction within oneself. They shake because of having an unconcentrated mind. What is called 'upanibandhanathambhamūla' (the base of the pillar of binding) is the tip of the nose or the sign at the mouth (upper lip). It is said that at that very sign of the nose-tip etc., it is as if one sees both ends and the middle on either side of a swing-plank.

In this context, it means as in the simile of the saw (kakacūpama). 'Desato' means from the place of contact. 'Nimittaṃ paṭṭhapetabbaṃ' means mindfulness should be established on the sign. It is called 'garukabhāvanā' because it should be developed by the teachers. Some meditation teachers (jhāyino) have said so.

Because of the statement 'saññānānattatā' (diversity of perception), the words spoken by some teachers are also to be accepted as authoritative. It is said so because it has not come down in the Commentaries since the time of the Councils (Saṅgīti). Even if there is no such thought as "Does a star-shape appear to me?", due to the diversity of elements, just as these elements arise, it appears in various ways to one who is just developing the meditation. It is said, "It is not proper to say 'it is not the sign,' because that would be a deliberate lie." In this context, 'kammaṭṭhāna' refers only to the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) already mentioned.
153:
In the nimitta, in the paṭibhāganimitta. "Nānākāra" means the various and diverse states described as "the four colors occur." "Vibhāvayaṃ" means making clear while knowing. "Assāsapassāsa" refers to the various states of mind in the nimitta arising from that in-breath and out-breath, or in the in-breath and out-breath itself. Indeed, only one who places the mind on the nimitta makes the various states clear; otherwise, it is said that he binds his mind to the in-breath and out-breath. [It is made clear] by the appearance and color of stars, etc., or by characteristics such as hardness, etc.

"Rejected in the Commentaries" means it is rejected in the Sihala Commentaries, giving the reason "due to proximity to the bhavanga." Why? Because if absorption (appanā) occurs in the sixth or seventh javana moment, there is no opportunity for the fruition-impulsion (phala-javana) in the path-process (magga-vīthi). If one asks, "Let it happen here?", it cannot be. This is because mundane absorption also follows the same course as supramundane absorption in the absorption-process. Therefore, when a monk who has attained jhāna wishes to dwell for seven days in the happiness of the present and enters jhāna, he reaches absorption at the fourth or fifth moment, not the sixth or seventh. Absorption occurs only in those [fourth or fifth moments]. Beyond that, it no longer serves as a support for absorption-impulsion. Because of proximity to the bhavanga, it reaches only the fourth or fifth moment; the teachers say this is because it stands between javanas like a pot standing on the ground.

Reflecting only on the jhāna factors without reflecting on many objects is called mastery in advertence (āvajjana-vasī). The subsequent arising of four or five reviewing consciousnesses is called mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-vasī). For this reason, it was said, "Mastery in reviewing is stated only by mastery in advertence." Mastery in attainment (သမာပဇ္ဇနဝသီ - samāpajjana-vasī) is the entering [into jhāna] for as long as one desires; it is the ability to establish the desired time limit. It is also said, "This is the difference between mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī) and mastery in emerging (vuṭṭhāna-vasī): by the power of resolve, the javana runs; by the power of emergence, it runs longer than the desired time." Alternatively, after reflecting on an object such as the earth kasina and the javana has run, reflecting again, the fifth jhāna consciousness arises; this is said to be the highest limit. For the Blessed One, however, jhāna occurs immediately after the advertence; all this is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada.

"Vatthu" refers to the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), "dvāra" refers to the doors such as the eye-door, and "ārammaṇa" refers to objects such as visible objects—so it is written. One sees the consciousness that has the apprehended visible object, or one sees it in another way. How? It is said, "Also the consciousness that has the apprehended form, base, door, and object." For the consciousness that has the base, door, and object in the apprehended forms, that consciousness...
154:
...sees that consciousness which has the apprehended visible object, base, door, and object. Or, it should be noted that one instance of the word "ārammaṇa" is elided; this thought of mine should be accepted only after careful consideration.

Furthermore, in the three tetrads, two terms each should be counted as one. Here, the experiencing of rapture (pīti) should be understood through samatha by way of the object, and through vipassanā by way of non-delusion (asammoha). In "Dukkhametaṃ ñāṇaṃ" etc., where it is said "by way of object and non-delusion," in this [context of mindfulness of breathing], it is stated in reverse (not in the usual order) from that aforementioned method. To explain: in those knowledges of suffering etc., because the delusion that covers that suffering is destroyed and it is no longer unmanifest, and because one is able to review at any desired time in such knowledge, knowledge is said to be by way of non-delusion in the three truths such as suffering. In the truth of cessation (nirodha), experiencing rapture associated with cessation by way of the object is not possible by way of non-delusion, because delusion has not yet been abandoned and because it would contradict the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali.

In that Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, "Dīghaṃ assāsavasena" etc. is stated to show [experience] by way of the object. By that mindfulness and by that knowledge, that rapture is experienced; the meaning here is that it is because the object is experienced. "Āvajjanto" etc. is stated to show the experiencing of rapture by way of non-delusion. For the person who knows, sees, and reviews by way of impermanence etc., and for the person who resolves and attends by way of focusing on that rapture, and likewise establishes energy etc. with momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), that rapture is experienced.

"Abhiññeyya" means what is to be known by full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). "Pariññeyya" means what is to be known by full understanding as investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). All the truth of suffering is to be known by higher knowledge and to be fully understood. In that Pali, it is written "this rapture." "Abhiññeyya" etc. is said referring to the path-moment (magga-khaṇa). Because the task of vipassanā called non-delusion is completed by the path, the path is also spoken of as if making "abhiññeyya" etc. its object. The phrase "to show the ground of vipassanā" is said because there is no bodily pleasure (kāyika-sukha) in samatha. "In the two terms of mental formations (citta-saṅkhāra)" refers to these phrases: "experiencing mental formations... he trains," and "calming mental formations... he trains." "Modana" and all such words are synonyms for rapture (pīti). Contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) etc. abandons the defilements and the formations of aggregates (khandhābhisaṅkhāra) rooted in those defilements. "Developed in this way" means it is not developed merely by producing the fourfold or fivefold jhāna, but it means developing it by making it complete in all aspects. Even in the times of vipassanā, the path, and reviewing, the Blessed One, who is skilled in means, showed everything by taking the occurring out-breath (assāsa) as the starting point.

## Why do we say this? This is the meaning.
155:
## Explanation of the Word-by-Word Commentary

In this context, the word 'ussukka' (exertion) is said to be a well-known designation; it means a word with the same meaning. Just as in the phrase 'sutvā bhuñjanti' (having heard, they eat), for one who has the intention to kill and desires to deprive of life, the word 'sañcicca' (intentionally) is similar to the exertion (ussukka) of the word 'voropana' (depriving). It means that the intention to kill and the depriving of life are one and the same. Elder Upatissa said that it does not occur merely by mental impulse alone; the effort (payoga) is also certainly required. Although it is said, 'knowing, well-knowing, intending, transgressing,' the depriving of life is also shown as 'knowing... transgression'; therefore, the meaning is shown without regard for the syllables. Indeed, because of the accomplishment of the result called transgression, the initial intention is the achiever of the purpose.

This phrase, 'all subtle forms of existence (attabhāva),' is said with reference to materiality (rūpa), not immateriality (arūpa). Just as in the Khandha Vibhaṅga, the state of gross or subtle existence of the immaterial phenomena called 'atta' is not intended here in this Third Pārājika. The phrase 'in the mother's womb' is a general statement; in the case of a spontaneously arisen (opapātika) human being, killing also constitutes a Pārājika. If it is asked, 'Why is that (mother's womb) taken when there is no effort in the physical aggregate?' it is because the life faculty (jīvitindriya) of that physical aggregate can only arise at that moment together with the mental aggregates. Therefore, it is established that only a living being is called a 'human being' (manussa-viggaha). Here, 'in the mother's womb' means either in the womb of a human mother or an animal mother. It is also stated in the Parivāra:

'One may kill a woman who is a mother,
And one may kill a man who is a father;
Having killed the mother and father,
One would not reach the state of anāntariya kamma because of that killing.
This problem has been considered by the wise who are skilled in the Vinaya.'

'First' (paṭhama) refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) itself. Indeed, in the mental continuum included in a single life, the rebirth-linking consciousness is called the first consciousness. The death consciousness (cuti-citta) is called the last (pacchima). In another way (if an interpretation other than being included in a single life were taken), there is no such thing as a first consciousness in the beginningless Saṃsāra, because there is no arising of consciousness apart from the conditions of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata). If it were to arise apart from them, it would lead to the flaw of a new being appearing. In the sense that 'this is the very first human form,' even if one is unable to deprive this very first human form of life, it is known as 'the very first' among the countless human forms that arise in the continuum from that beginning until death. When a certain human form reaches the continuum in sequence...
156:
...one is able to deprive it of life. One who destroys the continuum (santati) is said to deprive of life. In this context, if the method of diversity (nānatta-naya) is intended, the phrase 'the very first' is appropriate. However, it is not appropriate in the method of unity (ekatta-naya) due to the oneness of the continuum. If it is argued that because of the phrase 'destroys the continuum,' only the method of unity is intended here, and thus the phrase 'the very first' is inappropriate—no, it is because of the multiplicity of the continuum-present (santati-paccuppanna). Since the sequence of many mental and physical phenomena arising is called a continuum, it is said 'this is the very first.' In this way, both methods are included here. Otherwise, this phrase 'destroys the continuum' would not be established.

In this context, although it seems that only the continuum-present is intended by the phrase 'destroys the continuum' and not the duration-present (addhā-paccuppanna), nevertheless, if the continuum-present is destroyed, the duration-present is also destroyed. There is nothing to be said against the fact that if the duration-present is destroyed, the continuum-present is also destroyed. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: 'Both of them can be deprived of life; therefore, referring to both types of present, it is said "destroys the continuum".' Because of the phrase 'destroys the continuum,' if there is a transgression against a being who is about to die naturally at the end of its lifespan, there is no offense because the continuum is not destroyed by the transgression. If the transgression causes death in the interval before the end of the lifespan, there is an offense; the teachers say it is also connected to kamma. Based on the text, 'One might praise the beauty of death, or incite to death; he is also a Pārājika, one who is no longer in communion,' it should be understood that the Pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment of the intention to kill, because it is definitely unwholesome, involves painful feeling, is a bodily or vocal action, and is an act (kiriya).

'Seven or eight turns of the impulsion process' (javana-vāra) is said by way of similar objects. For that very reason, 'by way of similar continuum' etc. is stated. When it becomes the condition for the immediately following consciousness while being endowed with its opposite, it becomes weak, unlike before. Such an occurrence is the destruction of the life faculty.

'Īti' (calamity) refers to releasing seven kinds of scorpions and so forth in battle to bite and kill. 'Pajjaraka' is a mantra that causes the body to burn. 'Sūcika' is a stake. 'Visūcika' is the disease of indigestion (cholera). 'Pakkhandiya' is the disease of bloody dysentery. Creating a large body two or three hundred fathoms long, extracting Nagas, or causing death by poison or causing burning in others' bodies when looking with anger is called an effort (payoga).
157:
"Some teachers" refers to the teachers of the Mahāsaṅghika sect. This woman (possesses psychic power). Kulumba is the name of a fetus or a child. If it is asked: how does that power affect another child? When that person with power gazes intently with a corrupt mind, both that child and that power perish simultaneously, just as the breaking and extinguishing of a fire in a pot occurs in a single moment. It is written that their view does not agree with the instructions found in the Suttanta texts. Other teachers say that if one takes the view of those Mahāsaṅghikas and says, "This view is also suitable for permanent things," it should be rejected by way of the Triads (tika).

In the cases of sāhatthika-payoga (effort by one's own hand) and nissaggiya-payoga, the state of being sāhatthika is to be understood by the bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) that arises together with the seventh volition, which is the concluding decisive volition. In the case of āṇattika-payoga (effort by command), since vocal intimation (vacīviññatti) can occur along with all seven volitions, the sounds of the seven syllables come together to form individual syllables, making one's intention known through as many syllables as necessary; the state of being āṇattika is to be understood by the vocal intimation born together with the seventh volition that produces the final syllable. The same applies to vijjamaya-payoga (effort through magical knowledge). In the case of āṇatti (command) by bodily gesture, the method is the same as that stated for sāhatthika. In thāvara-payoga (permanent effort), as long as the other person dies, the perpetrator is bound by the action and incurs an offense. In further arrangements, if many others die, the multiplicity of being bound by the action (kammabaddha) and so on should be understood, provided the others die. However, in this case, there is only one pārājika offense. Since the goal-achieving volition (atthasādhaka-cetanā) is found only here in the third pārājika and in the second pārājika, and not elsewhere, these verses common to both pārājikas are spoken:

Those phenomena which are fixed by the law of past phenomena are known as fixed (niyata) phenomena.
Those phenomena which are fixed by the law of future phenomena are alone unfixed (aniyata) here in this case of pārājika.

For phenomena fixed by the law of past phenomena, the stability of the cause is indeed established.
For phenomena fixed by the law of future phenomena, the stability of the cause is dependent (upon the result).

Therefore, there is also another state of natural law (dhamma-niyāmatā) that arises due to a cause.
The result of that volition is unfixed; the volition that depends on the result is the state of law (niyāmatā).

Thus, for all phenomena, the state of natural law exists.
That volition which has attained the natural law is the goal-achieving volition (atthasādhaka-cetanā).

Before the completion of the volition, and afterwards because of the completion of its goal,
Without distinction, every goal-achieving volition is of six kinds.
158:
Because it is possible to make it known in detail in the case of command (āṇattika-payoga), that volition is called 'goal-achieving' (atthasādhika) only in command.

Fixed and unfixed states should be known in the nature of wrongness (micchatta) and rightness (sammatta). In the Abhidhamma method, not all fixed and unfixed natures are fruitful; therefore, only in that Abhidhamma would that volition be fixed (niyata).

All volitions to steal, whether by one's own hand or by command, would be absolutely fixed volitions according to the Abhidhamma method.

Based on taking life, there are many varieties of effort such as by one's own hand or by command; by the power of Abhidhamma, each of these volitions occurs and falls into that Triad of Fixedness (niyata-tika).

The cutting of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and the volition to cut it—these two are not the same as an act done by one's own hand (sāhatthika), much less could they be the same as an act by command (āṇattika).

The cutting of the life-faculty and the volition to cut it—these two are not the same as an act done by one's own hand (sāhatthika), much less could they be the same as an act by command (āṇattika).

At the moment of cutting the life-faculty, the murderous volition has lasted a long time; if so, what state determines the offense?

At the time of cutting the life-faculty, if the killer is dead, or asleep, or awake, would the killer be [acting with] wholesome [consciousness]?

There would be a breakdown of the Wholesome Triad (kusala-tika) and the Feeling Triad (vedanā-tika). In such a manner, the volition of the one who kills by his own hand is accomplished (as the cause of the offense).

Among the five laws shown in the Commentary—the law of seeds (bīja-niyāma), the law of temperature (utu-niyāma), the law of action (kamma-niyāma), the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma), and the law of mind (citta-niyāma)—some consider that this goal-achieving volition (atthasādhaka-cetanā) enters into association. If it is said, "This law of goal-achieving volition does not exist," then volitions that are fixed in wrongness or fixed in rightness would also come to the state of non-existence. Therefore, it should be understood that all those volitions, as appropriate, are included within the law of action and the law of mind. In the case of living, the disadvantage is analyzed by showing the advantage of death. However, in this training rule, because the terms "perception of death" (maraṇasaññī), "volition for death" (maraṇacetana), and "intention for death" (maraṇādhippāya) are not clearly manifest in the word "intention" (saṅkappa), they are analyzed; or else, because they are not clear or not coarse, they are not analyzed.

In the place where it is said, "This is not merely the name of thought (vitakka)," it should be taken that it is not only the name of thought, but indeed also the name of perception (saññā) and volition (cetanā). This is also stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī. Because it is said "from the body"...
159:
Or a critique should be made. In the phrase "This is not just the name of vitakka," it should be understood that it is not only the name of vitakka, but in fact, it is also the name of saññā and cetanā. It is stated similarly in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī.

Because it is stated as "kāyato," although it should be said as "sattiñusū," it is expressed as "ususattiādinā" for the sake of smoothness of speech. In a case where there is no specific designation, the object of the kamma is either the intended being or another being. In the phrase "ubhayehi" (by both), even if the first blow is not capable on its own, because it becomes capable upon receiving the second blow, it has become the cause for the destruction of the life-faculty. In truth, the killer delivers that first blow solely for the purpose of destroying the life-faculty. The second blow, however, is delivered with a different mind. Therefore, the phrase "by the first blow alone" is well-stated. Regarding the phrase "volition is harsh," the teacher wrote that the preliminary volition (pubbabhāgacetanā) which arises by taking a heavy object as its focus is the natural murderous volition (vadhakacetanā) and is not "harsh." It is said, "The preliminary volition is the accompaniment; only the murderous volition is harsh." In the phrase "as desired," both beasts are pierced. It is said that even one who throws with his own hand is not exempt because of the prior agreement.

Specific details of the action do not appear in the commentaries. It is said that the teacher considers it to be consistent with the Pali: "Pierce in this way, strike in this way, kill in this way." The passage beginning with "striking from the front" is said to be merely a deviation from the intended object (vatthu-visaṅketa). By the phrase "this person in the village," only the individual is specified. If a person commands by way of gender/characteristic, "Kill the tall one," without specifying further. If he speaks with specification, other teachers say he would say, "This tall one." However, the teachers say that when "dīgha" (tall) is said, it is already specified; thus he speaks without [further] specification, and the meaning is that the commanding monk does not say to kill any particular one among the tall ones. It is written, "Even if he intends a single person with a mind that marks the moment, he commands without specifying." It is stated that "If the other person kills another who possesses such characteristics, the commander is exempt because it did not happen according to his intention." In another Gaṇṭhipada, it is written, "In this way, even by the power of being tall, etc., it seems appropriate to say that it is only what is not specified by the mind." All should be accepted after careful investigation. In the phrase "because of specifying the place," by specifying the place, he only intends to kill the one sitting in that place. He himself, however, is not in that place at that time. Therefore, his own life-faculty along with the place does not become the object. Thus, one who commands to kill himself [unintentionally] is said to command the killing of another. How? Although he himself is short and thin and intended himself in the preceding stage, at the moment of commanding, "Kill the tall one," the mind of the commander—because those characteristics such as tallness do not exist in himself—arises by taking the life-faculty of another person who is similar to the one to be killed as its object. Therefore, the commanding monk is bound by the kamma. It should be noted that fulfillment occurs in this way.
160:
The mind of one who commands, "Kill the short one, the fat one, the strong one," because those characteristics do not exist in himself, arises by taking the life-faculty of another person who possesses such characteristics as its object. Therefore, the original commander (mūlaṭṭha) is bound by the kamma. It should be understood that it is fulfilled in this way.

In the instructions regarding the succession of messengers: "He commands, an offense of dukkaṭa is incurred. He informs another, an offense of dukkaṭa is incurred." This is stated with reference to the dukkaṭa offense arising from the informing and accepting between teacher and pupil as it may occur. If the executioner (vadhaka) does not accept, the fact that he incurs a dukkaṭa offense is established by implication, but it was not stated because there was no occasion [to preach it]. Because the occasion for the offense to be incurred by the original commander (mūlaṭṭha) is not limited, it is stated that he incurs a thullaccaya offense in that instance. If the executioner accepts, the original commander teacher incurs a thullaccaya offense along with the dukkaṭa offense previously incurred. Why? Because he has incited many people to evil. This dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offense is incurred if the executioner does not report that matter. If he reports it, he incurs only a pārājika offense. Why? Because of the absence of the volition that accomplishes the purpose (atthasādhakacetanā). In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is asked: "He accepts, and a dukkaṭa offense occurs for him. If so, why is it not stated in the Pali text?"—The executioner, having accepted saying "Very well, I will do it," does not perform the act. When such a record exists, for those who have doubt as to "What offense occurs for the commander? Does he incur a dukkaṭa offense?", it is stated that "The commander incurs a thullaccaya offense" to clarify that meaning. To say "If the executioner accepts, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred, and for the commander, a thullaccaya offense is incurred" is not fitting. Because the primary focus is to show the offense incurred by the commander, it was stated that "If the executioner accepts, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred."

In the instructions on the Visakkiyadūta term: "Although he wishes to speak, because there is no special benefit in speaking with difficulty in this matter, the Blessed One did not preach it." Regarding the statement in the commentary that "Only the original commander incurs a dukkaṭa offense," there is this investigation: When Buddharakkhita, who was commanded by the teacher, informs only Saṅgharakkhita of that matter, even if that Saṅgharakkhita accepts saying "Very well," because it is a deviation (visaṅketa), only the teacher incurs a dukkaṭa offense. It is not incurred by Buddharakkhita. Why? Because it was reached with the volition that accomplishes the purpose. For that very reason, it is stated in the Pali: "The commander and the executioner both incur a pārājika offense." However, that dukkaṭa offense to be incurred by the original commander was not stated because there is an occasion that is not limited by the Pali "There is no offense for the commander."
161:
When the agreement is not violated, it is stated that 'the instigator incurs a thullaccaya offense'; therefore, it should be understood as a settled conclusion that when the agreement is violated, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Regarding the statement 'If the executioner (vadhaka) accepts, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred,' this dukkaṭa offense applies only to the executioner, Saṅgharakkhita. In truth, that executioner monk first causes the instigator, Buddharakkhita, to fall into a pārājika offense, and then he himself will fall into a pārājika offense by taking a life. Therefore, although it is not directly stated in the Pali text as 'He takes that person's life; both the instigator and the executioner incur a pārājika offense,' it is already stated by way of meaning. Because it follows the method previously stated as 'From the time the pārājika was prescribed,' that statement is not repeated. Indeed, it has been previously stated: 'He takes that person's life; all those involved incur a pārājika offense.'

In this context, the previously mentioned dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses for the teacher and the disciples no longer apply from the beginning, because they directly reach the pārājika offense. Nevertheless, because the executioner's incurrence of the pārājika offense makes it clear that all of them have become pārājika, it is stated collectively as 'all those involved incur a pārājika offense.' However, in the phrase 'the instigator and the executioner incur a pārājika offense,' it is not stated collectively like that. Why? Because the executioner is currently in a state of having incurred a dukkaṭa offense. In fact, that executioner first incurs a dukkaṭa offense and only later reaches the pārājika offense.

If the disciples convey the message solely out of respect for the teacher, and if they themselves have no intention for the person to die, they do not incur a pārājika offense. However, they will inevitably incur a dukkaṭa offense due to the act of carrying an improper message. To clarify this meaning, some teachers cite as evidence the story from the Dhammapada where the wife of a hunter, who was a Sotāpanna, handed over bows, arrows, and stakes. That view accords with the Tittira Jātaka. Therefore, the teacher states that we consider it to be in accordance with the Pali and the Aṭṭhakathā.

In this case, as well as in the case of sending a message through a succession of messengers, since it is stated without specific restriction as 'Tell such-and-such a person; let such-and-such a person tell such-and-such a person,' there is no violation of the agreement whether the message is conveyed by speech, by gesture, by letter, or by sending a messenger. If the original instigator or an intermediate messenger has made a specific restriction, it should be understood that if that restriction is exceeded, it constitutes a violation of the agreement.

Now, I shall state the method mentioned in the Anugaṇṭhipada regarding both these matters. In the statement 'The executioner accepts; a dukkaṭa offense is incurred,' the offense applies only to the executioner and not to the instigator, Buddharakkhita. If that executioner definitely carries out either the death or the non-death of the person to be killed, then at the very moment of Buddharakkhita's command, among the pārājika and dukkaṭa offenses...
162:
...no offense occurs for Buddharakkhita. If that executioner monk definitely performs either the death or non-death of the person to be killed, then at the very moment of Buddharakkhita's command, one of either pārājika or dukkaṭa would occur. In the term 'iti cittamanos,' by way of context (adhikāra), just like the word 'iti' in 'cittasaṅkappo,' from the context 'The executioner accepts; the instigator incurs a thullaccaya offense,' it is indeed stated by way of context that 'the instigator incurs a dukkaṭa offense.' If one asks why it is not stated explicitly, it is to provide a method even beyond that. If it were said 'the instigator incurs a dukkaṭa offense,' because it is restricted only to the instigator, it would not be known that 'the one who accepts incurs a dukkaṭa.' If it is stated without restriction as 'The executioner accepts; a dukkaṭa offense is incurred,' it is possible to apply the dukkaṭa to both.

Therefore, the commentators, taking the context, said: 'When accepted by Saṅgharakkhita, it should be known that the dukkaṭa belongs only to the instigator.' They neither permit nor reject it for the one who accepts. Specifically, it is rejected because it does not restrict Buddharakkhita. This explains the meaning that for that Buddharakkhita, one of either pārājika or dukkaṭa would occur. Therefore, that statement is also well-said. Because it can be applied to both, the teachers said, 'This dukkaṭa belongs only to the one who accepts.' In that statement, because the word 'mūlaṭṭha' (instigator) is absent, it does not permit the instigator; and because the Pali 'the one who accepts incurs a dukkaṭa offense' is absent, it does not reject it. To provide the method that a dukkaṭa would occur for the executioner due to the acceptance, since 'mūlaṭṭha' is not mentioned in the Pali, the statement 'this dukkaṭa belongs only to the one who accepts' is also well-said. In that Pali, Buddharakkhita is rejected; by the method already stated, his offense is not fixed.

If one asks why the Aṭṭhakathā does not state the dukkaṭa for the executioner due to the acceptance, which is not explicit, but instead states the dukkaṭa only in terms of the instigator? It is to prevent an undesirable meaning. If it were said 'When Saṅgharakkhita accepts, he incurs a dukkaṭa due to the acceptance,' because it is stated explicitly by another method, it would follow that here too, the Aṭṭhakathā has already stated a thullaccaya for the instigator. Considering that the thullaccaya thus arrived at is not explicit, it states the dukkaṭa for the one who accepts without mentioning the thullaccaya. To prevent such an undesirable interpretation because it is not explicit in the Aṭṭhakathā, it says 'this dukkaṭa belongs only to the instigator.' By the method stated by the teacher, the dukkaṭa for the one who accepts is also indeed explicit.

If one asks why the commentator says 'our preference (khanti)' even though it is explicit? It is to show the method of practice (paṭipatti). Even teachers with unimpeded wisdom in the Three Piṭakas practice in this way in such places because it is not explicitly stated in the Pali and Aṭṭhakathā. 'How much more so for someone like me?' Thinking thus, noble sons with good hearts in the future will practice without exceeding the stated method, avoiding the fault of confusion, and without deviating from the order of the commentary (vaṇṇanā).
163:
Other teachers say, "Avoiding the fault of mixing, they practice without overstepping the boundaries of the commentary's sequence." Because this commentary passage is not mentioned in the commentary, or because the teacher later removed it in such instances, it is not found in some palm-leaf manuscripts; therefore, I shall write it in its entirety. If this is the case, would the offense not arise simply from acceptance? An offense occurs in acting as a go-between (sañcaritta), in acceptance, and in rejoicing in death; why then would it not occur in consenting to kill? Therefore, for the one who accepts, this offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) occurs; for that very reason, it was not said here, "for the one who stands at the root." Even in the previous method, it should be understood that this offense of wrongdoing applies to the one who accepts; it was not mentioned only because there was no opportunity. Therefore, whoever accepts, an offense is indeed incurred by that person due to that consent; this is our preference in this matter. As it is here, so it is in the case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna).

In the explanations such as arahorahosaññī (perception of secrecy in a secret place), although only a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is mentioned in the Pāḷi and the Commentary, nevertheless, if there is a specific designation for one who speaks with the intention "let him die" upon hearing it through a succession [of messengers], a Pārājika offense is incurred by the death of the designated person. If there is no specific designation, a Pārājika offense is incurred by the death of anyone at all. For one who speaks with a designation, saying, "Let such-and-such a person hear my words and tell that person [to die]," the nature of the deviation (vissaṅketatā) should be understood as stated in the section on the succession of messengers. If one says, "Let anyone hear and speak," and the person to be killed dies upon hearing it himself, it is not a Pārājika because of the deviation. If anyone hears and speaks, and that person [the target] dies, it is a Pārājika. If one says, "Let anyone hear my words and kill him," and anyone hears and kills, it is a Pārājika; however, if he hears it himself and kills himself, it is not a Pārājika because of the deviation. Thus, it should be understood according to the possibility.

In the phrase "he is released by giving the original price," it is already stated in meaning that he is released even earlier by destroying, breaking, crushing, grinding to powder, or throwing it into the fire. In the phrase "from whose hands the price was taken," it means the monk took the price from the hands of those relatives and attendants. Having taken back the price previously given from the hands of the owner of the manuscript, and giving it back to those very relatives, he is released; thus, it becomes the property of the manuscript owner alone. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is said, "If he, being remorseful, quickly gives the price to them and is released," that statement is made with reference to the wealth with which the manuscript was bought. Why? Because even if the manuscript is not yet given, he is released upon taking the wealth from the hands of the manuscript owner. If...
164:
...it were said with reference to other wealth, it would not be appropriate, because the manuscript has not yet been released from the state of being his own property. If he gives the manuscript to the owners but does not take the price, he is not released because it has not been released from the state of being his own property. If, while the manuscript is being given at its original price, he accepts it saying, "Let it be yours alone," he is released because it has been released from the state of being his own property.

Here is an investigation: If it is argued that just as when a stupa, an image, a pond, or a bridge is bought, the merit belongs only to the maker and not to the buyer, so too the demerit should belong only to the one who wrote the manuscript and not to the buyer—this is not so, because of the word: "He should search for a weapon for him." Indeed, just as it is established that a Pārājika is incurred by one who obtains a weapon made by another and places it [near someone with the intent to kill], so too it is established that a Pārājika is incurred if one obtains a manuscript written by another and places it nearby so that the person to be killed may see it and die. The teacher investigated this, saying that the example of the stupa etc. is an action caused by the act of making (karaṇappaccaya), whereas this [manuscript] has death as its cause (maraṇappaccaya). To me, however, it seems that the meaning can be established by the very example of the stupa etc.

"That many takings of life" means that a single intention (cetanā) is called "that many" by virtue of its function, just as the fourfold nature is mentioned in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and right efforts (sammappadhāna). "Setting a limit" means setting the limit according to one's own desire. If a killer, with the intention "Having dug a pit of such a nature, let him fall into it and die," digs it after determining the size of the pit, it is said "in this pit" with reference to that pit. Now, because the size of the pit to be dug is not determined, it is said "even in a single stroke of the hoe" and so on. Although the Suttantika elders set them apart, the teachers say that the concluding intention (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) exists in both cases.

If it is asked, "How is the object determined when many beings die?"—if the life faculty (jīvitindriya) of one among those to be killed is taken as the object, it means all have been taken as the object. Even in the death of a single person, it is not possible to take his entire life (jīvita) as an object; it is not possible to take as an object the life faculty that is arising, has arisen, or is ceasing. Because it exists, the intention of taking life (pāṇātipāta-cetanā) has both a present object and a pre-nascent object (purejātārammaṇa); therefore, that statement is also appropriate. At the final limit, having made that life which exists as pre-nascent in a single mind-moment the object, when an effort is made with the intention belonging to the seventh impulsion (javana), in effect, the entire life faculty of that being is taken as the object and is destroyed. It cannot be otherwise than this. Similarly, in the preliminary stage, having thought "I will kill many beings," at the time of making the decision, in such acts as administering poison, a single...
165:
In the preliminary stage, having intended, "I will kill many beings," at the moment of final decision, the volition (cetanā) of the aforementioned nature, which accomplishes a single effort (payoga) such as administering poison, arises by taking as its object the aforementioned life-faculty (jīvitindriya) of one among those many beings. By that single volition which has arisen in this way, all those beings are killed. This is because the act of death for all beings is accomplished by that very volition. It is not possible to deprive them of life or to take them as an object in any other way.

If it is asked, "How does the mass of unwholesome states (akusalarāsi) occur when many beings die through a single volition among those volitions?" the answer is: "Because it performs the function of the volitions occurring in each individual death." How so? All those volitions are only kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya-kamma). Therefore, if any one of those volitions gives rise to rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), all the remaining volitions—being obstructed by a more powerful wholesome kamma than the one that gave rebirth—fall into the category of 'lapsed kamma' (ahosi-kamma) and the like, and are no longer able to produce further results. Just as a wholesome volition gives rebirth-linking by obstructing an unwholesome kamma of the 'to be experienced in subsequent lives' (aparāpariyavedanīya) type, so too, because this upapajjavedanīya volition performs the remaining functions of those volitions by way of giving rebirth-linking and so on only in the immediately following existence, it is called a 'mass' (rāsi) even though it is a single volition. Due to the rebirth-linking given by that volition, an extremely intense resultant (vipāka) arises. This is the distinction here, as explained in detail in the Anugaṇṭhipada.

Because the meaning is 'even if they do not wish to die,' an offense is incurred even in the death of a spontaneously born (opapātika) being. If it is argued that 'falling' is not evident because the text says 'having been reborn,' it is written in the scriptures that spontaneous rebirth and falling are one and the same. Alternatively, according to the statement 'without specifying in any way,' since there can be the intention 'let them die in this pit,' the statement 'if one dies being unable to climb out, it is indeed a Pārājika' is well-stated. If a pit was dug with the specific condition 'let them die by falling,' and a spontaneously born human, after appearing, dies merely thinking 'I cannot climb out' based on the existing situation, the nature of a Pārājika is not evident. Therefore, it is stated, 'being unable to climb out.' If that spontaneously born human, being unable to climb out, falls back repeatedly and dies, then by such a death, the act of falling is also accomplished according to the intention of the monk who dug the pit. This is the meaning in this context.

In this regard, there could be this objection: Regarding the being of whom it is said 'dies being unable to climb out,' that being is living in the formless realm (arūpa-loka) at the moment of spontaneous falling. Furthermore, the volition to kill must take the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) as its object, according to the Paṭṭhāna teaching: 'An indefinite state (aniyata-dhamma) assists a state of certain wrongness (micchatta-niyata-dhamma) by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). The physical life-faculty assists the kamma of matricide, patricide, killing an Arahant, and shedding the blood [of a Buddha] by way of object-condition.' However, that physical life-faculty does not exist in formless beings (arūpa-satta). And that volition cannot have a future object, according to the statement: 'An indefinite state assists a state of certain wrongness by way of pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya): object-pre-nascence, base-pre-nascence, object-pre-nascence.'
166:
Because it is taught in the Paṭṭhāna (2.15.48, Micchattaniyatattika) that 'the physical life-faculty (rūpajīvitindriya) assists the act of matricide by way of the pre-nascence condition (purejātapaccaya),' it is not a future object. One might ask: if there were no other being who fell into this pit and died, what would be the object of the murderous intention? The present life-faculty of some living being in this group is the object. Even if that person does not die, it is still an act of taking life (pāṇātipāta).

How is this? For example: having first thought, 'I will kill seven people standing in order with a single arrow,' at the time of making the decision, one releases the arrow making the life (jīvita) of one of them the object. If the arrow misses that person but kills the other six, this person is still one who has committed the act of taking life. Similarly here, the murderous intention of one who thinks 'let anyone die' arises by making the life of someone the object. Even if the intended object does not die, because another dies, it is an act of taking life. If that person were an Arahant and attained Parinibbāna, the killer is indeed a killer of an Arahant (arahantaghātaka). This method applies to all such cases. This is said to be the appropriate decision and explanation handed down through the lineage of teachers.

Regarding the phrase 'the falling form is the standard'—if a mother falls into a pit, undergoes a change of sex (becoming male), and then dies, the person is a matricide (mātughātaka), not merely a killer of a man. Therefore, the offense is incurred by the power of the form at the time of falling. Why? Because the falling form and the dying form belong to the same continuum (ekasantāna). That falling form is indeed his life-faculty; there is no change in that life-faculty. It is only the female and male faculties that cease and arise during the course of existence (pavatti). In that context, 'woman' or 'man' is merely a conventional designation (vohāra). Therefore, he is a matricide, not a killer of a man. Just as the offense is incurred by the power of the falling form for him, so too in this case (regarding yakkhas and petas), a thullaccaya offense is incurred by the power of the falling form because it is the same continuum. This is the appropriate reasoning in the view of the first Elder (Elder Upatissa).

In the view of the second Elder (Elder Phussadeva): although a peta or a yakkha falls, because they have rootless rebirth-linking (ahetukapaṭisandhi) as a result of unwholesome kamma—like the rebirth of yakkhas mentioned in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary etc., 'vāmena sūkaro hoti'—because they are associated with all forms and are of non-human birth, if they die with an animal form, a pācittiya offense is incurred by the power of the form at the time of death. The change to a light offense (lahukāpatti) by the power of the object (vatthu) does indeed occur, just as the pācittiya for cutting a tree growing on a pot of gold changes (to a dukkaṭa). This second view is more appropriate; therefore, it is mentioned last. In the case of a Pārājika object, however, if one of human birth falls in any way and dies in any way, it is a Pārājika only, because of its gravity. For it is said that there is no change in a grave offense (garukāpatti).
167:
When an animal dies, a thullaccaya offense is incurred; the reason for this distinction is that they die as a peta or yakkha after discarding their animal form. If interpreted in another way, it is thought to be the views of Tissa and Phussadeva.

In the Gaṇṭhipada, it is written: 'In the second view, it is stated by the power of one who falls as a worldling (puthujjana) and dies after reaching Arahantship.' Regarding the word 'tiracchāne' (in an animal), some teachers say 'devas are intended.' Others say 'death occurs only with one's own form, not with another form.' Even when dying with the form of a yakkha or peta, the method is the same, meaning a thullaccaya offense is incurred. It is written: 'as in the case of killing a human who has the appearance of an animal.' The phrase 'having received a blow' (pahāraṃ laddhā) is said because it was done to cause the death of beings.

One utters the words, 'Good, good, let [them] die.' 'Vissabhāgaroga' refers to boils, pustules, and the like occurring in the body.

'Kālānuasārī' is said to be the root of a certain creeper. Or it is a flower made of the mahākacchapa (a type of plant/substance). 'Haṃsapuppha' refers to the feathers from both wings of a swan. Following the method mentioned below, the procedure of origination (samuṭṭhāna) through body, speech, and mind should be shown here by applying the methods of personal action and command.

## The Commentary on the Word-for-word Analysis (Padabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Commentary on the Decided Cases (Vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā)

Regarding the phrase 'being those who desire death' (maraṇatthikāva hutvā): because they desire to reach the heavenly world through the breaking up of this body, they are essentially those who desire death; such people with this intention are called 'maraṇatthika.' Because they do not know their state of desiring death, they incur the Pārājika offense. It is not that they do not know the occurrence of their own thoughts; they do indeed know. 'By the power of conventional usage' (vohāravasena) means by the power of the usage in the preliminary stage. However, in the final decision, this usage does not exist. It is not like the case of releasing a pig caught in a snare. 'According to the sequence' (yathānusandhinā) means without dying in the interval. 'Without reflecting' (appaṭivekkhitvā) means without investigating. If there is some object in the lower part, the fold is evident. 'When shown' (dassite) means when it has been taken out and placed. 'Obstruction' (paṭibandhaṃ) means 'do not cause an obstruction or hindrance to the use of the Saṅgha's property associated with you.'
168:
181-2. Since it is not possible to give the action, it is said 'that which was first obtained'. In the past, a monk who gave the most exquisite portion of the alms-food he had obtained was also giving the first portion of the alms-food that he himself had prepared with devotion. In the phrase 'unintentionally' (asañcicca), if one person falls while another is being pulled, there is no intention at all. In the phrase 'one who has no intent to kill' (na maraṇādhippāyassa), even if there is resentment and effort, there is no murderous intention (vadhakacetanā). In the phrase 'one who does not know' (ajānantassa), there is no fault for a monk who does not know due to ignorance of the object (vatthu). This is the distinction of those individuals. Although the phrase 'I did it unknowingly' is not found in the original Pāḷi, it is said that such Pāḷi should exist because it is mentioned in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). In the phrase 'If it is not a Thullaccaya (grave offense)', it is said that if painful feeling does not arise, it is only a Dukkaṭa (wrongdoing); this point should be investigated. 'Muggara' refers to mallets used for carving. 'Vema' refers to the sticks bound crosswise above and below those mallets. Below, both versions are read. It appears as if it has reached the hand. Thinking 'Let there be no distraction for that monk', he cuts it off. Having declared the attainment of a special distinction (dhamma), he cuts off his food out of shame for the offerings (sakkāra) that arise from that attainment, because he has already informed monks of similar standing. They inform him of what is allowable (kappiya).

'Unrequested intimation' (akata-viññatti) means not by way of intimation. Since it is permitted, even if it is done, it is like not being done, and thus it is called akata-viññatti. It is written that intimation in a place where one has not been invited with 'Venerable sir, please say what you need' is akata-viññatti. It is not proper to give directly with one's own hand to parents who are non-believers (titthiya). 'Pitucchā' refers to a paternal aunt. Even if they do not ask, one gives thinking 'It is difficult to ask', or if they themselves cannot say so, thinking 'It will be for them when they have need'. Because of the statement 'It is not medical practice', it is said that it is proper to provide medicine up to seven generations of the family lineage. 'Sabbapadesu' (in all cases) means the same method applies to the elder mother, younger mother, and so on.

Having searched by the method already mentioned, it is stated 'or by novices (sāmaṇera)', etc. They say, 'Not by unrequested intimation'. They say, 'If one gives while longing for it, it is a Dukkaṭa'. By way of what is allowable, it is said 'Bring flowers', etc. Because it is said 'He performed a worship (pūjā)', they say it is not proper to take it oneself.

If it is said 'Please recite', it should be done. For it is proper to preach the Dhamma. If the people do not know, one should not remove one's feet. For they take it as an inauspicious sign (avamaṅgala).
169:
If one gives alms-food that has been handled by someone to King Coranāga, he will become angry; yet, the first portion of alms-food that has not been handled is also not allowable for monks. Thinking thus, a monk took a small amount of rice between his fingers and then gave all the rice in the bowl; the king was pleased with that. 'Varapotthakacittattharana' refers to a special type of sewn floor covering. King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī (Piturāja), having been defeated by the Damiḷas, lived in the Rohana region for sixteen years. Then, surrounded by friends and ministers, he came saying 'I will retake the kingdom', and on the way, he had one minister executed for a minor matter. The remaining ministers, fleeing in fear, were plundered by robbers on the forest path and reached Hambugallaka Monastery. There, the Elder Tissa, who was proficient in the four Nikāyas, provided them with support and then sent them back to the King. After regaining the kingdom with those ministers, the King built Abhayagiri Monastery for the Elder Tissa of Hambugallaka. It is said that the remaining ministers each had a monastery built as well.

Sending someone near robbers is similar to this case: 'He sends him to Vāḷayakkha Monastery'. Why? Because of the intent to kill. A monk who, for the purpose of catching fish in tanks etc., sends a fisherman to the bank of the tank under another pretext saying 'Go to the edge of the tank', should be guilty of an offense of killing (pāṇātipāta). This is similar to 'He sent him to Vāḷayakkha Monastery'. Why? Because it accords with the words 'due to the intent to kill', and because it is also stated in the Commentary, 'Thus also to Vāḷayakkha'.

In the phrase 'taṃ tatraṭṭhitaṃ chindantaṃ' (cutting that which stands there), the word 'taṃ' (that) is not present in some versions. In other versions, it means they incur Pārajika and Thullaccaya offenses. Even with a wholesome mind, thinking 'I will cut this tree and go quickly to show the bowl and robes to the Saṅgha', it is not proper to cut it because it is not permitted. However, it is allowable for another monk because it is permitted.

How so? For the purpose of protecting a hut (kuṭi), the Blessed One permitted the giving of fire, etc. This hut is for the benefit of monks. Therefore, it is said, 'There is no need to say that it is allowable for another monk to cut a tree for the purpose of protecting a monk'. If the Blessed One permitted the destruction of plant life (bhūtagāma) for the purpose of covering the nakedness of a monk whose robes were stolen, and if it was permitted at the time of a snakebite for the purpose of saving life, then one should not say 'Even life should be sacrificed, but a tree should not be cut', etc. Therefore, that example is not the standard; only the decision of the teachers of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya) is the standard here. Here, this is the reasoning of the teachers: Even among Noble Ones (ariya-puggala), beings seeing them naked might develop lack of faith and go to hell...
170:
(In the future) they will come to be; moreover, it is permitted to destroy vegetation (bhūtagāma) so that snakes, having bitten, may be freed from their demerit. To protect the minds of the donors, [the Buddha] permitted the offering of fire and so forth. Otherwise, there would be an obstacle to the merit of the people and an obstacle to the gains of the Saṅgha. For one who intends to kill, there is no benefit to the mind. Because of seeing such non-transgression or the sacrifice of life, one might think, "How wonderful! He has done what is difficult to do," and thus gain only faith. Therefore, [cutting a tree] is not allowable for oneself, but it is allowable for another monk. Otherwise, if the meaning is taken [differently], it would lead to the establishment of the false Dhamma of the sectarians.

In the Ganthipada, however, it is written: "For a monk who cuts a tree for the sake of life, it is not allowable because it is unwholesome, being cut through the power of self-love; but it is allowable for another monk." When many trees have fallen upon [someone] or when they have fallen over a cliff, it is allowable for one to cut trees for the sake of another monk. Why? Because of the intention to protect others. Paritta means protection; to show that paritta, it was said: "shaving the ground all around" (samantā bhūmitacchanaṃ), etc.

Regarding the word vissaṅketa (misunderstanding) in the case of three people killing: even if [the victim] is killed by one of the three strikes, it is said to be a Parājika because it occurred within the designated area (khetta). Therefore, if all three kill together, they incur an offense. For this reason, it is said: "Within the designated limit, there is no vissaṅketa." Since it is said, "Beyond the limit, there is vissaṅketa in all places," it seems that if the third person kills by taking the strength of the two, he incurs an offense; this should be investigated. When it is said, "Let two people kill," if either one or two kill, it is a Parājika. They say: "If death occurs due to two strikes, it is called being killed by two; if death does not occur, it is only one; therefore, this should be understood."

## The Commentary on the Third Parājika is finished.

## 4. The Fourth Parājika

## Commentary on the Story of the Monks Dwelling on the Banks of the Vaggumudā River

In the Fourth Parājika, that river is beautiful (vaggu) and it gladdens (modayati) beings; therefore, it is called Vaggumudā. There is also a reading "Vaggumadā". The meaning of that word Vaggumadā is: that river is beautiful because it is full of clear, pure waves, and it is also subtle. As in the words nīluppala (blue lotus) and so forth, the meaning of being endowed with the state of prolonging life also has the sense of "long life". In the word madassa, the etymology should be understood as a river that is full of many foods, drinks, and so forth on festival days. Vaggu means pure, as it is recognized by the world. "They will be spoken" (bhāsito bhavissanti) is the remainder of the text.
171:
194-5. It is said that vaṇṇavā, vaṇṇavanto, and vaṇṇavantāni are also formed in the plural. Since there is no deficiency or fullness of the senses such as the eye, it is said: "due to the fullness of the seat of attention" (abhiniviṭṭhokāsassa paripuṇṇattā). The seat of attention for the sixth [sense], the mind, is the heart-base (hadayavatthu). It is the natural sense in the cycle of the four postures. Attanā dahati means placing by oneself, or making known by having penetrated [the truth] oneself. Santa means the present (vattamāna). Gotrabhū means it is only a name, as it occurs by merely following the lineage of the monks.

## Commentary on the Training Rule with its Analysis (Savibhaṅga)

In the Word-for-word Analysis (padabhājanī), since it says "the three knowledges" (tisso vijjā), if it is asked whether the formless-sphere jhanas are excluded—no, they are not. Because in the explanation of those three knowledges, in the term ñāṇadassana, it is specifically said: "Whatever is knowledge (ñāṇa) is vision (dassana); whatever is vision is knowledge." Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "The Word-for-word Analysis is stated with knowledge (vijjā) at the head." Dhurāṃ katvā means making it the lead (making it primary).

## Commentary on the Word-for-word Analysis (Padabhājanīya)

Lust (rāga) and so forth are called signs (nimitta) because they are the causes of lust and so forth that will arise in the future. If one says, "I am a possessor of the knowledges," referring to any one of the three knowledges, it is a Parājika. If one speaks referring to mundane arts (vatthuvijjā) and so forth, it is not a Parājika. If it is argued that only the abandonment of defilements is mentioned, and because it is only the moment of abandoning defilements, there is no occurrence of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)—no, that is not so, because it illustrates the function of the Path (magga). Therefore, it is said: "It does not exist without the Path," and so forth. Citta means the state of the mind being free from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). They say: "As long as the knowledge (the Fruit) has not yet arrived, if a person who says 'I am a possessor of insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa)' refers to the supramundane (lokuttara), and if the listener also understands it as supramundane, it is indeed a Parājika. This is because the supramundane also has that name 'insight-knowledge'."

"Even for one who speaks generally without specification, it is said to be a Parājika. It is appropriate to say 'Parājika' for one who speaks referring to the supramundane. How? Just as in the place where it is said 'Even one who says "I am a possessor of the knowledges" incurs a Parājika,' even though mundane arts (vatthuvijjā) etc. are possible, it is a Parājika because those mundane arts were not intended; so it is here as well. It is not possible to set another limit; if a monk, desiring to make his virtues known, speaks of the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) mixed with mundane [knowledge], it cannot be limited to saying he incurs a Parājika; it happens in another way"—so say other teachers. That statement is contradictory from beginning to end. Therefore, the example of vijjā is not a suitable example here. This is because in the Dispensation, mundane arts (vatthuvijjā) etc. are not prescribed as "knowledges" (vijjā). Or, it is written that another limit cannot be set because the Buddha did not use those synonymous terms in the section on the analyzed field (vibhattakhetta). When it is said, "I am a possessor of the analytical insights"...
172:
They say that because it is spoken figuratively, a thullaccaya (grave offense) is incurred; this statement should be examined. Having investigated and considered it: because of the connection with such words as "He who lives in your monastery," it is a figurative expression and is thus called a thullaccaya. Whether one says, "I attain the attainment of cessation," or "I am a gainer of it," or the statement beginning with "If it were so," the meaning is the same; for he speaks only to make known his own distinction. In words such as "He who lives in your monastery," the word "I" is absent, so being figurative is appropriate. Here, however, he points to himself saying "I am a gainer of that [attainment]," therefore it is as if a pārājika (defeat) should be incurred, so they say. The words in the Mahāpaccari and other commentaries say that among the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), not even one is [attained], therefore because it is spoken figuratively, it is not [a pārājika]; this should be well investigated. From the term "realization of the fruit" (phalasacchikiriyā) onwards, the text should be taken thus: even in the realization of the fruit, for each one, by the power of each fruit, a pārājika should be understood.

In the triad beginning with "abandoning of lust" (rāgassa pahānaṃ), only the abandoning of defilements is mentioned; that abandoning of defilements does not exist without the Path (magga). By the third Path, lust and hatred are abandoned; by the fourth, delusion. Therefore, for one who says "My lust is abandoned," etc., a pārājika is incurred. In the triad beginning with "the mind being free from the hindrance of lust" (rāgā cittaṃ vinīvaraṇatā), only the supramundane (lokuttara) is mentioned; therefore for one who says "My mind is free from the hindrance of lust," etc., it should be taken that only a pārājika is incurred. Some teachers living in the Uttaravihāra say, "Because it is an unshakable state (akuppadhamma)." If it is asked, "Why is it not [a pārājika]?" It is because in the Mātikā it is spoken only in the present tense as "Thus I know, thus I see." If so, in the word-by-word commentary (Padabhājaniya), because it is said "I attained, I have attained," etc., then for one who says "I was a stream-enterer in a past life," let there be a pārājika. It cannot be, because a meaning other than the past life is possible. How? It is said to make known that the present state should be taken by the power of the current duration, not the past life. The teachers say that speaking of a past life is a figurative expression, thus it is a thullaccaya.

The statement "Even if it is not so, it is only a pārājika" is said by way of assuming an impossible case. It will be said later: "Thus the speech has three factors." In saying "This does not exist," if the former factor exists, the latter does not; thus in the words "I attained" and "I have attained," although there is no difference in time in terms of meaning, there is indeed a difference in the expression.

Ukkhēṭito means frightened. The root khiṭ is in the sense of frightening.

## The Explanation of the Section on Pure [Offenses] is Finished.
173:
## Commentary on the Section on Desire for an Object (Vattukāmavāra)
Viññattipathe means standing in a place that should be known or can be known. Therefore it is stated: "A monk standing beyond the range of communication who hears with the divine ear-element (dibba-sotadhātu) does not incur a pārājika." In saying "He attains jhāna," if the hearer knows "This monk speaks thus with the intention of displaying his own virtues," it is a pārājika. If he knows otherwise, the teachers say not even a shadow of a pārājika appears.

## The Commentary on the Section on Desire for an Object is Finished.

## Commentary on the Variations of Non-offense (Anāpattibheda)
Anullapanādhippāyo means not having the intention to speak out. Other teachers say if there were an intention to speak out (ullapanādhippāya), it would only be a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense. It is said that this statement should be understood by connecting it with the story that comes later: "Friend, it is difficult for a worldling to endure."

## The Commentary on the Word-by-word Analysis (Padabhājaniya) is Finished.

## Commentary on the Decided Cases (Vinītavatthu)
225-6. In the cases of difficult work (dukkara), the house (āgāra), the desire for a pit (āvaṭakāma), and delight (abhirati), they say "If there were an intention to speak out, it is a pārājika." However, the reason for this is hard to see. It should be considered as if it were called a thullaccaya. The statement that one who goes by vehicle or by psychic power (iddhi) does not incur a pārājika is appropriate only in a situation where a promise was made to go on foot. "Those who go without falling behind or going ahead" means going as if holding each other's hands without leaving the distance of a forearm's length (hatthapāsa). In going together like "Arise, come, let us go," the teachers consider that even if one goes ahead or behind, no offense is incurred. "One who stays" means if a lay follower (upāsaka) sees him staying thus, it is a pārājika. It is said "One who stays during the night and then goes does not incur a pārājika." Nānāverajjakā means those living in various districts (janapada). Saṅghalābho means one's own portion received according to seniority.

Here, in the matter of the question "Who is it?", dhammadhātu means the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).
174:
Na uppaṭipāṭiyā means not recollecting by way of skipping like a lion's leap (sīhokkanta). Therefore, the meaning is that he penetrates [the knowledge] that it is a single birth which has become an intermediate existence (antarābhava).

## Conclusion (Nigamana)

In this place "twenty-four," those who kill their mother, father, or an Arahant reach the third pārājika. The violator of a nun and the four beginning with Lambi reach only the first pārājika. If asked why it is said to be twenty-four despite this? No, it is because of not knowing the intention. In truth, the four such as the mother-killer are intended here as unordained persons (anupasampanna). The four such as Lambi, although included in the first pārājika, are taught separately because in one sense they are not those who practice sexual intercourse (methunadhamma). With reference to the mere unfitness for communion (saṃvāsa) taught as "having one legal act, one recitation, and equal training," it is said "As it was before, so it is after." Otherwise, if taken in another way, it would follow that even their state of being a monk by designation and profession does not exist.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika is Finished.

## The Commentary on the Pārājika Section is Finished.
175:
## 2. Saṅghādisesa Section
## 1. Explanation of the Sukkavissaṭṭhi Training Rule

"Okkamantānaṃ" is the original reading. Here, the objector asks: "In this first Saṅghādisesa training rule, why is the subject 'a monk' (yo pana bhikkhu) not specifically mentioned?" It is answered: It is not specifically mentioned because the intention is to show that this rule is dependent on a specific purpose. How is it dependent? For a monk who is motivated by the intention to cure an itch, or who makes an effort to treat an itch, or who makes an effort regarding the bases of Dukkaṭa offenses such as the thighs due to sexual lust, or regarding the bases of Thullaccaya offenses such as wounds—even if there is an emission of semen, it is not a Saṅghādisesa offense. A Saṅghādisesa offense occurs only when there is an emission of semen while making an effort with the specific desire for the pleasure of emission; it is not so with any other desire. This is because of the statement: "If there is no intention to emit, there is no offense." Therefore, to show that such an intention is required, the subject is not specifically mentioned in this training rule. If the subject were mentioned as "Whichever monk should reach the state of emitting semen with intention," it would contradict the statement: "If one intends but makes no effort and semen is emitted, there is no offense." If it were expressed in the locative case as "In the intentional emission of semen, except in a dream," the same contradiction would arise. Therefore, without using those two modes of phrasing, it was stated: "The intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a Saṅghādisesa offense." In that phrasing, since there is no locative case in the sense of a cause (nimitta), the definition of the causal meaning is not fixed. Because it is not so fixed, it should be understood that this meaning is shown: the intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a Saṅghādisesa offense if there is effort, but if there is no effort, there is no offense.

236-7. In the word "Sañcetanikā," the first derivation shows the meaningfulness of the prefix (upasagga), and the second derivation shows the meaning of the suffix -ika. It means "due to the specific locations of wind, bile, phlegm, blood, etc." Regarding the word "Dhātu," it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada that it refers to the four elements such as the earth element, or the eighteen elements such as the eye element. "Vatthisīsa" means the base of the bladder. Some say it refers to the base of the male organ and not the tip. By the phrase "in the same way," one should take "due to the effort in the organ," etc. "Released from that" means not from the whole body, but merely moving from the respective location of the semen; so it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada. If it is argued that this does not agree with the phrase "merely upon entering the urinary tract (dakasota)," then the phrase "entering the urinary tract," etc., is stated.
