The meaning of that statement is: having made an effort in the organ and caused the semen to move from its place, one then intends to endure it to prevent it from entering the urinary tract due to subsequent remorse. Once it has come out of the urinary tract, one is no longer able to prevent it. Even if one is unable, if one tries to prevent it with the intention to do so, in the meantime...
176:
Because one is unable to prevent it above the urinary tract, it is said "or not yet come out." Why? Because semen that has moved from its place inevitably enters the urinary tract; thus the meaning in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) agrees with the meaning in the Gaṇṭhipada. "Released from that" means released from its own location. Indeed, it is only when it has come out of one's own body that the statement "whether it has come out or not yet come out" would be contradictory. Since semen that has moved from various parts of the body inevitably enters the urinary tract, it is said "merely upon entering the urinary tract." By this, the manifest time of the offense is shown. What is meant? For a monk who makes an effort in the organ for the pleasure of emission, even if a large amount of semen moves from its place in the body but remains stuck in various parts, as soon as an amount as small as what a tiny fly could drink enters the urinary tract, a Saṅghādisesa offense is committed.

In the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, it is also stated: "Even if it has not entered the urinary tract, it is a Saṅghādisesa," etc. If a monk does not notice that much semen coming out and, based on the statement "He intends, he makes an effort, it is not released, the offense is a Thullaccaya," confesses it with the perception of it being a Thullaccaya, he is still not released from the offense. He must be rehabilitated from the Saṅghādisesa offense either by seeing the color of semen in the urine or by knowing the slipperiness of the semen residing in the seminal vesicle. This is the logic in the view of the Third Elder in this matter. All the teachers are just these three Elders. The two decisions of those Elders—entering the urinary tract and making an effort in the organ—are common here; so Elder Upatissa says, it is said.

Considering that semen which has moved from its place inevitably enters the urinary tract, it is said: "In this case, the offense should be known merely by the movement from its place." An offense occurs only when it enters the urinary tract. It should be reflected that the entire body is the location of semen; if it has not entered [the tract], it is not called "moved from its place." Because the Elder is an Abhidhammika, since it is stated in the Kathāvatthu Commentary that "Sukkavissaṭṭhi is rooted in lust (rāga)," its production is rooted in the mind. From the Vinaya statement, "He took a portion of that impure thing with his mouth, and put a portion into his organ," it is also evident that it can be produced by physical conditions (utu). However, that semen produced by physical conditions occurs only in those who are not free from lust, because of the statement: "It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that an Arahant should emit semen." Since it is stated in the Parūpāhāra Commentary that "he has a storage for it," there is a place for that semen to reside, just like for feces and urine.
177:
In the Kathāvatthu Commentary (page 309), it is stated "it exists," thus the fact that there is a location (āsayā) for that semen is very clear. Because it is unmixed, like matter produced by the natural mind, and because of its emission, teachers conceive of three locations for semen: near the bladder, the waist, and the body. That semen should be understood like snake venom. Just as there is no fixed location for snake venom, but it arises when [the snake] is angry and bites, so too in this semen, there is no fixed location, but it is conceived to arise when one exerts effort through the power of passion (rāga).

The khobhakaraṇa-paccaya (disturbing cause) refers to causes such as medicine, lodging, and nutriment. In the phrase "saṃsaggabhedato," it means that dreams can vary due to two or three of these four causes. In the phrase "pahīnavipallāsattā," it means that whatever Sekhas and worldlings (puthujjanas) dream is entirely a distortion and is unreal. If that were so, it would contradict the statement: "A dream seen due to a prior sign (pubbanimitta) is definitely true." Therefore, that statement is not made with reference to the object (ārammaṇa). That object may be true or false. If it were said with reference to the object, one should say: "Asekhas, having abandoned distortion (vipallāsa), dream only the truth and not the false." In reality, it is said with reference to the vision (dassana). That vision is unreal. This is because even though one does not actually see, it is as if one sees; though one does not hear, it is as if one hears; though one does not touch, it is as if one touches. The teacher says, "That one also dreams the truth is not our opinion." That dream is not an object such as a visible sign (rūpa-nimitta); it is said with reference to an adventitious (āgantuka) present object such as a visible sign. Visible signs, etc., which are kamma-signs (kamma-nimitta) and destiny-signs (gati-nimitta), are indeed objects of the bhavaṅga-mind. Among those signs, the kamma-sign is only past, while the destiny-sign may be present for a short time.

"Īdisāni" means minds that have objects such as adventitious present visible signs, which were previously experienced or conceived in the present, and are associated with passion (rāga), etc. A monkey's sleep is quickly changing. Fearing a fall from a tree branch, it frequently opens its eyes and sleeps. Although humans also repeatedly open their eyes and look like those who are clearly awake, just as those who are awake repeatedly descend into the bhavaṅga, so too during the time of dreaming, their minds descend into the bhavaṅga. Because of this descent into the bhavaṅga, it is called "sleeping." Since it is said, "One sleeps with the bhavaṅga-mind," the descent into the bhavaṅga is called "sleep (niddā)" because it depends on the effortless and peaceful state of the physical body (karaja-kāya). That sleep is said to be "occurring" because, although one emerges from the bhavaṅga at the time of dreaming due to the weakness of the physical body, it reaches a state of effortlessness and peace. Because the physical body is effortless and peaceful, beings cannot be called "awake."
178:
The heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) depending on that physical body (karaja-kāya) is not very clear (serene). Because it is not clear, the mental process depending on that heart-base is like the light of a lamp depending on an unclear wick. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary: "That dream-volition (cetanā), having a weak base, is unable to pull for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)," and so on.

However, in the Ganthipada, it is written: "Having a weak base means the sign (nimitta) appearing in the dream is also weak." That weakness of the sign is not always the case; it applies to all signs. Volition is not weak because of the weakness of the object; the mental process is not weak because a mind with a past or future object, or a mind with a concept (paññatti) as an object, is not weak. The state of weakness of a volition without a base is not appropriate, because it possesses extremely great power due to the power of meditation (bhāvanā) which has no [physical] base. A mind endowed with the power of meditation, though it is merely a mental phenomenon (nāma), can take the very heavy physical body and place it in the Brahma world in just a single thought-moment. A sense-sphere mind (kāmāvacara-citta) that has not yet reached absorption (appanā) but is similar to that meditative mind can even enable the physical body to leap into the sky; what then need be said of other mahaggata and lokuttara minds?

If one asks what inferential reason there is to know that it is only the power of the mind, it is because one sees the occurrence of special functional activities such as repetition (āsevana) obtained through the power of the mind. Therefore, the teachers conceive that "having a weak base" means "having a weak heart-base." If the heart-base could produce the dullness or sharpness of the mind depending on it through its own dullness or sharpness, then the heart-base would be a faculty (indriya) like the eye-base, ear-base, etc. But this heart-base is not a faculty. This is because it is not presented as a faculty in the section on derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) in the Dhamma-saṅgaṇī Pali. Because it is not a faculty, it was not taught immediately after the body-faculty (kāyindriya); and because it is a base-matter (vatthu-rūpa), it was not taught immediately after the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), which is not a base-matter. Therefore, if one says, "The statement 'because that heart-base is not clear, the mental process depending on it is also not clear' is not established," [we reply] it is indeed established. This is because, even in matters that are not faculties, one sees the distortion of the mental process due to the combination of causes such as suitable or unsuitable climate (utu) and nutriment (āhāra), and because it is evident to direct perception. This is because one considers oneself as if awake even though one is not yet awake.

By this much, the specific mode of the physical body being effortless and peaceful is called sleep (niddā). That sleep occurs through the specific mode of the mind descending into the bhavaṅga. A being endowed with that sleep emerges from the bhavaṅga and sees a dream. Such a person is called "one possessed by monkey's sleep" (kapimiddha-pareta). The meaning that such a person is asleep but not yet awake is thus established.
179:
Because of the uninterrupted continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), one is said to be truly asleep. Therefore, it is said: "If a sleeping person sees [a dream], it would contradict the Abhidhamma," and so on. Since one is not considered awake during the moment of sleep, it is said: "If an awake person sees [a dream], it would contradict the Vinaya," and so on. Because there is a state where drowsiness has not yet ended and the life-continuum has not been fully entered, it is said: "One overcome by monkey-like drowsiness (kapimiddha) sees [a dream]." Otherwise, this person would neither be asleep nor awake, and would not have entered that sleep themselves. By this sequence of words, the Abhidhamma, the Vinaya, the words of Elder Nāgasena, and logical reasoning are all consistent with one another.

In this context, "kapimiddhapareto" means one overcome by drowsiness that has emerged from the life-continuum. That kind of sleep is called "kapimiddha" here. "Therein, what is torpor (middha)? It is the illness of the body, the unreadiness for work... sleep; this is called torpor." Thus it is stated. This torpor is a mental phenomenon (nāma-dhamma). The illness, drowsiness, and specific types of sleep of the physical body (karajakāya), which are the results of this torpor, are called "kapimiddha" by way of causal metaphor (kāraṇūpacāra). The statement, "Great King, only one overcome by monkey-like drowsiness sees a dream," is for this very reason.

In the phrase "yaṃ taṃ āpattivutthānaṃ," the Vinaya procedure by which one rises from that offense is called "āpattivutthāna" here. In the phrase "by a collective term for a part," the example is saying "one who cuts a tree" for one who cuts a branch, etc. The term "vedanākkhandha" (aggregate of feeling) etc., is an example of a conventional term (rūḷhī-sadda). In the phrase "na ca muccati," it is said with reference to the monk's action of the word "vīmaṃsana" (investigation), with reference to the decision in releasing, and by the nature of release.

"Geha" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Vanabhaṅgiya" refers to the breaking of a forest branch. Lust (rāga) itself, preceded by the associated pleasant feeling, is called "assāda" (gratification). The phrase "supantassa ca" should be understood as referring to one who is sleeping without interrupting the continuity of the life-continuum, like one overcome by monkey-like drowsiness; this statement should be reflected upon. "Jagganatthāya" means for the purpose of cleansing.

"Some say, 'Even by looking at the genitals of wooden dolls or painted figures, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred.' They write, 'When feverishness arises, there is gratification born of the lust for release.' In all versions, there is the reading 'āpatti tvaṃ' (you are an offense), as in the case of 'hatthikāmaṃ nassati' even in sand. Since it appears as 'Come, dear novice, take hold of my genitals,' it seems appropriate to call it 'verbal action' (vacīkamma). If this is so, [commanding] another, 'Do this'..."
180:
...if it is said that an offense can also be incurred by command (āṇatti), it would lead to confusion. Therefore, some teachers hold that it should not be said [that an offense is incurred by command]. It is said that there are two readings: "pupphāvaliyaṃ" and "sāsavaḷiyaṃ."

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen is Finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Bodily Contact

By the word "otiṇṇo" (descended), the monk's desire to indulge (in lust for bodily contact) is shown. By the phrase "vipariṇatena cittena mātugāmena saddhiṃ" (with a perverted mind together with a woman), the monk's effort (vāyāma) is shown. The word "saddhiṃ" (together with) indicates association. That association is indeed meeting and clinging. With what kind of mind does he cling? He clings with a mind perverted from its natural state. The meaning is that it is not a clinging with the intention of holding a bowl, etc. By the phrase "kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyya" (should fall into bodily contact), the perception of touch (phassa-paṭivijānanā) of that monk who is making an effort is shown. One who makes an effort and perceives the touch is said to "fall into" bodily contact. In this way, the fulfillment of the three factors of that monk is shown.

Alternatively, "otiṇṇo" means lust has entered him, just as a spirit (yakkha) etc. enters a being, by means of that perverted mind. Or, this instrumental case is in the sense of the accusative case. Lust enters the perverted mind just as a being enters a pit, etc. Alternatively, although he entered the monkhood thinking "I will transcend lust," he enters back into that very lust because of the perverted mind which is the cause [arising] from the desire to transcend. [He enters into lust] either with a woman who comes near him or by approaching her himself. By this (phrase "with a perverted mind"), whether the woman has lust or is free from lust, the woman's state is not the criterion in this training rule. Unlike in the training rule on bodily contact for bhikkhunīs, there is no requirement for both parties to have lust.

"Kāyasaṃsagga" means the physical contact and association of both the monk and the woman. In the Word-Analysis (Padabhājana), however, it is said: "Samāpajjeyyāti ajjācāro vuccati" (Falling into is called transgression). This statement is made with reference to the "falling into" (samāpajjana) and not with reference to "bodily contact" (kāyasaṃsagga). Indeed, only the falling into bodily contact is called "transgression" (ajjhācāra). In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said: "That which is called bodily contact is, in sense, a transgression." This statement seems to contradict the later Pali passage: "If there is the desire to indulge but one does not make an effort with the body and does not perceive the touch, there is no offense (anāpatti)." In truth, bodily contact is shown by the perception of touch. If that contact were [already] a transgression, how could there be "no offense"? Therefore, this statement in the Commentary is well-spoken [in its proper context].
181:
It is said that it contradicts the previously mentioned characteristic. For, by perceiving touch, bodily contact is shown. If that contact is a transgression (ajjhācāra), how can there be no offense? This is well-said. However, when extracting the phrase "kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyya" (should enter into bodily contact) and saying "ajjhācāraṃ vuccati" (it is called transgression), because both phrases are analyzed generally, and because there is no "entering" (samāpajjanā) when there is no object to be entered (samāpajjitabba), it should be said that "that contact is a transgression in meaning."

In this context of "hatthagāhaṃ vā" (grabbing the hand), the word "hand" includes the entire organic body (upādinnaka). It does not include ornaments such as hand-jewelry that are not connected to the body. By the word "veṇiggahaṇena" (grabbing the braid), it should be understood that hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, etc., which are produced by kamma and temperature (utu) and are not detached from the body although they are inorganic (anupādinnaka), are included. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "Even if one touches an organic or inorganic part with something inorganic like hair, etc., one still commits a Saṅghādisesa offense." Thus, it should be understood that inorganic parts like hair and body hair are also considered parts of the body.

If this is so, does it not contradict the method of the Pali and Commentary which says: "If one perceives touch, it is a Saṅghādisesa due to the fulfillment of three factors; if one does not perceive touch, it is a Dukkaṭa due to the fulfillment of two factors"? No, it does not, because of understanding that meaning. Knowing the state of being touched is also called "perceiving touch"; this is one way. Therefore, knowing the mutual contact of hair, etc., belonging to a woman's body or one's own body, and enjoying that contact, is also called "perceiving touch." It is not known only through the arising of body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa). In this context, body-consciousness is not constant (anekantika). When a bhikkhu's organic body is touched by a woman's organic or inorganic body, if his body-faculty (kāyindriya) is clear, body-consciousness arises in that monk; through that very body-consciousness, he is said to perceive touch. If it is an inorganic body, or if he is restless and his body-faculty is not clear, or if his body is afflicted by paralysis (timiravāta), body-consciousness does not arise in him. He is not said to perceive touch through that body-consciousness. However, one who makes an effort with the intention to associate sexually and enters into bodily contact is said to perceive touch through mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa). Therefore, it is said: "By this phrase 'should enter into bodily contact,' the perception of touch due to his effort is shown." Another monk also perceives touch by producing body-consciousness through contact with something connected to a woman's body or something she has released. Therefore, it has been said.
182:
"In this context, body-consciousness is not constant," it is said. Another monk, with lust for bodily contact, gently touches a sleeping woman covered in a cloth from above the cloth; although he does not specifically perceive the touch of the hair protruding through the cloth, because he makes an effort with his body with the intention to associate, he is said to perceive touch and commits a Saṅghādisesa offense. For it is said: "If one touches the body with the thought 'I will touch the blue cloth,' it is a Saṅghādisesa." This is the second meaning. Because of such multiple meanings and because the intention is difficult to know, "perceiving touch" (phassapaṭivijānanā) was not mentioned as a factor in the Mātikā Commentary. If that perception of touch were mentioned as a factor, there is a possibility that a monk, even after committing a Saṅghādisesa, might think he is not guilty, saying: "Although I saw the contact with the nails and hair, body-consciousness did not arise in me due to touching the hair, and since my body is numb as if paralyzed, I did not perceive the touch." Furthermore, he should be made to understand that meaning by showing the method stated in the Commentary regarding these words: "perceives touch" and "does not perceive touch." By this much, the reason "because of not knowing that meaning" has been explained in detail.

## Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

"Lustful mind" in this context means a corrupted mind; although this is stated generally, because it is said in the Vinītavatthu (Decided Cases) that "if one touches one's mother out of motherly love... it is a Dukkaṭa offense," it should be understood that "lustful" refers only to the lust for bodily contact. Similarly, although "woman" (mātugāma) is stated without distinction as "a human female," here only a human female with intact faculties (avinaṭṭhindriya) is intended. This is because it is said: "If one enters into bodily contact with a [dead] woman... it is a Thullaccaya offense." Although saying "human female" is sufficient, the statement "not a female yakkha, not a female peta, not a female animal" is made to show that not every woman with a human appearance is called a "human female" here, even if her faculties are intact. This is because yakkhas and others can create a human appearance through their inherent psychic powers. Among them, a female yakkha is a basis for a Thullaccaya offense, as it is stated in the Vinītavatthu that bodily contact with a female yakkha results in a Thullaccaya. Because they are similar to female yakkhas, female petas and female devas are also bases for Thullaccaya offenses. A female animal is a basis for a Dukkaṭa offense. Some teachers say that an animal in human form is also a basis for a Thullaccaya offense. In the Vibhaṅga, however, because the Pali "she is a human female and he perceives her as a human female" is absent, if there were statements like "she is a woman and he perceives her as a female yakkha," it would imply that yakkhas and others are not women...
183:
In the passage beginning with “She is a woman and he perceives her as a woman,” it should be understood that female yakkhas and others were not mentioned because of the danger of them becoming the basis for a Saṅghādisesa offense if they were included.

Some teachers, however, say: “In the Vinītavatthu, in the passage ‘A certain monk [touched] the body of a female animal... there is an offense of dukkaṭa,’ what is intended here is an ordinary female animal, not one in the form of a non-human (amanussa); therefore, it was taught as a dukkaṭa.” In the sections (vāra) beginning with “She is a woman and he perceives her as a female animal; she is a female animal and he perceives her as a woman,” only an ordinary animal is intended, and that animal is specifically a male animal. For that reason, in the Duṭṭhullavācā training rule and the Attakāmapāricariya training rule, the sections related to animals do not appear, just as the sections related to human men do not appear.

Likewise, in this context, a paṇḍaka refers only to a human paṇḍaka, and a man refers only to a human man. Therefore, these eight types of beings—female non-human, non-human paṇḍaka, male non-human, female animal, animal paṇḍaka, and the human, non-human, and animal hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka)—do not appear in this Kāyasaṃsagga training rule. One should understand without confusion the decision regarding the distinction of offenses and non-offenses, and the count of the future sections (anāgatavāra), based on the distinctions of the basis (vatthu), perception (saññā), and doubt (vimati) concerning those beings. Similarly, one should understand the sections such as the double-root combinations (dukamissaka) and the decision on what constitutes an offense or non-offense for them.

“Among those specific offenses, these four—non-human paṇḍaka, male non-human, female animal, and animal paṇḍaka—are bases for dukkaṭa. Female non-humans and human hermaphrodites are bases for thullaccaya. Non-human hermaphrodites and animal hermaphrodites are bases for dukkaṭa. In the Pali, because the female non-human does not appear, the non-human paṇḍaka, hermaphrodite, and male do not appear. Female animals, animal paṇḍakas, and animal hermaphrodites do not appear because they share the same status as the male animal. The human hermaphrodite does not appear because it shares the same status as the human paṇḍaka,” so they say. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated: “In the case of a Nāga maiden, a Supaṇṇa maiden, a Kinnarī, or even a cow, it is only a dukkaṭa.” Therefore, that statement of the Commentary should be taken as the authoritative standard.

In this matter, there is this investigation: In the Pali passage, “Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited to an animal sitting in the midst of the assembly,” the Commentary states, “An animal (tiracchānagata) is one for whom higher ordination (upasampadā) is forbidden.” Thus, an animal in human form is distinct from an ordinary animal. Likewise, in the case of the distinction of yakkhas, petas, and animals in human form, it is stated, “Even in causing suffering to an animal, it is only a dukkaṭa...”
184:
Because it is specifically stated here, and because of the statement regarding the specific offense in “The falling form is the standard, not the dead form,” and because of the general statement in (Pācittiya 661), “When both are oozing [with lust], if one touches with the body the body of a yakkha, a peta, a paṇḍaka, or an animal in human form, below the collarbone and above the kneecaps, there is an offense of thullaccaya,” it is established that such a being in human form is distinct. Because of this distinction, there is a specific case for a monk who enters into bodily contact with a female animal in human form; therefore, there must be a specific offense in that case. If a female animal in human form were also intended in the Kāyasaṃsagga training rule, then because the fading of perception (saññā-virāga) is impossible due to the similarity of form, that female should also be mentioned in the Duṭṭhullavācā and Attakāmapāricariya training rules; however, she does not appear there. If it is argued that she does not appear because those sections are summarized (saṅkhittavāra) even though she is not explicitly mentioned? Since the masculine gender (purisaliṅga) is used here in the passage “She is a woman and he is an animal, and he perceives both as women,” it is not appropriate. Therefore, the male animal also appears here. Even though the female animal in human form does not appear in the Pali, the Commentary states it is only a dukkaṭa; thus, the meaning is that the underlying reason for this statement should be sought. This statement is not appropriate. Why? Because when women and men are spoken of together, the masculine gender prevails. Here, the male animal, the paṇḍaka, and the female are all grouped together and called “animal” (tiracchānagata).

Among those animals, the perception of them as female, paṇḍaka, or male should be understood as they occur in those with human forms and those without human forms. In the two training rules such as Duṭṭhullavācā, because the sections are summarized, the male, the animal, etc., do not appear. Just as the offenses were stated previously, so it is in those rules as well. Alternatively, it is stated in the Mātikā Commentary that there is no offense for one who mocks a man, but a thullaccaya offense for one who mocks a paṇḍaka. Therefore, it is evident that those sections are summarized. Although there is a distinction for a monk who perceives a paṇḍaka, a man, or an animal as a woman, it is stated there as a dukkaṭa. Therefore, the teachers say that only the statement in the Commentary is the standard, and between these two views, one should investigate and adopt the one where the logic or reason appears superior. In such matters, one should speak only after careful investigation.

The count of the sections (vāra) appearing in the Pali should be understood in brief as follows: There are 5 sections with 'woman' as the root, and 5 sections each with 'paṇḍaka', 'man', and 'animal' as the root; thus, there are 20 sections with a single root (ekamūlaka). Similarly, there are 20 sections with double roots (dumūlaka) and 20 sections with mixed roots (missakamūlaka).
185:
There are sixty cases (vāras); these consist of three groups of twenty. In each group of twenty, taking one root case (mūlavāra) at a time, three cases of touching a body-connected object with the body are stated. The remaining fifty-seven cases are summarized. Similarly, three cases of touching the body with a body-connected object are stated, and the rest are summarized. Thus, in the case of touching a body-connected object with a body-connected object, in the case of touching the body with a Nissaggiya object, in the case of touching a body-connected object with a Nissaggiya object, and in the case of touching a Nissaggiya object with a Nissaggiya object, three cases each are stated, and the rest are summarized. Thus, by way of the six triads (tikas), eighteen cases are explicitly stated (sarūpato), and the remaining three hundred and forty-two cases are summarized. Furthermore, in the section on the lustful side (sārattapakkha) regarding a woman, by expanding each case as 'body with body,' the eighteen cases previously mentioned occur; thus, twenty-one cases are explicitly stated, and three hundred and ninety-nine cases are summarized. Beyond that, two sets of four (catukkas) occur: four based on the intention of indulgence (sevanādhippāya) and four based on the intention of release (mokkhādhippāya), which clarify offense and non-offense.

In this word-analysis (padabhājanīya), there is this distinction: because the twelve terms from 'āmasana' (touching) to 'chupana' (contact) are included by the term 'parāmasana' (handling) in the matrix (mātikā), it is stated as 'āmasana, parāmasana, chupana' without extracting the individual terms (paduddhāra). What is called 'parāmasana' is indeed 'āmasana.' It should be understood that if 'chupana' is mentioned, 'parāmasana' would also exist as a separate term. In this first case, 'She is a woman and he has the perception of her as a woman,' the twelve terms starting with 'āmasana' are shown in combination. Furthermore, it should be understood that four terms occur—two terms at the beginning, 'āmasati, parāmasati,' and two terms at the end, 'gaṇhāti, chupati'—while the remaining terms are summarized. In the cases of touching with a Nissaggiya object, etc., because they are not obtainable in all aspects, only the single term 'āmasana' occurs, and the other eleven terms do not. There is the text 'sañcopeṭi, harati,' and 'sañcopeṭi' also exists. In the Gaṇṭhipadas (glossaries), it is written: 'In wrapping with ropes, cloth, etc., as in the previous method,' and later, 'There is sammasana (handling) as in the previous method,' and 'Because an offense is prescribed for seizing a braid of hair, a saṅghādisesa offense also occurs in touching a hair,' and 'To clarify that meaning, it is stated starting from the word upādinnakena.'

'Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddese' means in this very detailed explanation as pointed out. When it is said 'sadisaṃ aggahesi' (he took something similar), it means he took an object similar to the one he intended to take; therefore, a heavy offense (garuka āpatti) should be imposed (decided) in that saṅghādisesa case, or it means in the Kāyasaṃsaggavibhaṅga. The other person is also one who touches a body-connected object. 'Gahaṇe ca' means 'and in taking.' 'Virāgite' means 'when it is missed.' 'Sārattaṃ' means...
186:
Infatuated (sāratta) means lustful with the desire for physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggarāga) with a woman whom one desires. If one intends to touch a woman who is free from lust, such as a mother or sister, and touches such a lust-free mother or sister out of familial affection, a dukkaṭa offense is appropriate in this instance. Or, if one intends to touch a lustful, infatuated woman but touches a lust-free mother, it is a case of touching an undesired mother. Here, according to the view of Elder Mahāsumma, a thullaccaya offense is incurred. This is because of the view that if one intends to touch the body but touches a body-connected object, it is a thullaccaya. Because of the word: 'If she is a woman, and he perceives her as a woman, and is infatuated, and the monk touches the woman's body with his body, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa,' a saṅghādisesa offense is also evident. If one intends to touch a lust-free person but touches an infatuated woman, here too, only a saṅghādisesa is evident. This is because of the word: 'If one intends to touch a blue (cloth) but touches the body, there is a saṅghādisesa.'

In this decision, however, the reason is given in the Anugaṇṭhipada: 'Because there is no lust for physical contact in the preliminary stage, a dukkaṭa offense does not occur.' Some teachers, however, say: 'If, out of fear of a heavy offense, one strives to touch only the blue (cloth) but touches the body, a dukkaṭa offense should occur for that monk because in the preliminary stage the thought "I will touch a body-connected object" had arisen.' It is said that Elder Dhammasiri says that in such a case, a saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. It is said: 'In the case of a female hermaphrodite (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) and a male hermaphrodite (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka), the distinction of offenses is according to the method already mentioned; even when the female organ is concealed, the offense is incurred by way of being a woman.'

## Explanation of the Cases (Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā)

'Tiṇannḍupaka' refers to an ornament made by taking roots such as grass. 'Tālapaṇṇamuddikā' is a ring made of palm leaf; by that statement, it is established that all ornaments such as anklets, waist-threads, and earrings made of palm leaf are not allowable. It is said that the monks living in the island of Ceylon (Sīhaḷa) do not touch even a drawn image of a woman or a waist-cloth. 'Ākarato' refers to a type of pearl (loose stone) produced from the ocean. 'Ratanamisso' refers to a conch shell entwined with gold creepers, etc., made for the purpose of ornamentation. 'Cooked together with gold' means cooking after adding liquid gold. 'Bījato' refers to things originating from ore-bearing stones. Because it was said, 'It is sent for the elders,' the Elder rejected it as unallowable. However, it is said that if it is said, 'Perform an offering to the shrine (cetiya),' it is allowable. 'Bubbuḷaka' means a star (or boss/stud). Brass (ārakūṭa) also has the nature of gold (is similar to gold).

For this has been stated in the Andhaka Commentary:
'Brass is just like gold; it conforms to gold; it is an untouchable (anāmāsa) object.'
187:
Because of the statement 'But for the sake of medicine, it is allowable,' a portion of the method mentioned in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is also permitted; this should be clarified by understanding the intention in each respective case.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule of Bodily Contact is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule of Lewd Words (Duṭṭhullavācā)

In the third training rule (regarding lewd words), twelve cycles (vāra) appear in their original form: three cycles of Saṅghādisesa, three cycles of Thullaccaya, three cycles of Dukkaṭa, and three cycles of Kāyapaṭibaddha (connected to the body). Among these cycles, since the three Saṅghādisesa cycles were already mentioned in the second training rule, they should be understood as cycles having a single root for each of the three sets of twenty. Therefore, fifty distinct cycles are summarized in this training rule. Otherwise, if there is a woman, and the monk is in doubt and has a lustful mind, and he speaks in praise of that woman's excrement path or urine path... (etc.)... there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). If there is a woman, and the monk perceives her as a paṇḍaka or an animal and has a lustful mind, and he speaks in praise of that woman's excrement path or urine path, or even insults her, there is a grave offense. If there is a paṇḍaka, and the monk perceives him as a paṇḍaka and has a lustful mind, and he speaks in praise of that paṇḍaka's excrement path, there is a grave offense. Although such instances where an offense occurs might become instances where no offense occurs, this does not happen. To show that there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives a paṇḍaka as a woman, it is stated: 'If one perceives both a woman and a paṇḍaka as a woman, the offenses range from Saṅghādisesa to Dukkaṭa.' Thus, it is already stated that 'there is a grave offense for one who perceives a paṇḍaka as a paṇḍaka.' Therefore, it should be understood that in all summarized cycles, a grave offense is already stated for the case of Thullaccaya, and a wrongdoing is already stated for the case of Dukkaṭa.

Likewise, in the manner beginning with: 'If there is a woman, and the monk is in doubt and has a lustful mind, and he speaks in praise of the area below the collarbone and above the kneecap, excluding that woman's excrement path and urine path... there is a grave offense,' such cases should be extracted as far as possible within the scope of Thullaccaya. Likewise, in the manner beginning with: 'If there is a woman, and the monk is in doubt and has a lustful mind, and he speaks in praise of something connected to that woman's body... there is an offense of wrongdoing,' the cycles of Kāyapaṭibaddha should also be extracted as far as possible. Although the triad of Nissaggiya cycles could be obtained like the triad of Kāyapaṭibaddha cycles, they are not extracted because there is no distinction in the offense. However, since the method is given in the triad of Kāyapaṭibaddha cycles, the cycles conforming to that...

They should be extracted. In all cases, young girls who are not discerning, elderly women, madwomen, and so forth are not intended. ## Commentary on the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā)

"In the same manner as stated" means it is written as "by the characteristic of a woman in the training rule on physical contact (Kāyasaṃsagga)." It is said that "by the characteristic of a woman" is the reading in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In this context, it does not amount to verbal abuse, but it occurs when there is contact. In this regard, there is this distinction: a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred only when there is contact with these three: sikharṇī, sambādhā, and ubhatobyañjanā. This is because they are specific terms for the excrement-passage and the urine-passage, or because they are extremely coarse. When there is contact with the other eight terms such as animittāsi, it does not reach the level of Saṅghādisesa.

Among those eight, these six terms—alohitāsi, dhuvalohitāsi, dhuvacoḷāsi, paggharaṇīsi, itthipaṇḍakāsi, and vepurisikāsi—are indefinite terms (aniyatavacana) for the passages. The two terms animittāsi and nimittamattāsi are also not extremely coarse. Since it is stated that those eight terms "do not produce a Saṅghādisesa," they are therefore grounds for a thullaccaya (grave offense). Some teachers say they are grounds for a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) because they are merely verbal abuse, as in the case of the wanderer (paribbājaka).

Only these terms, itthipaṇḍakāsi and vepurisikāsi, indicate a specific form of the whole body; if they occur alone, they do not produce a Saṅghādisesa because they pertain to the whole body. The remaining terms, however, produce a Saṅghādisesa because they do not pertain to the whole body. Those terms, like the term sikharṇī, indicate only the urine-passage.

The term ubhatobyañjanāsi is a term mixed with a case that does not warrant a Saṅghādisesa due to the male organ. For a male hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), the female organ is concealed and the male organ is prominent. Some say, "If that term also produces a Saṅghādisesa, why do terms like animittāsi not produce a Saṅghādisesa?" That statement is not appropriate. Because it is a name for the male organ, and because the characteristic is stated in the Matika as "a Saṅghādisesa is incurred by words related to sexual intercourse," some say: if one understands when being insulted with words related to sexual intercourse, it is a Saṅghādisesa; if one does not understand, it is a thullaccaya. If one understands when being insulted with other words, it is a thullaccaya; if one does not understand, it is a dukkaṭa. Everything should be carefully examined before being accepted.

"Laughing" means if it is said with reference to a certain woman, and if that woman understands, it is a Saṅghādisesa.

In the fourth training rule, three Saṅghādisesa cases are mentioned; it should be understood that the remaining fifty-seven cases, as well as the cases involving Thullaccaya and Dukkaṭa offenses, are summarized. "Nagaraparikkhārehi" means by the city surroundings such as walls and moats. "Setaparikkhāro" means white ornament, which signifies the ornament of virtue (sīla). What foul smell do I have?"

"Santike" refers to the place where one stands and makes it known. In the first analysis (viggaha), if constructed according to the Pali, the meaning is "Kāmahetupāricariyā" (service for the sake of sensual pleasure). The remaining word "adhippāyo" is merely a syllable (byañjana) because it has no special meaning. In the second analysis, according to the Pali, the words "kāmahetu" are merely syllables because they have no special meaning there. Thus, other teachers say that the four words are constructed by way of the two analyses.

In these training rules, if a transgression occurs with sexual desire, there is no instance where it is not a Saṅghādisesa (meaning it is definitely a Saṅghādisesa). Therefore, the statement, "Venerable sir, what is the highest gift? It is sexual intercourse," is said solely for the purpose of praising sexual intercourse; it should be understood that it is not said with the intention of sexual intercourse for the sake of obtaining it. In praising the service of sensual pleasure for another monk, a Dukkaṭa offense is committed. Even by the indirect statement (pariyāya), "Give the highest gift to the monk who resides in your monastery," a Dukkaṭa offense is committed. Some teachers say this is because it is stated, "One should speak praise of service to oneself, saying 'to one of such virtue as I...'" Some teachers say that if the five factors are fulfilled, it is indeed a Saṅghādisesa. This should be accepted after careful consideration. However, in the Gaṇṭhipada...

"Alāṃvacanīyā" means a woman who should not be approached; the word "alaṃ" is used in the sense of prohibition. "The Elder's father speaks" means the aged father speaks. As many sections (vāra) as possible should be extracted. 348-9. Since it is impossible to build by requesting, the meaning is that one should build with materials requested by oneself. The words agree, but the meaning does not. Why? Because in this training rule, both doing and causing to be done are intended. To show that meaning, he said "Yasmā pana," etc. By the method stated in this word-commentary (vibhaṅga) of the training rule, because of the word "saññācikāya" (by one's own request), one should practice by doing it oneself, and because of the word "parehi pariyosāpeti" (he has others finish it), one should practice by causing it to be done. Both these are the doer and the one who causes to be done. The words would be contradictory; for if the word "kārayamānena" (by one causing to be done) were said as "karontena" (by one doing), it would be contradictory because it does not reach that meaning. Indeed, the one who causes to be done is not called the doer. "By the method stated here" means by the method of the specified site and measurement (desitavatthuka-pamāṇika). If this is so, if it is said that because of the words "whether doing or causing to be done," the doer should also speak of what is being done until others finish it, it is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada that "Yadi pana," etc., was said to resolve that meaning. It is stated by the power of the words "building a hut by one's own request" (saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karonto). Since the word "vā" (or), which has an alternative meaning, is used without saying "by length and by width," an offense is incurred even if it is increased on only one side. A couch (mañca) that conforms to the measurement is said to be nine spans (vidatthi). It is said that the phrase "three cubits in width" also agrees with the phrase "four cubits in width." This is because the concluding statement "where it conforms to the measurement," etc., would not be possible. Even in a case less than the measurement, if it is four or five cubits in width but does not exceed the length, only the stated measurement is the "specified site" (desitavatthu). Indeed, an offense is incurred for one who builds what is not a specified site. Only a hut that exceeds the measurement (causes an offense), because it is said, "He should build a hut that exceeds the measurement." There is also a reading "thambhatulā." In the method of proclamation (anussāvana), some say, "It is also allowable in the Tamil language (Damiḷa-bhāsā)."

"Cārabhūmi" is the feeding ground (gocara-bhūmi). "Na gahitā" means not prohibited. In the Commentary, it is written: "Dhamma-gaṇ္ဍိကာ refers to a prison where punishment is inflicted, or a place where punishment is not inflicted, or a block for cutting off hands and feet." "With two bulls" means by the lower limit...
193:
It is said that it is impossible to turn back from the mentioned place because there is a steep precipice. It should be understood that this is stated to clarify the meaning of the conclusion. *Pācīna* refers to the location or foundation of the object. *Tadatthāya* means for the purpose of hewing. *Paṇṇasālā* (leaf-hut) refers to a hut that is plastered inside and out, but with a roof made of leaves. For that very reason, it is said to be 'with walls and roof.' If it is not plastered, the entire hut is allowable. Having increased the small amount of clay previously placed, if it is placed on the door-frame or the window. Regarding the phrase *Paṭhamameva*, Elder Dhammasiri says it means 'only at the time of arrival.' Elder Upatissa, however, says it means 'only at the time it was placed.' There is no offense for both monks because it is not connected with the first plastering and because it was done for the second time as a *vattasīsa*. If it is done by one who was commanded, because of the statement 'whether he does it himself or has it done by another,' if there is a personal designation for oneself, both incur an offense; if not, only the monk who gave the command incurs the offense. There is an opinion of the Teacher that a monk who builds a hut entirely made of clay, even though a smaller size is possible, incurs a *Saṅghādisesa* offense along with a *Dukkaṭa*.

The thirty-six sets of four (*catukka*) are: the set of four on the unpointed site, the set of four on the pointed site, the set of four on exceeding the measurement, the set of four on being within the measurement, the set of four on the unpointed site and exceeding the measurement, and the set of four on the pointed site and being within the measurement—thus there are six sets of four. Similarly, it should be understood in the five sections such as the *Samādisativāra*; therefore, there are thirty-six sets of four. Regarding the phrase *āpattibhedadassanattha*, because it is stated in the *Mātikā* without distinction, 'If a monk, in a site with danger, without an open space around it... he incurs a *Saṅghādisesa*,' the distinction of offenses is shown to dispel the wrong view that it is only a *Saṅghādisesa* even in a site with danger and without an open space; therefore, it means they are stated. If it is asked why the *Dukkaṭa* object is mentioned in the *Mātikā* without being stated thus in the *Vibhaṅga*: Monks should be invited to point out the site for a hut; those monks should point out the site. What kind of site? A site without danger and with an open space around it should be pointed out, not any other. In another place, it is stated by way of benefit: 'If a monk, in a site with danger, without an open space around it.'

Because what is called a 'site' has many varieties, such as: a site with danger, a site without danger, a site with an open space around it, a site without an open space around it, a site with danger and with an open space, a site with danger and without an open space, a site without danger and with an open space, and a site without danger and without an open space. Therefore, it means only a site without danger and with an open space should be pointed out, not any other. If it is asked what the purpose of this pointing out is: it is for the purpose of the means to avoid the cause for the prescription of a grave offense (*garukāpatti*). Indeed, by pointing out the site, both the *akataviññatti* (unrequested announcement), which is a cause for the prescription of a grave offense, and the state of having danger, which is a cause for one's own suffering and the suffering of others by harassing laypeople, are avoided through the means of pointing out the site. Monks, for the purpose of building an unallowable hut...
194:
Whether it is for a site with danger that causes distress to laypeople, or for the purpose of building an unallowable hut, this matter regarding pointing out the site has been established previously. 'Mixed offenses' (*vomissakāpattiyo*) refers to offenses where *Dukkaṭa* and *Saṅghādisesa* are mixed.

In those sets of four, although it should be said 'by two *Saṅghādisesas*' (*dvīhi saṅghādisesehi*), it is said as 'by the *Saṅghādisesa* of two' (*dvinnāṃ saṅghādisesena*) by changing the case and number. There is also a reading: 'the offense of two *Saṅghādisesas*' (*āpatti dvinnāṃ saṅghādisesānaṃ*).

Because there is no plastering of the roof, it is not connected; there is no offense, and that meaning is completed by the subsequent words. Plastering inside and out is stated referring only to the roof. Having said 'A house with a roof like a cock's eye is allowable,' the teachers who show that house by saying 'the roof with sticks,' etc., mean only a hut roofed with grass or leaves. In that case, because binding the roof with sticks lengthwise and crosswise like a net and then plastering it inside and out to cover it with grass or leaves refers only to the roof, it is appropriate. Therefore, it is written that for a monk who has a wall made of clay built and makes the upper part plastered inside or outside or both, connected with the wall, there is an offense even without plastering the wall. It is said that the statement 'referring only to the roof' is said by way of prominence and does not exclude the lower part; this point should be reflected upon.

Here (*ettha*) refers to the grass hut. *Yathāsamadiṭṭhāya* means according to the method already stated. In the Pali such as 'there are three *Dukkaṭa* offenses for the builders,' the sixfold set of 'he hears' (*so suṇāti*) is also obtained. Because it is well-established in both (the commander and the builder), there is no offense for the monk who gives the command. As for the one who was commanded, a *Dukkaṭa* offense is incurred due to not doing as pointed out by the commander. If he makes a personal designation, saying 'I too shall dwell here,' it is indeed a *Saṅghādisesa*. In a case where it is said without distinction, 'Build a hut,' because the training rule is *acittaka* (not depending on intention), the commander also incurs a *Saṅghādisesa*.

In this phrase 'I too shall dwell,' because there is no designation for any other person, and because it is restricted by the words 'and for the one who is building,' an offense is indeed incurred; or some say there is no offense because it is not specified. It is also written, 'In this case, the mind is merely the knowledge of the prescription.' In the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, however, regarding the phrase 'I too shall dwell,' an offense is incurred for one who desires, 'It shall also be my dwelling house.' If a monk desires it to be an *Uposatha* hall, there is no offense for him. Therefore, if it is said that after saying 'both are consistent,' and because of the statement 'one should stand in the grave offenses (*garuka*) that come in the *Vinayavinicchaya*,' the other view should be stated after the *Mahāpaccariya* view? No, it should not be stated because it is strong. Because of the statement 'except for a dwelling house, there is no offense in all places,' this monk has built it for the sake of a refectory (*bhojanasālā*), etc., so it is a mixture. For example, it is like two or three monks saying, 'Let us dwell together.'
195:
Because of being strong (balavattā). Because of the statement, "Except for a dwelling-house (vāsāgāra), there is no offense in all places," a confusion (saṅkara) arose because this monk built it for the sake of a dining hall, etc. How so? Two or three monks say, "We will live together," and they build it; it is protected for that long, just as in this case. Even if one builds it by dividing [the purposes], saying, "This place will be a dwelling-house, this place will be an Uposatha hall," it is still an offense. Between the two commentaries, the Mahāpaccari view is stronger; therefore, it is greatly expanded with "It is said later," etc. What is the benefit of such a distinction? Other tetrads should also be applied accordingly, such as "He himself finishes a hut begun by himself, or others finish it," etc. Although there is no offense of Saṅghādisesa in the case of caves (leṇa), etc., if there is a request for what is not yet made (akata-viññatti), there is indeed an offense because of that reason.
