## 8. Explanation of the First Training Rule on a Corrupt Mind

The statement "A disciple should attain" is said with reference to an ordinary disciple (pakati-sāvaka), not a chief disciple (aggasāvaka). It is said as "threefold knowledge" (tisso vijjā), etc., by way of the respective decisive support (upanissaya) and the respective person. It should be understood that it is said separately as "threefold knowledge" for some disciples, "four analytical insights" (catasso paṭisambhidā) for some, "six higher powers" (cha abhiññā) for some, and the "ninefold supramundane Dhamma" alone for some, as the case may be.

From the statement "Those monks who are bearers of the Suttas (suttantika)," etc., it is established that the division of the Three Piṭakas existed even while the Blessed One was still present. "Dhamma-preachers" refers to masters of Abhidhamma who think, "We will live with delight," etc. It appears as if Venerable Dabba was encouraging their delight in lowly talk (tiracchānakathā), but it should not be seen that way. Because of the association with Suttantika teachers, etc., it means creating an obstacle to the comfortable living (phāsuvihāra) of those Suttantika teachers; because those monks who delight in lowly talk have no delight [in the Dhamma], it means making them live without delight (anabhirati). Therefore, from their ascetic life...
196:
...falling away [from the ascetic life], he thought thus, wishing to avoid it—so it should be understood. They say, "The nature (dhammatā) of created forms (nimmitānaṃ) is only the nature of forms created by disciples, not those created by Buddhas." When it is said, "The instrument (karaṇa) is that which is most effective in accomplishing [an action]," it means the third case ending (instrumental) is used only in the sense of instrument.

383-4. 'Yaṃ' means 'by which reason' (yena). It is written, "Is the agent (kattā) one who acts, or one who does not act?" The accusation of the [Bhikkhunī] who says, "He treated me like a wife," is very strong. Therefore, just as in the case of remorse arising from mere touch, where the Blessed One prescribed a Saṅghādisesa without questioning because of the arising of lust for physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggarāga), so too it should be understood that He spoke because He knew beforehand the immoral nature of that Bhikkhunī. If she was expelled (nāsitā) based on a true confession, the Elder is the agent (kāraka). If it was based on a false confession, the Blessed One would not have said, "Expel her," yet He did say so; therefore, it is said, "If she was expelled based on a true confession, the Elder is the agent."

'Without confession' (appaṭiññāya) means she was expelled with reference to her naturally immoral nature, without this confession: "I have been corrupted by the noble one." In that case, the Elder is not the agent (akāraka). The dwellers of Abhayagiri also recite their own text and say, "In your view, the Elder is the agent." Why? Because one should not be expelled by destroying the marks (liṅga-nāsanā) merely because of an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to false speech. Only one who has committed a Pārājika should be expelled by destroying the marks. Because it was said, "Expel her," she became one who had committed a Pārājika; what did she refer to? Therefore, the Elder becomes the agent. However, when it was said, "Expel her based on her own confession," even if she had not committed a Pārājika, she became one to be expelled by her own words—this is the meaning. The dwellers of Mahāvihāra also recite their own text and say, "In your view, the Elder is the agent." Why? Because when it was said, "Expel her based on her own confession," the confession becomes true because of the word "Expel her." The meaning is that she should be expelled only by a true confession, not by a false one. The 'former method' refers to the view that says it is a dukkaṭa. It should be understood that the former method proceeds by way of logic, while the latter method proceeds by way of the words of the Pali text.

385-6. In the phrase 'pītisukhehi', where it should have been said 'sukhena', the inclusion of 'rapture' (pīti) is said with the rapture associated [with it] to exclude the happiness of the third jhāna and bodily happiness. If a groundless (amūlaka) accusation made by way of the accused is said as "not committed, not done," they will do [it]; therefore, there is a reading: "Being one who has the perception of having seen such a thing, he accuses." It is said, "In this way, accusations based on hearing, sensing, and suspicion should also be understood in detail."
197: ## Text. Regarding the phrase "With any one of the four [Pārājikas]," it is said by taking only what appears in the recitation of the Pātimokkha. The Teacher (the Commentator) understands that for one who accuses [another] groundlessly with any of the remaining [Pārājikas], only a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. This is because it is capable of causing one to fall from the state of a monk. Because of the phrase "standing nearby," for one who accuses behind [the other's] back, or causes another to accuse, it does not reach the "head" (the root Saṅghādisesa). If one accuses or causes another to accuse regarding a seen matter by way of hearing or by way of suspicion, or if one accuses or causes another to accuse regarding a matter of hearing or suspicion by way of seeing, etc., it certainly reaches the "head" (Saṅghādisesa) because of accusing without grounds. For it is said: "If one accuses a person who is committing a seen Pārājika offense, saying, 'I heard... etc... a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred'" (Pārā. 387). "If a person is impure, having committed one of the Pārājika offenses, and if another, being of impure view, speaks with the intention of causing him to fall without having asked for permission, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. If he speaks after having asked for permission, there is no offense" (Pārā. 389). This seems to disagree with the [former] Pali. Why? A person who commits a seen Pārājika offense is an impure person. Because of the statement, "If one, being of one of the impure views, accuses that person, saying, 'I heard that you have committed a Pārājika offense,' for every word, a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred," an offense is incurred according to the former method. Because of the statement, "If he speaks with the intention of causing him to fall, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred," a Saṅghādisesa offense [is mentioned] by the latter method; thus these two Pali methods seem to contradict each other. The Buddhas do not speak contradictory words; therefore, the logical reason (yutti) should be sought here. The Commentators first said: "There is no offense for one who accuses with grounds (samūlaka) or with grounds of perception (saññā-samūlaka). There is an offense for one who accuses without grounds (amūlaka) or without grounds of perception (saññā-amūlaka)." The meaning of that statement is: there is no offense for one who accuses with grounds consisting of seeing, hearing, or suspicion, or even without those grounds but with grounds of perception. There is an offense for one who accuses without grounds due to the absence of seeing, etc., or even with those grounds but without grounds of perception. Therefore, regarding a seen person... In the passage beginning with "when one commits a Pārājika offense," even if there are grounds of seeing, if one accuses without grounds of perception by saying "I heard," a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. To clarify that meaning, the sections (vāra) beginning with "one who has doubt in what is seen" should be understood as being stated.
198: In the passage beginning with "An impure person...," it should be understood that there is no offense because the accusation is made with grounds (samūlaka) or with grounds of perception (saññā-samūlaka). In this manner, those sections (vāra) were spoken to clarify that decided meaning. Among those sections, the sections beginning with "For one who has not seen" were spoken to show that an offense is incurred for one who accuses without grounds (amūlaka). The sections beginning with "One who has doubt in what is seen" were spoken to show that an offense is incurred for one who accuses without grounds of perception due to a mistake in perception (saññā). Otherwise, if the meaning were taken differently, the sections beginning with "For one who has seen" and "One who has doubt in what is seen" would be without distinction. The decision here is as follows: Just as a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred for one who accuses an impure person without asking for permission, and a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred for one who intends to revile by way of insulting speech (omasavāda), likewise, if one of impure view accuses an impure person without grounds, an offense is incurred. If he accuses with grounds, there is no offense. This decision should be understood as it accords with the statement: "There is no offense for one of impure view regarding a pure person, or for one of impure view regarding an impure person." If it were otherwise, the logical reason (yutti) should be sought. In the phrase "Sīlasampanno" (endowed with virtue), the word of one who is immoral is not authoritative. A bhikkhunī has no authority over bhikkhus; therefore, Elder Mahāpaduma spoke with reference to the procedure in the "excellent method" (ukkaṭṭha-naya). Elder Mahāsumma, however, spoke with the intention: "Even if a bhikkhunī accuses without knowing, or if sikkhamānās, etc., accuse, the bhikkhus, having heard their words, investigate and take action based on that monk's confession; what fault is there in doing so?" The third Elder said that even after hearing the words of heretics (titthiyas), the bhikkhus themselves investigate; therefore, it is not that no one can obtain [the result], but rather it can be obtained. Thus, others say that everything is consistent. "Tiṃsāni" means having thirty parts. "Anuyogo" means a reply (paṭivacana). "Ehiti" means will come (āgamissati). "Diṭṭhasantānena" means by the method of seeing, with the meaning "by the procedure as seen." "Patiṭṭhāya" means having gained a footing. "Ṭhāne" means in a shameful place. "Gāhaṃ" means undertaking responsibility for oneself (attādāna), thinking "I will accuse." "Cetanā" is the intention to undertake responsibility for oneself. "Vohāro" means making it known after knowing from here and there. "Paññatti" means the designation of names (nāma-paññatti). That designation is known by the mind-door consciousness that arises immediately after the sequence of consciousness occurring at the ear-door, which has the sound of speech as its object, and which has a previously acquired convention. Because that designation is known, its meaning—whether it be an ultimate reality (paramattha) or not an ultimate reality—is known by the mind-door consciousness that arises for the third time. This is revealed in the Pali by the six syllables such as "nāma," etc. The teachers have shown that designation in six ways, such as "concept of the existent" (vijjāmāna-paññatti) and "concept of the non-existent" (avijjāmāna-paññatti). Being part of that (tabbhāgiya) or not being part of that (atabbhāgiya) is appropriate only for produced phenomena (nipphannadhamma), not for concepts (paññatti).
199:
Because it is the object of a legal issue (adhikaraṇīyavatthu) and because it occurs within a legal issue (adhikaraṇa), it is called 'adhikaraṇa', just as a person situated on a couch is metaphorically called 'the couch'. It is written: "By way of figurative expression (pariyāya), there is no baseless name-designation (amūlaka nāmapaññatti); it is merely figurative, it does not exist in reality (sabhāva). It is only a name (abhidhāna), there is no designated meaning (abhidheyya)." "Only here" means only in this training rule. "Not everywhere" means not in legal issues arising from disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa) and so on. Why? It says "Na hi" etc. Because a baseless legal issue (amūlaka adhikaraṇa) does not exist in the same way that vivādādhikaraṇa etc. exist. "By the settlements (samatha) mentioned before" means by the settlements mentioned as "the settlements that proceed concerning which legal issue". Alternatively, "does not exist in reality" is said because its nature is not obtained. It is like consciousness (viññāṇa) etc. that have not yet arisen. Since the designation (paññatti) of vivāda etc. is not the meaning of adhikaraṇa, the settlements do not proceed based on the designation. Therefore, that designation does not have the quality of being a legal issue to be settled. Thus, the meaning is that the designation of vivāda etc. is not the meaning of adhikaraṇa. In this regard, there is this [verse]:

If a pārājika offense were groundless and merely a designation,
The Path and Fruit factors, which are the objects of the fourth pārājika,
Would likewise be merely designations.

Then the Path and Fruit factors would be of two kinds,
And likewise the past and the future;
Otherwise, the sixfold designation would not exist,
Therefore, He spoke the conventional teaching (sammuti-vāda) figuratively.

"Anuvadanti" means they abuse or scold. "Kiccayatā" means the state of having a duty to be performed. If asked "What is that kiccayatā?", it refers to acts of notification (apalokanakamma) and so on. "Kicca" (action/task) refers to the volition (citta) that originates communication (viññatti).

Regarding "being baseless due to the absence of hearing etc.", here, a person who, despite having seen, cannot say "I have seen" but says "I have heard" based on what they saw. For that person, there is an offense because of the impure view regarding that person. But here, it refers to one who, having heard before, was without offense, but later forgot and speaks with a pure view. "Others say this method applies to all cases" is stated. Poṭṭhabatika means one whose conduct is like Kāḷakadevī. "Yadaggena" means to whatever extent or whenever. "It is not allowable" etc. is stated only to show the absence of doubt (vematika). Therefore, only one who has doubt...
200:
...is called 'confused' (sammuṭṭha) because they cannot remember due to forgetfulness; this is the implication. That view is not appropriate because it occurs immediately after doubt etc. Therefore, the second Elder's view is mentioned later.

"Sabbattha" means in all the commentaries. "Okāsakamma" means the making of an opportunity (asking for permission). It is written: "An act done by giving opportunity is okāsakamma." In the example "The maiden does not see the sun" (asūriyaṃ passati kanyā), just as the maiden does not see the sun, when it is said "without making an opportunity" (anokāsaṃ kāretvā), it means without asking for permission.

## The Explanation of the First Training Rule on Corrupting with Malice is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Corrupting with Malice

"Only in Veluvana" is said with reference to the time when those Mettiya-Bhummajaka monks spoke. The statement "Previously, friends, we spoke only by hearsay" is said with reference to the words "We, being angry and displeased, instigated that Mettiya nun" and so on. "Belonging to another part" refers to this legal issue of the male goat's birth, which is a part other than the human or monk part, namely the part of an animal male goat (chagalaka). Or, "another part belongs to him" means that other part, known as being an animal male goat, belongs to this male goat; thus, this male goat is called a legal issue belonging to another category (aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa).

In that aññabhāgiya case, "the body of an image" or "the body of a stone statue" are examples. Here, the first derivation is stated according to the view of those who hold that "the class (jāti) is the meaning of the word (padattha)". That class is established in the nature of potentiality (satti) because it is predominant by way of being the master and being permanent. Because of deviation from that, the second derivation is stated by the power of the rule: "But the manifested form and the class are the meaning of the word" (vyattākati jātiyo tu padattho). "The support of the perception of naming"—here, the name itself is the naming. The perception of those who make a name is the "perception of naming", and it is the support of that. A human being is the support of the male goat class. The meaning is that the name is not without a support like a tortoise's hair. The name given to that male goat as "substance" (dabba) is called "point" (desa). Therefore, in accusing the Elder groundlessly etc., another object also clings to the Elder merely by way of common usage, not in reality; because it clings slightly, it is called a "pretext" (lesa). Since "point" (desa) and "pretext" (lesa) are not different in meaning, it should be understood that "based on some part which is a mere pretext" was extracted and stated as "ten pretexts, the pretext of class (jātilesa)" and so on. For example...
201:
In the Nidāna, in the formulation of the training rules (sikkhāpada), and in the Mātikā, this is the meaning. This is because 'aññabhāgiyaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ' refers to the legal issue (adhikaraṇa) concerning the he-goat (chagalaka). The phrase 'taking some part as a mere pretext' (kañci desaṃ lesamattaṃ upādāya) means taking the name 'Dabba' as a basis. Since this meaning is clear through the origin of the incident (atthuppatti), it was not explained in detail. In another way, it is because there is no fixed rule. Not for all monks is the he-goat (chagalaka) the only 'belonging to another category' (aññabhāgiya) legal issue, as it was for the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka. Other things related to cows, buffaloes, etc., can also be the basis. Not all monks, like Mettiya and Bhummajaka, rely only on a mere hint of a name. They also rely on a hint of birth (jāti), etc. Therefore, because there is no fixed rule and as stated above, it was not explained in detail. Furthermore, if it were stated as such (as chagalaka), it would seem that being 'belonging to another category' (aññabhāgiya) is possible only in the case of a he-goat and not in others; therefore, only that he-goat was shown. What is called 'lesa' (pretext) is just a pretext, not birth, etc. If it were shown as birth, etc., there would be a possibility of wrong grasping; therefore, it was not explained in detail.

'Aññabhāgiya' means the case of someone other than the accused (cuditaka). 'Adhikaraṇa' refers to a human, a non-human (amanussa), or an animal; this should be stated. If stated thus, it would mean the hint of birth, etc., of humans and so on. Otherwise, those (hints of birth, etc.) would apply to all four types of legal issues (adhikaraṇa). If it is argued that this is because the genitive case (sāmivibhatta) is placed first in the phrase 'adhikaraṇassa kañci desaṃ lesamattaṃ'? No, it is because there can be a fixed basis for birth, etc., in humans and so on, just as there is for a name, and because there is no fixed rule for the state of being a legal issue (adhikaraṇa). If there were a fixed rule, the basis of birth would be birth itself, the basis of gender (liṅga) would be gender itself, the basis of an offense (āpatti) would be the person who committed the offense (āpanna), and the basis of bowls and robes that are conflicting or not undertaken would be the owner (sāmika). If that were the case, it would reach a state that could be called a legal issue (adhikaraṇa), and thus the word 'adhikaraṇassa' should not be analyzed and should not be extracted. However, it should be extracted. Therefore, everything starting with 'due to the commonality of the term (vacanasamañña) adhikaraṇa' should be stated. These are not clear because they are not shown elsewhere besides this place. Vinaya experts (vinayadharas) should know this. This is because in the Parivāra, in a future passage such as 'a legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) belongs to the legal issue of dispute among the four legal issues,' if the question 'why' is asked, the reason would not be clear. Therefore, Vinaya experts should know the state of 'belonging to the same category' (tabbhāgiya) and 'belonging to another category' (aññabhāgiya) of those legal issues. If these are understood, then a legal issue of dispute belongs to a legal issue of dispute. Why? Because it belongs to the same category (tabbhāgiya). It does not belong to the other because it belongs to another category (aññabhāgiya). Thus, it is understood through an easy reason. Therefore, it should be understood that it is shown by depending on the legal issue obtained through the commonality of the term (saddasamañña).
202:
Among those categories (bhāgiya), because 'aññabhāgiya' regarding offenses (āpattaññabhāgiya) has a broad scope and because its explanation is different from the other three, even though it is included within legal issues (adhikaraṇa), it is stated separately as 'or it is an aññabhāgiya offense' (āpattaññabhāgiyaṃ vā hoti). Because it is included within legal issues, it should be understood that it is stated here as 'or it is an aññabhāgiya legal issue' (adhikaraṇaññabhāgiyaṃ vā).

Between these two categories as well, because it has a broad scope and because it appears in the Mātikā, the state of 'belonging to another category' (aññabhāgiya) is stated first, and the state of 'belonging to the same category' (tabbhāgiya) is stated later.

In that classification of categories, a legal issue that is established by the method of offenses (āpattinaya) through the term 'adhikaraṇaññabhāgiya' is called 'tabbhāgiya'. Therefore, without making a formal heading (uddesa) like 'a legal issue is tabbhāgiya,' an explanation (niddesa) preceded by a question is made: 'How is a legal issue a tabbhāgiya of a legal issue?'

In that sequence of the Pali, although the state of 'belonging to another category' (aññabhāgiya) of a legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) is stated only in terms of Pārājikas because it is the context of the sequel to a Pārājika, it should also be understood in terms of the remaining groups of offenses. There is an accusation (codanā) such as 'this monk is seen committing a Saṅghādisesa offense.' In such an accusation, the Pali such as 'one perceives a Saṅghādisesa as a Thullaccaya, or a Dubbhāsita as a Saṅghādisesa' should be understood as being stated either due to lack of skill in Vinaya or due to similarity with those respective objects (vatthu).

In all sections (vāra), it is not stated as 'perceiving it as a Pārājika.' Why is it not stated? Because for a monk who perceives it as a Pārājika, there is no offense. The phrase 'tabbhāgiya-vicāraṇāyaṃ' is stated because in the explanation of the term 'tabbhāgiya,' it is also shown as 'aññabhāgiya.'

'Vatthusabhāgatāya' means due to the similarity of the basis of the accusation (anuvādavatthu). Otherwise, the statement 'four failures (vipatti)' would be contradictory. 'Sabhāvasarikkhāsarikkkhato ca' means due to similarity or dissimilarity in nature. In that statement of similarity or dissimilarity, although the nature of the object such as jhāna is different, because the nature of jhāna is similar, the Pārājika offense of superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) is 'belonging to the same category' (tabbhāgiya) only to that same uttarimanussadhamma Pārājika.

Similarly, by the power of the object, although the legal issue of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) and the legal issue of duties (kiccādhikaraṇa) each have four types, the stated 'aññabhāgiya' does not occur. Therefore, when the state of 'belonging to another category' (aññabhāgiya) is known, even if the state of 'belonging to the same category' (tabbhāgiya) is not stated through the logical reasoning of seeking it, it is established; thus, it is appropriate to say 'only the aññabhāgiya is shown first.' In this context of 'it is certainly not tabbhāgiya,' because there can be a dispute (vivāda) as to whether one has reached the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) or not based on similarity, a legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) could also be 'aññabhāgiya' in an undetermined (abyākata) sense. Since the legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) is stated in the Pali, it is stated thus. 'Ādito paṭṭhāya' means starting from this term 'aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa.' 'Sexual intercourse (methuna) occurs through lust (rāga), a human being (manussaviggaho)...'
203:
It is written, "by way of similarity as well," starting with "dosenā" (by anger). That statement is established simply because the objects are different (vatthu-visabhāgatā). Regarding this statement, it is our opinion that even if the objects are similar, they are similar because the nature of the offense is the same. In truth, the Teachers say that even in a single object, there is a distinction of offenses. It should be understood in the manner to be explained later.

Because it is said, "The duty itself is the legal issue of duties" (kiccameva kiccādhikaraṇaṃ), this is a designation for the formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma). "The characteristic of the act" (kammalakkhaṇa) refers to the nature of the acts. "Depending on that act" means the Saṅgha performs the act having previously arranged it. Or rather, it is said that depending on preceding formal acts of the Saṅgha such as probation (parivāsa) or suspension (ukkhepaniya), acts like rehabilitation (abbhāna) or restoration (osāraṇā) arise. Therefore, although only a formal act of the Saṅgha is a legal issue of duties, it shows that the remaining distinctions are obtained.

In meaning, they are the same. Therefore, without stating the meaning of the region (desa), "pretext" (lesa) etc. are mentioned.

"Having made it with a basis" (savatthukaṃ katvā) means attributing it to a person. Even if they are of the same class, such as Khattiya, they become of another part (category) by way of height (tall or short), color (black or white), etc., which are seen, heard, or suspected. Seeing a tall Khattiya committing a transgression, one charges him with the pretext of class because he is the basis for the designation of a short Khattiya. Or, seeing one Khattiya committing a transgression, one takes the pretext of the class of another Khattiya who is distinct from the one seen, and charges him by way of another part such as what is seen, saying, "A Khattiya was seen; you are a Khattiya [who transgressed]." In this matter, it is written: "Tallness etc., and being seen etc., are legal issues (adhikaraṇa) because they are the basis for class, name, etc." That statement does not overcome the fault stated as "because the state of being a legal issue is not fixed." In the Commentary, it is said: "The state of being a legal issue should be understood by way of being the basis for the designation of the Khattiya class." That statement also is not universally applicable because no one has a designation of name and clan other than their own name and clan. Therefore, the extraction of the word "of the legal issue" is for the purpose of showing the four legal issues. It is our opinion, as the Teachers say, that it is for the purpose of showing a word similar to that term. In that context, in the phrase "either tallness etc. or being seen etc.," tallness etc. and being seen etc. are the "other part" (aññabhāga), which is the distinction of the accuser from the accused. Because of that part, he is called "another person."

"A light offense" (lahukaṃ āpattiṃ) refers to offenses lighter than a pārājika, such as saṅghādisesa. Therefore, at the end, showing that saṅghādisesa offense, it is said: "A monk [reaches] a saṅghādisesa..."
204:
"...is seen falling into a saṅghādisesa offense," etc., is stated. If it is asked why the pretext of an offense (āpattilesa) is not explained in detail like the pretext of class (jātilesa), etc., it should be understood that it is because it is not possible in that manner.

Sāṭakapatta means a bowl associated with the body (or a clay bowl). "Of an offense" (āpattiyā) refers to an offense belonging to another part from a pārājika offense, such as saṅghādisesa, and it is also the legal issue of the designation of offenses. Since it is said, "A pretext is a part of an offense," it should be understood that the pretext of the state of being an offense is meant. Therefore, taking the pretext of the state of being an offense of the group of offenses such as saṅghādisesa, which reaches the name "legal issue" in the sense of being the basis for the designation of an offense belonging to another part from a pārājika offense, the accusation is to be known as an accusation based on the pretext of an offense (āpattilesacodana).

In the statement "There is no offense for one who accuses or causes another to accuse while perceiving it as such," the absence of offense applies only to an accusation belonging to another part (aññabhāgiyacodana), not elsewhere. By this sequence of words, it is consistent with the investigation stated in the first Duṭṭhadosa training rule. If it is asked how that statement is evident in this training rule, it is evident from the words of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī. Indeed, it is said: "In that first Duṭṭhadosa and in this second Aññabhāgiya, in an accusation by way of another part of an offense, there is no offense even for one who perceives it as such (impure)."

## The monk who does not practice the Aññabhāgiya training rule in accordance with the logic of the regulations, will be considered by those wise in the Vinaya as having reached the state of belonging to another part.

## The Explanation of the Second Duṭṭhadosa Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the First Saṅghabheda Training Rule

There is also a variant reading: "Vajjaṃ na phuseyya."

Because of not knowing appropriately for those individuals, one would not be all-knowing. Since it is said, "Monks, one without a lodging should not enter the rains-retreat," it is indeed prohibited. "Pure in three respects" (tikoṭiparisuddha) is said to prevent the suspicion that another person might fall into sin; it is not said to prevent the act depending on it. "By respects" (koṭīhi) means by modes. "Pure" (parisuddha) means liberated. Ascetics enjoy meat prepared specifically for them through ten pretexts; "these are not ascetics"—this would lead to the state of reproach for the Dispensation. Because of that reproach, the multitude of people would also increase demerit, which is the cause for accusing the Noble Ones. It means meat that is free from those modes which are the cause of demerit. "Gara" is said to be a net for trapping deer. Since the suitability of meat prepared for one's own benefit or for the benefit of others is shown, the phrases "because of performing rites for the deceased" etc. are stated to show that suitability in meat prepared for the benefit of monks or for the benefit of others.
205:
Monks consume meat specifically prepared for them; such monks would reach the state of being criticized by the Dispensation, saying they are not true monks. Due to this cause of criticism, the multitude of people would also produce demerit by accusing the Noble Ones (Ariyas). Meat that is free from these causes of demerit is meant by 'vimutta' (released). 'Vāgurā' refers to a net for catching deer. Having shown the allowability (kappiya-bhāva) of meat prepared for the sake of others, such as 'for one's own sake,' etc., the phrase 'for the sake of funeral rites (petakicca) for the deceased' is said to show that allowability in meat prepared for the sake of monks and others.

The phrase 'Whichever...' etc., is stated to show that reason. Again, it is said that Elder Dhammasiri stated that meat prepared for the sake of the five co-religionists (sahadhammikas) is not allowable. In the Gaṇṭhipada (glossary), it is written: 'Meat prepared solely for the sake of monks, without being mixed with novices, is not allowable.' However, other teachers say: 'Even if it is said to be for the sake of funeral rites for the deceased, it is allowable; by the phrase "only for the sake of monks," it also means meat prepared with the thought "we shall eat after giving to the monks as well."' Again, they say that the phrase 'Among the five co-religionists...' etc., is stated to show the meaning that 'meat specifically prepared for one among the five co-religionists is not allowable for the remaining co-religionists.' In another Gaṇṭhipada, it is said that if one says 'for us' or 'for the king's ministers, etc.,' it is allowable; and having shown that it is allowable if one says 'for the sake of funeral rites' without saying 'for you (venerable sirs),' the commentator, establishing the characteristics of those mentioned in all places and the multitude of people included by the word 'ādi' (etc.), said 'only for the monks,' etc. In that context, it is said with the intention 'only in meat specifically intended for monks.' It is not to show that there is no offense if one says 'for you (venerable sirs) and for us.' Why? Because there is no 'mixed section' (missaka-vāra).

A 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) applies to those who have been mentioned and to those similar to those mentioned. They say: 'In the place where it is said "for the sake of funeral rites," they prepare it intending to offer a meal to the monks.' And because it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: 'In that section, if it is said "not for you (venerable sirs)," it is allowable.' Therefore, here too, by the power of the meaning previously stated, it is said: 'The same method applies to meat prepared for the sake of funeral rites or for the sake of auspicious ceremonies, etc.' If it is said: 'In the mixed section, it is allowable because of the word "eva" (only) having the sense of limitation (avadhāraṇa).' By the statement 'There is no offense in receiving allowable meat,' it follows that there is an offense in receiving unallowable meat. That statement, which says 'that should be accepted' and then 'it should be rejected,' seems good; it should be accepted after careful investigation.

'And in whatever place' means even in meat prepared for the sake of monks. To clarify that meaning, 'But if...' etc., is stated. Here, however, they say: 'For bhikkhunīs, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for the remaining co-religionists, it is a matter for disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma).' 'For an aeon in hell' means for an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa). Schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda) only occurs during the vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī period. 'Aeon' (kappa) refers to the life-span aeon (āyu-kappa).

'Kusala' means safety (khema). In this context, 'monks with shame who act out of fear of an offense,' the phrase 'the shameful one will protect' is stated to show that they will certainly report [the offense] out of fear of an offense. For a monk who does not report to a shameless person (alajjī), there is certainly an offense. This is because of the statement 'Those who see, those who hear...' In the phrase 'those who are not disciplined,' it is a term showing the agent in the passive voice (kamma-kāraka). It means a monk for whom the act of discipline by the formal act of a motion and announcement (ñatti-kammavācā) has not been performed. ## 13. Explanation of the Kuladūsaka Training Rule 

Not only the monastery is called Kiṭāgiri; that village is also called 'Kiṭāgiri'. Referring to the village, it is said later: 'The monks Assaji and Punabbasu should not reside in Kiṭāgiri'. 'Akatavatthu' means a new matter (the cause for incurring an offense). It is written: 'Flower bushes such as jasmine (jāti) and sumana, and moist green trees.' This distinction is by way of vegetation (bhūtagāma) and seeds (bījagāma). 'Vatatthāya' means for the sake of a fence (enclosure). 'Yaṃkiñci' means whether with water or without water (referring to a trench). 'Ārāmādi-atthāya' means for the sake of a forest grove, etc. The planting of small flower plants is mentioned only with reference to the act of corrupting families (kuladūsaka), not with reference to all acts such as stringing flowers. If it is asked: 'How is it known?' to show that point, it is said 'Buddhena dhammo', etc. There is also a variant reading of 'āveḷaṃ' as 'ābiḷaṃ'. 

'Gopphana' means stringing by knotting. 'Veṭhima' is a type of flower garland similar in nature to gopphana. 'Vedhima' is a flower garland made by piercing flowers with some other thread, etc. Regarding the tying of thorns, they say: 'It is not allowable to pierce for oneself; however, it is allowable for the sake of another'. 'Jālamayaṃ vitānaṃ' means a ceiling (canopy) made of netting. They make the flower-receptacle with holes like a lattice window. 'Tālapannaguḷaka' means a flower ornament made of palm leaves; even if made again, they only perform the cutting. For the purpose of inserting flowers at a stupa or a Bodhi tree, a Dhamma-rope (dhamma-rajju)...
208:
It refers to a rope that is pierced and tied. It is written: "Whether bound with dyed cloth or bound with threads, fibers, etc., it is like a strung flower." A shoulder bag (aṃsakoika) is like something placed inside a bag, so it is not considered vedhima (pierced or woven work); therefore, they say, "It is not proper to insert flowers in between a loosely tied shoulder bag." They also say, "It is proper to wrap it many times without letting them touch each other." Pūrita refers to a flower-cloth that is spread out lengthwise to fill it. Ghaṭikadāma-olambaka is written as "a cluster of garlands hanging in pairs." They say, "Since geṇḍu garlands and kharapatta garlands are rejected, a garland made of cloth etc. is also not proper as it conforms to what is unallowable (akappiya)."

It is written: "Recaka is the dance of those who dance in such a manner." This is described as "turning around." It is said that there is a reading: "Sāriya are barking dogs, and they stand in the manner of foxes or the play of deer." There is also the Pali reading "nibujjhanti."

The words abalabala etc. are spoken out of order. Just as the entire group is called "Assaji and Punabbasukas" by the power of the leaders, so too all the disciples belonging to the chief disciple are called "Sāriputtas" by the power of the chief disciple. Therefore, he said, "Go, you Sāriputtas."

By the words "One should not live in the village," it is clear that one should not live in another place within that village. Why is it said "or in that monastery"? Because of the possibility of meaning. If one has committed the act of corrupting families in a certain village, it is to show that it is not proper to live in that village, or in that monastery where one lived while corrupting families, excluding other monasteries. How is that? By the words "One should not live in the village," it follows that one cannot live even in a monastery in that village where the corruption of families was committed. Seeing that consequence, it was said "in that monastery." By saying so, it becomes clear that one is allowed to live in another monastery in that village. By the words "one who lives in that monastery," it is indicated that one who lives elsewhere in that village is allowed to wander for alms in a neighboring village.

Regarding "also in a neighboring monastery," a neighboring monastery means both a monastery near that monastery in the same village and a monastery near that village. By this, one who lives elsewhere in that village should not wander for alms in that village. However, it is proper to wander for alms in a neighboring village. Furthermore, if the corruption of families was committed in a certain village, one who lives in a monastery near the corrupter's monastery in a neighboring village is allowed to wander for alms in that village. If the corruption of families was not committed in a certain neighboring village, it is proper to wander for alms there, but not to stay in the monastery—this is the meaning.
209:
Some teachers say that because it is said "One should not wander in the town," it is indicated that it is proper to live in that village in another monastery. However, in the Gaṇṭhipada texts, there is no such investigation; therefore, it should be spoken after careful consideration.

## 1. Explanation of the first Aniyata training rule

444-5. "Uddesa" means recitation. "Āsāḷhī-nakkhatta" is the festival of entering the rains-retreat. In this context of "seclusion from the ear" (sotassa raho), although the word "raho" (seclusion) is present in a general sense, it is mentioned because of the generality of "duṭṭhulla" (grave offense), like the word "Pārājika" in the training rules on announcing grave offenses and concealing grave offenses. Therefore, the commentator said: "The definition must be made only by seclusion from the eye (cakkhussa raho)."

If it is asked: "How is this known?" It is known because of the statement "a woman (mātugāma) is even a girl born on that very day," and because of the statement "a woman capable (alaṅkammaniya) of practicing sexual intercourse." In this training rule, the defilement that delights in sitting in seclusion is only the defilement connected with sexual intercourse. It is not the defilement of delighting in lewd speech (duṭṭhullavācā) as in the second Aniyata. Therefore, it is clear that "seclusion from the ear is not intended."

However, some teachers say that the statement "that (lewd speech) is also obtainable" is mentioned to show this; by that statement, the "wise and competent" (viññū paṭibalā) woman mentioned in the second Aniyata is included.

In the phrase "yena vā sā," the word "vā" should be connected as "or that monk should be dealt with by that (offense)." That "vā" has the sense of alternative (vikappa). Therefore, it means: "the monk who confesses should be judged, or the monk who does not confess should not be judged." Thus, it is said in the Commentary: "Only the monk who confesses should be dealt with by that offense... should not be dealt with." For that very reason, in the Pāḷi, the statement "If that woman should say thus" etc., is mentioned to show those two meanings.

By the phrase "of trustworthy speech" (saddheyyavacasa), the view of those who say "Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) do not tell lies that destroy benefits, but they tell other lies" is refuted. Because it is said "seen" (diṭṭhaṃ), it is good to say "looked at" (olokesi). "You should protect" (rakkheyyāsi) means "Do not tell anyone about my special attainment."

If it is asked: "For what purpose is this statement mentioned here: 'If that woman should say thus: "I heard the venerable one speaking to a woman with lewd words while sitting"'?" Since it is considered that "seclusion from the ear" is not intended in this first Aniyata, this statement should not be intended. It should be known that it is mentioned to show that in a place suitable for sexual intercourse (alaṅkammaniyaṭṭhāna), lewd speech is also obtainable, but in a place not suitable for sexual intercourse, sexual intercourse is not obtainable. Just as this is so, some teachers say that the statement "If that woman should say thus: 'I heard the venerable one speaking in the presence of a woman in praise of ministering to his own lust'" is also obtainable in this first Aniyata, but not in the second Aniyata because it is not a place suitable for sexual intercourse. In the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, regarding this second Aniyata...
211: If it is argued that the offence of lewd speech is not mentioned in the first Aniyata because the Pārājika offence is excluded and only the offence of lewd speech is mentioned, then the original manuscripts of that Pali text beginning with 'Sā ce' should be corrected. In the Ganthipada (glossary), it is written: 'In this training rule, since only sexual intercourse, bodily contact, and sitting in seclusion are mentioned, only the seclusion of the eye (cakkhussa raho) is the standard.' Regarding the second Aniyata, it is written: 'One who is not blind sees bodily contact; one who is not deaf hears lewd speech. Bodily contact occurs through body and mind; lewd speech occurs through speech and mind; both occur through both.' Because it is stated in the Commentary that 'the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are just like the first Pārājika,' and because it is said 'born on that very day,' the argument for lewd speech (duṭṭhullavāda) is not sound.## The Explanation of the First Aniyata Training Rule is Finished.## 2. Explanation of the Second Aniyata Training RuleIn the second Aniyata, in some books, it is written: 'na heva kho pana paṭicchannaṃ āsanaṃ hoti āsanaṃ.' The word 'āsanaṃ' is redundant and should be written in accordance with what has been extracted. In this training rule, since bodily contact, lewd speech, and sitting in seclusion are included, both types of seclusion (eye and ear) are intended. If so, for what purpose is 'a wise and capable woman' mentioned? This wise and capable woman alone is the single basis (vatthu) for both bodily contact and lewd speech; therefore, it is so stated. Having shown the woman as the basis for bodily contact, and since the basis for the other (lewd speech) had not yet been shown, he said this, intending only lewd speech and wishing to show its basis.Here, a question arises: Just as in the first training rule, although not intended, lewd speech was mentioned to show a specific possibility, why is the seclusion of the eye not taken by virtue of bodily contact here as well? Indeed, it is not that it should not be taken, nor has it not been taken, but it is taken only by virtue of sitting (nisajja). This is because the sitting of the limbs is not a distinction. If it is asked, 'How can there be seclusion of the eye (cakkhu raho) when the place is not concealed?' It is possible because of distance. If it is asked, 'Why in the first training rule do even a hundred women not cause an offence, while here even one woman causes an offence?' The answer is not given because it is already established. It is established by the story where a certain monk in the Great Wood at Vesālī... etc., lay down with the door open... etc., and many women... and so on.

Because of the statement, "Having done as much as they desired, they departed" (Pārājika 77), a woman cannot be the second companion in the case of sexual intercourse (methuna-dhamma). This is because women tend to conceal each other's faults; for this very reason, the Pārājika offense for concealing a fault was prescribed for bhikkhunīs. Similarly, in the passage, "The venerable Udāyī, having shown those women the monastery, [showed] those women his private parts..." (Pārājika 283), it is understood that the conclusion is reached that a woman can be the second companion in the case of a gross offense (duṭṭhulla), because of the statement, "Those modest women, having left, complained to the monks" (Pārājika 283). In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: "In the rule on secluded seats in the Acelaka-vagga, in accordance with the Pali, 'A wise man is the second companion' (Pācittiya 288), it is said that 'Even if there are a hundred women, they cannot cause an offense'"; and it is also stated: "In the second Aniyata, the phrase 'Whether a woman or a man' should be understood as being said in accordance with the statement, 'Any wise man is the second companion,' found in the section on no-offense (anāpatti-vāra) of the final rule of the Bhikkhunī-vagga and the rule on unsecluded seats in the Acelaka-vagga."

## Miscellaneous Explanation

Furthermore, in this context, this miscellaneous method (pakiṇṇaka-naya) should be understood. How? If it is said that this Aniyata section is useless because it is not something new—it is not so, because it serves the purpose of showing the characteristic sequence of imposing or not imposing offenses, distinguished by heavy (garuka) and light (lahuka) offenses. In this Aniyata section, the characteristic sequence of imposing heavy and light offenses is shown by such passages as: "If that woman should say, 'Venerable sir, I saw [the monk] engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman,' and if that monk confesses, he should be dealt with according to the offense... etc." (Pārājika 446). And the characteristic sequence of not imposing an offense is shown by the word "kāretabbo" (should be dealt with).

If it is said that because it shows the characteristic, it should be presented at either the beginning or the end—it is not so, because it is not possible. Why? It is not possible at the beginning because the rules to which this characteristic belongs have not yet been shown. It is not possible at the end because it is mixed with heavy offenses. Therefore, it is appropriate to say it should be presented only in the middle of the heavy and light offenses, because it is mixed with both. In that Aniyata section, the light offense which...
213:
The light offense shown in that Aniyata section is also an offense starting with a heavy one. For this very reason, it is said, "By the secret enjoyment known as the defilement associated with sexual intercourse," and so on. Therefore, some teachers say that it should be recited immediately after the heavy offenses.

If it is asked: "In that case, since the purpose of showing the characteristic is already accomplished by the sequence shown in the first rule, the first rule alone is sufficient; what is the use of the second rule?"—it is not so, because it serves the purpose of preventing the wrong view (micchā-gāha) arising from the restriction of the place.

In fact, because the place is restricted by the words "in a concealed seat fit for lustful acts," a wrong view may arise that this characteristic should not be considered in any other place. To prevent that wrong view, the second rule is also meaningful. Why? Because of the difference in place, the desire to show the difference in privacy (raho), and the desire to show the difference in sitting and enjoyment in privacy. Due to the restriction of the place, the difference in sitting and enjoyment in privacy arises.

There should also be an understanding of the distinction between the two rules concerning sitting in privacy. Likewise, it is useful because of the desire to show the difference in physical contact (kāya-saṃsagga). Indeed, in an unconcealed place not fit for lustful acts, or even in a concealed place, physical contact can be obtained by holding the hair, etc., of a woman sitting there, which protrudes through windows, door-cracks, and so on; such methods should be understood in detail.

Some say: "Because it follows the method found in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, it should be understood that this section is absent from the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha." Others say that it is absent because the occasion (atthuppatti) for the offense did not arise in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha. That statement is inappropriate because it [the section] shows many meanings. In fact, during the time of all Buddhas, there are five recitations (uddesa) for monks and four recitations for nuns. Some say it is because the Saṃghādisesa and Pācittiya offenses specified there are not common (asādhāraṇa) in the prescription of the Pātimokkha recitations.

For those bhikkhunīs, by virtue of the rules on touching above the knees (ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika) and the eight grounds (aṭṭhavatthuka), a specific physical contact is a Pārājika matter. Because of the statement, "Should she consent to the taking of her hand, or should she bring her body forward for that purpose" (Pācittiya 674-675), consenting is a Pārājika matter; because of the statement, "Should she stand," standing is a Pārājika matter; because of the statement, "Should she go to a rendezvous," going is a Pārājika matter; because of the statement, "Should she enter a concealed place," entering a concealed place is also a Pārājika matter. Likewise, because of the statement, "In the darkness of the night without a lamp, in a concealed place, should she stand or converse one-on-one" (Pācittiya 838), gross speech (duṭṭhulla-vācā) is a Pācittiya matter. For this reason, it is the intention of those teachers that the Aniyata section is not mentioned for those bhikkhunīs because it cannot be stated in another way, and because there are no respective [Aniyata] offenses.

## Miscellaneous Explanation is Finished.

## The Aniyata Section is Finished.

## 4. Nissaggiya Kaṇḍa
## 1. Cīvara Vagga
## 1. Explanation of the First Kathina Training Rule

"Samitāvinā" means that this Blessed One has calmed the defilements; therefore, He is called "Samitāvī." [The term means] "by that Blessed One who has calmed the defilements." Although it should be said as "tīṇi cīvarāni," it is stated as "ticīvaraṃ." In this regard, the grammatical rule "a Digu compound preceded by a number is singular" should be understood. The name "ticīvaraṃ" refers to both robes that are determined (adhiṭṭhita) and robes that are not determined (anadhiṭṭhita). In passages such as "If a monk should stay away from the triple robe (ticīvarena) even for one night," it is the name for the robes determined by the determination of the triple robe. In this passage, "I allow you, monks, to determine the triple robe (ticīvaraṃ)," it is the name for robes not yet determined. In this context (the phrase "ticīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ"), both types of triple robes are possible. In the phrase "The triple robe is allowed to the monks by the Blessed One," it refers only to the determined robes. In the phrase "They enter the village with another triple robe," it refers only to the undetermined robes.

Indeed, the determination of the triple robe is valid only for a single set of triple robes; it is not valid for other extra robes, just as the determination of a bowl is not valid for others. Therefore, other robes remain in the status of extra (atireka) robes. Thus, it was said: "How can the group-of-six monks keep an extra robe?" and so forth.

460-1. In the laying down of this training rule, according to the primary regulation (mūla-paññatti), it was taught: "If one should keep an extra robe even for one night, it is a Nissaggiya offense." After that was taught, the Blessed One laid down the complete training rule thus: "I allow you, monks, to keep an extra robe for at most ten days. And thus, monks, should you recite this training rule: 'An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days; for him who exceeds that [limit of] ten days, there is an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya.'"

After that was laid down, during the later period of Enlightenment (pacchima-bodhi) in the time of King Ajātasattu, the Kathina was allowed. From the time the Kathina was allowed onwards, the monks recite this training rule: "When the robe is finished, when the Kathina is removed, for a monk... ten days... there is an offense of Pācittiya." This same method applies to the second and third Kathina training rules. Nevertheless, in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, it is stated only this much: "The phrase 'dasāhaparamam' (at most ten days) is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here." Therefore, it can be concluded that the words "When the robe is finished, when the Kathina is removed" are neither the primary regulation nor the supplementary regulation. Indeed, the matter concerning the Kathina is not evident in the context of the primary regulation nor in the context of the supplementary regulation; therefore, it should be concluded that only the aforementioned method is the essence. However, it might be argued: "From the time the Kathina originated, the word of the Blessed One was spoken as a supplementary regulation." If that were so, there would be two supplementary regulations. In that case, it would contradict the statement in the Parivāra...
215:
...which says "one supplementary regulation" (ekā anupaññatti). Furthermore, to demonstrate the aforementioned method, those words were not spoken at the time of the primary regulation in this training rule but were spoken later. Because it was established in this first training rule, it was spoken thus in the first regulations which were spoken later in the second and third training rules. Otherwise, those words would have to be spoken later in those second and third training rules as well. In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: "With reference to the fact that it was spoken later, it is a supplementary regulation in the passages beginning with 'niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ'."

The affection of trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana) is called love (pema); the respect of Arahants is called reverence (gārava). In the phrase "dasamaṃ vā navamaṃ vā," the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.

462-3. The phrase "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ" (when the robe is finished) is spoken merely to demonstrate the absence of robe-impediments (cīvara-palibodha). Therefore, it is said: "lost, destroyed, burnt, or the hope for a robe is intercepted." If it were spoken to show the robe that is to be kept for the ten-day limit, the monk would have to keep the lost robe and so forth. Here, "keeping" (dhāraṇa) means either placing it aside or using it. Both of these are applicable to a finished robe as well as to an unfinished robe. Therefore, it should not be said "if it is finished." This is because Nissaggiya does not occur only for one who exceeds the limit with a finished robe. Therefore, the robe referred to by the words "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ" should not be understood as the period for which it must be kept for ten days after the Kathina is removed. If that robe exists, it cannot receive even a single day of deferment (parihāra) after the Kathina is removed. Furthermore, it is said: "A robe is that which is the last [of the three] that is subject to assignment (vikappanūpaga)." In that robe subject to assignment, it is also called "finished." For that reason also, it should be understood that it cannot be said that it is kept with reference to that robe, as it is impossible.

In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, this is said: "In that statement, this objection might arise—if one of the robes of that monk were lost and so forth, which robe would he keep for the ten-day limit? Since there is no robe to be kept, the words beginning with 'niṭṭhita' are spoken to show the impediment of making [a robe] by way of extracting the meaning. This meaning should be taken when there is no other robe among the robes mentioned by the method beginning with 'lost' (naṭṭhaṃ vā). If it exists, for the monk who exceeds ten days with that robe, there is a Nissaggiya. This is the method in all cases. Only the robe mentioned as 'if it is finished' is intended. If it is asked why a finished robe is not explicitly stated as intended in this meaning, it is because it is obvious. How is it obvious? Since there is no keeping of lost or destroyed robes, it is obvious that only a finished robe is intended here. For example, how? Just as in the first Aniyata, since only sexual intercourse, physical contact, and sitting in private are mentioned, it is obvious that 'private from the ear' (sotassa raho) is spoken by way of extracting the meaning. Therefore, it is not said that 'private from the eye' (cakkhussa raho) is intended in the other sense. It should be understood that this is similarly accomplished. The phrase 'if it is finished' should not be said. Why? Because Nissaggiya occurs even for one who exceeds the limit with an unfinished robe. Although the Nissaggiya is slight..."
216:
In this context, the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of the triple robe (ticīvara) is intended. In making that determination of the triple robe, it is not proper to determine a robe that is unsewn, undyed, or not marked with the proper mark (kappabindu) by saying, 'I determine this outer robe (saṅghāṭi),' and so forth. To clarify this meaning, it is stated, 'Or it must be a completed robe.' Otherwise, it should have been said, 'When a completed robe is obtained.' If this were the case, one might ask: How can it be known that a monk who keeps the triple robe for more than ten days incurs an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya)? It can be known by the authority of the Pāḷi text. Because it was said, 'Monks, I allow you to determine the triple robe, not to assign (vikkappeti) it,' in this context also, it should only be said that 'A robe that has not yet been determined is called an extra robe (atirekacīvara).' By the phrase 'Or it must be a completed robe,' the Buddha intended to allow that the remaining robes, along with the robe intended here, cannot be kept for more than a maximum of ten days; thus He said, 'A robe that is neither determined nor assigned is called an extra robe.' In that regard, just as the meaning was extracted and stated as 'not assigned,' it could also be said as 'the last robe suitable for assignment.' Why? Because by the power of the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) beginning with 'When the robe is finished,' only the triple robe should be kept for a maximum of ten days. Otherwise, even by exceeding one day, an offense of forfeiture would be incurred because of the statement: 'If any monk should keep an extra robe, there is an offense of forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).' A robe other than the triple robe also must not be kept for more than ten days; if it exceeds that, an offense of forfeiture is incurred because it is stated as 'within ten days.' As it was said: 'There is no offense if one determines or assigns it within ten days.' Otherwise, it would merely be the statement 'He determines it within ten days.' Therefore, the meaning should be taken only according to the method stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). All of this is what other teachers say. In this context, if a robe that arises during the Kathina period is already completed, the statement that it should be kept for a maximum of ten days, and the words spoken to prove this, should not be accepted because they contradict the investigation (vicāraṇā) to be mentioned later in this very section and the logic already stated.

The investigation mentioned here is as follows: A monk who knows 'Tomorrow the Kathina will be revoked' but does not determine the robe he received today on that very same day, incurs an offense of forfeiture at dawn. Why? Because the training rule was laid down starting with 'When the robe is finished,' and so forth. During the Kathina period, even if it exceeds ten days, it receives protection (parihāra); after the Kathina is revoked, it does not receive protection even for a single day. For example, the Saṅgha that has spread the Kathina receives the benefits (ānisaṃsa) from the day it was spread until it is revoked, even if only one day remains; on the following day, they do not receive them. If, due to forgetfulness, the robe to be distributed is not distributed, on the following day it becomes common to even those monks who did not spread the Kathina. If days still remain, it belongs only to the Saṅgha that spread the Kathina. Similarly, from the day of spreading until revocation, a robe that is not yet determined or assigned is proper because it is within the permitted days.
217:
The day the Kathina is spread is included in the count. From the day the Kathina is revoked, a robe that has arisen can be kept for a maximum period of ten days; beyond that, it is not permitted. Why? Because of the statement: 'Monks, I allow an extra robe to be kept for a maximum of ten days.' Even during the Kathina period, this supplementary regulation, 'When the robe is finished, when the Kathina is revoked,' stands as a prohibition against the occurrence of forfeiture at the eleventh dawn. Those days should not be treated as non-days. Likewise, in the Third Kathina, it was investigated: By saying, 'When the robe is finished, when the monk's Kathina is revoked, if an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) should arise for that monk,' the Blessed One showed that 'The training rule I allowed below in the first training rule, stating that an extra robe should be kept for a maximum of ten days, also refers only to a robe arising outside the Kathina month, not within it.' Because of the statement, 'This robe, given even during the season with a specific reference, is called an out-of-season robe,' it is shown that after the Kathina is revoked, the ten-day protection is no longer received. Along with those days, the notion that one can again receive five days after the Kathina revocation is also prohibited because the time of arising of an out-of-season robe is defined by the statement: 'When the robe is finished... it should be made quickly.' For both these reasons, it is established that a robe arising during the Kathina period does not receive protection even for a single day after the Kathina is revoked. Therefore, referring to these two types of investigation, it should be understood that we said, 'It should not be accepted because it contradicts the investigation mentioned here and the logic already stated.'

In this matter, an objector asks: Does this word ending in the locative case (sattamī vibhatti), 'When the robe is finished, when the Kathina is revoked,' define the arising of the robe, or its keeping, or both? What is the case here? If it defines the arising, then if the Kathina is revoked only in the month of Kattika, a robe that arises must be kept for ten days from then on, even if that month has not yet ended. If it defines the keeping, then a robe arising during the Kathina period must be kept for a maximum of ten days even after the Kathina is revoked. If it defines both, it should be stated specifically as in the Third Kathina.

The answer is: Indeed, it defines both, but there is no benefit in specifying. The statement 'When the robe is finished,' referring to a robe arising during the Kathina period, does not mean 'it should be kept' with reference to that robe; this meaning has already been established. Because of the words beginning with 'If it is made,' that meaning is completed. Therefore, there is no benefit in specifying again; just as one does not perform a forfeiture that has already been performed, and just as one is unable to keep a lost robe and so forth. Or, according to the intention with which the Blessed One laid down this training rule,
218:
This meaning should be understood as being explained in the Third Kathina [Training Rule]. If it is asked why it is explained in that training rule, it is because there is an intention to show a specific provision. The specific provision (distinction) refers to 'no cassa pāripūrī' and so forth. In that Third Kathina Training Rule, by using the specific term 'akālacīvara' (out-of-season robe) and saying 'if an out-of-season robe should arise' instead of just 'if a robe should arise,' it indicates that even if the Kathina is removed, an in-season robe (kālacīvara) still exists. Furthermore, that robe is one that arises in the month of Pacchimakattika. For that very reason, it is stated in that training rule: 'a robe arising during the eleven months when the Kathina has not been spread.' Thus, the absence of fault stated in the rule of arising (uppattiniyama) is established. Regarding the statement in that training rule, 'This robe, though given specifically during the robe-season, is called an out-of-season robe,' there are two alternative interpretations of its meaning.

By virtue of designation, although it is named an 'out-of-season robe,' because it arises during the robe-season, it receives the robe-season privilege (kālaparihāra); if it were a robe without such designation, what more need be said? This first interpretation supports the absence of fault stated in the rule of arising. Furthermore, a robe named an out-of-season robe by virtue of designation, because it arises during the robe-season, does not receive the ten-day privilege beyond the robe-season; if it were a robe without such designation, what more need be said? This second interpretation supports the absence of fault in the rule of keeping (dhāraṇaniyama). If it is asked what the benefit is of it being an out-of-season robe by virtue of designation, it should be understood that such a robe, given specifically to the Saṅgha, has the benefit of being common to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha even if the Kathina is spread.

Furthermore, the days of an individual's Kathina are also just days. Because it enters into the count in this way, and by the power of receiving the name 'out-of-season robe,' and because of the dependence on the word 'Kathina' in the phrase 'when the Kathina is removed,' and because it is consistent with 'in-season robes' as well, it should be understood that the statement here is well-expressed in every way. Furthermore, there are robes that arise after the Kathina is removed by some [monks'] removal of Kathina, which are in-season robes for some monks and out-of-season robes for others. This occurs for a monk who has crossed the boundary, but not for one whose Kathina is removed. Setting aside the robe obtained after the removal of Kathina by virtue of two [reasons], it should be understood as a robe obtained after removal by one of the others. Indeed, for the one whose Kathina is removed, it is an out-of-season robe; for the other (whose Kathina is not removed), it is an in-season robe. Furthermore, there are robes that arise after the Kathina is removed by some [monks'] removal of Kathina, which are out-of-season robes for all monks. Such robes should be understood as being in accordance with how they were set aside. Furthermore, setting aside the robe that arises during the time the Kathina is removed, there are robes that arise in the last month of the rainy season (vassāna). Furthermore, there are out-of-season robes that arise after the Kathina is removed; such robes should be understood as arising in winter (hemanta) or summer (gimhāna). Because there are many varieties of robes arising due to differences in individuals and times, it should be understood that it is not simply stated as 'a robe arising after the Kathina is removed.' Because it has an indefinite meaning (anekāṃsika), this meaning also...
219:
To show the variety of meanings, it is said: 'When the Kathina is removed, the Kathina is removed for the monk.' Even though the meaning is established by this much, 'by any one of the eight headings (mātikā)' and so forth is still stated. The word 'dhārayāmi' (I shall carry) should be said to have come from the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga. By the word 'thus' (evaṃ), it means that there is no variation in the wording (vacanabheda) in that Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga.

The phrase 'the smallest robe that enters into assignment (vikkappanupaga)' is stated because it is all-inclusive. 'The smallest robe that enters into determination (adhiṭṭhānupaga)' is not all-inclusive. This is because, just as the Saṅghāṭi is the smallest that enters into determination, the Antaravāsaka and others cannot be the smallest that enter into determination, as determination is of many kinds. It should be understood that there is no such variation in assignment (vikkappanā), as it is of only one kind. In the phrase 'at the rise of dawn on the eleventh day, it entails forfeiture (nissaggiya),' the meaning should be understood as the days preceding it, excluding the final day. The final day refers to the first dawnrise of the following month of Kattika. Because that is the [robe] season, it does not cause forfeiture.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Commentary on the Accekacīvara Training Rule: 'Whether it is an urgent robe (accekacīvara) arising from the sixtieth day onwards, or a robe that has been set aside after being relinquished (paccuddharitvā), it certainly receives this privilege (parihāra).' Intending this very method, it is stated in that same commentary: 'For an urgent robe, if the Kathina is not spread, the period is one month and eleven days; if the Kathina is spread, it is five months and eleven days; beyond that, there is no privilege even for a single day.' According to this method, it is established that an urgent robe does not receive the privilege on the twelfth day. Therefore, in the phrase 'if one perceives what is not an urgent robe to be an urgent robe, there is no offense,' it is established that this refers to another robe similar to an urgent robe before it has been determined (anadhiṭṭhite). In that context, the phrase 'five months' is a statement of the maximum limit. It should be understood that a rainy-season cloth (vassikasāṭika), having reached the state of not being a rainy-season cloth, receives the privilege for eleven months.

In the phrase 'if ten days are exceeded, it entails forfeiture,' just as there are variations in wording in the context of rising from an offense (āpattivuṭṭhāna) such as 'concealed for ten days, a fortnight, more than a fortnight, a month, more than a month,' there is no such variation in wording here. Therefore, even if a year is exceeded, it is simply called 'exceeding ten days.' Similarly, in the Second Kathina Training Rule, even if one is separated [from the robe] for a year, it is simply called 'separated for one night.' In the Third [Kathina Training Rule], even if a year is exceeded, it should be understood as being called 'exceeding a month.' The statement 'if one perceives what is not determined to be determined, it entails forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya)' is an explanation of the opening term of one of the triads of Pacittiya offenses (tika-pācittiya). This method is the same for 'not assigned' (avikkappite) and so forth. Therefore, here, among the eight kinds of triads, having expanded on one, and having expanded on the opening term of each of the remaining triads, two by two...
220:
Because the Blessed One taught in brief, although many divisions of triads (tika) could occur, he spoke of only one; they say, "This is the nature of the Vinaya." However, in the sections on wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), after explaining one wrong-doing in detail, the remaining seven triads are likewise summarized. Similarly, it should be understood that at the very end, there is a portion for each case of "no offense" (anāpatti).

"No offense within ten days" means this summarized sense: that robe should be kept for a maximum of ten days. If one determines (adhiṭṭheti), assigns (vikappeti), or abandons (vissajjeti) that extra robe (atireka-cīvara) within ten days according to the appropriate time; or if it is lost, destroyed, or burnt by its own nature; or if another person takes it by force or takes it through intimacy (vissāsa), there is no offense of pācittiya. Regarding the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), however, there may or may not be an offense depending on the variation in perception (saññā). Here, by the power of the last two words, if one takes a robe thinking it was taken by force when it was not, a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred. If one takes a robe thinking it was taken through intimacy when it was not, a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred. Thus, it should be understood that the two triads of pācittiya and the two wrong-doings are summarized. In this section on "no offense," if one determines it within ten days, it should be understood that one determines it during the day after the dawn of the tenth day has passed. This is the decision according to the Pāḷi.

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), regarding the words "In matters weightier than this" and so forth, there is this decision preceded by an objection: In the Gaṇṭhipada, it is said that just as they perform even the formal act with a motion as the second (ñatti-dutiya-kamma), which is weightier than giving this forfeited robe, by means of an act of announcement (apalokana-kamma), so too it is proper to perform this act, which should be done by a motion (ñatti), with ordinary speech. If that were so, it would contradict what is said in the Commentary on the Chapter on Legal Procedures (Kammavagga) of the Parivāra: "A formal act with a motion (ñatti-kamma) must be performed only by establishing a single motion; it must not be performed by way of an act of announcement (apalokana-kamma) and so forth." Because of such contradiction, it is said, "For them, this announcement is suitable"; therefore, that statement was made only by way of conformity (anuloma). As for the rule (niyama), we say that just as the Uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha) for two monks occurs without a motion, so too is the giving of a forfeited robe for two monks; therefore, it is proper to say, "I give it to the venerable one." How is this to be known? Because it conforms to that [Uposatha act, etc.]. The teachers say it should be understood as a proof that "This formal act with a motion is also proper to be performed by announcement at times." In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, however, having raised an objection in this matter, it is said: "This point is established. A formal act with a motion must be performed only by establishing a single motion," referring to what appears in the Pāḷi. Although this statement does not appear directly in the Pāḷi, because it is spoken of by drawing from an implication (lesato), it is said that this is proper even by announcement.

468. In the phrase "In this same way," the meaning should be understood that the third Kathina training rule, being of the same category and same sense, is identical to the first Kathina training rule, because of the words "The evidence... performed by another," such as "When the robes of others are eaten by termites and so forth, my robes are also eaten."

469. In the phrase "To determine the triple robe," the triple robe (ticīvara) refers to the robe suitable to be determined by the determination of the triple robe. I allow a monk who wishes to determine that robe, for which I allow determination by the triple robe and not assignment (vikappanā), to determine it at all times because there is no limit to the period of determination. I do not allow one to assign it by making a time limit. If there is a reason, however, it is proper to withdraw the determination and assign that robe at any time. This meaning is understood from the words "No offense in determining or assigning within ten days."
221:
This method [applies] both in comparison, such as "When the robes of others are eaten by termites etc., my robes are also eaten," and because of the word of the Buddha, "The word which is the evidence... performed by another," it is evident that the third Kathina, which has the same category and the same sense, is identical to the first Kathina.

In this context of "ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ" (to determine the triple robe), the triple robe refers to the robe suitable to be determined by the determination of the triple robe, or that robe which the Blessed One allows to be determined by the determination of the triple robe and not to be assigned. Because there is no limit to the period of determination for that robe, He allows only the determination for a monk who so desires at all times; He does not allow assignment by limiting that time. If there is a reason, it has been stated that it is evident from the words "He determines or assigns within ten days" that it is proper to withdraw the determination (paccuddharitvā) and assign it at any time. As for the rainy-season cloth (vassikasāṭika), after that [four months of rain], it is only for assignment and not for determination. Indeed, the meaning is that He allows the determination of a finished robe within ten days starting from the first day of the four months of the rainy season; when more than four months have passed, He allows assignment for a monk who wishes to keep it as his own property. "Smaller than the Sugata-robe" is the maximum measurement for all three robes. If there is a view that "The triple robe should be determined as a small accessory cloth (parikkhāra-coḷa)," it is proper if there is such a reason.
