Just as it is proper to assign if there is a reason, it is even more proper to determine it with another [type of] determination. Because it is spoken of without specification as "He determines or assigns within ten days," the names saṅghāṭi, uttarāsaṅga, and antaravāsaka are the same whether they are determined or not. In phrases such as "This is the saṅghāṭi," the undetermined robe is meant. In the phrase "He may spend the night apart from the triple robe (ticīvarena vippavaseyya)," the determined robe is meant.

"Or in a nearby monastery" (sāmanta-vihāre vā) means a monastery near the alms-village, according to Elder Dhammasiri. The teacher says it can be obtained even in a very distant monastery. In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada also, it is said: "The phrase 'or in a nearby monastery' is merely the head of the teaching (indicative); therefore, having noted the place where it was kept, it should be determined even if it is in a distant place." A "nearby monastery" is a place where one can go and return on the same day. It should be understood that it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that it is not proper for a monk guarding against spending the night apart [from his robes] to determine a robe that is further than that. Some teachers say: "If another person moves a robe kept on a robe-line and hangs it on a peg, the determination is valid even for a monk who determines it without knowing [the change], because the robe had already been noted." "Having determined" (adhiṭṭhahitvā) is by the power of [determining as] a small accessory cloth (parikkhāra-coḷa) and so forth. "Only larger" and so forth...
222:
The general characteristic common to all determinations (adhiṭṭhāna) is as follows. In that characteristic of determination, because [the newly added part] becomes a portion of the robe that has already been determined, it is only necessary to determine it again. If the undetermined part is a minor portion of the determined robe, it falls under the count of the determined robe. Similarly, if the determined robe becomes a portion of an undetermined robe, it falls under the count of the undetermined robe. This is the characteristic. In achieving this determination, not only double-layered robes but also robes of three layers and so on should be joined and determined again. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "I allow a double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭi) made of four layers of cloth to withstand the cold... in the case of rag-robes (paṃsukūla), as many as desired."

"The remaining monks" refers to the monks who were sitting at the time of the statement. Therefore, just as it was said, "Monks, I allow the three robes to be determined and not to be assigned (vikappana)," the same was said regarding the accessory cloth (parikkhāracola). Neither the maximum limit nor the numerical limit of that accessory cloth was stated. Therefore, it means that it is allowable to use them by rescinding (paccuddharaṇa) all three robes and determining them with the words, "I determine these robes as accessory cloths." If it is asked, "How is it known that 'this is the introductory way (nidānamukha)'?"—it is known because, in the case where "at that time, the monks had a complete set of three robes, but they were in need of water-filters and bags," it was allowed: "Monks, I allow an accessory cloth." Since there is no prohibition stating that only one water-filter or one bag is allowable for monks and that two or three are not, it is established that accessories such as water-filters of a small size suitable for assignment or of an extra size are allowable.

If it is asked, "If this is allowable, does it not contradict the statement, 'I shall set a limit and establish a boundary for the robes of the monks'?"—it does not contradict. This is because of not knowing the context (anusandhi) and because of the apparent contradiction. What does this mean? In the Cīvarakkhandhaka, first, lay-robes (gahapaticīvara) were allowed. Then, silk (pāvāra), silk-cloth (koseyya), woolen rugs (kojava), woolen blankets (kambala), and so on were allowed. Then, in the case where "at that time, various kinds of robes arose for the Saṅgha, and the thought occurred to the monks, 'Which robes has the Blessed One allowed, and which has he not allowed?'"—the six kinds of allowable robes, such as linen (khoma), were allowed, but the numerical limit was not yet allowed. Then, "The Blessed One saw... many monks coming with bundles of robes on their heads, on their shoulders, and on their waists. Seeing this, the thought occurred to the Blessed One... 'Even those sons of good family in this Dispensation who are sensitive to cold and afraid of cold...'"
223:
Monks are able to suffice with the triple robe (ticīvara). Thinking, "It would be well if I were to establish a limit and set a boundary for the robes of the monks and allow the triple robe" (Mahāvagga, 346), the Blessed One allowed the triple robe. In doing so, He allowed only a single set of the triple robe. However, the monks of the group of six (Chabbaggiya) misunderstood and carried many robes. Those robes became extra robes (atirekacīvara) for them. Subsequently, this point is known because He allowed, "Monks, I allow an extra robe to be kept for at most ten days" (Mahāvagga, 347). While those Chabbaggiya monks were carrying many extra robes, the Blessed One, saying, "I allow those robes to be kept for only ten days, not just one," showed the procedure for carrying many triple robes by way of a time limit, even though a boundary and limit had previously been established for the robes known as the formal determination of the triple robe (ticīvara-adhiṭṭhāna).

Furthermore, by allowing, "Monks, I allow an extra robe to be assigned (vikappeti)" (Mahāvagga, 347), He showed the procedure for carrying an extra robe without a time limit. Therefore, it is established that both of these are sources (nidānamukha). Similarly, the formal determination of accessory cloth (parikkhāracola-adhiṭṭhāna) may also be possible. Otherwise, it would contradict the allowance of other robe determinations, because it would contradict the setting of boundaries and limits. Only the regulation of the triple robe determination is the limit of the triple robe. Therefore, it is said, "This is a separate source."

It is stated: "First, the triple robe must be determined by the triple robe determination; later, when one is unable to carry it, one should revoke the determination and determine it as accessory cloth (parikkhāracola). This was not said [to be done] from the very beginning." "Just as for a sick monk who is unable to carry the triple robe, the formal agreement to stay apart from the robes (vippavāsa-sammuti) is allowed; and even for one who is not sick, in the training rule concerning suspicion (Sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada), the depositing of that robe in a house is allowed; and beyond that, if there is a reason, staying apart for six days is allowed; and beyond that, if one is unable, the revocation of the determination is allowed; and for a robe whose determination has been revoked, if one is unable to determine it within ten days, assignment (vikappanā) is allowed. Similarly, in both cases of assignment—in the presence [of the recipient] or in the absence—since it becomes the property of another, if there is no reason for assignment, the Blessed One might allow it to be used after determining it as 'accessory cloth' (parikkhāracola). Thus, teachers who know His intention say so"—this is also stated in the Mahāpaccariya. The words beginning with "Pubbe" are spoken to show the application of what was called "a separate source." The statement that it is difficult to carry in an unbound boundary (abaddhasīmā) is because there is the possibility of going beyond the precinct (upacāra) for the sake of assignment and so forth.

The statement that the rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭikā) must not exceed the [prescribed] measure is because the maximum limit for that rainy-season robe has been stated. Regarding the point that a floor covering (paccattharaṇa) must also be formally determined: a covering offered with the words, "Venerable sir, we offer this covering to be spread upon the bedding in our monastery," etc., should not be formally determined. A covering offered with the words, "I offer this covering to you," one should...
224:
The phrase “I give to you” implies that the spread offered should be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) according to one’s own wish. It is written that once determined, it remains determined and does not need to be withdrawn (paccuddharīyati) again, as there is no time limit. Other teachers say it is valid even with a single utterance. Regarding items for medicine, monastic work (navakamma), parents, etc., a monk who sets them aside thinking, “I will acquire medicine with this,” or “I will give this to my mother,” should determine them. Other teachers say that for a monk who has already partitioned them, saying, “This is for medicine, this is for my mother,” there is no need for the act of determination. It should be noted that this is said with reference to setting them aside by releasing them from one’s own possession.

The statement “It should be determined again” is a commentary view (aṭṭhakathā-vāda) descending from the Councils (saṅgīti). It is said that thereafter, teachers applied logical analysis in various places. “A robe of [minimum] measurement” (pamāṇa-cīvara) refers to a robe of the smallest size. “Two robes” means two robes including the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). This method is the same as the “wherever it fits the size” method. Because of the statement, “For one exceeding that [size], it must be cut and [the Vinaya act] performed,” exceeding the limit is prohibited; since it is not prohibited if it is less than that size, it is allowable. In that regard, it should not be said that the minimum measurement of the triple robe (ticīvara) is not separately mentioned in the Vinaya Pali, because it is established by the Sekhiya training rules. What does this mean? Because of the words, “I will wear [the inner robe] all around,” “I will dress [the upper robe] all around,” and “I will go well-covered into the village,” the extent to which “being all around” and “being well-covered” are fulfilled according to the method stated in the Commentary should be known as the minimum measurement. That measurement is indeed the “five fist-lengths” (muṭṭhipañcaka) and so on, as previously mentioned. Therefore, it is said “not separately in the Pali” only by way of a brief indication.

In truth, although it is desired here, it does not quite fit; therefore, the connection starting with “If” is certainly well-stated. Because the limit is consistent. In other views, however, in some teachers’ doctrines there is no limit, and in some, the preceding and following do not agree. Determination is indeed determination, but at the time of use, an undyed robe is not allowable. All this applies only to the triple robe (ticīvara). The summary decision of this training rule is: when the Kathina has not been spread, starting from the first day of the cold season (hemanta); when the Kathina has been spread, starting from the first day of the hot season (gimha), the phrase “when the robe is finished” etc. is said with reference to the robes that have arisen.

Here, an objector says: “Because of the statement, ‘For one having [robes] washed and made white by laundrymen, the determination is still determination,’ determination is effective even on an undyed robe. Therefore, one should not make a mark [thinking] that it must be determined only after sewing with a needle and making a proper mark (kappabindu).” The answer is: It should be understood like a bowl (patta) that has been determined. Once determined... even if it becomes white or red again, the determination is not relinquished. Just as such a bowl does not return to the state of needing determination again, this undyed robe should be understood in the same way. Teachers say: “From the time use etc. are allowable, it should be determined within ten days.”

In this context of “words spoken without specification”: without specifically saying “it should be determined,” “he determines,” “it should be assigned (vikappetabba),” or “he assigns (vikappeti),” the statement “without assigning” (avikappetvā) seems contradictory. Therefore, I shall further state this miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) method by combining the Khandhaka Pali and the Parivāra Pali concerning the methods of determination and assignment. In the Khandhaka, it is first said: “Monks, I allow the triple robe... later to be assigned.” In the Parivāra, however, it is said: “Nine robes should be determined, nine robes should be assigned.” In the Dasaka (Tens), it is said that ten robes should be determined, and in the Ekādasaka (Elevens), eleven robes should be determined, but they should not be assigned.
225:
Should one not make the mark of determination after sewing, dyeing, and applying the smudge-mark (kappabindu)? (It is asked). (The answer is:) It should indeed be done, just like a bowl that has been determined. Just as a bowl does not lose its determination even if it becomes white or red again, and such a bowl does not undergo determination again, so should an undyed robe be understood. It is said: "From the time when use and so forth are allowable, within ten days from that time, determination should be made."

The "statement made without distinction" means that it seems to contradict the words "it should not be assigned" by not specifying "that which should be determined is determined, and that which should be assigned is assigned." Now, I shall speak of the miscellaneous method (pakiṇဏaka) by combining the Khandhaka and Parivāra texts regarding this method of determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and assignment (vikappanā). First, in the Khandhaka, it is said: "Monks, I allow the triple robe (ticīvara) to be determined, not to be assigned... I allow the rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭika) to be determined for the four months of the rainy season; beyond that, I allow it to be assigned," and so forth. In the Parivāra, however, it is stated many times, making it firm: "Nine robes should not be determined, nor should they be assigned," and "In a group of ten, ten robes, and in a group of eleven, eleven robes should be determined, not assigned," and "All robes should be determined, not assigned." Therefore, these two texts seem to be contradictory.

In the Khandhaka itself, it is said: "The rainy-season robe is to be determined for the four months of the rainy season; beyond that, it is to be assigned." In its commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated: "The rainy-season robe of standard size should be determined for the four months of the rainy season by the aforementioned method of taking the name; beyond that, having withdrawn the determination (paccuddhara), it should be assigned." This statement also seems mutually contradictory because withdrawal of determination is possible in the winter, and assignment is not possible in the rainy season. Similarly, in this training rule, the commentary's statement—"It should be understood that assignment is not prohibited in all cases according to the authority of the Pali text: 'Within ten days, one determines or assigns'"—seems to contradict the Parivāra text. In truth, the Buddhas do not speak contradictory words; therefore, the method of the Commentary is the refuge (the decision) here, by which the entire decision becomes of one flavor (consistent). In the Parivāra Commentary, it is also said: "'They should not be assigned' means they should not be assigned from the time they have been determined." It means that from the time the triple robes are determined, and within the period of determination for the rainy-season robes and so forth, they should not be assigned against one's will. Since the remaining Pali and its meaning have already been stated in this Commentary, all of this is indeed of one flavor.
226:
In this context, the objector says: If this is so, it should also be said, "The nine robes should not be determined." This is because from the time of assignment (vikappanā), they should not be determined.

The reply is: In this Pali passage, "To determine the triple robe, not to assign... to determine the accessory cloth (parikkhāracola), not to assign," since a prohibition against determination is not seen for all robes, and since assignment is shown, and since the limit is shown only for two types in the phrase "beyond that," it should be understood that it means "The nine robes should be determined and should not be assigned."

Another method: Monks, I allow the triple robe to be determined even without desire (unwillingly). Why? Because for a monk who does not determine a robe that arises during the robe-season (kāla), an offense may occur due to the lapse of the season; and for a monk who does not determine a robe that arises outside the robe-season (akāla), an offense may occur due to the lapse of ten days.

Among those robes, a robe that arises during the robe-season causes an offense due to the lapse of the season even if ten days are not yet complete. When forfeiting that robe, it should be forfeited thus: "Venerable Sir, this extra robe of mine, having been kept beyond ten days, is to be forfeited; I forfeit this robe to the Saṅgha," and so on. Other robes (arising outside the season) should be forfeited exactly as stated in the Pali. Of these two methods, the first is stated by way of the first regulation (paṭhamapaññatti): "Whatever monk should keep an extra robe, it is to be forfeited." The second is stated by way of the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti).

Just as when the object to be forfeited is not present, one does not recite according to the Pali but merely confesses the offense; and just as in forfeiting a rain-cloth, if it was merely sought, one does not recite according to the Pali but forfeits it as appropriate; so too should it be understood for this robe. Just as an extra robe that has exceeded a year is simply called "exceeded ten days"; and a triple robe separated for a year or a month is called "separated for one night" or "separated for six nights"; so too, some teachers say this robe is simply called "exceeded ten days." Therefore, this statement is established: "Monks, I allow the triple robe to be determined even without desire." Likewise, it should be understood to mean "I allow it not to be assigned even without desire."

If there is a desire, however, having withdrawn the determination, permission is given to assign it for the sake of the comfort of being separated (vippavāsasukha); because of the statement "there is no offense even if ten days have passed," it means assignment is permitted. Likewise, I allow the rain-cloth to be determined even without desire, because an offense may occur if ten days have passed. If it is asked, "For how long a period?"—it is for the four months of the rainy season. If there is a desire, it should be assigned beyond that.

It is said: "It should be understood that assignment is not prohibited for all robes." It is also said: "An offense occurs in the winter, not in the summer or the rainy season." Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "Beyond that, having withdrawn the determination, it should be assigned."
227:
In this regard (concerning the performance of paccuddhāra and vikappanā), there is this investigation: When should the paccuddhāra (withdrawal of determination) be performed, and when should the vikappanā (assignment) be performed? In this investigation, because it is stated, "after that (four months)," your statement is only a little; speak further. As soon as winter arrives, that (rainy-season robe) loses its determination; therefore, because there is no longer determination, it should not be said, "having performed paccuddhāra." Otherwise, it should not be said, "it should be assigned within the four months of the rainy season." Is it not stated, "to assign after that (four months)"? In this investigation, some teachers say, "this (statement regarding paccuddhāra, etc.) should indeed be said."

Just as a person who has completed the parivāsa period or a person who has practiced the mānatta remains evident even after the days of parivāsa and mānatta are finished, similarly, some teachers say that even when the periods for determination are finished, this stated period is still with determination. The decision of the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariya), however, is: "Withdraw the determination on the full moon day of Kattika and perform assignment on the first waning day." For it is stated in the Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā: "A monk who wears a rainy-season robe that was assigned on the first waning day, which is the end of the Kattika full moon day, incurs an offense in winter." In the Kurundī, however, it is stated: "Because of not withdrawing the determination on the Kattika full moon day, he incurs an offense in winter." That statement is also well-said. For it is stated: "To determine for four months, and to assign after that." Among those views, the method of the Kurundī should be regarded as the essence because it was stated later; the view of the earlier teachers should not be taken. A monk who wears it in summer also incurs an offense if it exceeds half a month. Here, however, it is stated, "he incurs an offense in winter, not in summer," so this is clearly the meaning of the Kurundī statement.

"If one does not withdraw the determination on the Kattika full moon day and does not assign on that same day, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense on the final first waning day due to the reason of not withdrawing; however, he does not incur an offense due to the reason of not assigning, because there is the possibility of a ten-day grace period (dasāhaparihāra)." Some teachers state this as the reason. If that were so, it would mean that determination is lost as soon as winter arrives, and that is inappropriate. For it is stated: "Determination is lost through these nine reasons: giving to another... etc... becoming holed"; it is not stated, "due to the expiration of the determination period (adhiṭṭhānakkhettātikkamena)." Should it be said that it is not mentioned because it is not common (applying only to the rainy-season robe)? It should not be said so, because it would lead to the conclusion that "due to becoming holed" should also not be said. In fact, the loss of determination due to becoming holed is stated in all commentaries only regarding the triple robe (ticīvara).

Therefore, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense due to not withdrawing the determination on the first day of winter, but not due to failing to assign after having withdrawn. From the words "to assign," it is understood that determination is not lost even if that determination period has passed. The intention is that he does not incur an offense in winter due to not assigning on the first waning day, which is the end of the Kattika full moon day. The reason is that, due to not withdrawing that robe, the dukkaṭa offense is incurred at the very moment of dawn on the first day of winter; thus it is said, "without withdrawing on the Kattika full moon day." As for the robe that has been withdrawn, in winter...
228:
One receives a ten-day allowance. It is stated (in the Pārājika Commentary), "If ten days are insufficient, one should not let the robe-time pass." This statement applies if the robe arises during the robe-season, not outside of it. A robe managed in such a way, even if not yet de-determined (paccuddhaṭa), does not incur a Nissaggiya offense; however, one should not wear (or store) that robe. Therefore, it is established that de-determination and assignment (vikappanā) must be performed on the full moon day of Kattika.

In this context, it should be understood that a person who performs vikappanā on an extra robe on the tenth day is considered to have kept it for a maximum of ten days and to have performed vikappanā within those ten days. Similarly, by performing vikappanā on the full moon day of Kattika, it is as if the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for the four months of the rainy season has been made, and thereafter, vikappanā is performed only during the period when no offense is incurred. By this much, it is shown that determination can exist during the period for vikappanā, and vikappanā can exist during the period for determination. Otherwise, in the dyads (duka), two types of dyads would have to be stated: "An offense is incurred through determination; an offense is incurred through non-determination. An offense is incurred through vikappanā; an offense is incurred through non-vikappanā."

Among those two dyads, the first clause of the first dyad is possible. This is because a Dukkaṭa offense regarding Vinaya transgression is incurred by determining a rainy season robe, etc., during the period when vikappanā should be performed. In this way, the second clause regarding the second Dukkaṭa has also been stated. There is no such thing as an offense being incurred through non-determination. Because no offense is incurred within ten days and because vikappanā, etc., are possible, there is also no such thing as an offense being incurred through vikappanā. This is because vikappanā is not prohibited in all cases. Therefore, those dyads were not mentioned as "not obtainable."

Here, the objector says: The Dukkaṭa offense shown based on the evidence of the statement "An offense is incurred in the winter" is appropriate only for a monk who intentionally does not de-determine. If it is due to lack of mindfulness, there is no offense. For a monk who intentionally does not perform vikappanā on a robe already de-determined on the full moon day of Kattika, a Nissaggiya offense is incurred on the following day along with a Dukkaṭa. If one fails to perform vikappanā due to lack of mindfulness, only a Nissaggiya offense is incurred according to this first regulation.

In the Mātikā Commentary (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī), it is said: "The rainy season robe loses its determination through the passing of the four months of the rainy season, and the itch-covering cloth (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi) loses its determination through the recovery from the illness; therefore, one should perform vikappanā on those robes after that period." This statement contradicts what was said before. Not only this statement, but also the commentary's words "One should de-determine and perform vikappanā after that period" are contradictory. This is because "after that period" refers to the winter season, and if one were to de-determine in the winter, the statement "the rainy season robe (loses its determination) through the passing of the four months of the rainy season" would no longer be appropriate. This is because if there is no longer a determination, there is no need to de-determine. Only a non-contradictory meaning should be desired. Therefore, if it is argued that the view "de-determination is merely a custom (vatta)" is possible here as well, it must be said that it is not possible. This is because it contradicts the words in the Kurundī Commentary. In that Kurundī Commentary, de-determination is stated to be performed on the full moon day of Kattika.
229:
Therefore, because it is a day of the rainy season, the rainy season robe, which is still under determination, should be de-determined; thus, de-determination is not merely a custom. Therefore, when saying "after that," it should be understood as up to the full moon of Kattika. This method of performing vikappanā, as well as the statement "through the passing of the rainy season months or through the recovery from illness," should be understood as being stated because de-determination must definitely be performed. In this way, it agrees with the absence of that statement in the Samantapāsādikā commentary for this training rule. Otherwise, that statement would have to be made here as well; thus, only the aforementioned procedure is possible here. Although it is possible, it is stated for the sake of easy understanding for the people of the world who find it difficult to understand.

Because that rainy season robe loses its determination through the passing of the rainy season, and it is shown that a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to non-de-determination at the first dawn of the winter season, one should de-determine and perform vikappanā only on the full moon day of Kattika. If vikappanā is not performed, it must be said that "a Nissaggiya offense is indeed incurred." Not being satisfied with just this much, the decision should be sought further. In this regard, there is this:

"In this way, one who wishes to know the existence or non-existence of the Vinaya Pāḷi,
Whether it is divided or undivided, and the logical consistency of its meaning,
Should seek out those who are experts in that meaning
In order to understand the Vinaya Piṭaka."

When it is said, "Take it for yourself," even without the words "I take it for myself," it is well-given. If the other person accepts it with approval, it is well-received by him. If he does not accept it, although it was well-given by the donor, that object belongs to no one. Similarly, when one says, "I take it for myself," if the owner accepts it with approval, it is well-received even without the words "Take it." If he does not approve, that object remains the owner's. If one takes it for the sake of a Vinaya act, it is not allowable. It should be understood that if one takes it not only for one's own benefit but gives it back to that person, it is allowable.

Similarly, if one relinquishes an object to another without lingering concern and then uses what that person gives back, or uses it out of intimacy with that person, it is allowable. Regarding such usage, some teachers say it is not allowable by the power of the Vinaya act. Those same teachers say regarding the phrase "makes a large robe small": "In the case of the three robes (ticīvara), one makes it by cutting it without exceeding one span in length; the same applies to the remaining robes." In such matters, one should well-note the path of the discourse of the ancient teachers by serving the lineage of teachers, and in coordination with the words of those ancient teachers, being mindful and endowed with clear comprehension, one should speak without confusing the minds of the listeners. This is our request.

## The Explanation of the First Kathina Training Rule is finished.
230:
## 2. Udositasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

(Those monks) departed for a tour of the countryside with only their inner and upper robes (*santaruttarena*). Why did they depart so? Although it was initially stated, "Monks, one should not enter a village with only the inner and upper robes; for one who enters, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," later it was stated, "Monks, there are these five reasons for laying aside the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), or the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*): being ill, a sign of rain or wind, desiring to go to the other side of a river, having a monastery with a secured door (*aggaḷagutti*), or having the Kathina robes spread."

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) of that Pali text, it is also stated: "Among these five, only the secured door is the standard. It is allowable to go outside only after leaving (the robe) in a secured monastery; it is not allowable in an unsecured monastery." Therefore, even if the Kathina has not been spread, it should be understood that they departed for the countryside tour after gaining the allowance to enter a village with only their inner and upper robes, having said, "Keep those monks in a monastery with a secured door," and entrusting the robes into the hands of compatible monks.

"Designation for non-separation" (*avippavāsa-sammuti*) means a designation for the purpose of not being separated, or giving a designation so that there is no offense caused by separation (*vippavāsa*). From the time of receiving that designation, it is allowable. For how long is it allowable? It is allowable for a month or more, as long as there is effort to travel. Therefore, it is said, "One who gives up the responsibility should revoke (the designation)." Furthermore, there is no need for another act of giving the designation; if twelve years pass and another illness occurs, it remains valid. It should also be understood that, like the act of higher ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*), a single designation is valid for life.

Phrases such as "It is also made" (*kataṃ vā hoti*) should not be mentioned in this training rule. Why? Because even if the obstacle of making (*karaṇa-palibodha*) is cut off, it is impossible for an offense to occur due to separation since the robe has not yet been assigned (*anadhiṭṭhita*). Therefore, if it is asked, "Should it only be said: 'When the robe is finished means the monk's robe is assigned'?"—No, because it depends on that (making). Assignment depends on the completion of the obstacle of making. Therefore, it is said, "It is made," and so on. In that word-analysis (*padabhājanī*), the word "*kataṃ*" (made) is just as previously stated.

477-8. In this context of "for the purpose of defining the characteristic of non-separation," the characteristic of non-separation is defined by the words, "Having left the robe inside the village, one should stay inside the village," and so on. The characteristic of separation should be understood by the reverse method. In the words "A village has a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*)," etc., except for a caravan, the foot of a tree, and the open air, the status of being a single precinct or multiple precincts in other places should be understood by way of having or not having an enclosure. Because...
231:
A caravan (*sattha*) is of two types: halted (*niviṭṭha*) and not yet halted (*aniviṭṭha*). Among them, a caravan not yet halted, whether belonging to a single family or various families, is always without an enclosure. A halted caravan may or may not have an enclosure. Therefore, in that case, it is taught by way of internal distance (*abbhantara*) rather than by showing an enclosure. The same applies to the open air (*abbhokāsa*). At the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūla*), it is defined by way of the shadow. Otherwise, because it is not shown in the *Vibhaṅga*, there might be a contradiction with the summary (*uddesa*) such as "A caravan is a single precinct or multiple precincts." Therefore, seven *abbhantaras* in front and behind the caravan, and one *abbhantara* on each side, is called a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*). Beyond that is multiple precincts (*nānūpacāra*). Similarly, at the foot of a tree, the area where the shadow falls at noon is a single precinct. The rest is multiple precincts. Why? Because at the foot of a tree, an enclosure is not the standard; the shadow alone is the standard. The definition of the open air is already stated in the Pali.

It is written: "Caravans etc. are a single precinct by way of belonging to a single family." Therefore, the definition stated for a house or a storehouse (*udosita*) also applies to a platform (*aṭṭa*) etc., and is thus summarized. Furthermore, in fields, threshing floors, gardens, and monasteries, the term "enclosed or unenclosed" is extracted again because the authority of the caravan's word-analysis is finished. The phrase "various rooms" etc. is not extracted for fields, threshing floors, and gardens because it is impossible there. Although possible in a monastery, it is not extracted because it was already defined there.

An owner is called "*kula*" (family). Therefore, by the words "of a single family or various families," the common or uncommon nature of the fourteen places for depositing robes, such as villages, is shown. It is not mentioned for the open air because it is impossible. The reason is that in these places for depositing robes, whether belonging to one family or various families, there is no special protection in unenclosed villages etc., but there is in enclosed ones. Therefore, the use of "single/various families" (*eka-nānā-kula*) and "single/multiple precincts" (*eka-nānūpacāra*) is meaningful. Even so, there is this distinction: in a caravan and at the foot of a tree, the distinction is only by the difference of family, not by the difference of precinct. In the open air, there is a distinction by the difference of precinct, but that distinction is not shown in the Pali. Because of the words "having exceeded that measure," they say there is no fault within the measure of two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyya-ratana*) even in the sky.

"*Sabhā*" (hall) is feminine. "*Sabhāyaṃ*" is neuter. Therefore, it is said "by the method of clarifying the gender." To show the neuter gender, "*sabhāyaṃ*" is indicated by way of the nominative case (*paccatta*). Because of its association with that, "*dvāramūlaṃ*" (the foot of the door) is also shown in the neuter. Because one is not at the place where the robe is deposited, the reach of a hand (*hatthapāsa*) of the street does not protect. One must stay in the house where the robe is deposited. One should stay in the hall or at the foot of the door...
232:
It is said: "One should not be separated from the hand-reach (hatthapāsa)." If it is argued that it is impossible to know because it is specified that "one must let the dawn rise only within the hand-reach," it is also impossible to know within a village, for it is stated for such reasons. Therefore, it is said: "Reason (yutti) alone is the standard (pamāṇa)." This meaning is also explained in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Again, in a small village, it is explained by way of the common village gate. It is said: "If that village has two gates, one should stay wherever one wishes, whether in the middle of a house or in the middle of a meeting hall."

480-1. Those dwellings and so forth which do not fall under the category of "village" are intended here. In an open space, even if there is no suspicion, if a robe is kept beyond seven abbhantaras (sattabbhantara), it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya). In this case, being within a boundary (sīmā) does not protect [from the offense], but being in a caravan (sattha) does. Since it is said, "The vicinity of a river (nadīparihāra) is also obtained," it is established that the vicinity is obtained in a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepasīmā). If a nearby monastery is within the same boundary, the robe does not become nissaggiya.

Now—
"A cut robe, the ascetic practice of the triple robe, going with only the inner and upper robes in a place designated as dangerous;
There is no offense for a monk without a robe, because it is accomplished through revocation (paccuddhara) and so forth."
This is the miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) method.

In that statement, this is the decision preceded by an objection: Some teachers, because of the words "a double-layered saṅghāṭi," say, "A single-layered saṅghāṭi should not be determined; if it is determined, it is not valid," and they give only a double-layered saṅghāṭi to candidates for ordination and ordain them. Those teachers should be informed by this scriptural fragment. Indeed, the Blessed One first allowed "a cut saṅghāṭi, a cut uttarāsaṅga, and a cut antaravāsaka." Then, in the case where "when the triple robe was being made for a certain monk, all the cut pieces were not enough; two cut pieces and one uncut piece were not enough; two uncut pieces and one cut piece were not enough," He allowed: "Monks, I allow an extra piece (anvādika) to be added." Therefore, it is established that even a single-layered saṅghāṭi is allowable. How could there be a double layer for a robe that is not enough even when cut? In the Commentary, it is also said: "To add an extra piece means to give an additional cloth (āgantukapatta). This should be added when it is not enough. If it is enough, the additional cloth is not allowable; it must be cut." In the case of a Kaṭhina robe, because it has a specific characteristic and because there is no statement saying "a cut double-layered robe is not enough," it should be concluded here that only a cut robe is allowable.
233:
Here, "ascetic practice" (dhuṭaṅga) means that since there is no specific triple-robe practice for novices (sāmaṇera), one who possesses the triple-robe practice does so with only three robes. If it is said, "Since there is no formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for those novices, let it be said 'only with determined robes,'" that should not be said. Why? Because it does not lead to a contradiction with the breaking of the ascetic practice.

Indeed, the ascetic practice is broken only by accepting a fourth robe. It is not broken by being separated from the triple robe. It is not broken by accepting an extra robe, nor by wearing an extra robe. Since the Blessed One allowed nine robes by way of determination only for monks, and spoke by way of the type of cloth, it is not so for novices. Therefore, since there is no rule (niyama) of Vinaya procedures for robes for those novices, He did not allow that triple-robe practice for them, just as for laypeople. Therefore, since it is not mentioned in the procedure for undertaking that ascetic practice, a final decision should be reached here.

"Designated as dangerous" (sāsaṅkasammata) means that in the Kankhāvitaraṇī, under the Sāsaṅka training rule, the factors are not stated separately. It is said, "The rest in this training rule should be understood according to the method stated in the second training rule of the Robe Chapter." However, it is not stated so. In that second Kaṭhina training rule, being separated for a night is the fourth factor. In this sāsaṅkasammata training rule, however, being separated for six nights is the factor. This is the distinction between these two training rules. Therefore, because of the similarity of factors and the similarity of designation (sammuti), they call this training rule the Sāsaṅka training rule. This training rule is without remainder (nippadesa), while that training rule is with remainder (sappadesa) because it has a limit of one month.

In that sāsaṅkasammata training rule, there is no offense for a monk who, even outside a village, enters a village boundary, stays, and then departs. In this Kaṭhina training rule, it is not so. Here, an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya) occurs immediately upon the rising of the dawn. In that sāsaṅkasammata training rule, however, the nissaggiya occurs at the rising of the dawn on the seventh day. This is the distinction between these two training rules. The factors are not stated because they are established by the reversal of the factors for laying down a robe and by the method stated here. Even if those factors are not stated, the fourth factor should be specified, but it was not specified. Why? Because by forfeiting according to the sequence of forfeiture stated in this Kaṭhina training rule and confessing the offense, it is for the purpose of showing the release from the offense that has arisen in that sāsaṅkasammata training rule.

Even if one is separated for a whole year, it is only called being separated for one night; what need is there to mention being separated for six nights? Even so, if the factors stated in that sāsaṅkasammata training rule are fulfilled, one should forfeit according to the method stated there. If one forfeits in winter or summer, my teacher says that the fourth factor was not specified to make it known that it is also proper to forfeit by the method stated here. Even a robe that has exceeded one month is forfeited by saying "it has exceeded ten days." Some teachers say it has exceeded one month by saying "it has exceeded ten days" even if it is less than a month by two [days]. Nevertheless, if it is a robe in expectation (paccāsācīvara), the nissaggiya robe should be forfeited by saying "it has exceeded ten days," while the original robe should be forfeited by saying "it has exceeded one month."
234:
In the words 'santaruttara', 'saṅghāṭi', or 'cīvara', does it mean only the three robes (ticīvara) or other robes as well? In this matter, if only the three robes were prohibited, it would contradict the rules regarding the seizing, cutting, washing, or requesting of robes by way of inclusion. If it means other robes as well, it would contradict the words 'when the robe is finished' and so on. If there is such a contradiction, I shall provide the answer: it should not be understood as a fixed rule, but should be taken according to the circumstances.

Indeed, in passages such as 'having left the robes behind, they wander the countryside with only the inner and upper robes (santaruttara)', it refers only to the three robes. However, in passages such as 'Monks, one should not enter a village with only the inner and upper robes; one should take at least one more robe beyond that', it refers to any robe. Similarly, in passages such as 'they give the saṅghāṭis after folding them', 'one gives the inner robe (nivāsana)', 'one gives the saṅghāṭi', 'friend, take this saṅghāṭi', 'give me the cloth', it refers to any robe at all.

It has been said: 'Every robe is called a saṅghāṭi because of the sense of being folded (saṅghaṭita)'. Likewise, some teachers say that in the phrase 'when the robe is finished', it also refers to any robe. Since as many robes as desired are permitted during the robe-season (cīvarakāla), if all those robes were being made, when would they ever be finished? Therefore, some say it refers only to the three robes. When it is said that there is no offense for being without a robe because of the accomplishment of relinquishing (paccuddhara) and so on, what does it mean? Some say that because of the danger of the Udosite Sikkhāpada becoming useless, an offense is incurred for the three robes when one is separated from them. In this regard, it is said: there is no offense because of the accomplishment of relinquishing and so on. For it is said: 'There is no offense if one relinquishes or gives it away before dawn'. Otherwise, for one who relinquishes or gives it away before dawn, an offense is incurred according to the stated method as long as another person does not formally determine (adhiṭṭhāti) it. In another way, regarding separation within seven abbhantaras, it should be understood literally: if there is separation, it is by way of separation; if there is no separation, it is by way of non-separation.

## The Explanation of the Udosite Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Third Kathina Sikkhāpada

'It is not enough' means it does not reach the minimum measurement; therefore, the minimum measurement of the three robes, such as five fist-lengths, is mentioned. 'Expectation for a robe' is called cīvarapaccāsā. By this, it is shown: whether that robe is obtained later or not, as long as that expectation is not cut off, the Buddha allows this original robe to be kept. In the term 'cīvarapaccāsā', the ablative case is used in the sense of a limit, or the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative.
235:
499-500. In the passage beginning with "When the robe is finished... the expectation of a robe is cut off," if one of the three robes has been made and there is still an expected robe remaining, that robe must be looked after. When the kathina has been removed because the robe-impediment (cīvara-palibodha) is cut off, or during the winter season (hemanta), if an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) arises, it should be made quickly. If the robes are complete, one does not look after the expectation; even if they are not complete, if there is no expectation, one does not look after it. Because of the statement "a robe that arises during the eleven months when the kathina is not spread," the month of Kattikā is the proper time (samaya) for making robes, whether the kathina is spread or not. If the kathina is spread, the winter season is sometimes called the proper time (samaya); if the kathina is not spread, it is sometimes called the improper time (asamaya). Beyond that, it should be known as definitely the improper time.

The phrase "given specifically [to someone]" (ādissa dinnaṃ), although not found in this training rule, is mentioned in the second Nissaggiya of the Bhikkhunīs by way of extracting the meaning. The rest is like the out-of-season robe. In that Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, if an out-of-season robe is given specifically to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha with the words "Let the arriving bhikkhunīs distribute it," and a bhikkhunī distributes it after determining it as a "seasonable robe" (kālacīvara), she incurs an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya). However, just as in that Vibhaṅga it is said by way of extracting the meaning that "an out-of-season robe means a robe that arises during the eleven months when the kathina is not spread, or during the seven months when the kathina is spread," this training rule should be understood in the same way.

If this is so, for what purpose is the statement "a robe given to a certain individual with the words 'I give this to you, venerable sir'" made? If it is asked, "Is it not because the robe given specifically to that person is not to be distributed?" It is mentioned because of the similarity of being undistributable. Just as a robe given specifically to the Saṅgha becomes an out-of-season robe because it cannot be distributed by monks who have spread the kathina, so too should the meaning be understood that a robe given to an individual cannot be distributed by other monks who have spread the kathina.

Even so, someone might think, "A robe given specifically to an individual also receives protection for only ten days." That person's thought is merely a doubt. This is because in the first Kathina training rule, the Pali "When the robe is finished, when the kathina is removed for the monk" would be purposeless. If it is argued that since it is known that even if the kathina is not removed, it should be kept for only ten days, this statement might be intended only for robes given without specifying an individual. Even so, a robe given without specification also receives protection for only ten days for monks who have not spread the kathina in the month of Kattikā, because it is said, "When the robe is finished, when the kathina is removed for the monk." If one says, "That is true," it contradicts the statement "a robe that arises during the eleven months when the kathina is not spread." Therefore, a conclusion should be reached in this matter only according to the method already mentioned.

It is said in another Gaṇṭhipada: "In the first training rule, all robes, by virtue of being 'robes as needed' (yāvadattha-cīvara), do not result in an offense even if ten days are exceeded within the kathina month, because protection is given." Just as an out-of-season robe given without specification within the kathina month receives only the protection of an out-of-season robe, so it is also in the time outside the kathina month. For that reason, although the training rule beginning with "When the robe is finished, when the kathina is removed for the monk, if a robe should arise..." is completed, it is called "if an out-of-season robe should arise" because the month of Kattikā is permitted for monks who have not spread the kathina. If this were the meaning, the teaching "an out-of-season robe means a robe that arises during the eleven months when the kathina is not spread" would not be possible. In fact, because of such a statement, just as monks who have spread the kathina do not incur an offense of forfeiture for exceeding ten days, it means that for monks who have not spread the kathina, all robes in the month of Kattikā do not result in an offense of forfeiture for exceeding ten days.
236:
It should be understood that an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) given specifically to an individual within the kaṭhina month receives the same protection as a season robe (kālacīvara), and similarly in other months. Therefore, although the matter is settled by the training rule beginning with 'When the robe is finished, when the kaṭhina is removed, if a robe should arise for a monk...', the Buddha, in allowing the late month of Kattika for those who have not spread the kaṭhina, said 'if an out-of-season robe should arise'. If this were not said, a robe arising during the eleven months when the kaṭhina is not spread could not be called an 'out-of-season robe'. Because of this statement, it should be understood that for those who have not spread the kaṭhina, just as for those who have, a nissaggiya offense does not occur if ten days are exceeded in the late month of Kattika for all robes. 

Furthermore, it is said: My allowance in the first kaṭhina training rule that 'an extra robe may be kept for at most ten days' refers only to robes arising outside the kaṭhina month, not within it. How? By the supplementary regulation 'when the robe is finished, when the kaṭhina is removed', the offense that would be incurred by exceeding the ten-day protection of an extra robe is prevented within the kaṭhina period; and to prevent the offense that would be incurred by exceeding ten days for robes arising after that period, it was said 'if an out-of-season robe should arise'. By that statement, 'this robe given specifically to an individual even during the kaṭhina period is called an out-of-season robe', it is shown that it does not receive the ten-day protection after the removal of the kaṭhina. The possibility of receiving another five days after the removal of the kaṭhina along with those days is also barred because the time of arising of an out-of-season robe is specified by the words 'When the robe is finished, when the kaṭhina is removed, if an out-of-season robe should arise for a monk... it should be made up quickly' (akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyya... khippameva kāretabbaṃ). By both [rules], it is established that a robe arising within the kaṭhina period does not receive even a single day of protection after the removal of the kaṭhina. Thus say other teachers. 

Again, it is said: Teachers might say this. In the phrase 'When the robe is finished, when the kaṭhina is removed, if an out-of-season robe should arise for a monk', the Buddha, by saying 'When the robe is finished, when the kaṭhina is removed', makes it known that within this interval, the three types of out-of-season robes do not arise. Why then are they detailed in the word-for-word commentary (padabhājana)? It is said: This training rule is stated with reference to the determination (adhiṭṭhāna). However, by allowing ten days in the first training rule, and if that is insufficient but there is hope [for more], by extending that same [period] and allowing a month, He also shows this special meaning of the out-of-season robe.
237:
It is also shown that it should be distributed by the monk who is present. That robe is mentioned by extending it with this training rule: 'It should be accepted by a monk who so desires'; therefore, all three are detailed in the word-for-word commentary (padabhājana). 

The phrase 'it should be made up quickly' (khippameva kāretabbaṃ) means 'it should be made up within ten days'; this is said to show the characteristic of the previous training rule regarding the sufficiency [of the cloth]. Therefore, instead of saying 'thus quickly' or 'speedily', it says 'ten days'. Whether this applies to one with a spread kaṭhina, or what if the kaṭhina is not spread? It is said that it shows the rejection for one whose kaṭhina is not spread; the questioner, not seeing the special benefit, merely comes to exhaustion. 

Regarding 'it is nissaggiya at the rise of dawn on the thirty-first day', even if joined with a large robe held with hope, if it follows the nature of the original robe and the minimum size is possible, it is nissaggiya. If not possible, it is not. If joined again, it is. If joined with another [type of] cloth, it is not. A cut piece becomes a different object. Some teachers say that a robe joined after exceeding the previous limit receives a new limit; this should be accepted after careful investigation. 

In another gaṇṭhipada (glossary), regarding 'this out-of-season robe is given specifically for the Saṅgha', there is no offense in a robe given to the Saṅgha. As in 'secrecy for the ear' (sotassa raho) etc., it is stated by extracting the word. If it is asked whether it refers to the gain of that Saṅgha? Since it is established by the phrase 'it may arise from the Saṅgha', it is redundant. There is also a reading: 'The Saṅgha will receive robes, or the group (gaṇa)...' etc. I have written everything in the gaṇṭhipada for the sake of proficiency; it should be spoken after thorough consideration. 

## The Explanation of the Third Kaṭhina Training Rule is Finished. 

## 4. Explanation of the Purāṇacīvara Training Rule 

503-505. Bhattavissagga means the arrangement of a meal. Ancient teachers say it is the classification of the arrangement of a meal. There, 'nāma tvaṃ' means: 'While you have such a duty performed, why do you have [a robe] washed in such an improper gift?' Or it means 'such a person as you'. 'Ordained by both Saṅghas' (ubhatosaṅghe upasampannā) is said because ordination in the presence of monks was rejected [for her], and for fear of following such rejection. In the context of 'old robe' (purāṇacīvara), it is said 'even if worn once, even if draped once' only to show the state of being old. Therefore, there is no room for the statement 'a robe means one of the six kinds of robes, at least of a size fit for formal assignment (vikappana)'.
238:
Some teachers say, "Na jāto" (Not born). Since the smallest robe suitable for assignment (vikappanūpaga-pacchima) is not intended here, but only the robe suitable for wearing as an undergarment or upper robe is intended, for that very reason, a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) is stated for sitting mats and bedspreads. Therefore, some teachers say [the smallest robe, etc.] is not mentioned. Because the type of cloth (jāti-pamāṇa) is not specified, for a monk who has any old cloth washed, it is a nissaggiya (forfeiture) offense. For that very reason, it is said, "If one has other requisites washed, excluding the robe, there is no offense (anāpatti)." If one has a bag smeared with impurity and used [by a nun] washed, it is a nissaggiya offense because it is coarse and unsuitable. For that very reason, some teachers say in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī that the limitation of the robe is not mentioned here; one should investigate and accept what is most appropriate.

It is said, "Only a robe that is allowable, having been dyed and marked with a kappabindu, is suitable to be worn as an undergarment or an upper robe; other robes are not suitable." By this statement, the Majjhimattheravāda (The Middle Elder Tradition) is supported; it is not unsupported. My opinion is that the words "having been dyed," etc., are stated to show the Vinaya procedure. Just as there are three sets of four (catukka) in the section where one perceives a non-relative as a non-relative, likewise, there are nine sets of four in the sections concerning doubt and relatives.

In this matter, it may be asked: If a nun, having washed once, lays down the burden of washing and then washes again, thinking "It is not yet clean," would there be no offense? Would it be considered washing without being asked for the second time? It is answered: If the monk forbids her, saying, "Washing this much is enough," and the bhikkhunī washes again, it is appropriate to say she washes without being asked. If he does not forbid her, it should be understood as being asked. In the case of a monk's change of gender (liṅga-parivattana), the occurrence of an offense by virtue of a bhikkhunī ordained on one side (ekato-upasampannā) is like that of the Sakyan princesses.

"Ekena vatthunā" means by any first object without distinction. There is a reading, "By virtue of the three sets of four." Because the ordination by the eightfold proclamation (aṭṭhavācikā) in the presence of monks is well-known, it is not mentioned; the Sakyan princesses are mentioned because they are not well-known.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Old Robes is Finished.

## 5. Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

508-510. Regarding the phrase "Apannatte sikkhāpade" (Before the training rule was laid down), it is written here as "Gaṇamhā ohīyana sikkhāpade" (The training rule on falling behind the group). Some teachers say it means before the training rule prohibiting forest-dwelling was laid down; they say, "That statement is not good." "Vihattatāya" means through exhaustion. "Upacāro" refers to an area of twelve cubits. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya and Kurundī that in this matter, when many robes are offered to a Dhamma-teaching monk by the public at night...
239:
...when robes are piled up by way of gifts of faith, if a monk takes them the next day with a pure heart, thinking, "These are gifts of faith from lay followers," there is no fault. If he takes them knowing, "Robes given by bhikkhunīs are also here," there is a fault. That fault occurs due to the state of being unintentional (acittaka-bhāva). It means that even if he knows they were given by bhikkhunīs, he takes one without knowing it is that specific bhikkhunī's robe among many robes. Regarding "resolving on it as a rag-robe (paṃsukūla)," it is allowable for a monk who takes it thinking, "I shall take a rag-robe," without specifically considering, "Could this be a robe given by bhikkhunīs?" The meaning stated in the Kurundī and other commentaries is the same as this. Other teachers say that by the words "acittaka-bhāvena," the wrong path of thinking "it is allowable to take it anyway" is refuted. The Elder Dhamma-siri does not say this; it has been explained in detail that he speaks straightforwardly. It is the scope of that Elder; his intention is: Just as it is said that it is allowable to take even the property of a bhikkhunī that has been set aside with the thought "I will take it as a rag-robe," provided one resolves on it as a rag-robe without specific consideration, likewise, it is allowable for a Dhamma-teaching monk if the robe given by a bhikkhunī is not evident (as being hers). Therefore, it is said that this meaning does not agree with the Mahāpaccariya and Kurundī because it is not stated by way of acittaka-bhāva. The prohibition, however, applies only to taking with specific consideration. Otherwise, the preceding and following statements would contradict each other. That statement is not appropriate because it is not the same as a rag-robe. A robe placed by bhikkhunīs on a rubbish heap as a rag-robe does not remain as that bhikkhunī's property. A rag-robe is ownerless and common to all; others also have the right to take it. Even if one knows beforehand, "This is a bhikkhunī's robe," a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika) has the right to take it, because at that time it is no longer her property. Although the phrase "resolving on it as a rag-robe" is stated to show the sequence of effacement (sallikhana), the Tathāgata, while giving meat, used an allowable object through effacement and spoke of the nissaggiya robe. The meaning is: "If a monk eats meat, how should he point out that meat?"

If it is asked: How is a rag-robe allowable due to being unintentional? It is allowable because she did not give it to that monk, and the monk did not take it from that bhikkhunī's hand. Even if it is an ownerless rag-robe, if one takes it from the hand of another bhikkhunī, it is not allowable because it meets the characteristic stated as "One should [not] accept a robe from the hand of a non-relative bhikkhunī." Some teachers say that if one takes the property of a non-relative bhikkhunī from the hand of a relative, it is allowable. Just as there is no offense for a monk who accepts from the hands of a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), etc., the factor is also stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī as "taking from the hand of a non-relative." Likewise,
240:
Some teachers state that there is no offense for a monk who takes the property of a relative from the hands of a Sikkhamānā, a Sāmaṇerī, an Upāsaka, an Upāsikā, a Bhikkhu, or a Sāmaṇera, or even from the hands of a non-relative Bhikkhunī, because it does not meet the aforementioned characteristics. For this very reason, it is stated (in the Pārājika) that 'If he receives a robe from the hand [of a nun], except in exchange, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),' without specifying 'receives a robe from a one-sidedly ordained nun (ekato-upasampannā).' Therefore, they say that even if it is the property of a non-relative, there is a dukkaṭa offense for a monk who receives it from the hand of a one-sidedly ordained nun. Both of these views should not be taken as the essence; rather, the underlying reason must be investigated.

Regarding the phrase 'What need is there to mention bowl-bags and so forth?' it refers to many layers of cloth that are not to be formally determined (anadhiṭṭhatabba). For this reason, it is stated in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: 'In the case of requisites that are not to be formally determined, such as bowl-bags and so forth.' Alternatively, even in the case of items suitable for formal determination, there is no offense because they are requisites, similar to a bolster-cover (bhisi-chavi). Is a cloth water-filter not a requisite? It is. However, they say it is not allowable because that water-filter has the shape of a robe, such as an inner cloth. Therefore, in this context, 'robe' refers to the smallest cloth that is suitable for formal assignment (vikappanā) and serves the purpose of a robe like an inner cloth. In the immediately preceding training rule, the decision was made regarding only the inner cloth and the outer robe.

If this is the case, should it not be stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī that there is a fourth factor, namely 'not being a requisite,' instead of mentioning only the three factors: being the smallest size suitable for vikappanā, not being an exchange, and receiving from the hand of a non-relative? It should not be stated. This is because in this training rule, requisites such as bowl-bags are designated as 'non-robes.' In the first Kathina and so forth, suitability for vikappanā is the standard, but in this training rule, suitability for bodily use is the standard. Since it is stated, 'anything such as a bowl-bag,' after extracting 'other requisites,' it is allowable to take bowl-bags and so forth that are suitable for vikappanā. In the place where it is stated 'even a cloth water-filter,' because it is said 'the smallest cloth suitable for vikappanā is called a robe,' a cloth water-filter is indeed a robe and not a requisite. Some say that the concluding statement 'What need is there to mention...' is also evidence. It is an 'acittaka' offense (independent of intention) due to ignorance of the regulation, not due to ignorance of the object. It is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: 'It is an acittaka offense due to not knowing that it is the property of a non-relative Bhikkhunī and due to not knowing that it is a robe.'

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving Robes is Finished.
241:
## 6. Aññātakaviññatti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

The word 'parikkhārānaṃ' is a genitive case (sāmivacana) used in the sense of the accusative (dutiyā). The word 'ekasāṭakaṃ' is a neuter noun expressing a state. By the statement 'A non-relative, foolish man,' it is shown that even if one is invited (pavārita), if they are unwilling to give, they stand in the position of a non-relative or one who has not invited. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement 'There is no offense for those who are invited' (anāpatti pavāritānaṃ).

One should not yet request [a new robe] nor break [branches] because one still possesses one's own robes that have not been snatched away, and because there is still hope of recovering those robes. For how long does that hope protect? Some teachers say: as far as the distance between one village and another, or up to half a league (yojana). Some say: as long as one is within the vicinity (upacāra) of sight and hearing. Some say: as long as others do not see [the robes]. Some say: until the hope is completely cut off. Others say: until the time limit for searching, breaking, and preparing branches and leaves. All these views are appropriate according to the circumstances. How is this known? It is known from the commentary statement: 'If none of these aforementioned items, from lay clothes to bolster-covers, are obtained, he should come covered with grass or leaves.'

'Should not yet be given to the elders' means they should not yet be given of one's own accord. Only when the elders say, 'Give, friend,' should they be given. In this case, junior monks whose robes have been snatched away also stand in that position; they should break branches and leaves, and not otherwise. For it is said, 'By whomever [the robes] have been snatched away.' However, the Teacher (Ācariya) says: 'They are allowed to give even of their own accord.' Thus, it is stated in the commentary: 'In the case of robes snatched away from teachers, preceptors, and so forth, a robe given by oneself after covering them with grass and leaves is also fit to be included.' If it were the case that they should be given only when the teachers say 'Bring it, friend' and not when they do not say so, the second point in the reason 'snatched away by someone' would have no distinction. Then why is it said 'Should not yet be given to the elders'? As long as one is breaking branches and leaves for the sake of the elders, they should not be given. After that, having personally worn those branches and leaves intended for the elders, they should be given of one's own accord even without the elders' command. Because the Blessed One himself has allowed it, there is no Pācittiya offense for destroying vegetation (bhūtagāma-pātavyatā). If it is asked whether the phrase 'with grass or leaves' refers only to allowable (kappiya) things, the answer is no; if those are not obtained... (pe)...
242:
It is because it contradicts the word "dukkaṭassa." Here, one might ask: "If, out of fear of a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing), one must transgress an object of pācittiya (expiation), and if that pācittiya object is not available, should one also transgress a thullaccaya (grave offense) object belonging to the Saṅgha? And if that thullaccaya object is not available, should one even transgress a pārājika (defeat) object?" No, because a pārājika is a lokavajja (a worldly fault/reproachable by the world). Furthermore, not all bhūtagāma (vegetation) are solely objects of pācittiya. Within that bhūtagāma, there are also objects of dukkaṭa and objects of anāpatti (no offense). Therefore, it should be understood that these grasses or leaves, etc., are objects of anāpatti at the time of that robbery.

By what measure is a monk considered one whose robes have been snatched away or one whose robes are lost? Some teachers say he is so by the measure of being naked. Some teachers say that for a monk who requests robes starting from the minimum robe suitable for vikappanā (legal assignment), an offense is committed. Some say it is due to the absence of robes suitable for wearing and covering. Some say it is due to the absence of the three robes. Some say it is due to the absence of the measure of the inner robe (antaravāsaka) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga).

Only this last view is appropriate. This is because of the statement: "One should accept that robe to the extent of the inner and upper robes." Therefore, for a monk who, while possessing the inner and upper robes, requests the minimum robe suitable for vikappanā, a nissaggiya (forfeiture) offense is committed upon obtaining it. If that is so, one might ask: "Should there not be a training rule stating 'if one requests and obtains it, it is a nissaggiya'?" That should not be said. This is because that meaning is accomplished by the verb "viññāpeyya" (should request) itself, and because roots have various meanings.

What is meant? Just as when it is said, "He performed (abhiviññāpesi) the act of sexual intercourse three times," it means "he engaged in it," so too here, when it is said, "he should request (viññāpeyya) a robe," it means he should bring it about or obtain it through requesting.

"Tena nivattho" means he is clothed in that robe. When he uses only that robe because no other is available, it wears out; it is not wearing out through a mere pretext. "Attanā" (by oneself) is suitable to be said for the act of hiring. Therefore, wearing out while using it in a proper manner, rather than an improper manner, is called "pari-bhoga-jiṇṇa" (worn out through use). The meaning is that giving to monks of similar nature when their robes have been snatched away also falls under proper use. It is said: "The Elder Dhammasiri stated that these two pretexts are the opinions of the teachers who teach the commentaries."

"He does not get to sit or lie down" means he does not get to do so as he pleases. In the phrase "for the sake of another," the words "of relatives or those who have invited" also follow. For whose sake? For the sake of that other person who is a non-relative or uninvited. To show that just as there is a triad of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya) regarding a non-relative, it is the same regarding an uninvited person, it is said: "of relatives or those who have invited." Otherwise, because it is accomplished by the phrase "one who perceives a relative as a relative," the remaining words would not always lead to an offense. Furthermore, in this context, by taking the term "aññātaka" (non-relative), the term "appavārita" (uninvited) is also taken...
243:
By including the appavārita (uninvited), the aññātaka (non-relative) is also included. This is because non-relatives are those who are uninvited. Similarly, by taking the ñātaka (relative), the pavārita (invited) is included, but in some places, it is not. To show this specific meaning—that by taking the pavārita, the ñātaka is not necessarily included—it is said "ñātakānaṃ pavāritānaṃ" (of relatives and those who have invited). Indeed, there is an offense for a monk who accepts a robe from a non-relative Bhikkhunī or an uninvited Bhikkhunī, except in exchange. However, if he takes it out of trust (vissāsa) from a relative Bhikkhunī or an invited Bhikkhunī, there is no offense (anāpatti). Similarly, in the case of washing an old robe, if it is for a relative Bhikkhunī, there is no offense, but if it is for an invited (non-relative) Bhikkhunī, it is only a tika-pācittiya (pācittiya of the triad). While it is allowable to give an old robe to some relative Bhikkhunīs, it is not allowable to give it to those who are invited (non-relatives). It should be understood that the determination of the offense (tikaccheda) occurs only through the mātikā (matrix/heading) and not by any other word. Even in that case, it occurs by only one word and not by the second word, etc.; this is the nature of the Vinaya.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting from Non-relatives is Finished.

## 7. Tatuttari-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Training Rule on More Than That)

522-4. "Paggāhika-sālaṃ vā" refers to a cloth market or a rest house where cloth is sold. People criticize, saying they are spreading out cloth that should be spread out in a rest house by holding it up with their hands. "Ti-cīvarikeneva" means only by a monk who possesses the three robes according to the Vinaya. Such a monk who possesses the three robes, even if he has accessory cloths (parikkhāra-coḷa) that have been determined (adhiṭṭhita), is allowed to request and take up to the measure of the inner and upper robes if all three of his robes are snatched away. Regarding the phrase "aññathāpi" (also in another way), some say: "For a monk who uses the three robes of proper measure by determining them as accessory cloths, if those robes are lost, he is allowed to take many robes, not just the measure of the inner and upper robes." Therefore, they say that such a distinction is only for a monk who possesses the three robes and not for one who possesses accessory cloths. The Teacher (Ācariya), however, says only this much: "aññena" means by a monk with more than the three robes, and "aññathā" means in a way other than the measure of the views stated here. Some say "aññathā" means that if all three are lost, the measure of the inner and upper robes should be taken, and if two or one are lost, the phrase "aññathāpi" is said to show that situation. Since there is no investigation (vicāraṇā) in the glossaries (gaṇṭhipada), one should examine and take them. Normally, he wanders with the inner and upper robes, or he wanders due to the training rule concerning dangerous areas (sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada), or due to such a formal agreement (sammuti), or due to not obtaining the third robe.
244:
"Only the measure is allowable" is stated to show the practice of effacement (sallekha). If one mistakenly takes this meaning and asks whether an offense is committed by a monk who takes more than that measure from relatives and so on? That statement does not agree with the Pali. For the Pali states: "There is no offense for relatives or for those who have given an invitation." Here, "those who have given an invitation" (pavārita) refers to those who invited him even before the time the robes were snatched, not at the time of the snatching. Because it is said, "One should invite beforehand," it should be understood that both the one who invites for the sake of the monk whose robes were snatched and that monk himself are considered as not yet invited. They give only because of the reason of the robes being snatched or lost.

Alternatively, just as a monk who, having caused a thought to arise at a later time, obtains a rainy-season cloth from a place where relatives had invited him, incurs a Nissaggiya offense through that training rule; so too in this training rule regarding snatched robes, even if it is a place where relatives have invited him, it is not allowable (to take more than the measure) due to the reason of the robes being snatched or lost. Therefore, Elder Dhammasiri said, "The statement in the Commentaries 'Only the measure is allowable' is the standard (pamāṇa)." That statement is improper. Why? Because this training rule was laid down for one who requests more than that [measure]. And in that training rule, the Mātikā Pali says, "An unrelated householder or householder's wife." In the Vibhaṅga, the Pali says, "Unrelated means one who is not related from the mother's side... and so on." In the section on 'no offense', the Pali says, "There is no offense for relatives or for those who have given an invitation." Therefore, since it does not agree with the three types of Pali, [the Elder's statement] is indeed improper. Thus, other teachers say that this statement was made solely with reference to effacement (sallekha).

However, in the Commentary on the Kāṇamātā training rule above, it is said, "Since it was prepared for them for the sake of travel provisions and gifts, only the measure is allowable," but it does not say "it does not agree with the Pali." There is no distinction between that training rule and this one. Therefore, the Elder's view appears to me as excellent; yet it should be further investigated.

Since this training rule was laid down only in the case of requesting for the sake of another, the phrase "for the sake of another" is not mentioned here. There is a reading, "The rest is clear in meaning." The reason "for the sake of another" is not mentioned is that it would contradict the origin story (nidāna). Nevertheless, the teachers say it can be obtained by the method mentioned immediately after.
