In such training rules related to householders (gahapati), although it is said, "A householder is anyone who lives in a house," it should be understood that this excludes the five classes of co-religionists, and includes those who have given up the training and those of other sects (titthiya).

## The Explanation of the Tatuttari Training Rule is finished.
245:
## 8. Explanation of the First Upakkhaṭa Training Rule

527-8. "Api" is thought to have the meaning of "hoti" (it is). The meaning of the reading "meyya" should be understood as "mayhaṃ" (for me). Where there is "na ime sukarā", there is also a reading "na imesaṃ sukarā". The meaning of that reading is written as "It is not easy to offer robes to these monks." Because of the phrase "pubbe appavārito" (not previously invited), it should be understood that even if invited at that moment, he is considered as not invited.

## The Explanation of the First Upakkhaṭa Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Second Upakkhaṭa Training Rule

What is the use of the Second Upakkhaṭa rule? There is no special benefit; it is merely laid down according to the circumstances, like the training rule for a nun sitting in private (rahonisajja). If this were the case, since the meaning is accomplished even without that second rule, and since there is no authority over not including it in the Pali, and since permission was given not to include it, it should not have been included in the Pali. Did not the Buddha say this Pali: "Ānanda, if the Saṅgha wishes, it may abolish the minor training rules"?

All this is not the reason. The reason is that the Buddhas do not utter even a useless word, let alone a training rule. Therefore, it was said in the Commentary: "That second rule is similar to a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) of this first rule." A supplementary regulation is not useless, and since this rule is similar to that, it implies it is not useless.

If so, what is the specific distinction here? To that question, it is said: "In the first training rule, one person is pressured; in the second, two are pressured. This is the distinction here." By this specific meaning, what further meaning is shown? In the Ancient Glossary (Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada), it is said: "This further meaning is shown: it is proper to pressure two persons even regarding a single object." Therefore, it shows this meaning: "The count of offenses is not only by the count of robes received, but also by the count of objects consisting of the persons pressured."

There are summary verses (Saṅgaha Gāthā) here:

"Even when counting by way of the object, there may be many offenses; to clearly show such a meaning, the Second Upakkhaṭa rule was spoken in this Dispensation.

How is this rule like the analysis (vibhaṅga) of the training rule on physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga)? Even with a single woman, there may be many offenses according to the efforts (payoga)."
247:
If the one not requested gives at the word of the one requested, there is no offense. Similarly, in the Upakkhaṭa training rules, the method should be understood as far as possible. The Commentary on the Second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Rāja Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Friends, we do not accept robe-funds... we accept only what is allowable at the proper time." This was said because the training rule on the acceptance of money (Rūpiya-paṭiggahaṇa) had been laid down prior to this training rule. Otherwise, if the Venerable Upananda would accept even a single kahāpaṇa for the purpose of buying meat with his own hand, why would he not accept a robe-fund which is much greater than that? Even so, because it is connected with robes, it was recited in the Cīvara-vagga.

538-9. Some teachers say: Since it is said "he destroys the reason for coming," he does not get the chance to request again. Some say: The coming is not fruitful; he will not get the robe because the hospitable reception (paṭisanthāra) has already been made. Some say: It is said because it does not have the characteristic of requesting. Some say: A monk who comes thinking "I will stand and request" destroys that standing; if he performs one [of the three actions like sitting], or even if he performs all three, he destroys only one "standing" because the word is in the singular. Some say: He destroys all three positions.

The Elder Upatissa says: "He does not destroy the requesting, etc.; the one who wishes to request has done what should not be done; because of that, there is a Dukkaṭa for the breach of conduct (vattabheda)." The Elder Dhammasiri says: "If he sits on a seat, by that one sitting he destroys two standings. If he accepts material gifts (āmisa), by that one acceptance he destroys two standings. If he speaks Dhamma, by that one speech of the extent mentioned in the Dhamma-desanā training rule, he destroys two standings; it is said with reference to such destruction."

When it is said "in which place," it is as if saying one should go only to one's own presence. Therefore, it is said: "But the phrasing does not match." One who does not delight in that robe-fund commanded by the lay followers (i.e., when the robe-fund is unallowable, one who does not delight in it), that non-delighting is only by mind, not by speech. If, thinking "he will give an unallowable object if I say this," and while desiring the unallowable by mind, he indicates the allowable by speech saying "Give me a robe," it is not allowable. Upon receipt, there is an offense according to the Rūpiya-paṭiggahaṇa training rule.

In this matter, there is this investigation: Even if he delights in it by mind, if he speaks with allowable terminology saying "Bring such and such an object with allowable goods worth a kahāpaṇa or worth a pāda," even if he says it with reference to money, it is allowable. Why? Because of the statement: "If one says 'We give a boundary' with reference to a certain piece of land where crops grow, it is allowable," and because of the statement: "If it is said 'We give to the monastery,' it is not proper to reject it." In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "An object given with reference to the Sangha, saying 'We give to the monastery,' is not heavy property (garubhaṇḍa); for the purpose of accepting the water of donation and for the purpose of saying 'Sādhu'..."
249:
In all cases, 'acceptance' (sampaṭicchana) means the characteristic described as: 'one should take it oneself, or have another take it, or consent to gold and silver placed nearby.' Even so, in some cases it should be rejected, in some cases it should not be rejected, in some cases it is proper to consent to a rejected object, and in some cases an unrejected object is proper. To show all these decisions, the detailed explanation beginning with 'Sace pana' is undertaken. In that commentary, because it says 'for a Cetiya... it is not proper,' it is established that it is proper to consent to an unrejected object given to a monastery (vihāra). Furthermore, even if it is said to an elder, 'We give this for your mother,' an offense of Pācittiya is incurred due to acceptance.

In the phrase 'he becomes one who has an offense,' by which offense does he have an offense? Some teachers say by an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). It is not by any specific offense, but he is called 'one who has an offense' simply because he asks in an improper situation. How is this? In the passage, 'Monks, a co-resident (saddhivihārika) endowed with five factors should be dismissed... the teacher who dismisses him is without fault,' it is not said that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a teacher who does not dismiss a student who does not practice well. Therefore, because it is said, 'Monks, one should not fail to dismiss a student who does not practice well; whoever does not dismiss him, there is an offense of dukkaṭa,' it is seen that there is no offense for a teacher who does not dismiss him even if there is no excessive affection etc. Rather, it is said, 'he becomes one with a fault.' See the completeness of this illustration. If one asks, 'Is it improper because the commentary says "he becomes one with a fault means he is with blame, he incurs an offense"?' No, it is not so; immediately after that sentence, it serves the purpose of removing such a wrong view. Therefore, it should be understood that because it is said 'a student who does not practice well should be dismissed,' it is made so that there is no offense. Teachers say it is a dukkaṭa offense; it should be examined. When it is said, 'Even an allowable object is indeed unallowable,' it means that even the taste of cow's milk obtained by bartering with grain produced from a tank is not allowable.

I shall also speak of the procedure regarding allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra), namely: 'by means of water' etc. The phrase 'it is difficult to distinguish' is not the same as the subsequent phrase 'it is unallowable only for that person; why? because the grain has been managed.' Therefore, it is well said. This refers to what is called 'new crop' (nava-sassa) which has not existed before, because it is mixed with other grain from the beginning by the power of the monk's effort (payoga). Standing on the threshing floor and guarding means if one guards with effort such as saying, 'Do not take this much, it is allowed to take this much,' or 'Remove it from this place, make a heap in this place,' that grain is unallowable (akappiya). If one guards with the thought, 'If I stay here, it is guarded,' or if seeing those who take it, one says, 'What are you doing?', it is said to be allowable; that statement is appropriate. In the training rule on receiving silver, it is said, 'One who guards by closing the door should stay.'
250:
Indeed, that object is unallowable only for the monk who arranged it so. Why? Because a new crop should not be caused to arise. However, it is not allowable to say below, 'Having prepared the crops, bring them.' The same method applies to a bed of leaves. It is said, 'Because it causes effort in those who are doing it of their own accord.' Why? It is evident because of the statement 'Because of managing kahāpaṇas,' and because it was caused to arise beforehand.

If donors, or people who have rented the Saṅgha's village, field, or monastery, or householders in that place say, 'We have brought these kahāpaṇas for the Saṅgha,' one should only say, 'It is not allowable.' If the kappiyakārakas say so, one should say, 'Kahāpaṇas are not allowable for the Saṅgha; only ghee and so forth are allowable.' Therefore, having said, 'Tell the Saṅgha's kappiyakāraka or [point out] a secure place,' and since no monk should handle the ghee etc. provided by them, one should conclude the management by saying, 'Bring ghee with this object.' Then it is allowable for other monks, like the fourth bowl among the four bowls to be mentioned later.

In that training rule, it is said: 'Having given the kahāpaṇas, saying "Take these kahāpaṇas and give this bowl," the bowl thus obtained is unallowable only for that monk. Why? Because it was improperly managed. For other monks, however, it is allowable because they did not accept the price.' If so, is it unallowable for all monks? If it is asked, 'Is this because of managing kahāpaṇas, and is this statement poorly said?' No. Because this was said with reference to the place where the price is accepted, it is like the second and third bowls among the four bowls. Therefore, in the section on doing it oneself, it is said only this much: 'It is not allowable.' Beyond that, it is called accepting the price.

This Rāja Sikkhāpada is difficult to understand because it has a wide scope, and like the king's mind, it is hard to know, or because it has a profound meaning.

## Rāja Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## Niṭṭhito Cīvara Vaggo Paṭhamo.

## 2. Kosiya Vagga

## 1. Kosiya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In this word 'kosiyakāraka', 'kosiya' refers to what is produced from the cocoons of insects known as 'kosakāra' because they make cocoons. If one makes it oneself, at the time of forfeiture, one should say, 'It is a nissaggiya made by oneself.'
251:
If it was made by both oneself and others, it should be stated exactly as in the Pali text. The fourfold set (catukka) that could occur, such as finishing by oneself what was started by oneself and others, is not shown even though it is possible. This is the nature of the Vinaya: when one threefold set (tika) or fourfold set (catukka) is shown, other possible cases are not mentioned.

## Kosiya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 2. Suddhakāḷaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In this place 'suddhakāḷakānaṃ', just as it was said in the first training rule, 'even with one silk thread,' here, because the phrase 'even one thread without mixing with other wool' is absent, it should be understood that even if mixed with other wool, if the appearance [of other colors] is not evident, it is called 'suddhakāḷaka' (pure black).

## Suddhakāḷaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 3. Dvebhāga Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

According to the words 'having weighed, two parts should be taken,' in weighing, to ensure the black wool does not exceed [the limit], two parts of black wool should be taken as the maximum limit. How is this known? It is known by the reason of the prohibition of pure black wool. 'The third part is white, the fourth part is brown'—this is the minimum limit.

In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇီ), however, it is said: 'If even one black hair is in excess, it entails forfeiture (nissaggiya).' Although this statement does not agree with weighing, since this training rule is acittaka (an offense regardless of intention), I do not consider it to mean that if even one black hair falls into the rug being made after it was previously weighed, it entails forfeiture. Otherwise, one would have to take less than the full two parts. One cannot weigh by counting hairs. If it must be done by counting, some ask, 'What is the use of weighing?' They say, 'It is allowable to take double of either brown or white.' Since this has not been investigated in the Commentary, it should be examined.

## Dvebhāga Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
252:
## 4. Commentary on the Six-Year Training Rule

The phrase "navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāya" (new is said in reference to the making) indicates the counting of years starting from the beginning of the making. The phrase "karitvā vā" (or having made) indicates the counting from the day of completion. The phrase "dhāretabbaṃ" (should be worn/used), however, indicates the counting from the time of use. This is because a monk who has received formal permission (sammuti) may have many rugs made before the completion of six years in whatever place he arrives. Therefore, regarding the term "aññaṃ navaṃ" (another new one), the question arises: does it mean other than the making, or other than the wearing?

In this matter, if it means other than the making, it would be proper to make one of those rugs again, either because it was poorly made or because it has become worn out through use. Such making could also occur without taking a sugata-span from the old rug, because such an act does not fall under the prohibition. Since making another rug is prohibited, and this rug was also previously made, it would be in opposition to that (Nissaggiya Pācittiya) training rule. If it means other than the wearing (using), then the formal permission (sammuti) would become useless. Does it mean that if the rug made first has not yet been used, it is not proper to make another new one even if there is formal permission?

The demonstration of the conclusion in this matter is as follows: the period of six years should be understood as starting from the day of completion. Within those (six years), when the seventh year is reached, the six years are completed. This completion is by the measure of months, not by the measure of years. A year that is either complete or incomplete in the seventh year is called a "year." Therefore, even for a rug that is unfinished, if six years are completed, it gains another six years starting from the day of completion. Whether that rug is used or not, it is simply called "worn" (dhārita).

Because it is said, "navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāya vuccati" (new is said in reference to the making), when six years have passed, if one unravels that very rug made previously and makes it again because it was poorly made or worn out through use, it should be worn for a maximum of six years starting from the day of completion, or even longer. If one makes it within six years, that very act is called "another new one" in reference to the making; therefore, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. Otherwise, there would be no distinction made by this phrase "navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāya."

If this is so, what happens? There is an origin story (atthuppatti). For it is said there, "They live with much begging and much requesting," and that phrase indicates making for another. If so, does that (origin story) lead absolutely to a Nissaggiya? It does not. This is its distinction: it is distinct because of the meaning stated as "There is no offense if one obtains and uses a rug made by another." What does this mean? When it is said, "navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāya vuccati," the arising of that rug through acquisition becomes "new," just like the arising of an extra robe (atireka-cīvara). From the day of such acquisition...
253:
...starting from that day, it should be worn for a maximum of six years. If one has it made within six years... pe... it is a Nissaggiya. Therefore, it is said only in reference to the making of a new one, not in reference to the acquisition. Because it has not yet arisen for oneself within six years, it falls under the designation of "new." If one has it made without having acquired it, it does not happen that "as it is obtained, so he may make it or have it made." Why? Because there is a distinction: "There is no offense if one obtains and uses a rug made by another."

## The Commentary on the Six-Year Training Rule is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Rugs for Sitting

In the phrase "nāssudha koci," the word "assudha" is a particle (nipāta) in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). In that Pali, although the plural "Those monks replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir'" is used, it should be understood that after those monks had given their assent to the Blessed One, among those monks staying there, no one except for the one monk who brought the alms-food approached the Blessed One. This interpretation is a good grasp of the meaning, as in "Venerable Sir, I alone pay homage to the Blessed One," etc. "I allow... pe... let them approach to see me as they please" means let them approach for the purpose of seeing.

566-7. The phrase "We [approach] the Venerable Upasena..." is said because the Venerable Upasena was the leader of the group (gaṇapāmokkha). All [practices] are mentioned by way of being a forest-dweller, an alms-food-eater, and a refuse-heap-rag-wearer. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary, "Because of the perception of the rug as a fourth robe." If one asks, "Do all those monks not even know what a robe is?" let it be so. What is called a robe? Among the six robes, any one robe that is suitable for assignment (vikappanā) and is the least (pacchima) is called a robe. Is that robe woven or non-woven? It is only woven. By which Pali is this known? That person likely does not even see the Pali. He regards the pair of cloths from the Sivi country, robes made by psychic power, and robes given by devas as non-robes. If he does so, one should say that even a non-woven cloth is called a robe. This being so, the perception of the rug as a robe is established because of the commonality of being made of wool, starting with woolen blankets. Did those monks formally determine (adhiṭṭhāna) the rug? They determined it improperly. Why? Because the rug is not a robe and because it is not suitable for formal determination. Or, if they did not formally determine it, those monks previously had the perception of those rugs as non-robes. Having considered it thus, it is answered that both the woven and non-woven are improper because of the perception of those rugs as robes. In this matter of rugs, is there no rug suitable for formal determination?
254:
It is stated in that very place: If an object not suitable for formal allocation (vikappanā) is not a robe, then by the mere Pali statement, "A robe means any one of the six kinds of robes," the matter is settled; thus, it should not be said that "An object suitable for formal allocation is the last." If an object not suitable for formal allocation does not qualify as a robe, then objects not suitable for determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and objects not suitable for formal allocation should be grouped together and come under the count of "robe." For this very reason, it is said: "If a fourth robe arises for a monk who wears only three robes (ticīvarika), only an aṃsaka-kāsāva (shoulder cloth) is allowable."

Furthermore, the perception of a rug (santhata) as a robe does not occur only to those monks; it follows other monks as well. This is because of the statement: "A so-called old rug is one that has been worn even once or wrapped even once." However, the Teacher of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya), referring to its status as a non-robe, explains the meaning as a place for sitting and lying down. The meaning of the words 'worn' (nivattha) and 'wrapped' (pāruta) is simply sitting and lying down. Furthermore, even if this is the case, the perception of a rug as a robe still follows. This is because it is stated in the Khandhaka (Mahāva. 358), "One should determine (adhiṭṭhāna) the sitting mat (nisīdana), but not formally allocate (vikappanā) it"; and in the Parivāra (Pari. 329), "Nine robes are to be determined"; and in the Nisīdana Training Rule, "The border (dasā) must be one span"; and here, "A so-called sitting mat is said to be with a border (sadasa)."

In the Commentary on that Pali, it is also stated: "Having spread it like a rug, at one end, in a place about one span long by the Sugata-span, it is split in two places to make three borders; because it is with those borders, it is called 'sadasa' (a sitting mat with a border)." And, "The sitting mat must be determined in the manner mentioned; and that sitting mat must be only one of the proper dimensions; two are not allowable." Therefore, a sitting mat is one of the nine kinds of robes and should be determined. It is established that the sitting mat is a special kind of rug made of sheep's wool, similar to a rug. Likewise, it is established that the sitting mat itself is the sitting-mat-rug (nisīdana-santhata). In the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, it is also said, "Only one." When that meaning is established, the perception of a rug as a robe is also established. Why? Because of the commonality of being a rug.

In this regard, the objector asks: Why does a rug without a border not come under the count of a robe? Even a large rug that is not determined is allowable. Since only a rug with a border comes under the count of a robe, it is therefore fit for determination. Because it is not included in the category of 'rug' (santhata), it comes under the count of a robe even without formal permission (sammuti) within six years. This happens only after discarding the old rug, not without discarding it. This is because of the statement: "That sitting mat must be only one of the proper dimensions; two are not allowable." If it is held that a rug is made only for sleeping and a sitting mat is not a rug, that view is not absolute. This is because it is said: "A so-called old rug is one that has been worn once or wrapped once." Here, it is replied: One should not seek a reason here, for the Vinaya regulation is not the domain of anyone other than the Buddha.
256:
The meaning is concluded that there is no offense for a monk who has reached his destination. Indeed, in distinguishing these various meanings: if sheep’s wool should arise for a monk... etc... the construction should be understood as: even if there is no carrier, if a monk who has set out on a journey carries it beyond three yojanas, he commits a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. By the words "A monk who so desires should accept them," it is shown that an offense is committed only by carrying one's own wool beyond three yojanas. Because of this demonstration, it is clear that there is no offense for a monk who, without such desire, accepts wool belonging to another and carries it beyond three yojanas. This meaning is illustrated by the phrase "should [wool] arise for a monk" and by the phrase "having regained wool that was snatched away."

In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is also stated: "If he goes while making another monk carry it, there is no offense for either of them." Therefore, if two monks reach the three-yojana limit and exchange their goods to carry them, the conclusion is that there is no offense. For this very reason, it is stated in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra): "He makes another carry it." What kind of person does he make carry it? One who knows, or one who does not know? In this context, if he makes one who knows carry it, and leaves it thinking "Another will carry it," it cannot be said with certainty that an offense is committed even if that person carries it. This is because even one who knows sometimes carries it of his own accord. If it were so, it would contradict the Commentary. On the other hand, if he makes one who does not know carry it, it would contradict the Pāḷi text which says: "If he places it on another's vehicle or among another's goods without that person knowing and causes it to exceed three yojanas, it is a Nissaggiya offense." Furthermore, if both together make one set of goods be carried, that too would be a Nissaggiya. If it were said not to be a Nissaggiya, it would contradict the logic of the Pāḷi text which states without qualification: "If there is no carrier, it should be carried by one's own hand for a maximum of three yojanas."

A carrier (hāraka) is of two types: conscious and unconscious. A conscious carrier is also of two types based on whether they know or do not know the nature of the sheep’s wool, or think "I am carrying this," or "This person is making me carry this." Among these, an unconscious carrier is a river current, a boat, or an ownerless vehicle. A conscious carrier is obvious. In such a case of making someone carry, the method of the Anugaṇṭhipada states: if he makes another person or an animal carry it, and they know at least this much—"This person is making me carry this"—there is no offense. This is the consistent decision in both the Pāḷi and the Commentary. Although the phrase "if there is no carrier" is stated without qualification, it is understood from the words "without the other person knowing, on their vehicle or among their goods" that a conscious carrier is intended there. And that does not refer to one who knows the nature of the sheep’s wool and thinks "I am carrying this." Therefore, it is said: "If he leaves it thinking another will carry it, even if that person carries it, it is an offense," and so on. This is because in that case, he is not the causative agent (hetukattu). In the Pāḷi, however, by the power of the causative agent, it says "he makes another carry it"...
257:
...is stated. The other two types of persons who know are possible in this context. In the Pāḷi phrase "having placed it [on the vehicle] of one who does not know," it illustrates that if he places it on the vehicle or among the goods of one who knows—thinking either "This person is making me carry it" or "He is making me exceed this place"—and causes it to exceed three yojanas, it is not a Nissaggiya offense.

The word "harāpeti" (causes to carry) establishes the status of a causative agent (hetukattu). Therefore, in the Commentary, the phrase "only while the owner does not know" is said in reference to one who does not know that "This person is making me carry this." The words "drives, urges, makes follow" are said in reference to one who knows that "This person is making me exceed this place." Even one who does not know does not exceed the place where they are stationed, nor do they follow, because of driving and so on. However, if they exceed it of their own accord without being driven, an offense is indeed committed for the bhikkhu because the status of being a causative agent is not possible.

Now, I shall speak starting from the fixed location: in the phrase "even if there is no carrier," because he carries it himself due to the lack of a carrier, it is a Nissaggiya offense; how much more so if there is a carrier? This is one meaning. Taking the word "api" in the sense of limitation (avadhāraṇa), a Nissaggiya offense occurs only when there is no carrier; but if there is a carrier, there is no Nissaggiya for the one who makes that person carry it. This is the second meaning. By the words "from the Saṅgha... or with one's own wealth," it shows that although this training rule is one that occurs regardless of intention (acittaka), an offense occurs only when sheep’s wool accepted by one's own desire from the Saṅgha etc. is carried beyond three yojanas; there is no offense for exceeding the limit with wool that is unknowingly unaccepted and merely stuck to one's robe etc. from somewhere. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "For one who travels while lying on a woolen blanket, if even a single hair remains stuck to the robe, an offense is committed because it has detached from the blanket." This statement is appropriate because, since the blanket was accepted, it is considered accepted by one's own desire. Since it is said "no offense for finished goods (katabhaṇḍa)," that item stands in the place of many finished goods. He has accepted that finished article, not the raw wool. In that case, the wool is also considered not accepted; a finished article is defined as a manufactured item where the wool cannot be easily separated. If this is the case, one should show the Pācittiya of the triad for unfinished goods and the Dukkaṭa of the triad for finished goods according to the method; otherwise, it is because the triad has been shown. "With effort" (sa-ussāhattā) means because of the unceasing movement. "And because of being regardless of intention" (acittakattā ca) means that as the wool exceeds three yojanas in accordance with the bhikkhu's exertion, he commits the offense even without the specific application of mind or the intention to carry. That non-offense is not [found] in the Pāḷi...
258:
"Sameti" means that there is no offense because the distance of three yojanas has been exceeded. However, within the three yojanas, there is no offense due to the effort (payoga). By the phrase "he carries it for three yojanas," it is shown that even if one intends to carry it for three yojanas on foot, one does not incur a dukkaṭa offense for every step within those three yojanas. This explanation is appropriate. It is said because there is the Pali statement: "Having gone with the intention of staying for three yojanas, he carries it further than that."

Furthermore, "he causes another to carry it" means causing another person who has the effort to carry it, thinking, "I will carry this." Otherwise, if it is placed on the head of someone who is walking, even if that person does not know, it is said that there would be no offense. However, because it is stated in the manner of "even on a vehicle that is not moving," etc., Elder Upatissa said that an offense is not incurred only when the thought "I will do this" or "I will carry it" arises in animals such as elephants that have been made to exert effort by carrying, etc.; if such a thought does not arise, it is not that there is no offense (i.e., there is an offense).

In the context of "placed by exchanging," Elder Upatissa says there is an offense because both items are placed outside. Some say there is no offense for one who takes a bundle placed outside the sīmā and puts an item from inside the sīmā outside, but this does not seem good.

"He carries it after regaining it" means he carries it further from the first three yojanas, and not from the second gāvuta, etc. There is no offense because there is no opportunity for an offense to arise regarding the finished goods.

## The Commentary on the Sheep's Wool Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Washing of Sheep's Wool Training Rule

Although it is stated in the section on no-offense (anāpattivāra) in the training rule for washing old robes that "he causes another requisite to be washed" after setting aside the robe, some say that from the time this training rule arose, an offense is incurred for causing sheep's wool to be washed, etc. Others say that the lack of offense is only due to the original offense and not because of this training rule. Some say that because sheep's wool is not a requisite, it is simply a matter of not taking damaged sheep's wool.

To clarify the meaning of this final method, this problem should be understood: Is the word "causes to be washed" (dhovāpeti) a term that expresses a comprehensive meaning (nippadesa) by including dyeing (rajāpana) and carding (vijaṭāpana), or is it a term that expresses a partial meaning (sappadesa) by not including them? If it is a term expressing a comprehensive meaning, then only this word should be used in all places, and not the other words. If it is a term expressing a partial meaning, then there is a contradiction in the context of "he causes to be washed that which he himself has not used." This is because it would lead to the undesirable conclusion: "He himself dyes it, he carded it, and a nissaggiya offense is incurred."
259:
The words of the Blessed One are merely for the beauty of the teaching (desanāvilāsa). In some Pali passages, it is stated with three terms (tikapada), and in some, with one term (ekapada). Those terms (such as dhovāpeti) express only a comprehensive meaning (nippadesa). If it is asked: "If there is a contradiction here in 'he causes finished goods to be washed,' would it not simply be no offense, as it leads to the undesirable conclusion that 'if he causes finished goods to be carded, there is no offense'?" The answer is: No, the carding of pure wool that is not yet finished goods is also to be taken from this training rule. If it is said that carding is allowed for those things that are clumped together due to washing with water, etc., it should be that there is no offense in carding an old rug; however, that is not appropriate because of the statement "he causes to be washed that which has not been used." Therefore, it is established that causing to be washed, dyed, or carded that which has been used is indeed a nissaggiya offense. And that which is "used" is indeed finished goods. It is not possible to use sheep's wool (without making it into something); otherwise, the statement "he causes to be washed that which has been used" would be meaningless. In this training rule, there is no such statement as "if he should cause old sheep's wool to be washed," as there is in the training rule for old robes (purāṇacīvarasikkhāpada). In that (purāṇacīvara) training rule, this Pali was written here by way of what was previously stated. If it is asked: "Is it a scribal error (lekhadosa)?" The answer is: No, because there is no special reason. In the training rule for old robes, "unused finished goods" are said to be "blankets, rugs, mats, etc." Although this meaning is established by this word (dhovāpeti), this term "dhovāpeti" may be comprehensive (nippadesa) in some cases and partial (sappadesa) in others. It is comprehensive in places such as "he washes it himself, without being told," etc. It is partial here in "he causes finished goods to be washed." If it is said that there is no offense based on the authority of the Pali statement "if he causes unfinished goods to be washed or dyed, there is no offense" and "if he causes them to be carded, there is no offense," the answer is: No, because by the very authority of the statement, it leads to an offense. If the statement "he causes to be washed that which has not been used" itself indicates that there is no offense for a monk who causes an unused rug to be carded, then it is already clear that there is an offense for a monk who causes a used one to be carded.

## The Commentary on the Washing of Sheep's Wool Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Money Training Rule

583-4. "Sabbampi" means all three. Although "pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, conch shells," etc., were mentioned incidentally as "not allowable" in the Rājasikkhāpada, they are mentioned again in their own place by way of showing the offense. How is this? It has become the proper place for pearls, etc. Because those objects are not found in the Pali of this training rule, they are mentioned in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) of this Pali and in the commentary of the Rūpiyasikkhāpada. No...
260:
It is not only gold and silver; other things such as fields and buildings are also generally intended by the phrase "unallowable objects should not be accepted," though not by specific enumeration. In the Pāḷi, however, only this much is stated by specific enumeration: "gold, silver, pearls, or gems called robe-fund." Therefore, the Rāja Sikkhāpada (Rūpiya Sikkhāpada) is the appropriate place for those pearls and so on. Since the inclusion of pearls and gems also establishes the inclusion of objects of the same class, they are not mentioned further. This is also because this training rule was laid down first. If this is so, and since they are not mentioned by specific enumeration in this training rule, one might ask: what is the appropriate place for those pearls and so on? The answer is that this training rule itself is the appropriate place in terms of meaning, though not in terms of specific enumeration.

How so? In the Ratana Sikkhāpada, those objects appear collectively as "jewels" (ratana), including both Nissaggiya objects and Dukkaṭa objects. Allowable objects appear as "designated as a jewel." Among those ten jewels, the two types—gold and silver—are Nissaggiya objects in this training rule, and it is established that the remaining objects are Dukkaṭa objects. Because it is already established in this training rule, in the non-offense section of the Ratana Sikkhāpada, it is stated: "taking an object designated as a jewel out of trust, taking it on loan, or taking it thinking it is discarded (paṃsukūla)"; it does not say "jewel." However, seven kinds of grain, female slaves, male slaves, fields, and so on are established as unallowable objects by the power of Suttas such as the Brahmajāla Sutta. Therefore, it is established that they are Dukkaṭa objects in this training rule. That is why in the Anuyoga-vatta, it is stated: "He knows the Dhamma, he knows what is in accordance with the Dhamma, he knows the Vinaya, he knows what is in accordance with the Vinaya."

Similarly, does raw meat also fall under Dukkaṭa objects? It does not. This is because in this Vinaya, it is allowed by such statements as: "Monks, I allow raw meat in the case of an affliction by non-humans." Therefore, although raw meat appears in the Sutta, it does not become a Dukkaṭa object. Nevertheless, the teachers state that if one accepts it for one's own consumption, a Dukkaṭa offense is indeed incurred. If one says, "Put it here," it is merely consenting to the gold or silver placed nearby. If it is argued that "Only unallowable management is unallowable," then in the context of "standing dependent on allowable and unallowable objects," it means that the object itself is unfit for consumption, but the allowable goods of equal value to that gold are fit for consumption. It is also said: "It stands dependent on an allowable object because it exists as a discarded item (paṃsukūla) and because pointing out a secure place is allowable. It stands dependent on an unallowable object because of the unallowability of the person saying 'Take this,' and so on." Thus, standing dependent on both allowable and unallowable objects means: words such as "It is placed in this spot; do you not see these excellent kahāpaṇas?" are allowable, so it stands dependent on an allowable object. If one says "Take this," it is unallowable for oneself because it is poorly managed, and thus it stands dependent on an unallowable object coming from that. When that person takes it because of the words "Take this"...
261:
...it does not reach the procedure called "or have it accepted." Merely because of poor management, that object becomes unallowable (akappiya) only for that monk who receives it. Because the acceptance of the original value is pure, it is like the third bowl among the four bowls mentioned later—so says the Elder Upatissa in the Anugaṇṭhipada. What is the use of saying much? Because it is obtained purely, it is allowable (kappiya). The teacher says their thought is that if there is poor management, it stands dependent on the unallowable. Similarly, even if relinquished for the sake of the Saṅgha or a group, because it follows the same course as that individual, it is stated excluding the specific offense.

When it says "no allowable goods are caused to be purchased," it shows the lack of means if they are indeed caused to be purchased. In saying "excluding the deposit (upanikkhepa)," if that lay follower says, "Venerable sir, this gold and silver is very much; this gold and silver should not be exhausted today," and places it himself in a place of deposit, or has another place it, then the Saṅgha, enjoying the profit obtained from that deposited object, is said to be "enjoying the requisites."

This monk (of the Rūpiya-chaḍḍaka) is thus endowed with such characteristics to the highest degree. Even a monk endowed with such qualities, if later, out of greed or for another reason, he marks it and drops it, he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. Regarding "at every use" in the context of lodgings (senāsana), it does not mean at every entry. That reflection is also allowable for a monk living at the foot of a tree or in the open air due to special reasons. If there is an intention to reside by way of sitting or lying down, etc., one should reflect at every use. Some teachers say that the status of medicinal requisites should be reflected upon at all times. The teacher says their thought is: for an unstored object, only in the afternoon; for a stored object, even in the morning, it should be reflected upon. It is said: "If one accepts... for the sake of food... time-limited (yāmakālika), seven-day-limited (sattāhakālika), or life-long (yāvajīvika), he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense. At every swallow, he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense." The Dukkaṭa mentioned in the training rule on eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana) is incurred in the afternoon; it is not incurred in the morning because it is the time for food. But the Dukkaṭa mentioned in the training rule on storage (sannidhi) is incurred even in the morning because it has become "stored." That is why in that storage training rule, only the two—seven-day-limited and life-long—are mentioned.

If one asks, "Can this distinction not be obtained because of the words 'if there is a reason'?" No, it can be obtained because otherwise it would lead to an undesirable conclusion and because the wording is not fixed. In the storage training rule, it says: "There is no offense if one stores and eats a period-limited (yāvakālika) item for the duration of the period; or if one stores and eats a time-limited (yāmakālika) item for the duration of the watch (yāma)." Here, by taking the Pāḷi text as the standard, it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that a time-limited item is not allowable in the morning, nor in the afternoon, nor during the day, nor at night, but only for someone who stores and eats it for exactly one watch. In such a training rule, it only says: "He stores and eats a time-limited item for the duration of the watch; he stores and eats a seven-day-limited item for seven days." It does not say "if there is a reason." Therefore, the phrase "if there is a reason" exists in some versions and not in others. Since the Pāḷi text is not fixed, the non-fixity of the offense is also established. Even so, one simply incurs the aforementioned Dukkaṭa offense. If one asks, "Are time-limited items, etc., Dukkaṭa because they have no nutritional benefit?" No, because food mixed with ghee, etc., becomes "sumptuous food" (paṇītabhojana). Alternatively, among all the kālikas, the period-limited (yāvakālika) is coarse. That period-limited item...
262:
"No offense" refers to an undesirable implication. Similarly, in that very training rule, it is only stated, "one stores and consumes yāmakālika for a watch, one stores and consumes sattāhakālika for seven days," but it does not say "if there is a reason." Therefore, since the phrase "if there is a reason" appears in some places and not in others, the usage is inconsistent, and thus the occurrence of an offense might also be inconsistent. Even so, one indeed incurs the aforementioned offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If it is argued that a wrongdoing does not occur because yāmakālika and such are not for the purpose of nutrition, that is not so; because food mixed with ghee and such attains the status of choice food (paṇītabhojana). Alternatively, among all kālikas, yāvakālika is coarse; if there is no offense for one receiving that yāvakālika for the purpose of nutrition at the proper time, what need is there to mention receiving the refined yāmakālika and such, which are permitted specifically for the purpose of nutrition? If it is argued that there is no offense only in the case of yāvakālika, that is not so; because an offense can occur for one who receives it not for the purpose of nutrition, just like one who receives other kālikas for the purpose of nutrition. Therefore, the aforementioned decision in this matter conforms to both the Pali and logic.

In this context of "purity through confession" (desanā-suddhi), confession refers to a Vinaya act; therefore, the act of rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna) is also called confession. Since it is said "consumes" (paṭisevati) instead of "receives" (paṭiggaṇhāti), there is no offense for one who consumes without being mindful during the act of receiving. Arahants (khīṇāsava), having completed their tasks, are like those who have received their inheritance; therefore, their consumption is "consumption as an owner" (sāmiparibhoga). Otherwise, it would be contradictory as it does not exceed the nature of yāvakālika. "Consumption as a debt" (iṇaparibhoga) is not proper, because of the offense regarding medicine, because it is an improper consumption of other requisites, and because it is consumed without permission, like a debt. It is written, "From the beginning, there is no such thing as a shameless person (alajjī); therefore, no one should be suspected." Co-residents (saddhivihārika) and others are like burdens. In the phrase "because of receiving as given," it is stated, "If one gives with one's own hand, it is not proper," and "If one takes the excess portion and has that same person give the portion set aside for oneself on the next day, it is proper." Giving in exchange is proper if it is according to the Dhamma; it is not proper if it is not according to the Dhamma. It is stated, "It is proper to learn that text as a support for the Dhamma." If asked for what reason, it is because of the justification in the Upasampadakkhandhaka Pali: "When harmony cannot be obtained, there is no offense in communal enjoyment and communal living."

In the phrase "given without mindfulness," giving without mindfulness means it has not yet been relinquished; therefore, if the donors regain mindfulness regarding the coins and such tied to the edge of the garment...
263:
...and take them back again, only the nissaggiya offense should be confessed. If those donors buy ghee and such with that unallowable object and offer them to the Sangha, it is allowable for that monk as well, because it is the property of the donors themselves. For the monk received it with the perception of "cloth" (vatthasaññāya), thinking "I am taking cloth," not with the perception of "money" (rūpiyasaññāya). Furthermore, this training rule was spoken with reference to receiving for one's own sake, and he did not receive it for his own sake or for the sake of others. However, if those donors do not come and take it, and if it was relinquished for his own sake after questioning the donors, he must forfeit it to the Sangha and confess the offense. If they did not relinquish it, it is said that he should only confess the offense; that statement is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. For if there is a confession of an offense, it is established that money was received; once that is established, the statement "the object produced from that is also allowable for him" is not logical.

If it is argued that it is indeed allowable, no; it is not logical to say that the offense should be confessed without forfeiting the object. If it is argued that it is logical because the training rule is acittaka (independent of intention), no; because of the statement "receives money" in all instances. For it is said, "he receives money"; otherwise, the word "money" (rūpiya) would be meaningless in all instances, as the meaning could be established even without it. And by this monk, cloth was received, and by the donor, only cloth was given; one who takes money that has gone along with the cloth with a thieving mind should be punished according to the steps (padavāra). And in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated, "Perceiving money as non-money means perceiving gold and such as mother-of-pearl and such," by virtue of the statement "he receives money."

The phrase "api ca puññakāmā" and so on is stated to show another procedure; therefore, it is said, "It should be noted that this was obtained in this house." Otherwise, it would occur by virtue of doubt in the marking; and if there is doubt, it would be only nissaggiya because of the statement "one who is doubtful about money," and so on. This procedure would then become meaningless, but it is not meaningless. Why? Coins and such tied in the edge of a garment are given without mindfulness and received with the perception of cloth; therefore, it is neither "giving money" nor "receiving money." In this case, there is no duty of confessing an offense, but that money should be returned to the donors themselves. My teacher said that "api ca puññakāmā" and so on is stated to show this other procedure: "The allowable object produced from that is allowable for all."

## The Explanation of the Money Training Rule is finished.
264:
## 9. Rupiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

This phrase, "exchanging gold and silver," is taught in terms of the highest limit. Likewise, the words of the Pali text such as "Rupiya means a kahāpaṇa bearing the image of the Teacher," etc., are also taught in terms of the highest limit. It is established that the lowest limit is also obtained in this training rule because of the triad (tika) beginning with "perceiving what is not rupiya as rupiya, one causes it to be bought," and because of the commentary statement: "For one who causes a nissaggiya object to be bought with a dukkaṭa object... a nissaggiya pācittiya occurs because of causing a heavy object to be bought." Here, the combination should be understood as: gold, kahāpaṇa, and whatever other things enter into common usage (vohāra).

In this training rule, five triads are taught based on the three types of gold and silver—wrought (kata), unwrought (akata), and both wrought and unwrought (katākata)—which are analyzed in the phrase "various kinds," and based on the two types of objects, rupiya and arupiya. The teachers of the commentaries showed one more triad in accordance with those five, making six in total.

Here, there is a question: While it is possible to show other triads when one limit of a triad is shown in other training rules, they are not shown; why are they shown only in this training rule? The answer is: Because it is stated in the Matika as "various kinds," they are shown only here to demonstrate the state of having various kinds. If it is asked, "Should this not also be stated in the Kayavikkaya (Trading) training rule because of the similarity of the meaning?" No, because the method has already been shown in this training rule.

Furthermore, since it is stated at the end of the Rupiya Vibhaṅga, "whatever things enter into common usage," it is established that gold and the like are only those objects that are fit for use. Because of that, it would follow that there is no nissaggiya offense for transactions with gold and silver that are not fit for use. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the arrival at that nissaggiya offense, taught the triads such as "one causes wrought gold to be bought with wrought gold." If this is so, it might be said that "whatever things enter into common usage" should not be stated in the Rupiya Vibhaṅga; for if that word is not stated, objects not fit for use would also be included, and thus there would be no purpose in stating the three triads such as "wrought," etc. The answer is: No, because it would then follow that exchanging allowable (kappiya) goods for allowable goods would also become a monetary transaction (rupiyasaṃvohāra).

If it is asked, "By the phrase 'whatever things enter into common usage,' would not exchanging things such as areca nuts, potsherds, bronze vessels, and robes also become a monetary transaction?" No, because by the words "wrought," etc., it is shown that only unallowable (akappiya) objects such as gold are intended. Therefore, by both statements, the intended meaning of "rupiya" is established as both the natural rupiya, which has the distinctions of wrought and unwrought, and the kahāpaṇa, etc., which are called kahāpaṇa and māsaka and enter into common usage as kahāpaṇa, etc., both in this training rule and in the preceding training rule. Rice and the like are not called rupiya because the terms "wrought," etc., cannot be applied to rice and the like. By this much, the purpose of the three triads such as "wrought," etc., has been stated.
265:
Now I shall speak of the remaining triads. Herein, only the Nissaggiya object of the aforementioned variety is called Rupīya (money). The remaining Dukkaṭa objects and Kappiya (allowable) objects are called Arupīya (non-money) because they are not money. Therefore, the statement "There is no offense for the five classes of fellow-practitioners if they perceive non-money as non-money" is not absolute, because a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred in the case of a Dukkaṭa object. In this training rule, if the Pāḷi text is taken as the standard, other things besides Nissaggiya objects, even pearls and so forth, are also called Arupīya.

Should it be said that there is no offense for the five classes of fellow-practitioners regarding such Arupīya objects? No, because it would contradict the Rāja Sikkhāpada. In that Rāja Sikkhāpada, it is said, "whether a pearl or a gem." Therefore, it is clear that unallowable objects such as pearls are Dukkaṭa objects because they are not among the Nissaggiya objects. This being so, the statement "There is no offense for the five classes of fellow-practitioners if they perceive non-money as non-money" refers only to purely allowable (Kappiya) goods, not to all Arupīya. However, in other cases, such as the Dukkaṭa triad beginning with "perceiving money in non-money," and in the triad shown in the Commentary, everything is to be understood as Arupīya. Therefore, the second triad is spoken to clarify the nature of Arupīya.

The Commentary shows that same meaning with one triad. Why is that triad not mentioned in the Pāḷi? Because in the Pāḷi, there is no function of perception regarding money in the purchased Arupīya. If that triad were mentioned, it would follow that the formal agreement (sammuti) for discarding non-money must also be given for allowable objects. Should it be said that because of discarding non-money, even the formal agreement for discarding money should not be taught? No, because it would lead to the conclusion that there is no function of formal agreement even for money.

Therefore, if one purchases an allowable object while perceiving money as money, it is like the third bowl in a set of four bowls. That object must be forfeited to the Saṅgha and so forth. Once forfeited, the object is allowable for other monks, just like the third bowl. If it was purchased with gold or silver that was accepted, it is like the second bowl. Any monk may discard that Nissaggiya object even without a formal agreement, and it is allowable. Thereafter, one should proceed according to the method already mentioned, beginning with "If an Ārāmika or someone else comes there." In that Pāḷi, wherever the locative case (bhumma) is used, as in "in money" (rupiye) or "in non-money" (arupiye), it should be understood as one's own property; where the accusative case (upayoga) is used, it should be understood as another's property.

Herein, the Elder Upatissa said: "By the previous training rule, the acceptance of gold and silver is prohibited; by this training rule, trading based on allowable objects in the hands of a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) is prohibited."

In the Pāḷi "with a Nissaggiya object, a Nissaggiya object... etc... in exchanging back and forth, by this [rule]," the simultaneous occurrence of offenses by virtue of two training rules regarding a single object is stated. That object must be forfeited by virtue of the latter rule. Some teachers say that a monk who has already incurred a Nissaggiya offense also incurs an offense by this rule. In the case of accepting and exchanging another's money, if the money is not accepted, that offense does not exist; therefore, the offense is incurred only by this rule, not by the previous one, similar to the Omasavāda training rule.
266:
Even if one speaks a falsehood (musā) through false speech (musāvāda), the offense is incurred only by the Omasavāda rule. Wishing to show the logical reasoning for "a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred because of a Nissaggiya object," etc., he said "Yo hi ayaṃ."

Regarding one who manages interest: if one takes this object and says, "Give this much" after a month or a year, it constitutes Rupiya-saṃvohāra (trading with money). For a monk who says, "Let there be this much interest, take this much" without a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka), a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred because the characteristics of buying and selling are absent. The passage beginning with "Mūle mūlasāmikānaṃ" is spoken to show the means of making it allowable. It is not only that the forfeited object should not be used; after doing this, it may be used again. In using it, if there is no means of making it allowable, the allowable way should be explained. As it appears in the Pāḷi, the means of making it allowable here also exists for the third bowl. "Just as there is such a means when taken for one's own sake, so it is when taken for the sake of the Saṅgha and so forth," it is said. As long as these first and second bowls are exchanged by a householder, it is not yet a means of making them allowable; even through many generations of people, the Commentary says, "they are simply unallowable."

In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is repeatedly stated: "Even the coins (kahāpaṇas) obtained by selling allowable goods belonging to the Saṅgha must be accepted only after being freed from [the act of] acceptance. Therefore, if a lay attendant says, 'These are those coins,' it is simply not allowable; they must be rejected and not managed. If they are managed, they are unallowable for all monks. If one manages objects that were accepted after being freed from [the act of] acceptance, they are unallowable only for that managing monk."

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Trading with Money is finished.

## 10. Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

"Paṭapilotikānaṃ" means with coarse cloths. The point "he transgresses, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa" should be understood in the previous training rule as well. By the reversal of the terms "it is bought and it is sold," the phrase "one's own goods" and so forth is spoken. Why? Because it conforms to the statement "this with this." Herein, the destruction of a gift of faith (saddhādeyya) should be understood by virtue of the wrong grounds.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Trading is finished.

## The Second Chapter, the Kosiya Vagga, is finished.
267:
## 3. Patta Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Patta Sikkhāpada
In the phrase "bahū patte sannisayanti," the word "sannisayanti" is a neuter verbal noun. It means "they will make an accumulation by taking many bowls." It is written: "They contain thirteen and a half palas." In this context, some teachers elaborate by showing the worldly usage of measurements which increase fourfold in sequence: "Four palas make one kuḍuva, four kuḍuvas make one pattha, and four patthas make one māsa."

"Khādananti" refers to eatables such as bean curry and the like. Since it is stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta Commentary that "the measure of curry is one-fourth of the rice," a portion of curry equal to one-fourth of a morsel of food should be taken as appropriate. The statement that "because the accumulation of bowls is forbidden for a bhikkhunī, a second bowl is also forbidden for bhikkhus following that rule" is not correct. This is because in the Pāḷi it is stated: "One may make an accumulation of a bowl that is not determined (anadhiṭṭhita) and not assigned (avikappita)." In the Kathina Khandhaka, even a single bowl is called "sannisaya" (accumulation) on the following day, similar to the accumulation and storage (nicaya-sannidhi).

In the subsequent training rule, however, the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is fixed such that a second bowl is forbidden. Therefore, one does not have the right to determine two bowls. If one determines them together, both determinations are invalid. If one determines them separately, the second one is not determined. For the purpose of assignment (vikappanā), however, one may obtain many bowls. Intending what is to be said now, it is stated: "There is a difference only in name." Here, "name" refers to terms such as medium (majjhima), medium-low (majjhimomaka), medium-high (majjhimukkaṭṭha), and so on.

If it is asked: "Because of the statement 'it does not count as a bowl because it is deficient in firing,' does even a determined bowl lose its determination if it is white due to harsh firing?" No, because it is not included among the nine causes for losing determination. Therefore, it is only due to the deficiency in the initial firings that it does not count as a bowl; in that case, it is not proper to request another. For it is said: "With less than five mends." Only when there is a hole or a crack does it lose determination through those flaws. Once determination is lost, this prohibition no longer applies. Therefore, one has no right to request another bowl even by withdrawing (paccuddharaṇa) or by assigning (vikappanā).

In the phrase "the bowl-maker having received the price," it means from the day it was fired and set aside. In the phrase "being one who wishes to give," it means from the day it was given or from the day it was heard...
268:
...or from that day, it should be understood as ten days. In the case of a change of gender (liṅgaparivatta), if ten days have passed, a Nissaggiya offence is incurred by the monk who is the owner of the bowl; for a bhikkhunī, however, it is incurred if one night has passed.

## The Commentary on the Patta Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Ūnapañcabandhana Sikkhāpada
612-3. "Bahū patte viññāpenti" means many monks requesting bowls one by one request many bowls, or many monks request bowls. Does this training rule, "Monks, a bowl should not be requested; for him who requests one, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," get repealed by the Ūnapañcabandhana training rule or not? Some say it is not repealed. This is because, taking that very training rule, it is said: "If he requests, there is a dukkaṭa in the effort (payoga)." Because that dukkaṭa is mentioned even after exhausting the obtained bowl, it is repealed by the statement: "By the acquisition, it becomes a Nissaggiya." Otherwise, one would incur a Nissaggiya along with a dukkaṭa, which would contradict the section on non-offence (anāpattivāra). An unmade request (akataviññatti) made at an unpermitted time is merely a dukkaṭa. "Bhinna" is the instrumental case in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa), or it means "bhedena" (because of breaking), being the instrumental case in the sense of cause (hetuttha).

## The Commentary on the Ūnapañcabandhana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Bhesajja Sikkhāpada
Based on the statement "That was a golden garland," the Teacher says that, excluding the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika), it is allowable to give gold and silver to others as they wish, to have them accept it, and to have them engage in trade. This should be reflected upon as it is the domain of the psychic power of one possessing such power.

By the statement "for those whose meat is allowable," it should be understood that although the butter and so on of those animals whose meat is not allowable are also not allowable, they are not objects of a Nissaggiya offence. Likewise, they are not objects of sumptuous food (paṇītabhojana). "Set aside after being taken (uggahitaka)" means set aside for the purpose of swallowing. Other butter (not for swallowing) is allowable to be swallowed after being formally received (paṭiggahita). "Of both kinds" refers to those made with milk and curd received after the meal (in the afternoon) and those received before the meal (in the morning). Having stated a semblance of a reason, "because the meat is unallowable," if one who wishes to eat desires to eat only pure fresh butter (navanīta) at the wrong time (vikāla), the lumps of curd and buttermilk should be removed. For one who wishes to cook, it does not become "cooking for oneself" (sāmaṃpāka); this is the meaning intended by the Elder Mahāsīva. Because of the statement "that which is in the cow (milk)," ghee cooked by adding milk is allowable at the wrong time. It exists (as medicine) during an interim famine. Here, "with medicines" refers to oil made together with lifelong (yāvajīvika) medicines. "Before the meal" here refers to uncooked oil; some say that the word "uṇhāloka" shows the state of being hot. That statement is not good. In the phrase "because it has arisen," since it is taken from sesame powder etc. for the sake of oil, because of the statement "it is only a dukkaṭa," it is implied that oil made from mustard seeds etc. received for a purpose other than oil is allowable for seven days starting from the day it was made.
269:
## 
It is said that in the afternoon, one who wishes to eat only butter should remove the lumps of curd and whey; it is the intended meaning of the Elder Mahāsīva that for one who wishes to cook, it does not constitute 'self-cooking' (sāmaṃpāka). Because of the phrase 'it will reach exhaustion,' it is established that butter cooked with milk added is allowed in the afternoon.

'With medicines' means with lifelong (yāvajīvika) medicines. 'Oil made before the meal' refers only to oil made without cooking. 'With hot water'—some say this indicates the state of being heated, but that is not appropriate. 'Because of being produced' means produced from sesame powder and so on. Because of the statement 'accepted for the sake of oil... it is only a dukkaṭa offense,' the appearance is seen that oil made from mustard seeds etc., which were accepted for a purpose other than oil and have passed seven days, is allowed for seven days starting from the day it was made. Some say 'karamanda' is the heartwood of a tree.

Since they cook oil by adding milk etc. to the fat-free residue, the residue is not allowed, only the oil is allowed. Therefore, it is said, 'He feels remorse as if for the residue of cooked oil.' If it is said that it is not allowed because it is cooked with animal fat, please speak, venerable sirs; in butter, there is a connection (relationship) with lumps of curd and so on. In honey, the four kālikas should be applied as appropriate; the same applies to sugarcane. How? Honey with bees and larvae is yāvakālika. Honey without bees but mixed with water is yāmakālika; if not mixed with water, it is sattāhakālika. Pure beeswax is yāvajīvika. Similarly, it should be known that sugarcane or its juice with residue is yāvakālika; sugarcane juice without residue but mixed with water is yāmakālika; if not mixed with water, it is sattāhakālika; and dry sugarcane residue is yāvajīvika. Why? Because of the distinction of mixing with water.

What is meant? Among the four kālikas, the preceding ones are heavy (garuka) and the succeeding ones are light (lahuka). Among those kālikas, this mixing with water makes the heavy light and the light heavy. Indeed, mango juice and so on are heavy because they are yāvakālika, but mixing with water gives them names like mango-drink (ambapāna) and makes them light yāmakālika. Because of the Commentary statement 'Molasses (phāṇita) is produced from sugarcane, depending on sugarcane juice,' it is established that sugarcane juice is sattāhakālika. Regarding that sugarcane juice, much has been said and applied, such as 'mixing with water makes it yāmakālika.'

Alternatively, in this sugarcane juice, because it was allowed by the Buddha saying, 'Bhikkhus, I allow sugarcane juice,' like molasses-water (guḷodaka), even if not mixed with water...
270:
## 
It is allowed even for a monk who is not ill; therefore, it was said in the Commentary: 'Sugarcane juice without residue is allowed in the afternoon.' The teacher says, 'All this decision is our own reasoning (vinicchaya).' Some teachers, however, say that because of the statement 'Molasses (phāṇita) is produced from sugarcane' and the Commentary statement 'depending on sugarcane juice,' sugarcane juice is indeed molasses; therefore, it should be treated like molasses (guḷa). Some teachers say, 'According to the method mentioned, although it is sattāhakālika, because it is separately allowed as "Bhikkhus, I allow sugarcane juice," it is allowed for a monk who is not ill even if not mixed with water.' Some teachers say, 'Because it is separately allowed according to the method mentioned, whether mixed or unmixed with water, it is only yāmakālika; molasses-water (guḷodaka), however, is only sattāhakālika.' Some teachers say, 'Like molasses-water, that sugarcane juice in both forms is only sattāhakālika.'

Among those views, the investigation into the first teacher's view is as follows: Since the allowance for sugarcane juice would be established by the allowance for molasses itself, the separate allowance for 'sugarcane juice' would become useless. Likewise, the Commentary statement 'Sugarcane juice without residue is allowed in the afternoon' would also be useless. It should have been said, 'It is allowed for seven days,' but it is not possible to say so. If it is asked, 'Is it because it falls under the category of liquids allowed in the afternoon?' No, because in that category, it would lead to the fault of not being able to mention it as sattāhakālika. If it is asked, 'Is it mentioned because it enters the category of liquids without regard to the difference in time?' It is not possible to say, 'Sugarcane juice with residue is allowed for seven days.' If it is asked, 'Should it not be mentioned because it falls under the category of liquids allowed in the afternoon?' No, for if it were said so, this juice, like other juices, would be allowed only in the afternoon and not after that. If it is asked, 'Is it said to be allowed in the afternoon because it is not to be consumed after that afternoon?' No, because it would lead to the fault of becoming yāvakālika. That fault does not occur because sugarcane juice that has passed the night can become molasses through cooking. This very same investigation applies to the third and fourth teachers' views. The investigation into the second view has been stated; the final decision here will become clear in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka.

The statement 'Molasses (phāṇita) is produced from sugarcane' is a specific statement regarding the molasses that is a nissaggiya object, which is a superior substance compared to molasses produced from Madhuka, palmyra, or coconut. By this, it is understood: 'In this context, what is called molasses as a nissaggiya object is only that produced from sugarcane, not that produced from Madhuka and so on.' By this much, it is established that not everything produced from sugarcane is called molasses. Therefore, in the Khandhaka, after first allowing molasses, sugarcane juice was allowed later; likewise, in that same Khandhaka, molasses-lumps (guḷa) and molasses-water (guḷodaka) were also allowed.
271:
## Regarding the view of those who hold that "sugarcane juice is yāmakālika" in the passage beginning with "Depending on sugarcane juice, uncooked," etc.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Depending on sugarcane juice, uncooked," etc., there is a view held by certain teachers that "sugarcane juice is yāmakālika." Those teachers explain the meaning of "uncooked" as being only that which is not cooked by the bhikkhu himself; and "cooked without the substance" as being cooked apart from the substance. That statement is not appropriate, because it would lead to the purposelessness of the phrase "depending on sugarcane juice," and because a bhikkhu has no authority or right regarding the act of cooking. If it is argued that "self-cooking" is intended here, that statement is also inappropriate, because of the fact that sugarcane juice not cooked by oneself becomes molasses (phāṇita) according to their own preference, and because of the demonstration of the method in later passages such as "molasses made with unstrained sugarcane juice received before the meal."

In that context, the statement "molasses made by oneself with unstrained sugarcane juice is indeed allowable if unmixed with food (nirāmisa)" indicates that the sugarcane juice, which does not produce self-cooking along with the dregs in that commentary, is made only into molasses that is received along with the substance. Therefore, the ancient teachers said that it is not allowable to receive it at the wrong time (after noon). It is stated: "Molasses made from crushed sugarcane is called 'cooked with coarse substance' like the boiling of dye-water, and is allowable only before the meal, based on that perception."

The teachers of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā said: "Receiving molasses in this way is not sweet (or not abundant); therefore, it is not allowable after the meal." The Elder Upatissa reportedly said that this was stated in the Mahāpaccariya only to show this meaning, whether it be sweet or not sweet. That statement is appropriate; it was said because it originates from sugarcane. For that very reason, it was stated: "But sugar candy (khaṇḍasakkharā)... is allowable." It is written: "They cook that sugar candy by putting it into a pot of milk." Jallikā refers to foam and such.

When the Blessed One spoke referring to medicine (bhesajja), He spoke of the remaining matters by way of extracting the meaning (atthuddhāra). In the Khandhaka, it is stated: "Whatever medicine is designated as medicine, and is recognized as medicine in the world, and can pervade for the purpose of nutriment," therefore it is said: "They are able to pervade for the purpose of nutriment." The investigation of this matter will become clear in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka.

"Dvāravātapānakavāṭāni" refers to the door-leaves of doors and windows. By merely applying the astringent liquid (kasāva), those substances (butter, etc.) give up their original nature; therefore, it is said: "They should be smeared." They say: "Kasāva (astringent liquid) also refers to liquids with a golden hue and such." "Adhiṭṭheti" (he determines) means he produces the thought: "Now this shall not be for consumption; it shall be for external use." The word "vikappeti" (he assigns) is not present here. Determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is also expressed by verbal utterance, because it is not proper to say, "I determine this fresh butter" without speaking.
272:
The statement that it is not allowable to use it is said with reference to relinquishing without intimacy (vissāsa). If there is intimacy, by merely saying "You use it," it is already relinquished; therefore, it should be noted in connection that there is no offense for both. If it has not yet been relinquished, it is evident that an offense is incurred. Therefore, the robe owned by two persons must be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) by one of the two who is present. If he does not determine it, it is also fitting to say that a nissaggiya offense is incurred.

If the value of even a kākanika has not been given, this case is not similar to the statement "It is not fit for determination... it does not reach the state of one's own property," nor is it like the property given to the group of Ābhidhammikas. Why? Because among the Ābhidhammikas, there may be unordained persons (laypeople or novices), and that property is common even to those who become Ābhidhammikas later. In this case, however, both are indeed ordained (bhikkhus), and both have the right to do as they wish and have a sense of ownership (mamatta) over that robe. It is not common to others in that way. Even if two or three bhikkhus do not act with the thought "We shall live together," they still protect it. This case is also similar to the statement "There is no offense because it is undivided."

If the one who received it with a price is given it by the other, or if he gives it to the other, since it becomes nissaggiya if seven days pass while it is in possession, that robe must be determined by one of the two who is present. Although the effort (payoga) of determination is not apparent here, it is because there is no determination-effort for two persons with equal requisites. Nevertheless, it is said "it must be determined" because an offense can occur when the time elapses for the one who received the oil and such among two persons with all identical goods, and because it is difficult to obtain a special benefit if it is not determined.

That statement is not appropriate because the regulations for bowls, robes, and seven-day medicines (sattāhakālika) are not the same. In this matter, for a bowl or a robe, an offense is incurred only when the time elapses for one who does not determine it after it has reached the state of being his own property. However, for a seven-day medicine, even if it is shared with another's property, it causes an offense for the one who received it if the time elapses. In this case of seven-day medicine, the act of receiving (paṭiggahena) is the standard, not the state of being one's own property. And if the seven-day medicine becomes nissaggiya, it is not to be consumed by anyone at all. As for the bowl and robe, there is no offense if another person uses them. Furthermore, this seven-day medicine, even if the time has elapsed, is allowable if it is received back after being forfeited. But for a bowl or robe, it is allowable only after performing a Vinaya act (vinayakamma).

The gift of this undivided seven-day medicine is valid, but not so for a bowl or robe.
