For it is said in the Commentary: "It is the property of two... even if they give it to their co-residents (saddhivihārika) and others without dividing it, it is as if it were not given." In a case where even the gift is not valid, how could there be determination? If one bhikkhu gives a bowl or robe to the other on the tenth day, from that day onwards, that bhikkhu has the right to carry it for ten days...
273:
It is obtained; it is not like the sattāhakālika (seven-day medicine). Upon investigating in every way, such consideration is not acceptable. Therefore, the teacher’s thought is that this entire statement should not be regarded as the essence. It is stated that if one fails to forfeit it according to the Vinaya procedure and suddenly violates the rule, even if it is forfeited to someone else, it is not proper to take it back and use it. If a robe becomes nissaggiya (forfeitable) while separated by another region or by the sea, the monk staying here, having abandoned it with a mind of relinquishment and without lingering concern, should confess the offense; then, through the intimacy with that monk, he may take it back and determine (adhiṭṭhāna) it. It is also stated, "The same method applies to alms-bowls and so on," and "Palm-molasses and coconut-molasses are also only sattāhakālika." Some teachers say, "Sattāhakālika medicine owned by two persons but received by one does not cause an offense even after seven days have passed; however, it is not proper for either of them to use it," and "The same method applies even if one receives and keeps property belonging to another." A procedure stating that butter and so on, which are the basis for an offense of dukkaṭa (wrongdoing), may be used again after being forfeited is not found.

## The Commentary on the Medicine Training Rule is Finished.

## 4. Vassikasāṭika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Regarding the phrase "having made only one," Elder Dhammasiri says that a monk who reminds even his relatives of the characteristics of the rainy-season cloth should take only one. In this context of "the four types of fields (khetta)," although only three types are seen, the fields should be understood as follows: The field where one is allowed to seek is called the pariyesana-khetta (field of seeking). It is stated, "In this way, the karaṇa-khetta (field of making), nivāsana-khetta (field of wearing), and adhiṭṭhāna-khetta (field of determination) should also be known." Among these fields, the teacher says that the inclusion of the earlier field by the later field should be understood, but the inclusion of the later field by the earlier field is not to be understood; it occurs according to what is obtained (yathālābha). The meaning is: the last field, the adhiṭṭhāna-khetta, includes all three earlier fields. Likewise, the nivāsana-khetta includes the two earlier fields. The karaṇa-khetta, however, includes only the first field, the pariyesana-khetta. Here, although there is no difference in terms of time between the karaṇa-khetta and the nivāsana-khetta, they are stated as two types because of the difference in action (kiriya), based on the Pali statement, "One should wear it, noting that there is still a month and a half of summer remaining," and because of the accomplishment of those two purposes. If it is asked, "How is it known that there is no difference here?" It is known through the Pali. For the Pali says, "One should wear it, noting that there is still a month and a half of summer remaining." It is also known from the Mātikāṭṭhakathā.
274:
That is indeed true; by this method, "The last half-month is also the field for making and wearing," it is established that there are only three types of fields. However, in some manuscripts of the Samantapāsādikā, the following text is found: "From the first day of the waning moon of Jeṭṭhamūla until the Uposatha of the dark fortnight, this half-month is both the field of seeking and the field of making. Within this interval, if the rainy-season cloth is not yet obtained, it is proper to seek it; if obtained, it is proper to make it; it is not proper to wear it or to determine it." That text is an incorrect reading because it contradicts the aforementioned Pali, Mātikā, and Commentaries. Therefore, it should be understood that the reading there ought to be: "If not yet obtained, it is proper to seek it; it is not proper to make, wear, or determine it." Thus, first, the inclusion of the earlier field by the later field should be understood as established; the inclusion of the later fields (such as the field of making) by the earlier field is not possible. Is it not said only this much: "In the one month remaining of summer, the rainy-season cloth should be sought"? If it is argued that this is because the Commentary says, "This half-month is both the field of seeking and the field of making"? No, that is because of a scribal error (lekhanadosa), as has been demonstrated. The field of making can include the field of wearing because there is no difference in terms of time. For that very reason, the "taking according to what is obtained" (yathālābhaggahaṇa) was mentioned previously, and it has been so established; although there is no distinction, the benefit has already been stated. The field of wearing can never include the field of determination, because the inclusion of a later field by an earlier field is not to be understood. If it is argued that this is not because of a contradiction with the Pali? No, it is because the meaning of that Pali is not understood. In the phrase "one month remaining of summer," meaning "half a month remaining of summer," the word 'iti' here has the meaning of "starting from this." Since the field of offense is shown later, it has already been shown that for the other (the monk who wears it), it is a field of non-offense. For a monk who procures it from those who have given before, from relatives, or from those who have invited him, a nissaggiya offense occurs because it is the after-time (piṭṭhisamaya). If the regular donors of rainy-season cloth are those who give annually to the Saṅgha or to an individual without being invited, then only reminding them (satup-pāda) is proper. It is meant that for others, if they fail in their duties, an offense of dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) occurs.

By the statement, "If it has been made... it should be determined on the day of entering the vassa... it receives a period of use (parihāra) for six months," it is indicated that even during the vassa, if it has not been made until the last day of the rainy season, it receives the period of use. If it is asked, "Why is this not investigated?" It is because it is established by implication (atthuppatti). By the statement, "It receives a period of use for six months," it is already established that it is received even if not yet made. Although that meaning is established, because it does not appear in its own form (sarūpa), and in order to show it in its own form, and because it is difficult to believe, in order to show it by logic...
275:
The commentator began thus: "Just as in this case, a robe obtained during the Kathina period should also be dealt with according to the method mentioned below." This statement is found in the Anugaṇṭhipada. That statement is poorly stated because it contradicts itself within that same Anugaṇṭhipada. The commentary passage cited as evidence here also does not establish that meaning. The phrase "If it is insufficient, he receives an extension (parihāra) until the full moon of Kattika" indicates that for a monk with an insufficient robe, the period of extension is only until the full moon of Kattika; after that, not even a single day is granted. Therefore, it is clear that if it has not been made due to being insufficient, he receives the extension until the full moon of Kattika, and after that, he does not. Likewise, that same statement indicates that once the extension is completed, he does not receive it again. Therefore, the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) must be made on the full moon day of Kattika itself. It is written: "If it is insufficient within ten days, the end of the making during the rains is the measure."

Regarding this, an objector says: "One should not say 'by one day, two days, etc.'" Why? Because the days of the summer are a time when formal determination is not to be made. Therefore, one should not say generally, "The formal determination should be made within ten days or on that very day," because it would imply that summer days become the proper time (khetta) for formal determination. To this objection, it is replied: It is not that it should not be said; it should indeed be said. Why? Because the meaning of that Pali is not understood. Ten days before the commencement of the rains (vassūpanāyikā), there are ten days of summer. A rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭika) obtained and completed on the first day, even if ten days have passed, does not yet incur a Nissaggiya offense because it has not yet reached the proper time for formal determination, which is the day of the commencement of the rains. The statement "There is no offense even if ten days pass before the commencement of the rains" is also correct.

The phrase "The formal determination should be made within ten days" is not meant to show a general meaning that it should be determined even during the summer days within those ten days. Rather, it is meant to show that if a rainy-season robe is obtained in summer and it is within ten days of the proper time for formal determination, it should be determined only within that proper time; one should not exceed ten days thinking it is not the proper time. Why? Because summer days are also included in the count. Therefore, counting even the days that are not the proper time, it is said, "The formal determination should be made within ten days" only within the proper time.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rainy-Season Robe is finished.
276:
## 5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Snatching Back a Robe
The word 'sāmaṃ' (by oneself) is stated for the purpose of limiting it to the perception of it being one's own property (sakasaññita). For it is only with the perception of it being one's own that Nissaggiya is incurred in causing to snatch or snatching. Therefore, this word 'sāmaṃ' indicates a primary factor of the Nissaggiya. Because 'robe' (cīvara) is mentioned, it is already stated that for a monk who snatches a requisite that is not a robe, there is no Nissaggiya.

In the word 'datvā' (having given), although the explanation in the Padabhājanī as 'having given oneself or having caused another to give' is appropriate, it was not stated that way for fear of undesirable implications, such as causing someone to give another's property to a different monk and then snatching it oneself or causing that same person to snatch it. However, in terms of meaning, it should be understood that if one causes his own property to be given by a co-resident, etc., or causes another's property to be given through intimacy, and then snatches or causes that gift to be snatched, a Nissaggiya is incurred. This is because it was given without any lingering expectation (anapekkha).

If so, what about the statement: "One who snatches and takes property given after relinquishing it should be punished according to the value of the goods"? This refers to taking with a thieving mind without perceiving it as one's own. Therefore, it is said: "Because he takes it perceiving it as his own, there is no Pārājika offense for that monk." Furthermore, from the statement "There is no offense if he gives it himself or takes it through intimacy," that point is established. By this much, it is established that there is no offense for a monk who takes back a robe given temporarily (tāvakālika). The phrase "He will take the preceptor in our presence," etc., indicates giving to a novice. That kind of giving is not intended here.

If it is asked: "In the Pali, just as there is a triad of Pācittiya offenses for an ordained monk (upasampanna), is there also a triad of Dukkaṭa offenses for an unordained person (anupasampanna)?" No, because the intention of that Pali is not understood. If, after giving in this way during the time he was unordained, one snatches it back in anger upon seeing him ordained under another, or if one gives to a monk who says "I will renounce the training and be ordained in your presence" and then snatches it back again, a Nissaggiya is incurred—this is the intention here.

If one is commanded once and snatches many items, a Nissaggiya is incurred. Because it is connected as one act, there is only one Pācittiya; referring to that, it is said: "If commanded, he takes many, there is one Pācittiya." However, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, it is said: "Offenses are according to the count of objects." That refers to the taking by a monk who says "Take all of them" because of the plurality of the command. Therefore, it is said there: "With a single speech, many offenses are incurred." In this way, the Pali statement and the two commentary statements agree with each other. Even if it is another's property or a paṃsukūla robe, Nissaggiya is incurred. Therefore, it is said: "Like money tied in the hem of a garment."
277:
That statement is made to show the constancy of that meaning. It should be understood that even for a monk who, with a mind to snatch away covered property, through a conscious verbal act, personally or by commanding another, takes it by force saying "Give it!" If it is argued that "If that person gives it, there is no offense," that statement is not appropriate. Or if it is argued because the Mātikā Commentary says, "Whether he gives it out of pleasure or out of anger, there is no offense," it is not so. This is because in both cases, the statement refers to giving according to one's own will, and because it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that there is no offense in taking by force. 

Teachers say that because of the Pāḷi statement, "Having personally given a robe to a monk," and because "being ordained" (upasampannatā) is mentioned in the definition of factors in the Mātikā Commentary, it shows that being a monk is required in both giving and taking. Our teacher considers this view inappropriate. Why? Because it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that there is no offense for a monk who gives a robe to an unordained person and then snatches it back when that person becomes ordained. If it is argued that a dukkaṭa offense occurs there because it is said, "Having given a robe or other requisite to an unordained person... there is an offense of dukkaṭa," that argument is not established. The point that being ordained at the time of giving is the only criterion is not evident in the Commentaries, the Pāḷi, or by logic. Therefore, that statement is not appropriate. 

Another variation (vikappa) of that statement is possible: if one gives a robe to an unordained person and snatches it back while he is still unordained, it is a dukkaṭa; or if one gives it while he is ordained and snatches it back when he is no longer ordained, it is a dukkaṭa. Therefore, because other variations are possible, it is not appropriate. This is because a separate dukkaṭa offense is not prescribed for one who gives while the recipient is unordained and snatches it back when he is ordained. Therefore, as in the training rules such as having an old robe washed, being ordained at a later time is the criterion here. Thus, because "being ordained" is mentioned among the factors, that statement is not appropriate. In this regard, it is heard that the Elder Dhammasiri said, "It refers only to giving to a monk who expects the item, not to giving by relinquishing it completely"; this should be reflected upon.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Snatching Back Robes is finished.

## 6. Sutta-viññatti-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, although it is said, "Having personally requested thread," in the Mātikā Commentary, it does not say "thread personally requested for the sake of a robe," but only "thread requested for the sake of a robe" is mentioned in the factors. Therefore, it should be understood that thread requested by another for the sake of a robe is also included. The word "personally" (sāmaṃ) here is to restrict the requesting of a certain person.
278:
Why is it said "having personally requested"? Nevertheless, in the phrase "having it personally woven," the connection and meaning should be understood as having it woven for one's own benefit. In the Pāḷi, however, the construction is made with the proximate word. Therefore, by saying "thread personally requested," thread requested by another becomes allowable (kappiya). A weaver obtained by requesting manual labor is also allowable.

If it is a cloth of the minimum size suitable for formal assignment (vikappana), it should be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) only once after being woven on the loom. There is no need for a further act of determination because it has become one with what was already determined. However, it is said, "If it is determined at intervals, showing the boundaries like a Cīna cloth, then it must be determined again." By the word "by obtaining," it is said that such acts as "I will have it woven and keep it" are included within a single robe.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread is finished.

## 7. Mahā-pesakāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

The criterion is the special instruction and what is specially made because of that monk's word; the giving of material gifts (āmisa) is not the criterion. In some books, the detailed explanation extracted as "robe" does not agree with that Pāḷi.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Great Weavers is finished.

## 8. Acceka-cīvara-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

"I allow you, monks, to accept and set aside an urgent robe (acceka-cīvara)," and "until the Pavāraṇā has been held," were the words spoken. Those monks, however, misunderstood the meaning of those words and, while setting aside urgent robes, let the robe-season (cīvara-kāla) pass. Is this robe one that has been distributed (vibhatta) or undistributed (avibhatta)? It is a distributed or individual (puggalika) robe. That is why it is said later, "Friends, our urgent robes..." An undistributed robe, being communal (saṅghika), does not cause an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya) to any individual monk.

Furthermore, by this general statement, "to accept and set aside an urgent robe," starting from the day of entering the rains (vassūpanāyika) or starting from the later period... until.
279:
Since it is communal (saṅghika), it is indeed proper to store it until the Pavāraṇā. Even an individual robe (puggalika) is allowed to be stored because it was given with the instruction, "Take it when the rains retreat is over." Such a robe does not belong to that monk throughout the rains retreat; it still belongs to the donor. Similarly, a robe given in the third or fourth year from now with the instruction "Take it on the Pavāraṇā day," etc., should be stored and accepted only according to the donor's wish. This meaning is clear in the Commentary.

If it is asked, "Do these robes not become subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya) even after the robe-season (cīvarakāla) has passed?" No, they do, because they were given specifically to an individual. Because this time is mentioned as "kāla" in the phrase "given specifically during the time (kāla)," and as "samaya" in the Gaṇabhojana training rule and others, it should be understood that "cīvarakālasamaya" is used here as a combined term to show that they have the same meaning.

In the matrix (mātikā) of this training rule, however, it refers to such an individual robe that has come into one's possession. Therefore, it was said, "If an urgent robe (acceka-cīvara) should arise for a monk." A donor who cannot give to a monk spending the rains retreat in his own monastery completes the act of giving during the rains and leaves; the same applies to the Saṅgha. Therefore, there are urgent robes that, from the time they arise, become the property of the Saṅgha or an individual, but were not given as rains-residence robes (vassāvāsika). There are also robes given during the season as rains-residence robes that do not become the property of an individual or the Saṅgha immediately upon arising, but only when the rains retreat is over. There are also robes given during the season that do not become the property of an individual but become the property of the Saṅgha or the donor. Referring to this [third type], it is said, "It should be stored after making a mark." Since this robe has not yet become one's own property, it is permissible to store it for more than a year. Therefore, it is established that the phrase "ten days before" (dasāhānagata) refers to robes other than this.

Since a robe received more than ten days before cannot be stored until the Pavāraṇā, one must determine (adhiṭṭhāna) only the robe that has become one's own property. Referring to such a robe, it is said "ten days before." This is because it is stated in the section on non-offence (anāpattivāra): "He determines it or assigns (vikappeti) it within the season." However, a robe that must be stored after making a mark does not become one's own property because it is to be given to another. One cannot say "he determines it or assigns it" regarding that robe. Nor does that robe become subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya) in this case, because there is no forfeiture for the Saṅgha. This meaning is very clear in the Commentary.

If it is asked, "What kind of robe should be stored after making a mark?" A robe belonging to another...
280:
(That robe) is indeed communal (saṅghika). Then, by the words "it will be easy to give after marking it," the ownership of another is shown.

It is written: "Beyond that (ten days), there is no allowance for even a single day, because it has not reached the period beyond ten days." This means that since it does not reach ten days beyond this robe-season, one does not get ten days after the season. In the phrase "he certainly gets this allowance," the reason is written as "he lets the dawn of the eleventh day rise during the robe-month." In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "Other teachers say that the Blessed One, by way of the urgent robe (acceka-cīvara), also allows other robes that are not urgent, saying 'one is allowed to store it on the eleventh day without determining it'."

Which of these two statements is well-spoken? Some say both are well-spoken. How? The first (Gaṇṭhipada) statement agrees with the meaning: "For an urgent robe, if the Kathina has not been spread, it is one month plus ten days; if the Kathina has been spread, it is five months plus ten days." According to the view of the Anugaṇṭhipada, it would result in saying "eleven days plus." The second statement agrees with the Commentary's words: "Not yet ten days... the meaning of not having reached by ten days." By this method, the text "the storage period of a robe arising from the fifth day onwards is shown" is appropriate. Likewise, according to the Gaṇṭhipada view, it would result in saying "the full moon of Kattika, nine days before." By the power of that Gaṇṭhipada, the text "In fact, it is established by the rule that this urgent robe should be worn as an extra robe for a maximum of ten days; however, by the power of the circumstances (atṭhuppatti), the training rule was laid down showing the meaning as if it were something new" is appropriate. What is the essence here? Only the latter statement is the essence. That is why the commentator said, "starting from the fifth day." Because it is consistent with the ancient Gaṇṭhipadas and the Commentary, and because it is consistent with the Pali "ten days before," the Gaṇṭhipada view here also agrees with the Pali.

How does it agree? Because a monk has completed the rains retreat only when the dawn rises on the Pavāraṇā day, therefore, including this tenth day, there are ten days starting from the sixth day, consisting of nine days [plus the tenth]. With those ten days (the instrumental case is used in the sense of association/sahayoga). Considering that the full moon of Kattika has not yet reached the robe-season, it is called "not yet reached" (anāgata).

Regarding the assignment (vikappanā) of the rain-cloth (vassikasāṭika) after withdrawing it (paccuddharaṇa) on the full moon of Kattika, it is said: "to determine it for four months, and to assign it beyond that"...
281:
It is said that the fulfillment of this illustration should be understood in this way. If it is said in this context, "It is fulfilled in this way," it should not be said so. The reason is that this training rule would then become purposeless. If it is said, "The period for accepting an urgent robe (acceka-cīvara) is determined," it should not be said so. The reason is that it is stated in the ancient Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) and Glossaries (Gaṇṭhipada) that "A robe arising from the sixth day onwards is no longer an urgent robe because it is settled by the first Kathina." Beyond that, it is called an "urgent robe." It is also stated that an offense (āpatti) is incurred by a monk who accepts it. Such an offense is not possible according to the Pāḷi, the Commentary, or logical reasoning. If it is said, "It is stated merely by way of the originating incident (atthuppatti)," it should not be said so. This originating incident, which involves keeping a robe for more than ten days, is not found in the Pāḷi. In this context, the originating incident is only this: "Monks, having accepted an urgent robe, let it exceed the robe-season." Therefore, it should be understood that in the Parivāra, starting from the question "On what matter?", only this much is stated. If it is said, "This training rule was prescribed to show that an urgent robe should not exceed the robe-season, while other robes may exceed it," it should not be said so. This is because only the fault of the urgent robe is shown, there is no special reason, and it contradicts statements such as "If desired, this extra robe (atireka-cīvara) may be kept for at most ten days," making the aforementioned statement impossible.

How is this so? When it is said that the Kattika full-moon day, along with the ten days, "has not yet arrived," it implies that the full-moon day is distinct from the ten days. If it were not distinct, the word "saha" (along with) would not be possible. This is because it is impossible for something to be associated with itself. The word "anāgata" (not yet arrived) would also not be possible, because that full-moon day has already arrived. If it is argued, "Since it is not yet one with the robe-season as there is no interval, it has not yet arrived and is thus 'not yet arrived'," it should not be said so. Even if it were not yet one, the meaning of the word "anāgata" would still be possible. The word "anāgata" is possible only when there is the possibility of arrival; Nibbāna or a designation (paññatti) is never called "anāgata." Like Nibbāna, the three moments (of time) are not so called. Since that full-moon day never reaches the state of being the robe-season, it is simply inappropriate. However, the statement "Thereafter, it should be assigned (vikappana)" is possible because it refers to the subsequent period. Furthermore, when dawn rises on the Pavāraṇā day, that full-moon day is indeed ten days away from the robe-season. This is because it was previously associated with the ten days. In this case, even if they become one, that full-moon day has simply not yet arrived. Therefore, it should be understood that no word expresses the grammatical definition (vacanattha) through analysis (vigraha) in that manner at all times.
282:
For what purpose is it stated here, "One month and ten days," and so on? It is stated because the fulfillment (of the period) is possible. Indeed, for an urgent robe (acceka-cīvara) that arises before dawn on the fifth day, one month and ten days is exactly the full period; thus it is so stated. Furthermore, even the daytime of that fifth day is called "yesterday" when the night arrives, let alone the time before dawn. Therefore, it was said, "Yesterday, friends, for us..." and so on.

Despite this, the writing that says, "By the power of the first text which states 'from the sixth day onwards', even a robe that is not an urgent robe, or the triple robe (ticīvara) that has been formally removed (paccuddhāra) and set aside, also receives this allowance," and "one month and ten days," etc., is not correct. Only if the text is established as "from the fifth day onwards" can the aforementioned meaning be possible through this method; therefore, those points should not be re-established. Our teacher (ācariya) considers that they should be regarded just as they stand. The Elder Upatissa said that this training rule is only for the purpose of preventing a forfeiture (nissaggiya) on the full-moon day. If the text is established as "from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the Pavāraṇā month," the storage period for the robe that has arisen is shown by this method. There is a text stating, "Acceka-cīvara means an urgent robe (accāyika-cīvara)," and so on. The writing that says "from the sixth day onwards" and "this robe is at most ten days," etc., is not the (original) text. Therefore, assuming that one receives an allowance of eleven days, the teacher (Commentator) reportedly had it written as "from the fifth day onwards." Some elaborate here, saying, "There is a text: 'Even a robe that is not an urgent robe arising from the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the Pavāraṇā month, or the triple robe that has been formally removed and set aside, also receives this allowance'," and "There is a text: 'For an urgent robe, if the Kathina has not been spread, it is one month and eleven days; if the Kathina has been spread, it is five months and eleven days'." Therefore, one should speak only after careful consideration, or else one should remain silent.

## The Explanation of the Acceka-cīvara Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Sāsaṅka Training Rule

Regarding the phrase "any one robe of the three robes," they say this is stated to show that this procedure applies only to the triple robe (ticīvara), while other requisites may be kept as one pleases. In the phrase "staying away for more than six nights," it is stated based on the view that staying in that very lodging (senāsana) is not "staying away." Why? Because the status of the robe can be known. In this context, although it says "a forest dwelling (āraññaka)..."
283:
A forest dwelling is said to be at least five hundred [bow-lengths] away according to the statement. However, to protect the dhutanga, one should stay only in a forest dwelling because there can be the obstacle (palibodha) of knowing the occurrence of robes. If it is asked, 'How is it known that it can be obtained at a distance greater than a gāvuta?' it is known from the statement: 'Should there be any reason for that monk to be away from that robe.' If it is asked, 'Can it also be at a distance of a yojana?' No, it cannot. This is because it is permitted in the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra): 'Having entered the village boundary again and stayed, he departs.' If so, what is this statement: 'It cannot be obtained at a distance of a yojana'? This is said only in terms of a permanent residence. Does the dhutanga break in that case? It does not break. However, there is no scope for dhutanga in this training rule.

If so, why is it said, 'This person should be known as a dhutanga-thief'? It is because it is impossible. How is it known? It is because it is not present in the factors. By showing a dwelling suitable for a dhutanga-observer, that person's status as a dhutanga-observer is established. If it is asked, 'Is it because of the length of the statement?' No, it is not. The Pāḷi text itself is the authority rather than the length of the statement. This is because it is said, 'There is no offense if he enters the village boundary again, stays, and then departs.' If it is asked, 'How long should he stay after leaving the village boundary before departing?' it is on the very next day. Therefore, some teachers say that the eighth dawn should rise either at the permanent residence or at the destination. Some say within six nights. Some say as long as he does not make it a permanent residence. Some say until the fatigue of the journey is relieved. If there is a danger, there is no offense if he stays within six nights. If he makes it a permanent residence, an offense is incurred at dawn.

If that day is the seventh day, some say that the deposited robe should be taken or assigned (paccuddharaṇa) on that very day. If that dwelling falls short of the required factors due to the appearance of a new road or the establishment of a new village in between, the robe should be taken or assigned on that very day. Some say that if a monk who has been away for six nights finds the factors diminished, there is no offense because it is a permitted day. Others say that an offense is indeed incurred because it does not fulfill the factors. In this matter, one should consider and accept what is appropriate. If he is a dhutanga-observer, he should not stay in the village boundary but should stay in a place that fulfills the final measurement and then depart. If the village is one with a fixed boundary of non-separation (baddha-avippavāsa-sīmā), there is no offense for a monk staying within the boundary even in another month. In the Ancient Glossaries (Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada), it is said: 'Even when staying in a dwelling as described, with the intention that the robe should be kept in the village only within six nights, an offense is indeed incurred for a monk staying for another six nights or another period.'

## The Explanation of the Sāsaṅka Training Rule is finished.
284:
## 10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Diverting (Pariṇata Sikkhāpada)

'Friends, please give to us'—in this case, is it an unsolicited request (akataviññatti) or not? It is. If so, what is the difference between the training rule on requesting from non-relatives (aññātaka-viññatti) and this training rule? That training rule on requesting from non-relatives is prescribed for a monk who requests only from a non-relative who has not invited him. This training rule on diverting, however, is prescribed for a monk who requests even from a relative who has invited him. That training rule is prescribed only for a monk who has no robe; this training rule is prescribed even for a monk who has a robe. That training rule is prescribed for a monk who requests only a robe; this training rule is prescribed even for a monk who requests requisites other than a robe.

Even so, this training rule on diverting exists independently without including that training rule on requesting from non-relatives. Therefore, if the factors of both training rules are fulfilled, by which training rule should the offense be incurred? Some teachers say that the offense should be incurred only by this training rule because it is an absolute prescription (nippadesa-paññatti). Others say that the offense should be incurred by both because the factors of both are fulfilled.

The factors of that training rule on requesting from non-relatives are four: being a robe suitable for assignment (vikappanā), not being the proper time, requesting from a non-relative, and obtaining it through such a request. The factors of this training rule, however, are three: the gain having been diverted toward the Sangha, diverting it to oneself while knowing this, and obtaining it. Between these two views, only the former view is appropriate because the opportunity [for both to apply] is not provided in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) or the Parivāra.

If so, should it not be stated in those factors as 'not yet diverted elsewhere'? It need not be stated because it is established by the sense. Because the two training rules on diverting are established, because there is the perception of it being diverted, and because an offense can occur, if one says 'Give to me,' although it is not explicitly shown as allowable, it is allowable because it is said 'It is also for us.'

In the passage 'Diverted to the Sangha... an offense of Dukkaṭa is incurred,' the term 'to an individual' is not mentioned because it comes by way of the Suddha-pācittiya rules. The term 'to another shrine (cetiya)' is also not mentioned because the Sangha is not a shrine. For that very reason, in the passage 'Diverted to a shrine... an offense of Dukkaṭa is incurred,' the terms 'to another Sangha' or 'to another individual' are not mentioned.

Likewise, in this training rule, in the passage 'Diverted to an individual... an offense of Dukkaṭa is incurred,' although 'to oneself' is not taught, they say it is possible. Some say that the word is not mentioned here because this training rule concerns diverting to oneself. Others say it is like the word 'for the sake of another' in the subsequent training rule. That is not so, because it is not mentioned in this training rule on diverting to an individual.

Elder Dhammasiri, however, said:
'If one diverts a gain intended for the Sangha or another person,
From another person to oneself or to another,
There is a Nissaggiya, a Pācittiya, and also a Dukkaṭa.'

The meaning of that is: If one diverts to oneself a gain already diverted to the Sangha, a Nissaggiya offense is incurred. If one diverts that same gain intended for the Sangha to another person, a Pācittiya offense is incurred. If one diverts a gain intended for another person to oneself or to someone else, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Therefore, because the offenses mentioned in the training rules such as requesting from non-relatives can occur, the word 'to oneself' is not mentioned in these two training rules on diverting. In truth, if that word 'to oneself' were mentioned, a Dukkaṭa...
285:
Or if one diverts it to another, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, because the offences mentioned in training rules such as requesting from unrelated persons (aññātakaviññatti) and others may occur, the word "to oneself" is not mentioned in these two Pariṇata training rules. If that word "to oneself" were mentioned, it would only be an offence of wrong-doing. However, since it is not mentioned, both one of the offences already mentioned in those training rules according to the Pāḷi text and the offence of wrong-doing obtained by implication in this case occur together as two offences. Thus, an opportunity is provided for the exhaustive knowledge of the masters of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara).

Thus, in the manner described, there is the excellent ornament of virtue known as the Section of Thirty (Tiṃsakakaṇḍa).
This excellent ornament of virtue, the Section of Thirty, is worthy of adorning those of good family who possess the excellent ornament of virtue through the power of the Vinaya regulations.
The entire collection of the essence of virtue completed in this work purifies the person of good family who possesses the excellent essence of virtue by means of the Vinaya.

## The Commentary on the Pariṇata Training Rule is finished.
## The Third Chapter, the Bowl Chapter (Patta-vagga), is finished.
## The Commentary on the Nissaggiya is finished.
502:
In the phrase "and to the Dhamma" (dhammassa ca), it is said that a share equal to that of a single monk should be given to the shrines (cetiyas) and the Dhamma in all monasteries. If it is asked whether this contradicts the statement "to the Community of monks and to the shrine," the answer is that it does not. Because in those previous instances it was stated "to the Community of monks," and here it is stated in connection with the monastery, they explain that a share must indeed be received in each respective monastery.

Regarding the phrase "having caused it to reach oneself," if it is argued that the entire object should be allowable because it cannot be used during the wrong time (after noon), it is not allowable, because it was stated "carry it to the Community of monks," and because that monk accepted it saying, "I shall carry it."

In the phrase "pacchimavassaṃvutthānampi," the word "api" has the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa). It means only for those monks who have emerged from the later rainy season retreat (pacchimavassa). Otherwise, if it were taken in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), the statement "the experts in characteristics say" (lakkhaṇaññū vadanti) would be meaningless. They elaborate on why this is so. What is the benefit of such elaboration? Since it is already established by the later statement, "Starting from the robe-month... it reaches only those monks who have emerged from the past retreat," it need not be further examined. Therefore, it is stated as "lakkhaṇaññū" by way of the teacher Acala.

If it is said that it reaches all monks who have arrived... standing in the outer precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), it means for monks who have emerged from the retreat in any place whatsoever. This is because it is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary: "It reaches all those who have arrived, monks who have emerged from the retreat in any place whatsoever." However, when speaking from the first day of the summer season, they are said to have emerged from the retreat only in the immediately preceding winter season, not the rainy season. Therefore, it is said, "The schedule (mātikā) should be set up." Alternatively, it means it also reaches those monks sent by the elders.

## The Explanation of the Robe Chapter (Cīvarakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
503:
## 9. Explanation of the Campeyya Chapter (Campeyyakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Two Expulsions and So Forth
In the phrase "appatto nissāraṇaṃ," what is called "expulsion" (nissāraṇa) is an act (kamma) permitted only for monks who corrupt families (kuladūsaka). This monk is not a family-corrupter; therefore, it is said "appatto" (it does not apply). If it is asked, "If that is so, how is he properly expelled?" it is because it is stated in the Cūḷavagga: "If the Saṅgha desires, it may perform the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma)." According to the statement, "They perform the act of further punishment (tassapāpiyasikakamma) for a monk who deserves the act of further punishment," it should be understood that they carry out the cycle of procedures (cakkabandha).

## Explanation of the Discussion on Upāli’s Questions
"Parato" (further on) is written to mean after the questions of Upāli. In the Dosārita Pali, it is stated: "A person under twenty years of age (ūnavīsativassa) does not come because the basis is defective (vippannavatthuka)." In this Campeyyakkhandhaka, it should be understood that the unrighteous acts (adhammakamma) themselves are divided into two types, resulting in five kinds. For this very reason, it is stated in the Parivāra regarding this chapter: "Five unrighteous acts." By the statement, "The blind, the mute, and the deaf are admitted," it is established that higher ordination (upasampadā) can be attained even by one who has not yet been ordained as a novice (apabbajita).

## The Explanation of the Campeyya Chapter is finished.
504:
## 10. Explanation of the Kosambaka Chapter (Kosambakakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Kosambi Dispute
In the word "suttantiko," although it is said "expert in Vinaya, expert in the Mātikā," it is said with reference to the recitation of the two Vibhaṅgas (Ubhatovibhaṅga), and he is not a reciter of the Khandhakas (Khandhakabhāṇaka). Based on the statement "Friend, there is an offense here," it is said "He has the view of an offense regarding that offense." Later, the expert in Vinaya regained mindfulness, thinking, "If the basis (vatthu) exists, it is the standard; the regulation (paññatti) is not the standard," and he held the view of an offense regarding that offense. Therefore, it is stated at the end: "Other monks have the view of an offense regarding that offense."

The reason they write "yathā mayā ñattī" is because of the singular word "paññattā."

## Explanation of the Story of Dīghāvu
They write: "Monks, formerly in the city of Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta..." In the ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, the reading "in the city of Bārāṇasī" does not exist; they say, "Its absence is indeed better."

## Explanation of the Discussion on Going to Pālileyyaka
"Rakkhitavanasaṇḍa" (the Protected Forest Thicket) is stated by the Elders who conducted the Recitations (Saṅgītikāraka) to make it easy to understand. They also say, "Pālileyya is a village, and it is named after that village." This statement does not contradict the Dhammapada Commentary.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Eighteen Matters
In the phrase "I say it should not be prohibited," if a monk prohibits a monastery to a monk who is worthy of that monastery, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) falls only on that monk. There is no fault for the Buddha who, having stated the Community's agreement such as "There is no opportunity here for those who cause quarrels and strife," does not lay down that rule; nor for the Buddha who prohibits a monk who, acting overbearingly by saying "I am the Buddha," informs his own disciples and takes [the monastery], by saying "Take it according to what is proper." Here, for the monks of Kosambī who have come to settle the dispute, it is not said "according to seniority," but because it is stated "if there is no secluded monastery, it should be given after making it secluded," having made it secluded...
